body.text: ātmasiddhiḥ /
body.translated_text: <s>Ātmasiddhi</s> (Establishment of the Self)

body.text: siddhāñjananāmakavyākhyopetā /
body.translated_text: Accompanied by the commentary named <s>Siddhāñjana</s> (Collyrium of Established Truth)

body.text: yatpadāmbhoruhadhyānavidhvastāśeṣakalmaṣaḥ /
body.translated_text: Having all sins completely destroyed through meditation on whose lotus feet,

body.text: vastutāmupayāto 'haṃ yāmuneyaṃ namāmi tam // 1 //
body.translated_text: I, who have attained true existence, salute that <s>Yāmuna</s>. // 1 //

children.translated_text: Root text (<s>mūla</s>)
<s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature), <s>puruṣa</s> (individual soul), <s>kāla</s> (time), the manifest (<s>vyakta</s>), and the liberated (<s>mukta</s>) — all follow the will of that one
who eternally, with numerous eternally perfected beings,
who delight in serving and enjoying Him — may there arise in me abundant <s>bhakti</s> (devotion)

body.text: bhavatu mama parasmin puruṣe bhaktibhūyā // 1 //
body.translated_text: toward that Supreme <s>Puruṣa</s> (Person), resplendent with <s>Śrī</s>, in whom they find their joy. // 1 //

children.translated_text: Commentary (<s>vyākhyāna</s>)
We worship the one who is higher than the highest, who delights in the creation, sustenance, and dissolution of the world,
the Lord of all worlds, the consort of <s>Śrī</s> (<s>Śrīyaḥpati</s>). // 1 //
I take refuge in the treasure-house of <s>jñāna</s> (knowledge), <s>vairāgya</s> (dispassion), and <s>bhakti</s> (devotion), the ocean of compassion,
the best among sages, <s>Yāmuna</s>, the supreme <s>ācārya</s> (preceptor). // 2 //
Through compositions such as the <s>Śrībhāṣya</s>, revealing the supreme <s>tattva</s> (reality),
I take refuge in the blessed lord <s>Rāmānuja</s>, who is gracious toward me. // 3 //
Relying on the essence of the grace of the foremost <s>Deśika</s> (teacher), this commentary
on the <s>Siddhitraya</s> (Three Establishments) is composed by me in a lucid style. // 4 //

children.text: kka yāmunāryaśrīsūktisandarbhaḥ kka ca me matiḥ /
children.translated_text: Where stands the garland of sacred sayings of the venerable <s>Yāmunācārya</s>, and where my intellect?
Even though the subject matter is exceedingly limited, my rashness alone is at fault. // 5 //
Those who bear the burden of establishing the <s>Viśiṣṭādvaita</s> (Qualified Non-dualism) doctrine,
the <s>Deśikas</s> (teachers), whose essence is compassion toward those who seek refuge — they are my shelter. // 6 //
The ornament of the lineage of the illustrious <s>Vādibhīkṛt</s>, belonging to the <s>Vātsya</s> clan, <s>Kṛṣṇa Ārya</s>, rich in virtues,
my father, who bestowed upon me my name, who revealed the meaning of the sacred sayings of the <s>Draviḍa Nigama</s> (Tamil Veda) —
having bowed to him, and also to my great teacher <s>Rāmānujārya</s>, the lamp of the lineage of the author of the <s>Bhāṣya</s>,
and to <s>Hārīta</s> of beautiful fame, the ornament of the learned lineage — I expound the sayings of <s>Yāmuna</s>. // 7 //
Belonging to the clan named <s>Nāgapura</s>, known as <s>Vādibhīkara</s>,
I, <s>Aṇṇaṅgarāryadāsa</s>, elucidate the words of my teacher. // 8 //

body.text:
atha khalu bhagavān śrīmadyāmunaminiḥ śrīvaiṣṇavasaṃpradāyapravartakācāryeṣu prathamaparigāṇitasya yogarahasyanyāyatattvaśāstrapraṇeturbhagavataḥ śrīmannāthamuneḥ pautra riśvaramunitanujanmā viśiṣṭādvaitasiddhāntapravartanadhurandharaḥ prativādivāraṇaprakaṭāṭopavipāṭanakṣamaḥ paramācārya ātmasiddhināmakaṃ vedāntaprakaraṇamupakramamāṇo 'vighnaparisamāptipracayagamanādiphalaṃ maṅgalamāśīrūpaṃ vastunirdeśaṃ ca kurvāṇaḥ śiṣyaśikṣāyai nibadhnāti "prakṛtī' ti / prakṛtirmāyā, tatkāryāṇi samaṣṭivyaṣṭirūpāṇi vyaktāni, prakṛtiprākṛtapariṇāmahetuḥ kālaḥ, tadbaddho jīvarāśiśreti līlāvibhūtisthāḥ sarve saṅgṛhītāḥ śabdacatuṣṭayena / muktāḥ bhagavadupāsanāprabhāvādbhavabandhanātkarmapāśapragrathitādvinirmuktāḥ / ete prakṛtyādayo yasyaiva paramapuruṣasyecchāṃ saṅkalparūpāṃ sadā samanusaranti svarūpasthitipravṛttiṣu, tasmin pūruṣa ityanvayaḥ / imāni ca
sarjanāvanasaṃharaṇasaṃsāravimocanāni saṅkalpaikaniṣpādyāni bhagavato līlārasāya kalpante / evaṃ līlāvibhūtiyoga uktaḥ / atha nityavibhūtiyogamāha

children.translated_text: with the word '<s>nitya</s>' (eternal)

children.text: iti / nityamiti pūrvottarayoranvitaṃ madhyamaṇinyāyena / sadodbhūtāpahatapāpmatvādisvarūpaiḥ sarvajñairbhagavadanubhavajanitaprītikāritāśeṣaśeṣavṛttyanvayata evādhigatabhogairanantairanantagaruḍaviṣvaksenādibhirnityasūribhiḥ śrīmati mahāvaikuṇṭhe divye 'kṣare dhāmni sadā niratiśayaprītimanubhavati nārīṇāmuttamāyāḥ śriyo vallabhe puruṣottame parabrahmaṇi mama bhaktipracayo bhūyādityāśaṃsā / ubhayavibhūtināthe ramānāthe bhaktirhi sarvaśreyaskarī / tattadbhaktyāśaṃsanamucitataram / bhaktireva bhagavati prārthyā cetanaiḥ / sa hi svayameva śreyo vidadhāti / tattasmin śvaśreyaḥprārthanā nocitatarā bhaktānāmiti cānena jñāpyate / acetanabhedaścetanabhedaśca paramārthataḥ, śrīmannārāyaṇasyaiva pāramyaṃ, sarvacetanācetanānāṃ tadvibhūtitvaṃ, niratiśayapremagarbhatadupāsanasyaivāpavargahetutvamavicchinnapūrṇabhagavadanubhavagarbhasevāyā eva paramapumarthatvaṃ ceti svābhimatāḥ prakaraṇārthā atra saṃsūcitāḥ // 1 //
children.translated_text: — the word '<s>nityam</s>' is construed with both the preceding and the following, according to the <s>madhyamaṇi-nyāya</s> (principle of the middle gem). With innumerable eternal attendants — <s>Ananta</s>, <s>Garuḍa</s>, <s>Viṣvaksena</s>, and others — the <s>Nityasūris</s> (eternal divine beings) who possess ever-manifest natures characterized by freedom from sin and other qualities, who are omniscient, whose enjoyment consists entirely in the service of every kind prompted by the love born of experiencing the Lord — may there arise in me an abundance of <s>bhakti</s> (devotion) toward the Supreme <s>Brahman</s>, <s>Puruṣottama</s> (the Supreme Person), the beloved of <s>Śrī</s>, the foremost among women, who eternally experiences unsurpassed delight in the divine, imperishable abode of <s>Mahāvaikuṇṭha</s> resplendent with <s>Śrī</s> — this is the prayer. For <s>bhakti</s> toward the Lord of both <s>vibhūtis</s> (realms), the Lord of <s>Ramā</s> (<s>Śrī</s>), is the cause of all highest good. Therefore praying for such <s>bhakti</s> is most fitting. It is <s>bhakti</s> alone toward the Lord that should be sought by conscious beings, for He Himself bestows the highest good. And by this it is also indicated that praying to Him for one's own separate good is not most fitting for devotees. The following doctrines favored by the author are here indicated as the subject matter of the treatise: the distinction between non-conscious (<s>acetana</s>) and conscious (<s>cetana</s>) entities is ultimately real; the supremacy belongs to <s>Śrīman Nārāyaṇa</s> alone; all conscious and non-conscious beings constitute His <s>vibhūti</s> (divine glory); worship imbued with unsurpassed love is itself the means to <s>apavarga</s> (liberation); and uninterrupted service containing the fullness of the experience of the Lord is itself the supreme goal of human life. // 1 //

body.translated_text: Now then, the blessed <s>Yāmuna Muni</s> — grandson of the blessed <s>Nāthamuni</s>, who is counted first among the founding <s>ācāryas</s> (preceptors) of the <s>Śrīvaiṣṇava</s> tradition, the author of the <s>Yogarahasya</s>, <s>Nyāyatattva</s>, and other works; born as the son of <s>Īśvaramuni</s>; the chief proponent of the <s>Viśiṣṭādvaita</s> doctrine; capable of shattering the brazen arrogance of opposing disputants; the supreme <s>ācārya</s> — commencing the <s>Vedānta</s> treatise named <s>Ātmasiddhi</s>, composing a <s>maṅgala</s> (auspicious invocation) in the form of a benediction that yields fruits such as unobstructed completion and progressive attainment, and also indicating the subject matter, he instructs his disciples with the verse beginning "<s>prakṛti</s>." <s>Prakṛti</s> means <s>māyā</s> (primordial matter); the <s>vyaktas</s> (manifest entities) are its effects in both aggregate (<s>samaṣṭi</s>) and individual (<s>vyaṣṭi</s>) forms; <s>kāla</s> (time) is the cause of the transformation of <s>prakṛti</s> and its derivatives; the hosts of <s>jīvas</s> (individual souls) bound therein — all those belonging to the <s>līlā-vibhūti</s> (realm of divine play) are comprehended by these four terms. The <s>muktas</s> (liberated souls) are those released from the bondage of <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence), tied by the noose of <s>karma</s>, through the power of worship of the Lord. These — <s>prakṛti</s> and the rest — always follow the will, in the form of <s>saṅkalpa</s> (divine resolve), of that very Supreme <s>Puruṣa</s> with respect to their essential nature, existence, and activity — the syntactical connection is with 'in that <s>Puruṣa</s>.' And these acts of creation, protection, dissolution, and liberation from <s>saṃsāra</s>, all accomplished solely by His will, serve the delight of His divine play (<s>līlā-rasa</s>). Thus the connection with the <s>līlā-vibhūti</s> has been stated. Now he states the connection with the <s>nitya-vibhūti</s> (eternal realm) —

body.text: viruddhamatayo 'nekāḥ santyātmaparamātmanoḥ /
body.translated_text: There are many mutually contradictory views regarding the <s>ātman</s> (self) and the <s>paramātman</s> (Supreme Self);

body.text: atastatpariśuddhyarthamātmasiddhirvidhīyate // 2 //
body.translated_text: therefore, for the purification of those [views], this <s>Ātmasiddhi</s> (Establishment of the Self) is composed. // 2 //

body.text:
saṃmataṃ hi sarvasamayeṣu ātmajñānaṃ niḥśreyasaheturiti / śrūyate ca 'pṛthagātmānaṃ preritāraṃ ca matvā juṣṭustatastenāmṛtatvameti' 'ātmānaṃ cedvijānīyāt' 'taratiśoka- mātmavit' 'brahmavidāpnoti para' mityādiḥ parāvarātmatattvajñānasyāpavargasādhanatvaṃ pratipādayan vedāntavākyagaṇaḥ /
tatrāsminnātmani parasmiṃścānekavidhā vipratipattayaḥ tīrthakarāṇām /

children.translated_text: They are as follows:

children.text: - ātmaviṣaye tāvat dehameva kecidātmānamācakṣate / indriyāṇyanye / mana ityanye / prāṇamapare / adhyastajñātṛ bhāvamanahaṅkāraṃ bodhamātramitare / dehendriyamanaḥprāṇabodhavilakṣaṇamākāśādivadacitkhabhāvamāgantukabodhasukhaduḥkhādyasādhāraṇaguṇādhāramahaṅkāragocaramapare / apare tu bodhaikasvabhāvameva, svabhāvadhavalamiva sphuṭikamaṇimupadhānaviśeṣāpāditāruṇimaguṇādinirbhāsamantaḥkaraṇopadhānāpāditarāgadveṣasukhaduḥkhādyaśivaguṇanirbhāsamanuditāvastamitasvarūpaprakāśaṃ svayañjyotiṣamimamabhidadhati / anye tu jñānānandasvabhāvam / āśrayānukūlyapratilabdhānandasukhādivyapadeśabodhaviśeṣa evāsya svābhāvika ityanye / tathā - anumānasamadhigamyaḥ ; āgamaikavedyaḥ ; mānasapratyakṣavedyaḥ ; grāhakatayaiva sakalaviṣayavittiṣu pratyakṣaḥ ; jñānasvabhāvatayānuditānastamitasvarūpaprakāśaḥ svayañjyotiḥ ; ridṛśo 'pyugamānumānayogajapratyakṣaiḥ svetarasakalavilakṣaṇasvābhāvyena viśadaviśadataraviśadatamatayāntato yathāvadaparokṣyata iti /
children.translated_text: Regarding the self, to begin with — some declare the body itself to be the <s>ātman</s> (self). Others say the sense organs (<s>indriyas</s>). Others say the mind (<s>manas</s>). Yet others say the vital breath (<s>prāṇa</s>). Some others say it is mere consciousness (<s>bodhamātra</s>), the superimposed knower-nature, devoid of ego-sense (<s>ahaṅkāra</s>). Others hold it to be distinct from body, sense organs, mind, vital breath, and consciousness — like space (<s>ākāśa</s>), an unconscious void-like entity that is the substratum of adventitious and uncommon qualities such as knowledge, pleasure, and pain, and is the object of ego-sense. Yet others declare it to be of the nature of pure consciousness alone — like a crystal (<s>sphaṭikamaṇi</s>) that is naturally clear but appears to have qualities such as redness imparted by particular adjuncts placed near it, so too the self appears to have inauspicious qualities such as desire, hatred, pleasure, and pain imparted by the adjunct of the internal organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>), while its self-luminous essential nature never truly rises or sets. Others say it is of the nature of <s>jñāna</s> (knowledge) and <s>ānanda</s> (bliss). Yet others say that the particular cognition designated as bliss, pleasure, and so forth, obtained through favorable conditions of its substrate, is alone its intrinsic nature. Likewise — some say it is knowable only through inference (<s>anumāna</s>); others that it is knowable only through scripture (<s>āgama</s>); others that it is knowable through mental perception (<s>mānasa-pratyakṣa</s>); others that it is directly perceived in all cognitions of objects by virtue of being the apprehender; others that by its nature as consciousness, its essential luminosity never rises or sets, being self-luminous (<s>svayañjyotis</s>); yet others say that even such a self is ultimately perceived as it truly is through perception, inference, and yogic direct experience (<s>yogaja-pratyakṣa</s>), with progressively increasing clarity — clear, clearer, and clearest — by virtue of its intrinsic distinctness from everything else.
Likewise —

children.text:
- paramamahān ; aṇuparimāṇaḥ ; śarīraparimāṇaḥ ; svataḥ parimāṇarahito 'pi vyāpyavastuparimitikṛtapariccheda iti / vyāptirapicaitanyamātreṇa ; svarūpeṇeti / tathā kṣaṇikaḥ ; yāvaccharīroṣmastāyī ; āprakṛtapralayāvasthīyī ; āmokṣasthāyī ; kūṭastho nitya iti / sarvaśarīreṣvekaḥ ; pratikṣetraṃ nānābhūta iti ca tathā tathā pratipadyante /
tathā paramātmaviṣaye 'pi - kecit samastavastusākṣātkāriṇaṃ sarvaśaktimīśvarameva nābhyupagacchanti / abhyupagacchanto 'pyeke pratyastamitamitimānamātṛmeyeśvareśitavyādibhedavikalpakūṭasthavijñā naikarasamanādyavidyopadarśitaviyadādibhedāvacchinnajñānaiśvaryādimahimavika
lpatayā kālpanikamācakṣate / apare tu yathoktasvarūpamevāvidyopadhānena tadguṇasāratayā prakalpitabrahmādisthāvaraparyantavividhajīvabhedaṃ svādhīnavicitravartasvabhāvamāyopahitatayā samāsāditasārvajñyādisaṃpadamupahitamimamabhidadhati / tathānye prakṛṣṭasattavopādānanimittasvatantrapradhānapariṇāmaviśeṣamātrani yamanirvāhitarvaiśvarya maryādamādriyante / anupahitamapi pariṇāminamapare pratipedire / apariṇāminamapi svamāyāṃśabhūtavicitrāntaḥkaraṇadarpaṇatalapratibimbitatayā pratipannaviśvataijasaprājñabhāvaṃ tamekameva cetanamitare rocayante / anye tu
svādhīnatrividhacetanācetanasvarūpasthitipravṛttibhedaṃ svābhāvikaniravadhikātiśayajñānabalaiśvaryavīryaśaktitejaḥprabhṛtisakalakalyāṇaguṇagaṇamahārṇavaṃ puruṣaviśeṣamīśvaramātiṣṭhante /
tathā tadviśeṣe 'pi hariharaviriñcabhāskarātmanā anabhimata tattanmūrtiparityāgena ca catusridvyekamūrtitayā vivadante / mūrtiviśeṣaviṣayāśca nityatvānityatvabhotakatvābhautikatvasvārthaparārthatvādivitarkāḥ prādurbhavanti ; parijanasthānādigocarāśca / tathā pramāṇato 'pi - ānuśrāvika evetyeke / ānumānikaścetyanye / viśiṣṭapratyakṣasamadhigamyaścetyapare /
tathā ātmaparamātmanoḥ saṃbandhe 'pi - anādyavidyopādānabhedāspado 'yamīśvareśitavyatādirūpasaṃbandhaḥ / paramārthatatsvekaṃ tattvamiti kecit / vyatirekābhāve 'pyatirikto jīva ityanye / svatastvaikyam, upādhito bheda iti viśiṣṭasvarūpabhāvena bhinnābhinnatvamitare / nānātve satyevābhedo nāmānvayaḥ aṃśāśibhāvalakṣaṇaḥ, samavāyaḥ paratantratālakṣaṇaḥ, śeṣaśeṣitvarūpaḥ, svasvāmibhāvaḥ, bhṛtyasvāmilakṣaṇa iti ca nānāvidyā vādāḥ /
tathā paramapuruṣārthabhūte brahmaprāptilakṣaṇamokṣe 'pi - svarūpocchittilakṣaṇaḥ, avidyāstamayalakṣaṇaḥ, niśeṣavaiśeṣikātmaguṇocchedalakṣaṇaḥ, kaivalyarūpaḥ, tadbhāvasādharmyalakṣaṇaḥ, tadguṇasaṅkāntilakṣaṇaḥ, catthāyāpattilakṣaṇaḥ, sāṃsiddhikānandādisvarūpāvirbhāvalakṣaṇaḥ, tadguṇānubhavajanitaniratiśayasukhasamunmeṣopanītātyantikatatkiṅkaratvalakṣaṇa iti tathā tathā vivadante /
tatsādhanato 'pi - karmayogalabhyaḥ, jñānayogalabhyaḥ, anyatarānugṛhītānyataralabhyaḥ, ubhayalabhyaḥ, ubhayaparikarmitakhāntasyaikāntikātyantika bhaktiyogalabhya iti /
tadevamanavasitaviśeṣavimarśakajanavimatidarśanāt, tatttatpakṣasādhanabalābalānagamācca tatastataḥ sandihānāḥ prekṣāvanto na tāvatparamapuruṣārthāya ghaṭeran, yāvadayamātmā paramātmā ca svarūpataḥ pramāṇataḥ saṃbandhataḥ prāptitaḥ tatsādhanataśca na nirṇiyeteti tatpratibodhāyedamārabhyate /
yadyapi bhagavatā bādarāyaṇenedamarthānyeva sūtrāṇi praṇītāni / vivṛtāni ca tāni pari
mitagambhīrabhāṣiṇā dramiḍabhāṣyakṛtā / vistṛtāni ca tāni gambhīranyāyasā(ga)rabhāṣiṇā śrīvatsāṅkamiśreṇāpi / tathāpi ācāryaṭaṅka-bhartṛprapañca-bhartṛmitra-bhartṛhari-brahmadaktaśaṅkara-śrīvatsāṅka-bhāskarādiviracitasitāsitavividhanibandhana śraddhāvipralabdhabuddhayo na yathāvat, anyathā ca pratipadyanta iti yuktaḥ prakaraṇaprakramaḥ // (ityupoddhātaprakaraṇam)
prakaraṇārambhaprayojanasabhidhatte 'viruddhe'ti / ātmaparamātmaviṣaye hi nānā vipratipattayaḥ santi / matīnāṃ viruddhatvaṃ viruddhārakārāvagāhitvam / yato mumukṣūṇāmātmaparamātmatattvaṃ jijñāsamānānāṃ tadviṣaye vādivivādinimittā vipratipattayaḥ santi, atastatpariśuddhyarthaṃ - ātmaparamātmatattvamateḥ tattadvādaprayuktāsadviruddhākāraprakārakatvarūpadoṣanirasanena yathāvasthitākārāvagāhitvalakṣaṇaśuddhiyogasaṃpādanārthamātmasiddhināmakaṃ prakaraṇaṃ viraccate satpramāṇatarkairātmaparātmatattvanirṇayaphalamiryarthaḥ / parāvarātmatattvaṃ pradhānaviṣayaḥ / parapakṣapratikṣepo nāntarīyakaḥ / ātmatattvanirṇayaśca sākṣātprayojanametatprakaraṇasyeti sūcitam / paramparayā niḥśreyasābhiṣvaṅgaścāsyābhipretaḥ / viṣayaprayojanokteḥ saṃbandhādhikāriṇau cākṣepagamyau / evamanubandhicatuṣṭayasaṃpattiranusaṃhitā / parāvarātmatattvapratipādakaścutyantānugrāhakanyāyaprapañcanaṃ prakaraṇasyāsya mukhyaṃ kṛtyam / tataścātmaparamātmamananopayogīdaṃ saṃpadyata iti bodhyam // 2 //
children.translated_text:
[The self is variously held to be:] supremely great; atomic in size; of the size of the body; or, though intrinsically devoid of measure, delimited by the extent of the pervaded object. And pervasion too [is held to be] through consciousness alone, or through [the self's] own essential nature. Likewise, [it is held to be] momentary; lasting as long as the bodily warmth endures; enduring until the state of cosmic dissolution (<s>prakṛtapralaya</s>); lasting until liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>); immutable and eternal. [It is held that there is] one [self] in all bodies; or that [the self is] manifold, distinct in each body — thus they variously maintain.
Likewise, regarding the supreme self (<s>paramātman</s>) too: some do not accept an omniscient, omnipotent Lord (<s>Īśvara</s>) who directly perceives all things. Others, while accepting [such a Lord], declare him to be merely imagined — since the immutable consciousness, in which the entire array of conceptual distinctions such as knower, known, Lord, and the ruled has subsided, is of a single, homogeneous, beginningless nature — [and maintain that his] glory of knowledge, sovereignty, and the like, delimited by distinctions such as space and the rest that are projected by beginningless <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), is merely a product of conceptual construction. Yet others speak of him as conditioned (<s>upahita</s>) — [saying that] this very [Brahman] of the aforementioned essential nature, through the superimposition of <s>avidyā</s>, being conceived as the essence of those qualities, has the manifold distinctions of individual selves (<s>jīva</s>) fabricated [upon it], ranging from <s>Brahmā</s> down to immovable [beings], and has acquired the perfections of omniscience and the like through being conditioned by <s>māyā</s> (illusion) whose nature is variegated and self-dependent activity. Others, again, accept [the Lord as having] a sovereignty whose compass is sustained solely by [his being] the specific transformation of an independent primordial matter (<s>pradhāna</s>), [operating as] the material and efficient cause, with preeminent existence. Others maintain that [the Lord is] a transformer (<s>pariṇāmin</s>) even without being conditioned. Yet others hold that there is only one conscious being, who — though non-transforming — is reflected in the mirror-surface of the variegated internal organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>), which is a portion of his own <s>māyā</s>, and thereby assumes the states of <s>viśva</s> (waking), <s>taijasa</s> (dreaming), and <s>prājña</s> (deep sleep). Still others uphold the Lord as a supreme Person (<s>puruṣaviśeṣa</s>) — [one who] independently [governs] the essential nature, existence, and modes of activity of the threefold sentient and insentient [reality], [and who is] a great ocean of all auspicious qualities including naturally unlimited and unsurpassed knowledge, strength, sovereignty, valor, power, splendor, and so forth.
Likewise, even regarding [the Lord's] specific [form], they dispute as to whether he has the form of <s>Hari</s>, <s>Hara</s>, <s>Viriñca</s> (Brahmā), or <s>Bhāskara</s> (the Sun), and by abandoning the respective forms not accepted [by them], [they debate whether he has] four, two, or one form. And regarding the specific forms, debates arise concerning eternality and non-eternality, being material and non-material, being for one's own sake and for the sake of others, and the like — as well as regarding his retinue, abode, and so on. Likewise, regarding the means of knowledge too: some [hold that the Lord] is known only through scripture (<s>ānuśrāvika</s>); others [say he is known] also through inference; and yet others [say he is] to be realized through a special kind of direct perception.
Likewise, regarding the relation between the individual self and the supreme self too: some [hold that] this relation of Lord and ruled, whose locus is a distinction based on beginningless <s>avidyā</s> as the material cause, [is such that] in the highest reality (<s>paramārtha</s>), that [Brahman] alone is the one reality (<s>tattva</s>). Others [hold that] even in the absence of difference, the individual soul (<s>jīva</s>) is distinct. Yet others [hold that there is] identity in essence but difference through limiting adjuncts (<s>upādhi</s>), and thus both difference and non-difference through the existence of a qualified essential nature. Others [hold that] even while there is real plurality, what is called non-difference is the relation (<s>anvaya</s>) characterized by the part-whole relationship; or [it is] inherence (<s>samavāya</s>) characterized by dependence; or [it is] the relation of accessory and principal (<s>śeṣa-śeṣin</s>); or the relation of property and owner; or one characterized by servant and master — thus there are doctrines of many kinds.
Likewise, regarding <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation), which is characterized by the attainment of <s>Brahman</s> and constitutes the supreme human goal (<s>paramapuruṣārtha</s>), too they variously dispute: [it is] characterized by the annihilation of [the self's] essential nature; characterized by the cessation of <s>avidyā</s>; characterized by the complete destruction of the particular qualities of the self according to <s>Vaiśeṣika</s>; in the form of absolute isolation (<s>kaivalya</s>); characterized by similarity of nature with that [Brahman]; characterized by the transfer of its qualities; characterized by attaining that [Brahman's] state; characterized by the manifestation of the innate nature of bliss and the like; or characterized by absolute and eternal servitude to that [Lord], brought about by the arising of unsurpassed bliss born from the experience of his qualities.
Regarding its means too: [it is] attainable through <s>karmayoga</s> (the discipline of action); attainable through <s>jñānayoga</s> (the discipline of knowledge); attainable through one [of the two] assisted by the other; attainable through both; or attainable through <s>bhaktiyoga</s> (the discipline of devotion), which is exclusive and absolute, for one whose [heart] has been purified through the preparatory discipline of both.
Thus, since we see the disagreements of people who have not settled upon a definitive determination, and since we have not ascertained the relative strength and weakness of the arguments for each position, discerning persons who are in doubt from every direction cannot exert themselves toward the supreme human goal until the self and the supreme self are determined with respect to their essential nature, the means of their knowledge, their mutual relation, their attainment, and the means of that attainment — therefore, for the awakening to that, this [work] is undertaken.
Although the blessed <s>Bādarāyaṇa</s> composed sūtras dealing with precisely these topics, and those were elucidated by the author of the <s>Dramiḍabhāṣya</s>, who spoke with measured profundity, and were expanded by <s>Śrīvatsāṅkamiśra</s> too, who spoke [as from] an ocean of profound reasoning — nevertheless, those whose intellects have been led astray by their faith in the various black and white treatises composed by <s>Ācārya Ṭaṅka</s>, <s>Bhartṛprapañca</s>, <s>Bhartṛmitra</s>, <s>Bhartṛhari</s>, <s>Brahmadatta</s>, <s>Śaṅkara</s>, <s>Śrīvatsāṅka</s>, <s>Bhāskara</s>, and others, understand [the truth] not as it is but otherwise — hence the undertaking of this treatise is justified. (Thus ends the introductory section.)
He states the purpose of commencing the treatise with the word 'viruddhe' (conflicting). For regarding the self and the supreme self, there are many conflicting views. The conflictedness of views means their apprehension of mutually contradictory forms. Since for those who seek liberation (<s>mumukṣu</s>) and wish to know the reality of the self and the supreme self, there exist disagreements occasioned by disputants and counter-disputants regarding that subject — therefore, for the purification of that — that is, for the purpose of producing the purity characterized by the apprehension of things as they actually are, through the removal of the defect consisting in the false and contradictory forms introduced by the various arguments in each position — a treatise named <s>Ātmasiddhi</s> is composed. Its fruit is the determination of the reality of the self and the supreme self through valid means of knowledge and reasoning (<s>satpramāṇatarka</s>) — this is the meaning. The reality of the lower and higher self is the principal subject. The refutation of opposing positions is an indispensable [part]. And the determination of the reality of the self is the direct purpose of this treatise — this has been indicated. Indirectly, the intention is the embrace of the supreme good (<s>niḥśreyasa</s>). The relation and the qualified student are to be understood implicitly from the statement of the subject and the purpose. Thus the possession of the four prerequisites (<s>anubandhi-catuṣṭaya</s>) has been noted. The principal task of this treatise is the elucidation of the reasoning that demonstrates and ultimately favors the reality of the lower and higher self. And from this it should be understood that this [work] is conducive to the contemplation of the self and the supreme self.

body.translated_text: For it is accepted in all philosophical systems that knowledge of the <s>ātman</s> (self) is the cause of the highest good (<s>niḥśreyasa</s>). And it is heard in scripture: 'Knowing the individual self and the impeller as distinct, being favored by Him, one attains immortality'; 'If one were to know the self'; 'The knower of the self crosses beyond sorrow'; 'The knower of <s>Brahman</s> attains the supreme' — thus the body of <s>Vedānta</s> passages establishes that knowledge of the reality of both the lower and the higher self is the means to <s>apavarga</s> (liberation). Therein, regarding this self and the Supreme, there are manifold conflicting views among the founders of philosophical schools.

body.text:
anarthakāyātmatattva na ko 'pi prekṣāpūrvakārī pravarteteti svagranthaphalasyāsya niḥśreyasābhiṣvaṅgamāviṣkaroti 'saṃmatam' iti / nanvastu nāmā'majñānasya mokṣasādhanatvam, atiriktaparamātmajñānasya tatkula ityatrā'ha 'śrūyate' iti / bāhyānāṃ vimatyāmapi vaidikavaryāṇāmātmana iva paramātmano 'pi tattvajñānasya mokṣasādhanatve na vimatiriti bhāvaḥ / parātmā-paraṃbrahma puruṣottamaḥ śrīmannārāyaṇaḥ / avarātmā-jīvātmā / śiṣṭaṃ spaṣṭam /
nanu sandhigdhe hi nyāyapravṛttiḥ / vedāntaireva parāvarātmatattvaṃ suniścitamiti kathaṃ tatra śaṅkā, kathantarāṃ ca
nyāyapravṛttiḥ ? ucyate / śrutibhirarthāvagame 'pi prasiddhamativibhavānāṃ tīrthakarāṇāṃ vividhavādaśravaṇataḥ śrutitātparya eva sandehapravṛtteḥ śrutyarthayāthātmye 'pi śaṅkā saṃbhavadudayā / imamevā'śayaṃ hṛdi nidhāyātmatattve sandehasandohikā vipratipattīrupakṣapati 'tatre' ti / tīrthaṃ - darśanaṃ tīrthasāmyāt / darśanaṃ hi āntarājñānamalanirharaṇapūrvakaṃ tattvajñānarūpāṃ śuddhimātmanāmupajanayati / tatkurvantīti tīrthakārāḥ - dārśanikāḥ / tadyathā - uktaṃ vipratipaccibāhuvidhyaṃ yathā - yena prakāreṇa, tadvarṇyata iti yāvat / 'dehameve'ti / dehādyātmatvavādinaścārvāka
bhedāḥ / 'mana ityanye' iti / mana ityaprasiddhaṃ kimapi kecidātmetyācakṣata ityarthaḥ / 'ātmānamācakṣata' ityuttaratrāpyanveti / saugatamataṃ śāṅkaramataṃ cāha tantreṇa 'adhyaste' ti / bodhamātrañcaitanyamātram / anahaṅkāram - ahaṃbuddhiśabdāviṣayam / āvidyamahaṅkāra granthisthaṃ jñātṛtvamātmanyāropyata ityekaḥ pakṣaḥ / anādivāsanayā jñānasyaiva jñātṛbhāvādyāropa iti cāparaḥ / tārkikamatamāha 'dehendriye' ti / bodhaḥ - jñānam / dehendriyamanaḥprāṇadhībhyo 'nyamacaitanyasvarūpamāgantukajñānasukhādiv iśeṣaguṇavantamahaṃbuddhiśabdagocaramātmānaṃ kāṇādā gautamāścācakṣata ityarthaḥ / acitsvabhāvamityanenākāśāderivātmasvarūpasya jaḍatvaṃ vivikṣitam / ahaṅkāraḥ, - ahamiti buddhiḥ śabdaśca / sāṅkhyamatamāha 'apare' iti / bodhaikasvabhāvameva-bodhaścaitanyaṃ, tadeva svo bhāvaḥ svarūpaṃ yasya tam, jñānasvarūpameva / upadhānam-upodhaḥ sannidhānam / imam - ātmānam / yathā svabhāvato dhavala eva sphaṭikādirjapākusumādyupādhisnidhānenāropitatattadraktādirūpeṇa pratibhāsate, evaṃ nityasvaprakāśaḥ svayañjyotirātmāntaḥkaraṇasannidhānata āropitasukhaduḥkhāditadguṇavattayā bhāsate kevalam / vastuto nityanirduṣṭa evāyamiti bhāvaḥ / 'anye tvi' ti / mīmāṃsakaikadeśinaḥ siddhāntyekadeśino vā / jñānānandau svābhāvikadharmāvātmana ityamīṣāmāśayaḥ / siddhāntināṃ matamāha 'āśraye'ti / ānando 'pi nātiriktaḥ, kintu ātmanaḥ anukūlatvena prāpta ānandasukhādinirdeśo yena, evaṃbhūto jñānaviśeṣa eva saḥ / sa eva cātmanaḥ svabhāvaḥ / saṃsāritvaduḥ khitvādi tu karmopādhikamiti bhāvaḥ / yāvaduktopapannaścātmeti hārdam / tattadvādyukteṣu yāvadupapannam, tāvadākāravattvaṃ cātmanaḥ saṃmatameva hi siddhānte /
ātmasvarūpe vipratipattīrūktvā tadgrāhakapramāṇe tā upakṣipati 'tathā anumāne'ti / sautrāntikīya ānumānikatvapakṣo 'yam / anumānaṃ ca ahaṃvijñānaṃ sālambanaṃ vijñānatvānnīlapītādivijñānavadityādyudāhāryam / vilakṣaṇa ātamā anumānagacara iti naiyāyikapakṣo vātrakīrtitaḥ syāt / agnimavivaraṇānusārāt / 'āgamaikavedya' iti / śrotriyāṇāṃ pakṣo 'yam / ahaṃbuddherdehālambanatayaivopapatteḥ saṅgātaparārthatvādyunumānasyāprayojakatvādinā ca śāstraikagamya ātmaityamīṣāmāśayaḥ / 'mānase'ti / tārkikāṇāṃ bhāṭṭānāṃ ca pakṣo 'yam / 'grāhakataive'ti/ prābhākarapakṣo 'yam / grāhakatayā-jñātṛtayā / jñānasya tritayāvabhāsakatvāddhaṭapratyakṣa eva ghaṭa iva tañjñānaṃ jñātā cātmā prakāśete ityamī / sāṅkyādimatamāha 'jñānasvabhāvataye' ti / svo bhāvaḥ svabhāvaḥ svarūpam / nityasyā'tmano jñānasvarūpatayā
itarānadhīnanityasvaprakāśo 'yamityete siddhāntināmāśayamāhar 'idṛśo 'pī'ti / viśadatamatayetyanantaraṃ 'gṛhīta' iti śeṣaḥ / pratyaktvādinaivāsya svaprakāśatvāddehādivyāvartakanityatvāṇutvajñātṛtvādiprakāreṇā'gamena viśadatayā, mananato viśadataratayā, yogajapratyakṣato viśadatamatayā ca gṛhīto 'yaṃ muktau svābhāvikāsaṅkucitāparokṣajñānaprabhayā kāstnaryenānubhūyata ityarthaḥ /
ātmanaḥ parimāṇe 'pi tā nirdiśati 'tathe'ti / naiyāyikapakṣamāha 'paramamahā' niti / tattvaṃ cāpakarṣānāśrayamahatparimāṇam / bibhutvasahacaritam / tatpratibhaṭaṃ siddhāntināṃ pakṣamāha 'aṇuparimāṇa' iti / mādhyamaṃ paramāṇaṃ manyamānānāmanaikāntyavādināṃ matamāha 'śarīraparimāṇa' iti / sasattvaikāntyavādināṃ sāṅkhyānāṃ matamāha 'svata' iti / parimāṇarāhityaṃ vibhutvādātmanām / parimāṇavattve hi paricchinnatvamavibhutvaṃ prasajyata ityeṣāṃ hārdam / aupādhikaṃ cāsya parimāṇamityāha 'vyāpye'ti / vyāpyāntaḥkaraṇaparimāṇaupādhikaparimāṇo 'yaṃ bandhe ityarthaḥ / vyāptāvapi tāmāha 'caitanye'ti / svadharmabhūtajñānadvārikaiva vyāptiriti siddhāntipakṣaḥ / yathāntaḥkaraṇādhīnaṃ parimāṇam, tathā jñānādhīnaṃ vyāpakatvamiti sādṛśyenopastitatvāt siddhāntapakṣasya
prathamanirdeśo 'tra / 'svarūpeṇe'ti / ātmā svarūpataḥ sarvagata iti naiyāyikādayaḥ / kālasaṃbandhe 'pi tā upakṣipati 'tathe'ti / kṣaṇikatvaṃ saugatānāmabhimatam / yāvaccharīroṣmasthāyitvaṃ cārvākāṇām / āprākṛtapralasthāyitvaṃ brahmadevādīnām, āmokṣasthāyitvāmauḍulomyupajñānām / kūṭasthanityatvaṃ naiyāyikādīnāṃ siddhāntināṃ ca / kūṭasthatvam-nirvikāratvam / nityatvaṃ sarvakālasattā /
saṅkhyāyāmapi tāmāha 'sarve'ti / ekajīvavādo māyāvādyekadeśinām / pratiśarīramātmabhedo naiyāyikādīnāṃ siddhāntināṃ ca / cakāro 'nuktavipratipattisamuccāyakaḥ / 'tathā tathe'ti / svasvābhimatatattadviruddhākāreṇātmānaṃ tete vādino manyanta ityarthaḥ / jīghātmasvarūpādau vipratipattīruktvā paramātmasvarūpādau tā upakṣipati 'tathā parame'ti / 'nānaiva vipratipattayaḥ tīrthakarāṇā'miti śeṣaḥ / 'keci'diti / cārvākā bauddhā ārhatāḥ karmaḍāścetyarthaḥ / saśvaravādiṣvapi naikamatyamityāha 'abhyupagacchanto 'pī'ti / ekekecidadvaitinaḥ / kālpanikaṃ kalpiteśvarabhāvam / kalpanāprakāramāha 'pratyastamite'ti / kūṭastham-avikāri nityaṃ vijñānamātraṃ satyam / yatreśeśitavyādibhedaprapañco mātṛmeyatadavacchinnamititvādirapi naivāsti / evaṃbhūte 'dhi
ṣṭhāne 'vidyayaiva nānāśaktimatyā viyadādinānācitpratibhāso rajjvāmiva sarpādyavabhāsaḥ / āvidyabhūtasamaṣṭivyaṣṭyavacchinnajñānaiśvaryādimahimabhedapratibhāsaśca / tat samaṣṭhyavacchinnajñānaiśvaryādimattayā bhāsamānaṃ caitanyamīśvaraḥ / vyaṣṭirūpadevādidehādyavacchinnajñānādimattayā nānātvena ca bhāsamānaṃ tadeva jīvajātamityeṣāmāśayaḥ / avidyāyā eva jīveśvarabhāvakalpakopādhitvametanmate / māyāvidyopādhibhedavādināṃ matamāha 'apare tvi'ti /
nirbhedacaitanyamātramevāvidyopahitaṃ nānājīvabhāvena māyopahitaṃ ceśvarabhāvena parisphurati / tatrāvidyākṛtatvājjīvabhedaḥ kāmakrodhalobhādyāvidyaguṇapradhāno 'vidyāparavaśaścar / iśvarastu svavaśavartivividhapariṇāmaśīlamāyāśaktyādhigatasārvajñyasarvaiśvayārdimahimetyamīṣāmāśayaḥ / yogatantraniṣṭhānāmīśvarasamādaraṇarītimāha 'tathānye' iti / aupādhikameveśvaratvametanmate 'pīti tathetyanenābhipretam / svatantraprakṛtipariṇāmaviśeṣasya yo viśeṣo nityodriktasattvakatvarūpaḥ prakṛṣṭasattvapradhānāṃśopādānatvaprayuktaḥ, tena saṃpāditā sarvaiśvaryavyavasthā yasya tamīśvaramādriyanta ityarthaḥ / sadā śudadhasattvātmakāntaḥkaraṇādirīśvaropādhiḥ / tadupahitacaitanyamātravapuḥ puruṣaviśeṣar iśvaraḥ / upādhiviśeṣādhīnameva tasyaiśvaryamiti bhāvaḥ / yādavaprakāśapakṣamāga 'anupahitamapī'ti / sindhuriva phenabudbudataraṅgabhedena brahmaiva jaḍajīveśvarūpeṇa bhavatīti pariṇāmavādo 'yam / pratibimbavādamāha 'apariṇāminamapī'ti / 'tamekameva cetana'mityanena māyopahitaṃ caitanyamīśvaraḥ / antaḥkaraṇeṣu tasyaiva pratibimbabhedā jīvā ityābhāsalakṣaṇatvaṃ jīvānāṃ vijñāyate / yadvā māyāyāṃ pratibimbitaṃ caitanyamīśvaraḥ / tasya māyāśabhūtavicitrāntaḥkaraṇeṣu pratibimbabhedā jīvā iti bhāvaḥ / viśvādirjāgṛtisvapnasuṣuptyabhimānī / siddhāntināṃ matamāha 'anye' tviti / trividhāścetanāḥjñātṛtvavanto baddhamuktanityāḥ / trividhāścātetanāḥ - jñātṛtvarahitāḥ prakṛtikālanityavibhūtayaḥ / jñānarūpatve 'pi nityavibhūterajñātṛtvādacetanatvam / teṣāṃ sarveṣāṃ svasvākārasaṃpattiḥ, niṣpannasvarūpāṇāmuttarottarakālānuvṛttirūpā sthitiḥ, pravṛttiviśeṣāśca tattatkāryānuguṇā yadadhīnā eva sadā, sar iśvaraḥ / sa ca na nirguṇaḥ / kintu svābhāvikotkṛṣṭatamaṣāṅguṇyaprabhṛtyanantakalyāṇaguṇagaṇaratnākaraḥ / nirguṇatvaṃ cāsya heyagandhābhāvāt / ayaṃ ca puruṣaviśeṣaḥ - trividhajīvātmavilakṣaṇaḥ puruṣottamaḥ śriyaḥ - patirityeteṣāṃ hārdam /
puruṣaviśeṣar iśvara ityuktama / sa kiṃnāmarūpa ityapekṣāyāmāha 'tathā tadviśeṣe 'pī'tir / iśvarīyanāmarūpādiviṣaye 'pi naikamatyaṃ vādināmityarthaḥ / tathāhi-eka evaiśvaro mūrticatuṣṭayaṃ
gṛhṇāti kāryavaśādityeke / trimūrtivādinastvādityarūpaṃ parityajanti / hariharaikyavādinastu brahmarūpamapi / śaivāstu hara evaiśvara ityabhimanyante / śrīvaiṣṇavastu harirevetyāmananti / evaṃ hairaṇyagarbhāṇāṃ saurāṇāṃ ca tattadekamūrtipakṣo 'pyanusandheyaḥ / riśvaramūrtigataviśeṣeṣvapi vipratipattīrāha 'mūrtī'ti / sārthatvam - svabogasiddhyarthatvam / parārthatvam - jīvānugrahaikārthatvam / vitarkāḥ - vipratipattayaḥ / 'parijane'ti /
parijanādayaḥ santi neti, nityāḥ anityā iti, prākṛtā aprākṛtā iti ca pakṣabhedāḥ parijanasthānādāvanusandheyāḥ / 'pramāṇato 'pī'ti / sārvavibhaktikastasil / pramāṇaviṣaye 'pītyarthaḥ / śāstraikapramāṇaka ityeke / āgamānumānapramāṇaka ityapare / śruto mataśca śrutito 'numānataśca premapūrvānudhyānasaṃskṛtamanogrāhyaśceti tu siddhāntinaḥ //
body.translated_text:
No discriminating person would engage in [investigating] the nature of the self (<s>ātmatattva</s>) if it were purposeless — thus he reveals that the fruit of his own treatise is the desire for the highest good (<s>niḥśreyasa</s>), with the word 'accepted' (<s>saṃmatam</s>). [Objection:] Granted, let the knowledge of the self be a means to liberation — but the knowledge of a supreme self beyond [the individual self] belongs to that same family [of soteriological knowledge] — to this he replies with 'it is heard' (<s>śrūyate</s>). The purport is that even when outsiders [i.e., non-Vedic thinkers] have doubts, the foremost among the Vedic [authorities] have no doubt that the knowledge of the true nature of the supreme self (<s>Paramātman</s>), just like [knowledge of] the [individual] self, is a means to liberation. The supreme self (<s>parātman</s>) is the supreme <s>Brahman</s>, <s>Puruṣottama</s>, the blessed <s>Nārāyaṇa</s>. The lower self (<s>avarātman</s>) is the individual self (<s>jīvātman</s>). The rest is clear.
[Objection:] But logical inquiry (<s>nyāya</s>) proceeds [only] when there is doubt. Since the truth about the higher and lower selves is well-ascertained by the <s>Vedānta</s> texts themselves, how can there be doubt there, and how, in turn, can logical inquiry proceed? [Reply:] It is said: Even when the meaning has been understood from the <s>śruti</s> (scripture), because of hearing the various doctrines of the founders of schools (<s>tīrthakara</s>) — who are renowned for their great intellectual powers — doubt arises regarding the purport of <s>śruti</s> itself; thus doubt with a plausible basis is possible even regarding the true meaning of <s>śruti</s>. Keeping this very intention in mind, he presents the conflicting views — which constitute a mass of doubts — regarding the nature of the self, with the word 'there' (<s>tatra</s>). '<s>Tīrtha</s>' means 'philosophical system' (<s>darśana</s>), because of the similarity to a sacred ford. For a philosophical system (<s>darśana</s>) generates in selves a purity in the form of knowledge of reality, preceded by the removal of the internal impurity of ignorance. Those who do this are '<s>tīrthakāras</s>' — the founders of philosophical systems. That is: the manifold variety of conflicting views that has been stated — in what manner [they hold their views], that is being described. '[Some say] the body alone [is the self]' — the varieties of <s>Cārvāka</s> [materialists] maintain that the body and the like are the self. 'Others [say] the mind' — some call something otherwise unknown as 'mind' the self — this is the meaning. '[They] declare the self' connects also with what follows. He states the Buddhist and <s>Śaṅkara</s> [Advaita] doctrines together with the word 'superimposes' (<s>adhyaste</s>). 'Mere awareness' (<s>bodhamātra</s>) means 'consciousness alone' (<s>caitanyamātra</s>). 'Without ego' (<s>anahaṅkāra</s>) — not an object of the ego-cognition or the word 'I.' One position is that the knower-hood (<s>jñātṛtva</s>), which resides in the knot of the ego-sense born of ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>), is superimposed upon the self. Another [position] is that through beginningless latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>), there is superimposition of knower-hood and the like upon knowledge itself. He states the <s>Tārkika</s> (Naiyāyika) doctrine with '[different from] body, senses' (<s>dehendriya</s>). '<s>Bodha</s>' means knowledge (<s>jñāna</s>). The meaning is that the <s>Kāṇāda</s> [Vaiśeṣika] and <s>Gautama</s> [Naiyāyika] schools declare the self to be different from body, senses, mind, and vital breath — having an unconscious own-nature (<s>acitsvabhāva</s>) — possessing adventitious special qualities (<s>viśeṣaguṇa</s>) such as knowledge, pleasure, and the like — and being the referent of the ego-cognition and the word 'I.' By 'having an unconscious nature' (<s>acitsvabhāva</s>), it is intended that the own-nature of the self is inert, like space and the like. '<s>Ahaṅkāra</s>' — the cognition 'I' and the word [expressing it]. He states the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> doctrine with 'others' (<s>apare</s>). 'Having awareness as its sole nature' — '<s>bodha</s>' is consciousness (<s>caitanya</s>); that alone is its own nature (<s>svabhāva</s>), its own form (<s>svarūpa</s>) — [i.e.,] having knowledge as its very essence. '<s>Upadhāna</s>' means proximity, placing near. 'This' (<s>imam</s>) — the self. Just as a crystal and the like, being white by nature, appear with the superimposed forms of red and the like due to the proximity of a <s>japā</s>-flower and the like — so the self, which is eternally self-luminous and self-effulgent, merely appears as possessing the qualities of pleasure, pain, and the like superimposed [upon it] due to the proximity of the internal organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>). The purport is that in reality this [self] is eternally faultless. 'Others indeed' (<s>anye tu</s>) — some among the <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s>s, or some among the Siddhāntins [i.e., Viśiṣṭādvaitins]. Their view is that knowledge and bliss are natural properties of the self. He states the view of the Siddhāntins with 'in the substrate' (<s>āśraya</s>). Bliss too is not something additional; rather, it is precisely a particular [mode of] knowledge that has come to be designated as bliss, happiness, and the like by virtue of being favorable to the self. And that alone is the nature of the self. The purport is that the state of being a transmigrating soul (<s>saṃsāritva</s>), suffering (<s>duḥkhitva</s>), and the like are due to the limiting adjunct (<s>upādhi</s>) of <s>karma</s>. The essential meaning is: 'the self is as far as it is established [by valid reasoning].' Whatever is established among the [arguments] stated by the respective disputants — to that extent the self's possession of [that particular] form is indeed accepted in the [Viśiṣṭādvaita] system.
Having stated the conflicting views regarding the own-nature of the self, he introduces those [conflicting views] regarding the means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) that apprehends it, with 'likewise regarding inference' (<s>tathā anumāne</s>). This is the <s>Sautrāntika</s> position that [the self] is known through inference. The inference can be illustrated as: 'The ego-cognition (<s>ahaṃvijñāna</s>) has a [real] object (<s>sālambana</s>), because it is a cognition (<s>vijñānatva</s>) — like the cognition of blue, yellow, and the like.' Or the Naiyāyika position — that the self, being of a different character, is an object of inference — is stated here. [This follows] from the <s>Agnimavivaraṇa</s> commentary. 'Knowable by scripture alone' (<s>āgamaikavedya</s>) — this is the position of the scriptural scholars (<s>śrotriya</s>). Since the ego-cognition is adequately explained as having the body as its object, and since inference from the purposefulness of the aggregate and the like is non-probative, the self is accessible only through scripture — this is their view. 'Through mental [perception]' (<s>mānasa</s>) — this is the position of the <s>Tārkikas</s> (Naiyāyikas) and the <s>Bhāṭṭa</s> [Mīmāṃsakas]. 'Through apprehender-hood' (<s>grāhakatā</s>) — this is the <s>Prābhākara</s> position. 'Through apprehender-hood' — through knower-hood. Because cognition illuminates the triad [of knower, known, and knowledge], in the very perception of a pot, just as the pot [is manifest], so too that cognition and the self as knower are manifest — this is their [view]. He states the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> and other views with 'through the nature of knowledge' (<s>jñānasvabhāvatā</s>). 'Own nature' (<s>svabhāva</s>) means 'own form' (<s>svarūpa</s>). Because the eternal self has the nature of knowledge, it is eternally self-luminous without depending on anything else — this is their [view]. He states the view of the Siddhāntins with 'even such [a self]' (<s>idṛśo'pi</s>). After 'with the greatest clarity' (<s>viśadatamatayā</s>), the word 'apprehended' (<s>gṛhīta</s>) is to be supplied. The meaning is: this [self], being self-luminous by virtue of its immediacy (<s>pratyaktva</s>), is apprehended through scripture — which distinguishes it from the body and the like by [specifying] its eternality, atomicity, knower-hood, and other modes — with clarity; through reflection (<s>manana</s>) with greater clarity; and through yogic direct perception (<s>yogajapratyakṣa</s>) with the greatest clarity; and in liberation (<s>mukti</s>) it is experienced with full intensity (<s>kāstnaryena</s>) through the radiance of natural, uncontracted, immediate knowledge.
He indicates the conflicting views regarding the size (<s>parimāṇa</s>) of the self too with 'likewise' (<s>tathā</s>). He states the Naiyāyika position with 'supremely great' (<s>paramamahā</s>). And that reality is a great magnitude not subject to diminution — accompanied by all-pervasiveness (<s>vibhutva</s>). He states the opposing position of the Siddhāntins with 'atomic in size' (<s>aṇuparimāṇa</s>). He states the view of those who hold a middle position — considering [the self to be of] the size of an atom — namely the non-exclusivists (<s>anaikāntyavādin</s>), with 'of the size of the body' (<s>śarīraparimāṇa</s>). He states the view of the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s>, who are exclusivists holding [the self] to be always existent, with 'by its own nature' (<s>svataḥ</s>). The absence of [determinate] size for selves is due to their all-pervasiveness. For if they had [determinate] size, limitedness and non-all-pervasiveness would follow — this is their essential view. He states that its size is adventitious (<s>aupādhika</s>) with 'in what is pervaded' (<s>vyāpya</s>). The meaning is that in bondage, its size is adventitious, [determined by] the limiting adjunct of the size of the internal organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>) that it pervades. He states the [conflicting views] regarding its pervasion (<s>vyāpti</s>) too with 'in consciousness' (<s>caitanya</s>). The Siddhāntin's position is that pervasion is only through knowledge that is its own essential property (<s>svadharma</s>). Since [in this view] size depends on the internal organ and pervasiveness depends on knowledge — the Siddhāntin's position is stated first because of the similarity [between the two cases]. 'By its own nature' (<s>svarūpeṇa</s>) — the <s>Naiyāyikas</s> and others [hold that] the self is all-pervading by its own nature. He introduces the [conflicting views] regarding [the self's] relation to time too with 'likewise' (<s>tathā</s>). Momentariness (<s>kṣaṇikatva</s>) is the accepted [view] of the Buddhists. Duration as long as the body's warmth lasts is [the view] of the <s>Cārvākas</s>. Duration until the cosmic dissolution of <s>Prakṛti</s> is [the view] of <s>Brahmā</s>, <s>Deva</s>, and the like; duration until liberation is [the view] of those who follow <s>Mauḍulomi</s>. Immutable eternality (<s>kūṭasthanityatva</s>) is [the view] of the <s>Naiyāyikas</s> and others, and of the Siddhāntins. 'Immutability' (<s>kūṭasthatva</s>) means 'changelessness' (<s>nirvikāratva</s>). 'Eternality' (<s>nityatva</s>) means existence at all times.
He states the [conflicting views] regarding number too with 'all' (<s>sarva</s>). The doctrine of a single individual soul (<s>ekajīvavāda</s>) belongs to some among the <s>Māyāvādins</s> (Advaitins). The difference of selves corresponding to each body is [the view] of the <s>Naiyāyikas</s> and others, and of the Siddhāntins. The word 'and' (<s>ca</s>) aggregates the unmentioned conflicting views. 'Likewise, likewise' (<s>tathā tathā</s>) — the meaning is that those various disputants consider the self to have such-and-such a form, contradicting their respective [opponents'] accepted [views]. Having stated the conflicting views regarding the nature of the individual self (<s>jīvātman</s>) and the like, he introduces those [conflicting views] regarding the nature of the supreme self (<s>Paramātman</s>) and the like with 'likewise regarding the supreme' (<s>tathā parama</s>). 'The conflicting views of the founders of schools are manifold' is to be supplied. 'Some' (<s>kecit</s>) — meaning <s>Cārvākas</s>, Buddhists, Jainas, and followers of [mere] <s>karma</s>. He says that even among those who accept <s>Īśvara</s> (God), there is no unanimity, with 'even those who accept' (<s>abhyupagacchanto'pi</s>). Some are Advaitins. '[Their Īśvara is] imaginary' (<s>kālpanika</s>) — meaning the [Advaita] conception of <s>Īśvara</s> is a product of mental construction (<s>kalpanā</s>). He describes the mode of construction with 'when [all differentiation] has set' (<s>pratyastamita</s>). The immutable (<s>kūṭastha</s>), changeless, eternal consciousness-alone is the [sole] reality. Where the manifold differentiation of lord and lordly subjects, of cognizer, cognized, and the delimitations of cognition — none of this exists at all. In such a substratum, through <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) alone — which possesses manifold powers — there is the appearance of diverse insentient [objects] like space and the like upon consciousness, like the appearance of a snake and the like upon a rope. And there is the appearance of the differentiation of the greatness of knowledge, lordship, and the like, delimited by the aggregate (<s>samaṣṭi</s>) and the individual (<s>vyaṣṭi</s>), which are products of <s>avidyā</s>. That consciousness which appears as possessing knowledge, lordship, and the like — as delimited by the aggregate — is <s>Īśvara</s>. That very same [consciousness], appearing as many — as possessing knowledge and the like delimited by the bodies of gods and the like in their individual forms — is the class of individual souls (<s>jīva</s>). This is their view. In this doctrine, it is <s>avidyā</s> itself that serves as the limiting adjunct (<s>upādhi</s>) that constructs the states of being a <s>jīva</s> and <s>Īśvara</s>. He states the view of those who distinguish between <s>māyā</s> and <s>avidyā</s> as [different] limiting adjuncts with 'others, however' (<s>apare tu</s>).
The undifferentiated consciousness-alone, when conditioned by <s>avidyā</s>, manifests as the manifold state of individual souls (<s>jīva</s>), and when conditioned by <s>māyā</s>, manifests as the state of <s>Īśvara</s>. In that case, the differentiation of <s>jīvas</s> is produced by <s>avidyā</s>, and is dominated by the qualities of <s>avidyā</s> such as desire, anger, greed, and the like, and is under the control of <s>avidyā</s>. But <s>Īśvara</s> — through the <s>māyā</s>-power that is under his own control and is capable of diverse transformations — has attained the greatness of omniscience and supreme lordship. This is their view. He states the manner in which <s>Īśvara</s> is revered by those established in the <s>Yoga</s> <s>Tantra</s> with 'likewise others' (<s>tathānye</s>). The word 'likewise' (<s>tathā</s>) indicates that even in this doctrine, the lordship of <s>Īśvara</s> is adventitious (<s>aupādhika</s>). The particular transformation of independently [functioning] <s>Prakṛti</s> — which has the specific form of being constituted by eternally predominant <s>sattva</s> — [and which] is occasioned by its being the material [cause] of the predominant <s>sattva</s> portion — through that [specific transformation], the state of possessing all lordship has been accomplished for him [<s>Īśvara</s>]. This is the meaning: they revere as <s>Īśvara</s> [such a being]. The limiting adjunct (<s>upādhi</s>) of <s>Īśvara</s> is the internal organ and the like that are eternally constituted by pure <s>sattva</s>. The body of <s>Īśvara</s> is consciousness-alone as conditioned by that [limiting adjunct]. <s>Īśvara</s> is a special <s>puruṣa</s> (spirit). The purport is that his lordship depends solely on the specific limiting adjunct. He states <s>Yādavaprakāśa</s>'s position with 'even without conditioning' (<s>anupahitam api</s>). Just as the ocean [appears] in the differentiation of foam, bubbles, and waves — so <s>Brahman</s> itself becomes [the triad of] insentient [matter], individual souls, and <s>Īśvara</s> — this is the transformation doctrine (<s>pariṇāmavāda</s>). He states the reflection doctrine (<s>pratibimbavāda</s>) with 'even of what is untransformed' (<s>apariṇāminam api</s>). By 'that one consciousness alone' — consciousness conditioned by <s>māyā</s> is <s>Īśvara</s>. The reflections of that very [consciousness] in the [various] internal organs are the individual souls — thus the nature of the individual souls as appearances (<s>ābhāsa</s>) is understood. Or: consciousness reflected in <s>māyā</s> is <s>Īśvara</s>. The reflections of that [consciousness] in the diverse internal organs, which are effects of <s>māyā</s>, are the individual souls — this is the purport. '<s>Viśva</s>' and the like [viz., <s>Taijasa</s>, <s>Prājña</s>] are the presiding [consciousness] of waking, dream, and deep sleep [respectively]. He states the view of the Siddhāntins with 'others, however' (<s>anye tu</s>). There are three kinds of conscious entities (<s>cetana</s>), i.e., possessing knower-hood: bound, liberated, and eternally [free]. And there are three kinds of non-conscious entities (<s>acetana</s>), i.e., devoid of knower-hood: <s>Prakṛti</s>, time (<s>kāla</s>), and the eternal divine realm (<s>nityavibhūti</s>). The eternal divine realm is non-conscious despite having the form of knowledge, because of lacking knower-hood. The possession of their respective forms for all of these, the continuity of those whose natures are fully established over successive times, and the specific activities appropriate to their respective functions — all of these depend forever on <s>Īśvara</s>. And he is not without qualities (<s>nirguṇa</s>). Rather, he is an ocean of infinite auspicious qualities (<s>kalyāṇaguṇa</s>), beginning with the naturally most exalted sixfold perfection (<s>ṣāḍguṇya</s>). And his being 'without qualities' means the absence of even a trace of what is to be rejected (<s>heya</s>). And this special <s>puruṣa</s> — distinguished from the three kinds of individual selves — is <s>Puruṣottama</s>, the Lord of <s>Śrī</s> — this is their essential view.
[The text] stated that the special <s>puruṣa</s> is <s>Īśvara</s>. In response to the question 'What is his name and form?', he says 'likewise regarding the specifics of that' (<s>tathā tadviśeṣe'pi</s>). The meaning is that even regarding the name, form, and the like pertaining to <s>Īśvara</s>, the disputants have no unanimity. For thus: some [say] a single <s>Īśvara</s> assumes four forms (<s>mūrticatuṣṭaya</s>) according to functional requirements. The advocates of the three forms (<s>trimūrtivādin</s>), however, discard the solar form. And the advocates of the unity of <s>Hari</s> and <s>Hara</s> [discard] even the <s>Brahmā</s> form. But the <s>Śaivas</s> consider that <s>Hara</s> alone is <s>Īśvara</s>. The <s>Śrī Vaiṣṇavas</s>, however, maintain that <s>Hari</s> alone [is <s>Īśvara</s>]. Likewise, the single-form positions of the <s>Hairaṇyagarbhas</s> (followers of <s>Hiraṇyagarbha</s>) and the <s>Sauras</s> (sun-worshippers) should also be considered. He states the conflicting views regarding the specifics of <s>Īśvara</s>'s forms with 'regarding the form' (<s>mūrtī</s>). 'For one's own purpose' (<s>sārthatva</s>) — for the purpose of his own enjoyment. 'For the sake of others' (<s>parārthatva</s>) — solely for the purpose of grace toward individual souls. 'Speculations' (<s>vitarka</s>) — conflicting views. 'Regarding the retinue' (<s>parijana</s>) —
whether the retinue and the rest exist or not, whether they are eternal or non-eternal, whether they are of <s>Prakṛti</s> or not of <s>Prakṛti</s> — these divisions of positions should be considered regarding the retinue, [divine] abode, and the like. 'Regarding the means of valid knowledge too' (<s>pramāṇato'pi</s>) — the <s>tasil</s> suffix is in the sense of all case-endings. The meaning is: regarding the subject of the means of valid knowledge too. Some [say the self] is known solely through scripture. Others [say] through scripture and inference as means of valid knowledge. But the Siddhāntins [say]: [<s>Īśvara</s> is] heard [through scripture] and reasoned about [through inference], and [also] apprehensible by the mind refined through loving meditation (<s>premapūrvānudhyānasaṃskṛtamanas</s>) — apprehensible both from scripture and from inference.

body.text:
atha jīvaparayoḥ saṃbandhe 'pi vipratipattīrnirdiśati 'tathā ātme'ti / advaitināṃ pakṣamāha 'anādī'ti / avidyākṛtabhedāvalaṃbanatvādīśeśitavyatvādevyarvihārikatvameva na paramārthatvamityāśayo 'mīṣām / pratibimbapakṣābhiprāyeṇā'h 'vyatireke'ti / bimbato bhedābhāve 'pi pratibiṃbānāṃ bhedapratipattyādigocaratvalakṣaṇo 'tirekoviśeṣo 'stīti bhāvaḥ / bhāskarapakṣamāha 'svata' iti / svarūpato 'bhedaḥ / aupādhiko bhedaḥ / bhedābhedayorviruddhayoḥ kevalasvarūpa evāsaṃbhavādityāśayaḥ / yādavaprakāśapakṣamāha 'nānātva' iti / aṃśāṃśibhāvalakṣaṇa ityasyānvaya ityanena saṃbandhaḥ / aṃśāṃśitvādbhedābhedopapattiḥ / bhedasamānādhikaraṇābhedasyaiva tādātmyasya sāmānadhikaraṇyārthatvamiti hārdameteṣām / 'samavāya' ityādiḥ siddhāntinā pakṣaḥ / nānāsaṃbandhopagamājjīvaparayoḥ siddhānte nānasaṃbandhakīrtanam / aṃśāṃśibhāvalakṣaṇa ityasya siddhāntapakṣatvamapi saṃbhavati / paratantratā-apṛthaksiddhiḥ tadrūpaḥ samavāyaḥ, na tvatirikto vaiśeṣikamatavaditi bhāvaḥ / paragatātiśayādhānecchāprakḷptasvarūpādikatvaṃ śeṣatvam / yatheṣṭaviniyogārhatvaṃ svatvam / preryacetanatvaṃ bhṛtyatvamiti bhidā / etatpratisaṃbandhitvalakṣaṇaṃ ca śeṣitvādīti bodhyam / bhṛtyasvāmīti bhāvapradhānanirdeśaḥ / bhṛtyasvāmitvalakṣaṇa iti yāvat / tathaiva vā pāṭhaḥ saṃbhāvyate /
atha muktisvarūpe vipratipattīrāha 'tathā parame'ti / brahmaprāptilakṣaṇeti svābhimatoktiḥ parābhimatānāṃ muktisvarūpāṇāṃ puruṣārthatvāyogasūcanārthā / cārvākāṇāṃ śūnyavādināṃ ca svarūpocchittipakṣaḥ / yogācārāṇāṃ māyināṃ vā pakṣo dvitīyaḥ / kaṇādādipakṣastṛtīyaḥ / viśeṣaḥ
eva vaiśeṣikaḥ / sāṅkhyapakṣasturīyaḥ / tadbhāvasādharmya lakṣaṇa ityadvaitināṃ syāt / tacchabdo brahmaparaḥ / brahmabhāva eva sādharmyaṃ muktiriti / yadvā - brahmarūpasāmyaprāpti, brāhmaguṇaprāpti, brahmakāntiprāptilakṣaṇamuktibhedaparaṃ padatrayam / 'sāṃsiddhike'ti mīmāṃsakādīnāṃ matam / 'tadguṇe'tyādi siddhāntinām / svarūpāvirbhāvo 'pyatra garbhitaḥ / kiṅkaratvaṃ sevākaraṇam /
muktyupāye 'pi tā āha 'tatsādhanato 'pī'ti / karmajñānasamuccayapakṣo yādavaprakāśīyaḥ / 'ubhaye'ti siddhāntipakṣaḥ / karmayogajñānayogābhyāṃ saṃskṛtacetasa eva bhaktiyogo nāma parabhaktirudaiti / karmajñānādyaṅgikā saiva parabrahmaprāptilakṣaṇamokṣasādhanam / tasyāścaikāntikatvaṃ bhagavadekaviṣayatvam / ātyatnikatvaṃ cāvicchinnatvam / parajñānaparamabhaktyoretadvipākarūpatvameveti bhāvaḥ /
vipratipattipradarśanasya vicārāmbhopayogitāṃ samarthayati 'tadeva'miti / parīkṣakāṇāṃ vipratipattibhede kasmiṃścidapi vā pakṣe yāvatsatpramāṇatarkamūlakatvādiviśeṣo nāvadhāryate, tāvattattve sandeho na nivartate / yāvacca niruktaviśeṣānavadhāraṇam, na tāvattattatsādhane vyāptipakṣadharmatāyogitvalakṣamabalanirdhāraṇam / na ca viruddhasādhyasādhanayorvāstavikavyāptipakṣadharmatopapattirekasminneva dharmiṇi / tathā ca samabalatayā pratīyamānānāṃ nānāpakṣasādhanānāṃ satpratipakṣabhāvena sādhyanirṇayo durghaṭaḥ / na cārthasandehādeva muktiḥ / tathā ca pakṣabhede jāgrati yatra vāstavo viśeṣa iti vicāraḥ prāptāvasaraḥ / vicāreṇānyatamapakṣe viśeṣāvadhāraṇe tu tatpakṣasādhanasyādhikabalatvajñānātsatpratipakṣabhāvanivṛttestenārthatattvanirṇayopapattiḥ / tat muktisādhanopayogyarthatattvanirṇayāyā'tmasvarūpādigocarānyatamapakṣasya satpramāṇatarkamūlakatvādiviśeṣavyavasthāpanaparasya vicāragranthasyā'rambho yukta eveti samuditāśayaḥ /
nanu - ātmaparamātmanornānāvipratipattinirasanārthaṃ pūrvācāryaprabandhānāṃ pravartanameva karyam / kṛtaṃ nūtnaprabandhapraṇayanapravṛttyetyāśaṅkāmantarnidhāyāha 'yadyapī'ti / idamarthānyeva - ātmaparamātmatatsaṃbandhādyarthatattvanirṇayārthānyeva, sūtrāṇi - brahmamīmāṃsāsūtrāṇi / eṣāmeva mukhyaṃ sūtratvamiti skāndoktam "nirviśeṣitasūtratvaṃ brahmasūtrasya cāpyataḥ / saviśeṣāṇi sūtrāṇi hyaparāṇi vido viduḥ // mukhyasya
nirviśeṣeṇa śabdo 'nyeṣāṃ viśeṣataḥ / iti vedavidaḥ prāhuḥ śabdatattvārthavedinaḥ //" iti / 'vivṛtānī'ti / parimitatvaṃ - śabdasaṅkṣepaḥ / gabhīratvam - arthagāṃbhūryaśālitvam / dramiḍabhāṣyakṛt - dramiḍācārya saṃjñakaḥ chāndogyavyānasya
vākyābhidhasya ṭaṅkācāryāparābhidhānabrahmanandikṛtasya bhāṣyakartā / brahmasūtrāṇāmapi bāṣyaṃ kṛtamaneneti etachrīsūktisandarbhādavagamyate / 'vistṛtāni ce' ti / tāni - dramiḍācāryakṛtabrahmasūtrabhāṣyavākyāni / 'vivaraṇagranthe' iti śeṣaḥ / tānibrahmasūtrāṇi vā / śrīviṣṇupurāṇavyākhyāne viṣṇucittīye vivaraṇavākyāni samuddhṛtāni santi / 'tathāpī'ti / ayaṃ bhāvaḥ - yadyapi pūrvācāryaprabndheṣvadhyātmatattvaṃ saparikaraṃ nirūpitamevāsti, athāpi pāścātyaiḥ brahmamīmāṃsādivyākhyācchalena nānāmatānāṃ pravartitatvādā cāprāmāṇyahetvavadhāraṇāt tadgrantheṣvapi śraddhāyāḥ siddhāntagrantheṣviva saṃbhavāt teṣu ca vipratipattibāhulyena vicalitabuddhayo nāñjasā tattvajñānaṃ prāpnuyuriti tattanmatasārāsāravivekopayogitattanmataparīkṣātmakaprakaraṇārambha āvaśyaka eveti / ācāryaṭaṅkādiṣu nirdiṣṭeṣu kecit siddhāntinaḥ, anye tu matāntarānuyāyinaḥ syuḥ / tatprabandheṣu ca sitāsitatvam - asphuṭapratipādakatvamanyathāpratipādakatvaṃ ca yathāsaṃbhavaṃ yojyam / yadvā - ṭaṅkaśrīvatsāṅkāvapi atra nirdiṣṭau matāntarasthau vākyavivaraṇakartṛbhinnau syātām / vākyakarturṭaṅkasaṃjñā ca vedārthasaṅgraṭīkāto 'vagamyate / 'tatpratipattaye ce'ti / kecidasphaṭatayār'thatattvamavagacchanti, kecitpunaḥ kenāpi hetunā matāntaragrantheṣu śraddhālavo 'ta eva vañcitabudadhayo 'nyathaiva pratipadyanta iti sphuṭapratipattaye anyaprabandhānāṃ sitāsitatvapratipattaye ca prakaraṇārambho yukta evetyāśayaḥ / pūrvācāryaprabandhānāṃ śāstrarūpāṇāṃ prakaraṇamidamātmasiddhyādīti ca hārdam / prakaraṇaṃ cedaṃ śārīrakamīmāṃsāyāḥ, nyāyatattvaśastrasya ca / śāstraikadeśārthapratipādanatatparatve sati śāstrārthapratipattyupayogi (virodhimatanirāsādi) kāryāntaravyāpṛtimattvaṃ prakaraṇatvam / taduktam "śāstrai kadeśasaṃbaddha śāstrakāryāntare sthitam / mataṃ prakaraṇaṃ nāma" iti //
body.translated_text:
Now he indicates the disagreements regarding the relation between the individual self (<s>jīva</s>) and the Supreme, [beginning with] 'tathā ātma' and so forth. He states the position of the <s>Advaitins</s> with 'anādī' and so forth. Their intention is: because the difference [between the individual and the Supreme] is based on <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), the relation of controller and controlled pertains only to conventional reality (<s>vyāvahārika</s>), not to ultimate reality (<s>paramārtha</s>). With the intention of the reflection-theory (<s>pratibimbapakṣa</s>), he says 'vyatireke' and so forth. The sense is: even though there is no difference from the original (<s>bimba</s>), there is a distinguishing excess in the reflections (<s>pratibimba</s>) characterized by being objects of the apprehension of difference and the like. He states the position of <s>Bhāskara</s> with 'svataḥ' and so forth. Non-difference is in essential nature; difference is adventitious (<s>aupādhika</s>). The intention is: because both difference and non-difference, being contradictory, are impossible in the bare essential nature alone. He states the position of <s>Yādavaprakāśa</s> with 'nānātva' and so forth. The construction 'characterized by the relation of part and whole (<s>aṃśāṃśibhāva</s>)' connects with 'thus is the relation.' Because of the part-whole relation, both difference and non-difference are explicable. Their core position is: the co-referentiality (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) itself, which is the identity of the non-difference co-located with difference, has the meaning of co-referentiality. The siddhāntin's (proponent's) position is [stated with] 'samavāya' and so forth. Because various relations are accepted between the <s>jīva</s> and the Supreme in the established doctrine, various relations are mentioned. It is also possible that 'characterized by the part-whole relation' is the siddhāntin's own position. Dependence (<s>paratantratā</s>) and inseparability (<s>apṛthaksiddhi</s>) — the <s>samavāya</s> (inherence) that has that nature, but not an additional [relation] as in the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> doctrine — this is the sense. <s>Śeṣatva</s> (subordination) is having a nature whose form is fashioned by the will to bestow excellence upon another. <s>Svatva</s> (being property) is worthiness of being disposed of as [the owner] wishes. <s>Bhṛtyatva</s> (servanthood) is being a conscious being that is directed. The distinction [is thus]. And one should understand that <s>śeṣitva</s> (being the principal) and the like are defined as being the correlates of these respectively. '<s>Bhṛtyasvāmī</s>' (servant-master) is a designation with prominence on the abstract state, meaning: having the nature of servanthood and masterhood. Or such a reading may be supposed.
Now he states the disagreements regarding the nature of liberation with 'tathā parame' and so forth. 'Characterized by the attainment of <s>Brahman</s>' is the proponent's own view, intended to indicate that the forms of liberation maintained by opponents are unfit to be the ultimate human goal (<s>puruṣārtha</s>). The position of the <s>Cārvākas</s> and the <s>Śūnyavādins</s> is the annihilation of one's own nature. The position of the <s>Yogācāras</s> or the <s>Māyāvādins</s> is the second [alternative]. The position of <s>Kaṇāda</s> and others is the third. '<s>Viśeṣa</s>' here means specifically the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> [position]. The position of <s>Sāṅkhya</s> is the fourth. 'Characterized by the similarity of its state' would be the <s>Advaitins</s>' [position]. The word 'tat' refers to <s>Brahman</s>. Liberation is precisely the state of <s>Brahman</s>, as similarity — this is [their view]. Or alternatively, the three terms [may] refer to the difference in liberation characterized by: attainment of similarity to <s>Brahman</s>'s form, attainment of <s>Brahman</s>'s qualities, and attainment of <s>Brahman</s>'s splendor. 'Sāṃsiddhike' is the view of the <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s> and others. 'Tadguṇe' and so forth is the siddhāntin's [view]. The manifestation of one's own essential nature is also implied here. <s>Kiṅkaratva</s> (servitude) means the performance of service.
Regarding the means to liberation too, he states those [disagreements] with 'tatsādhanato 'pi' and so forth. The position of the combination of action and knowledge (<s>karmaajñānasamuccaya</s>) belongs to <s>Yādavaprakāśa</s>. 'Ubhaye' is the siddhāntin's position: supreme devotion (<s>parabhakti</s>), which is <s>bhaktiyoga</s>, arises for one whose mind has been purified through <s>karmayoga</s> and <s>jñānayoga</s>. That [devotion] alone, having <s>karma</s>, <s>jñāna</s>, and the like as its auxiliaries, is the means to liberation characterized by the attainment of the Supreme <s>Brahman</s>. Its exclusivity (<s>aikāntikatva</s>) means having the <s>Bhagavān</s> alone as its object. Its perpetuity (<s>ātyantkatva</s>) means uninterruptedness. The sense is: supreme knowledge (<s>parajñāna</s>) and supreme devotion (<s>paramabhakti</s>) have the nature of being the result of this [combined practice].
He justifies the utility of displaying the disagreements for the commencement of investigation with 'tadevaṃ' and so forth. The overall purport is: until the inquirers ascertain the specific distinguishing feature — namely being grounded in valid means of knowledge and reasoning (<s>satpramāṇatarkamūlakatva</s>) — in any one of the positions amid the variety of disagreements, the doubt regarding the truth does not cease. And as long as the said distinguishing feature is not ascertained, the determination of the strength of the concomitance (<s>vyāpti</s>) and the presence of the property in the subject (<s>pakṣadharmatā</s>) in the respective proofs cannot be made. And there cannot be genuine concomitance and subject-property-hood for contradictory proofs of what is to be proved in a single subject. Accordingly, when the proofs of various positions are perceived as equally strong, the determination of what is to be proved is difficult due to their being matched by counter-proofs (<s>satpratipakṣa</s>). And liberation does not come from mere doubt about the truth. Therefore, when the difference of positions is at hand, investigation — into where the real distinguishing feature lies — has found its occasion. When, through investigation, the distinguishing feature is ascertained in one position, then from the knowledge of the superior strength of that position's proof, the status of being matched by counter-proofs ceases, and thereby the determination of the truth of the matter is explained. Thus, for the determination of the truth of the matter — which is useful for the means to liberation — concerning the self's essential nature and the like, the commencement of an investigative treatise aimed at establishing the distinguishing feature of being grounded in valid means of knowledge and reasoning in one position is entirely justified — this is the collective purport.
[Objection:] For the removal of the various disagreements regarding the self and the Supreme Self, the works of the earlier teachers should themselves be employed. What need is there for the enterprise of composing a new work? — anticipating this objection, he says 'yadyapi' and so forth. 'These very' — 'for the determination of the truth of the self, the Supreme Self, their relation and the like' — 'the <s>sūtras</s>' [means] the <s>Brahmasūtras</s> (the aphorisms of <s>Brahmamīmāṃsā</s>). That these alone are the primary <s>sūtras</s> is stated in the <s>Skāndapurāṇa</s>: 'The <s>Brahmasūtra</s> has unqualified sūtra-hood; the knowledgeable know that the other sūtras are qualified. The term [sūtra] applies to the primary [text] without qualification, and to the others with qualification — so say the knowers of the <s>Veda</s> who understand the meaning of the term.' 'Vivṛtāni' (expounded): 'limited-ness' means brevity of words; 'profundity' means being endowed with depth of meaning. The author of the <s>Dramiḍabhāṣya</s> is the one known as <s>Dramiḍācārya</s>, the commentator on [the work called] <s>Vākya</s> — the exposition of the <s>Chāndogya</s> [Upaniṣad] — composed by <s>Ṭaṅkācārya</s>, also known as <s>Brahmanandi</s>. That he also composed a commentary on the <s>Brahmasūtras</s> is understood from the compendium of <s>Śrīsūkti</s>. 'Vistṛtāni ca' (and elaborated): 'those' [refers to] the sentences of <s>Dramiḍācārya</s>'s commentary on the <s>Brahmasūtras</s>. The supplement is: 'in the commentary text (<s>vivaraṇagrantha</s>).' Or [it may refer to] those <s>Brahmasūtras</s> [themselves]. In the <s>Viṣṇucittīya</s>, the commentary on the <s>Śrīviṣṇupurāṇa</s>, sentences from the <s>Vivaraṇa</s> are cited. 'Tathāpi' (nevertheless) — this is the sense: Although in the works of the earlier teachers the metaphysical truth is indeed expounded with full apparatus, nevertheless, since various doctrines have been propagated by later [thinkers] under the pretext of commenting on the <s>Brahmamīmāṃsā</s> and the like, and since until the grounds for their invalidity are ascertained, faith in those works can arise just as in the texts of the established doctrine, and since people whose understanding is shaken by the abundance of disagreements in those [works] cannot straightforwardly attain knowledge of the truth — therefore, the commencement of a chapter devoted to examining those various doctrines, which serves to discriminate between the essential and the non-essential in those doctrines, is indeed necessary. Among those mentioned — <s>Ṭaṅka</s> and others — some are siddhāntins (proponents of the established doctrine), while others may be followers of other doctrines. And the 'being white or black' (<s>sitāsitatva</s>) in their works should be understood contextually as either unclear exposition or contrary exposition. Or alternatively, <s>Ṭaṅka</s> and <s>Śrīvatsāṅka</s> mentioned here may be adherents of other doctrines, different from the authors of the <s>Vākya</s> and <s>Vivaraṇa</s>. And the designation '<s>Ṭaṅka</s>' for the author of the <s>Vākya</s> is understood from the commentary on the <s>Vedārthasaṅgraha</s>. 'Tatpratipattaye ca' (and for the understanding of that): some understand the truth of the matter unclearly; others, being faithful to the texts of other doctrines for whatever reason, and therefore having their understanding led astray, comprehend it otherwise — so for clear understanding and for understanding the white-or-black nature of other works, the commencement of this chapter is indeed justified — this is the purport. And the core [point is that] this chapter — namely the <s>Ātmasiddhi</s> and the like — is a subsidiary text (<s>prakaraṇa</s>) of the works of the earlier teachers that have the nature of <s>śāstra</s>. And this chapter is [a subsidiary] of the <s>Śārīrakamīmāṃsā</s> and of the <s>Nyāyatattvashāstra</s> (the science of logical truth). The nature of being a subsidiary text (<s>prakaraṇatva</s>) consists in: while being devoted to expounding one part of the <s>śāstra</s>, also being engaged in other tasks of the <s>śāstra</s> that are useful for understanding its meaning (such as the refutation of opposing doctrines). As stated: 'What is connected with one part of the <s>śāstra</s> and is situated in another task of the <s>śāstra</s> — that is known as a <s>prakaraṇa</s> (subsidiary text).'

body.text: prathamaṃ tāvadātmatattvamupavarṇayati 'tatre'ti / 'deha' iti / nirūpaṇīyatayopakṣitpeṣu ghaṭakībhūta ātmā dehādito vilakṣaṇaḥ svayaṃprakāśaḥ nityaḥ sūkṣmatayā sarvavyāptikṣamaḥ pratiśarīraṃ bhinnaḥ ānandasvabhāva ityarthaḥ / dhīḥ - viṣayaprakāśakaṃ jñānamātmano dharmabhūtam / tadādhāratvāttadvilakṣaṇatvam / ananyena svena sādhanaṃ siddhiḥ prakāśo yasya so 'nanyasādhanaḥ / nityatvamutpattivināśarahitatvam / vyāpītyanenāṇusūkṣmatvaṃ phalitam / svataḥ sukhī - svarūpata evānukūlaprakāśalakṣaṇa sukhavān / sukhasvarūpa iti yāvat / yadvā svābhāvikamānanditvamasya; duḥkhitvaṃ tvaupādhikameveti bhāvaḥ // 3 //
body.translated_text: First, he describes the truth of the self with 'tatra' and so forth. 'Deha' and so forth: the self (<s>ātman</s>), which is the integral [element] among those mentioned as subjects of investigation, is different from the body and the like, self-luminous (<s>svayaṃprakāśa</s>), eternal (<s>nitya</s>), capable of all-pervasiveness due to its subtlety, different in each body, and of the nature of bliss (<s>ānanda</s>) — this is the meaning. <s>Dhī</s> (cognition) is the knowledge that illuminates objects, which is an attribute belonging to the self (<s>dharmabhūta</s>). Because of being its substrate, it is different from it [the cognition]. '<s>Ananyasādhana</s>' means: that whose establishment, [i.e.,] illumination, is accomplished by itself alone, not by another — [i.e.,] self-established. Eternity means being devoid of origination and destruction. 'Vyāpī' (all-pervading) implies being atomic and subtle as its consequence. '<s>Svataḥ sukhī</s>' (inherently blissful) means: possessing by its very nature the bliss characterized by a favorable luminosity. In other words, of the nature of bliss. Or alternatively: it has natural blissfulness; its suffering is merely adventitious (<s>aupādhika</s>) — this is the sense.

body.text: tatra - dehendriyamanaḥprāṇadhībhyo 'nyo 'nanyasādhanaḥ /
body.translated_text: There — [the self is] other than body, senses, mind, vital breath, and cognition; self-established;

body.text: nityo vyāpī pratikṣetramātmā bhinnaḥ svataḥ sukhī // 3 //
body.translated_text: eternal, all-pervading, different in each body — the self (<s>ātman</s>) is inherently blissful.

body.text: nanu dehamevātmānaṃ pratyakṣataḥ pratidyāmahe / ahaṃ jānāmīti jñātā hyātmā ahamiti cakāsti / dehaścāhaṅkāragocaraḥ, sthūlo 'haṃ kṛśo 'hamiti darśanāt / dehasya hi sthaulyādiyogaḥ / atastatsamānādhikaraṇatayāyamahaṅkāraḥ śarīrālambana ityavaśyāśrayaṇīyam / itarathā sakalalaukikaparīkṣakavyavahāroparodhaśca / na cāyaṃ lākṣaṇiko vyavahāraḥ, mukhyavṛttibhūmeḥ pṛthagasiddhatvāt / na cānekāvayavayogiśarīrālambanatve jñātravabhāsasya tadīyarūpāvayavādyavabhāsenānvayinā bhavitavyam, yena tadanvayābhāvāt jānāmīti pratyayaḥ śarīrātiriktamavagamayet / bāhyendriyapratyakṣa eva tathā niyamadarśanāt / svānta syā'ntaraguṇādhāratāvabhāsa eva sāmarthyaniyamāt / anavadhṛtāvayavaviśeṣasyāpyanekāvayavayogino mahimaguṇaśālinaḥ tryaṇukasya prathamapratyakṣābhyupagamāt / vāyośca tvagindriyeṇa sparśādhiṣṭhānamātratayopalambhadarśanācca / dehavyatiriktātmagocaratve 'pi yathā tadīyaguṇāntarāgrahaṇam, tathehāpi / yathā tatra bāhyapratyakṣagocara eva saṅkyāparimāṇādigrahaṇaniyamaḥ /
body.translated_text: [Objection:] But we directly perceive the body itself as the self through perception. For the self is the knower, as [indicated by] 'I know,' and it shines forth as 'I.' And the body is the object of the I-cognition (<s>ahaṅkāra</s>), as seen [from usages] like 'I am stout' and 'I am thin.' For it is the body that possesses stoutness and the like. Therefore, because of co-referentiality (<s>samānādhikaraṇatā</s>) with it, this I-cognition must necessarily be accepted as having the body as its basis (<s>śarīrālambana</s>). Otherwise, the conduct of all worldly people and investigators would be obstructed. Nor is this a secondary usage (<s>lākṣaṇika vyavahāra</s>), because the ground for the primary meaning (<s>mukhyavṛtti</s>) has not been independently established. Nor, when the body — which possesses many parts — is the basis [of I-cognition], need the appearance of the knower be accompanied by the appearance of its constituent forms, parts, and the like — such that, from the absence of such accompaniment, the cognition 'I know' would indicate something beyond the body. For in external sense-perception itself, such a restriction [that the substratum must appear with all its parts] is observed. The restriction of the internal [cognition's] capacity is confined to the appearance of being the substrate of inner qualities alone. [Consider also that] the first perception of a <s>tryaṇuka</s> (tri-atomic molecule) — which possesses many parts whose individual details are not ascertained, and which bears the quality of magnitude — is accepted [even without apprehending all parts]. And wind too is observed to be perceived by the tactile sense-organ merely as the seat of touch [without apprehending other features]. Even if the self beyond the body were the object [of I-cognition], just as other qualities of it are not apprehended, so too here [the non-apprehension of certain features does not disprove bodily selfhood]. And just as there, the restriction of apprehending number, measure, and the like [applies] only to external perceptual objects,

children.text: evaṃ ca pratyekaṃ paramāṇuṣu caitanyānupalabdheḥ, tadabhyupagame caikaśarīra evānekasahasracetanāpātāt, akāraṇaguṇapūrvakasya kāryadravyavartino viśeṣaguṇasyāsambhavānna śarīraviśeṣaguṇaścetanyam, ayāvaccharīrabhāvitvāccetyādayo 'numānabedāḥ pratyakṣabādhitaviṣayatayā na parākramituṃ kṣamante / viśeṣaguṇatve ca
