children.translated_text: accordingly, since consciousness is not perceived in each individual atom, and if it were accepted [in each atom], there would be the absurd consequence of many thousands of conscious beings in a single body, and since a specific quality (<s>viśeṣaguṇa</s>) that inheres in an effect-substance cannot arise without being preceded by that quality in the cause — [for these reasons] consciousness is not a specific quality of the body. And [further,] because it does not persist for the entire duration of the body's existence — these and other varieties of inference are not capable of prevailing, since their subject-matter is contradicted by perception. And if [consciousness were] a specific quality,

children.text: prītiṣidhyamāne dehaguṇatvābhyu pagamaprasaṅgaśca / api cecchānuvidhāyikriyatvendriyavattvādayaḥ śarīre dṛśyamānāḥ saṃpratipannācaitanyāddhaṭāderatyantavyāvartamānāḥ śarīrameva cetanamavagamayanti / kramukaphalatāmbhūladalāvayavādiṣu pratyekamavidyamānasyāpi rāgasyevāvayavini saṃyogaviśeṣāt, dehārambhakaparamāṇusaṃśleṣaviśeṣādeva dehe caitanyasyāpyāvirbhāvo nānupapannaḥ / carvaṇajanitahutavahasaṃyogasaṃpāditapāṭalimabhiḥ paramāṇubhirdvyaṇukādikrameṇa kāraṇaguṇapūrva eva tatra rāgodaya iti cet; na; pramāṇābhāvāt / api ca sitāsitāditantuṣu pratyekamavidyamānamapi citrarūpaṃ viśeṣaguṇaṃ tadārabdhe paṭe sphaṭamupalabhamānāḥ kathaṃ kāraṇaguṇapūrvakatvamuktaguṇasyādhyavasyema ? / na cāvayarūpātirekeṇāvavini citraṃ nāma rūpāntaraṃ nāstyeva / avayavino 'cākṣuṣatvaprasaṅgāt / avayavarūpaireva tadupapādane sarvameva kāryadravyaṃ nīrūpamāpadyet / anubhavaviredhaḥ, sarvavyavahā
children.translated_text: And if pleasure is denied [as a quality of the self], there would follow the consequence of accepting it as a quality of the body. Moreover, [properties such as] having actions that conform to desire, possessing sense organs, and the like — which are observed in the body and which are absolutely distinct from pots and the like that are acknowledged as non-conscious — indicate that the body itself is conscious. Just as redness, which is not present in each of the individual components such as areca nut, palm leaf, betel leaf, and the like, [manifests] in the composite through a specific combination — so too, the manifestation of consciousness in the body through a specific conjunction of the atoms that constitute the body is not untenable. [Objection:] The redness there arises through atoms whose crimson hue is produced by the conjunction with fire generated by chewing, and through the sequence of dyads and the like — the redness arises preceded by a quality of the cause. [Reply:] No, because there is no evidence [for this]. Moreover, when we clearly observe a variegated form — a specific quality — in a cloth produced from [threads], even though it is not present in each of the white, black, and other threads individually, how could we determine that the said quality is preceded by a quality of the cause? And it is not the case that there is absolutely no form called 'variegated' in the composite beyond the forms of the parts — for there would follow the consequence that the composite is invisible to the eye. If [the variegated form] were to be accounted for by the forms of the parts alone, then every produced substance would become formless. [This would involve] a contradiction with experience, and a contradiction with all conventional practice.

children.text: ravirodhaśca / viśaṣaguṇaśca kāṭhinya karakadravyavarti akāraṇaguṇapūrvakaṃ dṛśyata ityanekāntaśca / na ca saṃyogaviśeṣaḥ kāṭhinyam ; tasya dviṣṭhatvāt ; asya tu karakadravyaikavartitvāt ; sparśaviśeṣatayā padārthavidbhirabhyupagamācca / dṛśyasya dehasya kathaṃ draṣṭṛtvamiti cet ; ko virodhaḥ? / ayameva yadekasyāṃ kriyāṃyāmekasya karmatvaṃ kartṛtvaṃ ca na ghaṭata iti / yadyevam, vyatirekavāde vā kathamātmani ahamiti pratyayaḥ / rūpabhedāditi cet, samānamidaṃ dehātmavāde 'pi / api ca parasamavāyikriyāphalagāmi karma / svasamanetajñānaphalabhāginaḥ śarīrasya karmatvameva nāstīti na paryanuyogāvakāśaḥ / ato deha evātmeti bārhaspatyāḥ / tathāca "
children.translated_text: And hardness, which is a specific quality residing in a single substance such as a bracelet, is observed without being preceded by a quality of the cause — hence [the opponent's position is] inconclusive. And the specific combination [of atoms] is not hardness, because [combination] resides in two [substances], whereas [hardness] resides in a single substance such as the bracelet; and because those who know the categories [of reality] accept it as a specific form of touch. [Objection:] How can the visible body be the seer? [Reply:] What is the contradiction? This is precisely [the point]: that in a single action, one and the same [entity] cannot have both the status of object and agent. [Objection:] If so, even on the view that [the self] is separate, how is the cognition 'I' [directed] at the self? [Reply:] Because of the difference in form — [but] this is equally [applicable] on the view that the body is the self. Moreover, <s>karma</s> (action) is that which partakes of the result of an action that inheres in another. Since the body, which partakes of the result of knowledge that inheres in itself, simply does not have the status of <s>karma</s>, there is no scope for this objection. Therefore, the <s>Barhaspatyas</s> [i.e., the Carvakas/materialists] [hold that] the body itself is the self. And so [it is stated]:

children.text: pṛthivyāpastejo vāyuriti tattvāni, tebhyaścaitanyaṃ, kiṇvādibhyo madaśaktivat
children.translated_text: 'Earth, water, fire, and air — these are the realities (<s>tattvas</s>). From these [arises] consciousness, like the power of intoxication from fermented ingredients (<s>kinva</s>) and the like.'
Thus is the <s>sutra</s>.

body.text: prathamaṃ tāvadātmatattvamupavarṇayati 'tatre'ti / 'deha' iti / nirūpaṇīyatayopakṣipteṣu ghaṭakībhūta ātmā dehādito vilakṣaṇaḥ svayaṃprakāśaḥ nityaḥ sūkṣmatayā sarvavyāptikṣamaḥ pratiśarīraṃ bhinnaḥ ānandasvabhāva ityarthaḥ / dhīḥ - viṣayaprakāśakaṃ jñānamātmano dharmabhūtam / tadādhāratvāttadvilakṣaṇatvam / ananyena svena sādhanaṃ siddhiḥ prakāśo yasya so 'nanyasādhanaḥ / nityatvamutpattivināśarahitatvam / vyāpītyaneneṇasūkṣmatvaṃ phalitam / svataḥ sukhī - svarūpata evānukūlaprakāśalakṣaṇasukhavān / sukhasvarūpa iti yāvat / yadvā svābhāvikamānanditvamasya; duḥkhitvaṃ tvaupādhikameveti bhāvaḥ // 3 //
body.translated_text: First, [the author] describes the reality of the self with [the word] 'tatra' ('in that [context]') and [the word] 'deha' ('body'). The meaning is: among those [realities] introduced as requiring examination, the self — which is a constituent [of the whole] — is distinct from the body and the like, self-luminous, eternal, capable of pervading everything due to its subtlety, different in each body, and of the nature of bliss (<s>ananda</s>). <s>Dhi</s> (cognition) — knowledge that illuminates objects is an essential attribute (<s>dharmabhuta</s>) of the self. Because [the self] is its substrate, it is distinct from it. 'Self-established' (<s>ananyasadhana</s>) means that whose manifestation, i.e., illumination, is accomplished by its own [nature] and by no other. Eternality means the absence of origination and destruction. 'Pervading' — from this, subtlety is the result. 'Inherently blissful' (<s>svatah sukhi</s>) — possessing bliss, characterized as a favorable illumination, by its very nature. That is to say, of the nature of bliss. Or alternatively, this [self] has natural blissfulness; its suffering is merely adventitious (<s>aupadhika</s>) — this is the purport.

body.text:
uktamātmatattvamasahamānaḥ śarīrātmavātī cārvākaḥ pratyavatiṣṭhate 'nanu dehameve'ti / pratyakṣaṃ hi mukhyaṃ pramāṇam / na ca tadatilaṅghanena kaścanārthaḥ sādhayituṃ śakyate / pratyakṣaṃ ca sathaulyādiyoginaṃ dehameva jñātāramahamarthamātmānaṃ pratipādayatīti deha evātmeti bhāvaḥ / dehasyaivāhaṃbuddhiviṣayatvamupapādayati 'dehaśce'tyādivākyadvayena / 'ata' iti / tatsamānādhikaraṇatayā-dehābhinnārthaviṣayakatayā / itthaṃ bhāve tṛtīyā / ayamahaṅkāraḥ - sthūlo 'hamityahapratyayaḥ pratyakṣarūpaḥ / śarīrālambanaḥ - śarīraviṣayakaḥ / śiṣṭaṃ spaṣṭam / pratyakṣātikrame doṣamāha 'itarathe'ti / pratyakṣamūlā hi vyavahārāḥ samupalabhyante paṇḍitapāmarasādhāraṇā arthakriyākārimo mukhyā eva / tadvirodhaḥ pratyakṣātikrame prasajyata ityarthaḥ / nanu 'sthūlo 'haṃ jānāmī'ti pratītirbhrāntireva pāmarāṇām / paṇḍitānāṃ tvaritiktātmagocaraivāhaṃ jānāmīti / ahaṃ sthūla iti tu vyavahāraḥ paṇḍitānāṃ lākṣaṇika ityāśaṅkāmanūdya pratikṣipati 'na cāya'miti / ayaṃ vyavahāro lakṣaṇika ca netyanvayaḥ / vācyamiti śeṣaḥ /
pratikṣepayuktimāha 'mukhye'ti / ahaṃpadaśaktiviṣayasya dehavyatiriktasyānupalambhanirastatvāddeha eva mukhyatvamahampratyayavyavahahārayoriti bhāvaḥ / jānāmyahamiti jñātṛtvapratīterdehagocaratve 'nupapattimāśaṅkate 'na ce' tyādinā / anvayinā - niyatena / sāvayavārthapratyakṣatvavyāpakaṃ tadavayavādiprakāśakatvamiti niyamo neti bhāvaḥ / sati niyame yatprasaktaṃ tadā 'yene'ti / iti sidhyediti śeṣaḥ / tadanvayābhāvāt-śarīrāvayavādiprakāśānvayābhāvāttadaprakāśakatvāccharīrātiriktamevāvagamayedahaṃ jānāmīti / na tu śarīraṃ sāvayavamiti niyamaphalam / jñātṛtvapratyakṣaṃ śarīrāviṣayakam, tadavayavāviṣayakatvāt / yadyadakyaviviṣayaṃ tattadvayavagocaram, yathā ghaṭādi pratyakṣamityatra prayoge niruktaniyamasyopayogaḥ / niruktaniyamasyāsaṃbhave hetumāha
'bāhye'ti / sahacāradṛṣṭerhi niyamavijñānam / sahacāraśca bāhyapratyakṣa eva dṛṣṭa iti tadviṣaya eva niruktaniyama iti bhāvaḥ / nanu bhavatu sahacāradarśanaṃ bāhya eva / niyamastvasaṅkocātpratyakṣamātrāgocaro 'stvityatrāha 'svāntasye'ti / āntaro guṇo jñānasukhādiryogyaḥ / tadādhāratvamātreṇa dharmyavabhāsakatvaṃ manasaḥ / natu dharmāntarasya / bahirasvātatryānmanasaḥ / tathāca rūpasāvayavatvadigrahāsaṃbhavāt manasā jñātṛtvamātreṇa śarīragraha iti pratyakṣasāmānye niyamo nopasaṃhartuṃ śakyata iti bhāvaḥ / bāhyatve 'pi śarīrasya jñānādyuparāgoṇāntaratvamityabhimānaḥ / avayavigocarabāhyapratyakṣatvavyāpakaṃ tadavayavagocaratvamiti niyame 'pi vyabhicāramāha 'anavadhṛte'ti / tryaṇukacākṣuṣe 'tīndriyatvena tadavayavasyāgrahāvdyabhicāra iti bhāvaḥ / anekāvayavayoginaḥ - anekāvayavasamavetasya, svasamavetasamavāyenānekāvayavaviśiṣṭasya / mahimaguṇaśālinaḥ - mahatparimāṇavataḥ / trasareṇupratyakṣānantaraṃ cākṣuṣadravyatvādinā tasya sāvayavatvānumānādupanītadvyaṇukabhānaṃ dvitīyāditryaṇukapratyakṣe saṃbhavatīti vyabhicārasthalaṃ tryaṇukapratyakṣaṃ prathamatvena viśeṣitam / nanu yogyāvayavakāvayavibāhyapratyakṣasya tadavayavagocaratvamiti niyamo 'stviti cettatrāpi taṃ doṣamāha 'vāyośce'ti / sparśavattvamātreṇa vāyuspārśane tadavayavaviṣayakatvābhāvāttatra vyabhicāro niruktaniyamasyeti bhāvaḥ / satyevāvadhāne vāyvavayavādigrahaḥ / anyadā tu tvaksannikṛṣṭasya vāyoḥ sparśavattvenaivopalambha ityabhimānaḥ / ahañjānāmīti pratīte rūpādyaviṣayatvena śarīrāviṣayatvasādhane 'prayojakatvamāha 'dehavyatirikte'ti / jñātṛtvapratīterityādiḥ / tadīyaguṇāntaram - ātmaniṣṭhasaṅkhyādi / 'tathehāpī'tyanantaramupapadyata iti śeṣaḥ / ayaṃ bhāvaḥ - dravyagrāhīndriyasya yogyasannikṛṣṭatadguṇagrāhakatvamiti niyamaḥ / tathā cātiriktātmaṃvāde yathā saṅkyā
dīnāṃ tadguṇānāmayogyatvānna manasā grahaḥ evaṃ dehātmavāde 'pi tadīyarūpāderayogyatvādeva na manasā graha iti / na ca rūpavaddravyapratyakṣe rūpagrahaṇaṃ niyatamiti vācyam / ghaṭādisparśane 'naikāntyān / 'yathā tatre'ti / yathā tatra - atiriktātmavāde bāhyapratyakṣa eva dravyagrāhiṇastadgatasaṅkyādigrāhitvamiti niyamyate, tathā dehātmavāde 'pi niyamyatāmiti bhāvaḥ / 'tathehāpī'ti punaranusandheyam /
evamahaṃ jānāmīti pratyakṣasya dehaviṣayakatvaṃ samarthitam / anena dehacaitanyabādhakānumānānāṃ bādhitatvamāha 'evaṃ ce'ti / caitanyaṃ na śarīraviśeṣaguṇaḥ ākāraṇaguṇapūrvakatatvāt, ayāvaddravyabhāvitvādvā saṃyogavaditi dehacaitanye bādhakamanumānam / tatra prathamahetorasiddhiṃ pariharati 'pratyeka'mityādinā / nanu paramāṇuṣu dehāraṃbhakeṣu caitanyaṃ māstu / yenānekacetanaprasaṅga ekasmin dehe / akāraṇaguṇapūrvakaśca rūpādiḥ pākajo dṛṣṭaḥ / tadvadbhavatu caitanyamityatrāha 'kāryadravye'ti / pīlupāko 'trābhimataḥ / tathā ca kāryadravyaviśeṣaguṇatvavyāpakaṃ svasamavāyisamavāyivṛttisajātīyaguṇāsamavāyikāraṇakatvarūpaṃ kāraṇaguṇapūrvakatvam / vyāpakanivṛttyā ca caitanye śarīraviśeṣaguṇatvasya nivṛttiriti bhāvaḥ / dvitīyānumāne ca yo yaḥ kāryadravyaviśeṣaguṇaḥ sa sa yāvaddravyabhāvīti sāmānyato vyatirekavyāptiḥ pīlupākanayena vācyā / 'ityādaya' ityādipadena caitanyaṃ na dehasya viśeṣaguṇaḥ tanniṣṭhaviśeṣaguṇāntaravaidharmyādityanumānaṃ grāhyam / na parākramituṃ kṣamantedehacaitanyaṃ bādhituṃ na pragalbhante / kutaḥ ? pratyakṣabādhitaviṣayatayā / pratyakṣabādhena niruktānumānānāmeva nodayaḥ
saṃbhavati / prabala upajīvyatvena pratyakṣapramāṇabādhanaṃ ca durbalairetairanumānanairduṣkaramiti bhāvaḥ / ayāvaddravyabhāvināmakāraṇaguṇapūrvakāṇāmapi saṃyogādīnāṃ śarīraguṇatvadṛṣṭerniruktahetubhirapi caitanye śarīraguṇatvasyābhāvo na sādhayituṃ śakyata ityāśayenāha 'viśeṣe'ti / śarīra evopambhāccaitanyaṃ tadguṇa eva / niruktahetubhistadviśeṣaguṇatvaniṣedhane 'pi na kṣatiḥ / paribhāṣikaṃ hi viśeṣaguṇatvam / bhāvanānyo yo vāyuvṛttivṛttidharmasamavāyī tadanyatve sati gurutvājaladravatvānyaguṇatvaṃ viśeṣaguṇatvamityatra garutvādereva jñānāderapyanyatvaṃ prakṣipyatāmiti bhāvaḥ / akāraṇaguṇapūrvakatvādihetūnāmaprayojakatvāccharīraviśeṣaguṇatve 'pi jñānārdane kṣatirityabhiprayannāha 'api cecche'ti / śarīraviśeṣaguṇāntaravaidharmyājjñānasyāśarīraviśeṣagutvaṃ cediṣyate, tarhi saṃpratipannācetanaghaṭādividharmatvāddehasya caitanyavattvameva kuto neṣyate lāghavāditi bhāvaḥ / indriyavāttvādaya ityādipadena prāṇavattvaṃ grāhyam / icchānuvidhāyikriyatvaṃ - sākṣādicchādhīnapravṛttimattvaṃ dehasya / ghaṭādestu dehavyāpāradvārakameva taditi bhāvaḥ / śarīraṃ cetanāvat icchānuvidhāyikriyatvādindriyādimattvādvā yannaiva tannaivaṃ yathā
ghaṭādīti vyatirekānumānaṃ ca dehasya caitanye 'tra vākye garbhitam / kāryadravyaviśeṣaguṇatvasya kāraṇaguṇapūrvakatvavyāptāvanaikāntyamapyāha 'kramuke'ti / kramukaphalasaṃmiśricūrṇakopaliptatāmbūlapatrasya dantasaṅghaṭṭanaiḥ pūrvāvayavavināśe tadavayavānāṃ saṃśleṣaviśeṣato niṣpanne piṇḍitāvayavini raktaṃ rūpamavayaveṣvavidyamānaṃ saṃśleṣaviśeṣata eva teṣāmutpannamiti tatra vyabhicāra iti bhāvaḥ / ākṣipati 'carvaṇe'ti / dantasaṃmardaiḥ pūrvāvayavino vdyuṇukaparyantasya nāśe paramāṇuṣu svatantreṣu carvaṇodbhūtamukhyāgnisaṃyogalakṣaṇapākavaśādraktarūpasyotpatteḥ kāraṇaguṇapūrvakameva piṇḍitāvayavini raktaṃ rūpamiti na vyabhicāra iti bhāva ākṣeptuḥ / pariharati 'na pramāṇābhāva'diti / saṃśleṣaviśeṣasyaiva kvacidrūpāntaraprayojanakatvameṣṭavyam / yathā haridrācūrṇe cūrṇakajalasaṃyogenaiva hi raktaṃ rūpaṃ dṛṣṭam / tathātrāpi saṃbhavāt pākakalpanāyāṃ mānābhāva
iti bhāvaḥ / carvaṇasthale pīlupākenaiva rūpāntaramityāgrahe 'pi sthalāntare vyabhicāramāha 'sitāsite'ti / na hi citrapaṭasthale 'vayaveṣu pākasaṃbhavaḥ / na cāvayaveṣu citraṃ rūpam / tathā cacāvayaviviśeṣaguṇasya svasajātīyāvayavaguṇapūrvakatvamiti niyamasya citrarūpe 'naikāntyamiti bhāvaḥ / sājātyaṃ rūpatvādyavāntarajātyā vivakṣitam / na hi nīlatantubhiḥ śuklapaṭāraṃbhaḥ / rūpatvādinā sājātyavivakṣāyāṃ tu tasyāpi prasaṅga iti / nanu citraṃ nāma rūpāntaraṃ neṣyate / na caivaṃ nānārūpatantubhirārabdhaścintrapaṭo nīrūpaḥ syāt / rūpādervyāpyavṛttitvaniyamādavyāpyavṛttinānārūpavattvasya satminnupagamāsaṃbhavāditi vācyam / avayavarūpeṇaiva cākṣuṣatvopapattau citrapaṭasya nīrūpatve 'pi kṣativirahāt / samavāyasvasamavāyisamavetatvānyatarasaṃbandhenodbhūtarūpasya dravyacākṣuṣe hetutvopagamāditi cedatrāha 'sarvameve'ti / evamavayavarūpeṇaiva cākṣaṣopapatteḥ sarvasyāpyavayavino rūpavattavaṃ neṣyatāmityarthaḥ / iṣyata evameva lāghavādityatrāha 'anubhave'ti / sākṣādrūpavattvopalambhavyavahārayorabādhitayoḥ sattvādiṣṭāpattirnīrūpatve 'vayavinaḥ kartuṃ na śakyata ityarthaḥ / citraḥ paṭa iti cābādhitapratītivyavahārataśritraṃ rūpamapyeṣṭavyayamiti bhāvaḥ / nanvayavanānārūpairavyāpyavṛttyeva nānārūpaṃ citrapaṭa upeyate pratītibalāt / tathā ca na tatra vyabhicāra ityatrāha - 'viśeṣaguṇaśce'ti / jalīyasya karakasyāvayavasaṃśleṣaviśeṣādārambhakasahakārivaicitryācca dravatvarahitasya kaṭhinasparśa upalabhyamāno na kāraṇaguṇapūrvakaḥ / jalaparamāṇuṣukaṭhinasparśasyābhāvāt / tathā ca karakasparśe kāraṇaguṇapūrvakatvaniyamasya vyabhicāra iti bhāvaḥ / nanvavayavasaṃyogaviśeṣa evāstu kāṭhinyam / tathā ca kkānaikāntyamityatrāha 'na ca saṃyoge'ti / avayavasaṃyogaviśeṣasya kāṭhinyarūpatve tasyāvayavinyavṛtteḥ kaṭhinaḥ karaka iti pratītivyavahārau na syātām / kathañcittadupapādane 'pi cākṣuṣadravyavṛttisaṃyogasya cākṣuṣatvātkāṭhinyasya cakṣuṣāpyupalaṃbhaprasaṅga iti bhāvaḥ / 'sparśaviśeṣataye'ti / tvaṅbhātragrāhyaguṇatvātkāṭhinyaṃ sparśaviśeṣa
eveti sāmpratam / padārthavidbhiḥ kāṇādaiḥ sparśaviśeṣatayaiva ca tadabhyupagatamiti bhāvaḥ /
dehātmavāde kartṛkarmabhāvavirodhamāśaṅkya pariharati - 'dṛśyasye'tyādinā / 'ko viredha' iti / viruddhārthe hi kathantā / draṣṭurdṛśyatve 'virodhātkā nāma kathanteti bhāvaḥ / virodhamāha 'ayameve'ti / tatkriyāyāṃ tadaiva kasyacitkartṛtvaṃ karmatvaṃ ca na yuktam / kriyayā āptumiṣṭatamaṃ hi karma sādhyarūpam / kriyāśrayaḥ karttā ca siddharūpaḥ / siddhasādhyayornaikyaṃ saṃbhavatīti virodhaḥ kartṛkarmatvayoriti bhāvaḥ / ākṣepturmukhenaiva samādhiṃ vācayituṃ pratibandīmāha 'yadyeva'miti / samādhimāhākṣeptā 'rūpabhedā'diti / samādhitaulyamuttaramāha dehātmavādī 'samāna'miti / yathā ātariktātmavāde 'hantvādinā karmatvam, manaḥsaṃyogattvādinā ca kartṛtvaṃ jñānakriyāyāmityākārabhedādavirodha ucyate, tannyāyasya na dehātmavāde daṇḍanivāraṇamiti bhāvaḥ / vastuto yādṛśasya karmatvasya kartṛtvena virodhaḥ, na tādṛśaṃ jñānakarmatvam / ato 'pi na doṣa ityāha - 'api ca pare'ti / 'svasamavetajñānaphalabhāgini' iti / svaniṣṭhajñānanirūpitaviṣayatāvata ityarthaḥ / viṣayatāyā viṣayinirūpyatvāt jñānaphalatvopacāraḥ / 'karmatvameva nāstī'ti / mukhyaṃ karmatvaṃ nāstītyarthaḥ / ayaṃ bhāvaḥ - parasamavetakriyājanmaphalāśrayatvaṃ mukhyaṃ karmatvam / yathā grāmasya gamanakarmatvam / viṣayaviṣayibhāvalakṣaṇamamukhyameva tu jñānādikarmatvam / saviṣayārthadhātuyoge karmatvaṃ viṣayatārūpamiti hi tārkikāṇāṃ samayaḥ / asya jñānakartaryapyupagamānnātmānaṃ jānātītyāderanupapattiḥ / mukhyasyaiva
tu kartṛtvena virodha iti / nacāmukhyamidaṃ karmatvaṃ nānuśāsanasiddhamiti vācyam / 'karturīpsitatamaṃ karme'tyasyaiva tantreṇāsminnapi pramāṇatvopagamāt / kartuḥ jñātuḥ, kriyayā-jñānena, āptumiṣṭatamaṃ - jñātavyatvenābhimataṃ karmeti cātra pakṣe 'kṣarārtho vācyaḥ / aniṣṭasya jñātasya tu 'tathā yuktaṃ cānīpsita'mityanenaiva kriyāyuktaṃ - jñānena viṣayatayā saṃbaddhaṃ anīpsitaṃ jñeya
tvenecchāviṣayabhūtamapi karmeti cārtho 'mukhyakarmatvapakṣe / vyavahārasya jñānaphasatve 'pi tadāśrayatvābhāvānna viṣayasya mukhyaṃ karmatvam / ātmanaḥ svavyavahārāśrayatve 'pi taddhetusvagocarasvaniṣṭhajñānasya na parasamavetatvamiti na tat / vyavahārānuguṇyalakṣaṇajñānaphalavivakṣāyāṃ tu viṣayasya ghaṭāderjñānakarmatvaṃ mukhyaṃ syānnāma / adhikamarge vakṣyāmaḥ / samarthitaṃ dehātmatvaṃ nigamayati 'ata' iti / bārhaspatyāḥ - bṛhaspatipraṇītalokāyatatantraniṣṭhāścārvākāḥ / aiśvaryamahimakṣayāyāsurāṇāṃ vaidikaścaddhāvilopakaṃ mohakaṃ tantraṃ nirmitaṃ suraguruṇāsurendrānunayavivaśeneti ca prasiddhiḥ / dehasyaiva caitanye tatsūtraṃ pramāṇayati 'tathā ce'ti / pṛthivyādīti catvāryeva bhūtāni tattvāni / taiḥ saṃhatya niṣpādite dehe pratyekamasadapi caitanyamudbhavati / kiṇvādibhyo niṣpādite surādravya ivāpūrvā madaśaktiriti sūtrārthaḥ /

children.translated_text: Here [is] the counter-argument: the body is not the self, because of the contradiction from direct perception.
Indeed, the 'I'-cognition and the 'this'-cognition do not belong to one and the same person regarding one and the same object.

children.text: ahaṃ jānāmīti pratyagūvṛttirahamiti matiridaṅkāragocarāccharīrānnīṣkṛṣṭameva svaviṣayamupasthāpayati / ghaṭāderiva / parāgvṛttiridamiti śarīraviṣayiṇī ca śemuṣī svaviṣayamahaṅkāragocarādvivecayati yathāyaṃ ghaṭa iti / itarathā svaparavibhāgānupapatteḥ / na caikasminneva rūpabhedādevaṃ pratītiḥ / na hi devadatto daṇḍinamātmānaṃ daṇḍyayamiti pratyeti /
children.translated_text: The inward-directed cognition (<s>pratyagvrtti</s>) — 'I know' — the cognition 'I' — presents its own object as extracted [i.e., distinguished] from the body, which is the domain of the 'this'-cognition, just as [it distinguishes it] from a pot and the like. And the outward-directed cognition (<s>paragvrtti</s>) — 'this' — which has the body as its object, distinguishes its own object from the domain of the 'I'-cognition, just as in 'this is a pot.' Otherwise, the distinction between self and other would be untenable. And it is not the case that such cognition [arises] regarding one and the same thing merely due to a difference of form. For <s>Devadatta</s> does not cognize himself, who carries a stick, as 'this one to be beaten with a stick.'

children.text: anyacca, niyamitabahirindriyavṛtteravahitamanaso 'hamiti svātmānamavayataḥ karacaraṇodarādyavayavā na bhāsante / svathīyasi cāvayavini śarīre 'hamiti matigocare 'bhyupagabhyamāne 'vaśyamavayavapratibhāsenāpyanvayinā bhāṣyam / na hyāsti saṃbhavaḥ - avayavī sthavīyān pracakāsti ; avayavāstu na kecana prathanta iti / yattu tryaṇuke vyabhicāra iti ; tanna / vātāyanavivaradṛśyani
children.translated_text: Moreover, when the external sense organs are restrained and the mind is concentrated, one who cognizes one's own self as 'I' — the parts such as hands, feet, belly, and the like do not appear [in that cognition]. And if the body, which is a composite possessing parts, is accepted as the domain of the 'I'-cognition, then it must necessarily be accompanied by the appearance of its parts too. For there is no possibility of this: 'the composite, being gross, shines forth; but none of its parts are manifest.' As for the [alleged] counter-example in the <s>tryaṇuka</s> (triad of atoms) — that is not [valid], because in the absence of accepting atoms as distinct from the visible rays of dust seen through a window aperture, there is no ground [for it].

body.translated_text:
The <s>Cārvāka</s>, who is a proponent of the body-is-the-self view and cannot tolerate the stated reality of the self, objects: 'But it is the body alone.' For perception is the primary means of valid cognition, and no object can be established by transgressing it. And perception presents the body alone — which possesses corpulence and the like — as the knower, the referent of 'I,' and the self. Thus the purport is: the body alone is the self. He establishes that the body alone is the object of the 'I'-cognition with the pair of sentences beginning with 'dehaś ca' and so on. 'Ataḥ' means: by virtue of co-referentiality (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) — that is, by having as its object something non-different from the body. The instrumental case [in the original] is in the sense of 'in this manner.' This <s>ahaṅkāra</s> (ego-sense) — namely, the 'I'-cognition in the form 'I am stout' — is of the nature of perception. It has the body as its support — that is, the body as its object. The rest is clear. He states the fault in transgressing perception with 'itarathe' and so on. For conventions rooted in perception are observed [to be] common to both the learned and the unlearned, primary in effecting purposeful action (<s>arthakriyā</s>). The meaning is: conflict with that [perception] would absurdly follow upon its transgression. [Objection:] But the cognition 'I am stout, I know' is merely an error of the unlearned; for the learned, the cognition 'I know' has as its object the self that is distinct [from the body]; and the convention 'I am stout' is, for the learned, secondary (<s>lākṣaṇika</s>). Having stated this doubt, he rejects it with 'na cāyam' and so on. The construction is: this convention is not to be called secondary. He states the reason for rejection with 'mukhye' and so on. The purport is: since what is the proper referent of the word 'I' — [namely,] something distinct from the body — is negated by non-apprehension, the body alone has primacy in both the 'I'-cognition and the [corresponding] convention. He raises the difficulty of the cognition of knower-ship 'I know' having the body as its object, with 'na ca' and so on. 'Anvayin' means: invariable. The purport is: the rule that the perception of a composite object is pervaded by the illumination of its parts and the like does not hold. If the rule held, then what would follow is [stated with] 'yena' and so on. The remainder is: 'thus it would be established.' Because of the absence of such invariable concomitance — because of the absence of the concomitant illumination of the body's parts and the like, and because of [the perception] not illuminating them — [such a perception] would make known something distinct from the body alone, [via the cognition] 'I know.' But [in fact] the result of the rule is not that the body is composite. The perception of knower-ship does not have the body as its object, because it does not have the body's parts as its object. [The rule:] whatever has [something's] parts as its objects also has [that thing's] parts within its scope — as in the case of the perception of a pot and the like — here in this application, the stated rule is useful. He states the reason for the impossibility of the stated rule with 'bāhye' and so on. For the knowledge of the rule comes from observing co-occurrence (<s>sahacāra</s>). And co-occurrence is observed only in external perception — hence the stated rule applies only to that [external perception]. The purport is this. [Objection:] Let co-occurrence be observed only in external [perception]; but the rule, being unrestricted, should apply to perception in general. To this he replies with 'svāntasya' and so on. The internal quality — knowledge, pleasure, and the like — is fit [to be apprehended by the mind]. The mind's capacity to make the substratum (<s>dharmin</s>) manifest is only by virtue of being the locus of that [quality], not of any other property — because the mind lacks independence with respect to external [properties]. And thus, since the apprehension of form, compositeness, direction, and the like is impossible through the mind, the apprehension of the body through the mind is by knower-ship alone — hence the rule cannot be extended to perception in general. The purport is this. [Regarding the view that] even though the body is external, it is internal due to being affected by knowledge and the like — this is [mere] presumption. Even granting the rule that the perception of a composite external object is pervaded by [apprehension of] its parts, he states a counter-example with 'anavadhṛte' and so on. The purport is: in the visual [perception] of a triad-atom (<s>tryaṇuka</s>), since its parts are beyond the senses, there is deviation [from the rule] because the parts are not grasped. 'Of what possesses many parts' means: of what inheres in many parts, [or] of what is qualified by many parts through the relation of inherence in what inheres in it. 'Possessing the quality of greatness' means: having a large magnitude. Since, immediately after the perception of a triad-atom, the appearance of a dyad — derived through inference by [the rule that] what is a visible substance and the like must be composite — is possible in the perception of the second and subsequent triad-atoms, the perception of the triad-atom is specified as the first [instance] of the counter-example. [Objection:] Let the rule be: for the external perception of a composite having fit parts, there is [also] apprehension of its parts. Even to this, he states the fault with 'vāyoś ca' and so on. The purport is: since wind is apprehended by touch through [the property of] being touch-possessing alone, without [apprehension of] its parts being the object, there is deviation from the stated rule in that case. [It is held that] the apprehension of the parts of wind and the like occurs only when attention is [specifically directed]; otherwise, wind, being in contact with the skin, is apprehended solely as possessing touch. He states that the non-objecthood of the body in the cognition 'I know,' [even if established] through the non-objecthood of form and the like, serves no purpose, with 'dehavyatirikte' and so on. The cognition of knower-ship and so on [is the subject]. 'Its other quality' means: number and the like that inhere in the self. The remainder is: 'tathehāpi' ('so here too') applies after this. The purport is this: the rule is that a sense-organ that apprehends a substance also apprehends the qualities [of that substance] with which it is fitly connected. And thus, in the view of a distinct self, just as number and the like — qualities of that [self] — are not grasped by the mind because of unfitness, so too in the body-is-the-self view, form and the like of that [body] are not grasped by the mind precisely because of unfitness. Nor should it be said that in the perception of a substance possessing form, the apprehension of form is invariable — because of inconclusiveness in the case of touching a pot and the like. 'Yathā tatra' means: just as, in the view of a distinct self, it is restricted that only in external perception does the substance-apprehending [sense] also apprehend the number and the like belonging to it — so too let it be restricted in the body-is-the-self view. The purport is this. 'Tathehāpi' should be connected again.
Thus it has been argued that the perception 'I know' has the body as its object. By this, he states that the inferences that would refute the consciousness of the body are themselves refuted, with 'evaṃ ca' and so on. [The inference:] Consciousness is not a particular quality of the body, because it is not preceded by a quality of the cause, or because it does not last as long as the substance — like conjunction. This is the inference that would refute body-consciousness. Regarding the first reason, he resolves the unestablishedness with 'pratyekam' and so on. [Objection:] Let consciousness not exist in the individual atoms that constitute the body, lest there be the absurd consequence of many conscious beings in a single body. And color and the like that arise from baking (<s>pāka</s>) are observed to be not preceded by a quality of the cause. Let consciousness be like that. To this he replies with 'kāryadravye' and so on. The <s>pīlupāka</s> (atomic baking) [theory] is intended here. And thus, being preceded by a quality of the cause — in the form of being the non-inherent cause of a quality of the same kind residing in what inheres in what inheres in oneself — pervades [the property of] being a particular quality of the product-substance. And through the cessation of the pervader, the cessation of [the claim that consciousness is] a particular quality of the body [follows]. This is the purport. And in the second inference too, the general negative concomitance — that whatever is a particular quality of a product-substance lasts as long as the substance — should be stated according to the <s>pīlupāka</s> method. The 'ādi' in 'ityādayaḥ' includes the inference: consciousness is not a particular quality of the body, because of its dissimilarity from other particular qualities inhering in it. [These inferences] are unable to prevail — they are not bold enough to refute body-consciousness. Why? Because their subject-matter is contradicted by perception. Since the stated inferences simply cannot arise when contradicted by perception, and since it is difficult for these weak inferences to override perception, which is the stronger and more fundamental <s>pramāṇa</s>. This is the purport. Since conjunction and the like — which do not last as long as the substance and are not preceded by a quality of the cause — are also observed to be qualities of the body, even by the stated reasons the absence of body-quality-hood in consciousness cannot be established — with this intent he says 'viśeṣe' and so on. Since consciousness is observed only in the body, it is a quality of the body alone. Even if the stated reasons negate its being a 'particular quality' (<s>viśeṣaguṇa</s>) [in the technical sense], there is no loss. For 'particular quality' is a technical term: a quality — other than heaviness, fluidity of water, and other [listed] qualities — that inheres in what inheres in an entity other than the inherence-base of that [entity's qualities], while being different [from those listed qualities], is a 'particular quality.' [The suggestion is:] let the otherness of knowledge and the like, just like that of heaviness and the like, be included [in the list]. This is the purport. Since the stated reasons such as not being preceded by a quality of the cause are ineffective, [consciousness] being a quality of the body — even if a particular quality — causes no harm. Intending this, he says 'api ca icchet' and so on. If it is desired that consciousness is not a particular quality of the body because of its dissimilarity from other particular qualities of the body — then why is it not desired, by the lighter [explanation], that the body possesses consciousness, precisely because of its dissimilarity from admittedly non-conscious things like pots? This is the purport. 'Indriyavattvādayaḥ' — the 'ādi' includes possession of vital breath (<s>prāṇa</s>). 'Having activity that conforms to desire' means: the body possesses activity directly dependent on volition. But for a pot and the like, that [activity] is only through the intermediary of bodily effort. This is the purport. The body is conscious, because it possesses activity conforming to desire, because it possesses sense-organs and the like — whatever is not like this is not like this, as a pot and the like — this inference by negative concomitance (<s>vyatireka</s>) for the consciousness of the body is also implicit in this passage. He also states the inconclusiveness in the pervasion of being a particular quality of a product-substance by being preceded by a quality of the cause, with 'kramuke' and so on. When a betel leaf smeared with a paste of areca nut and the like is crushed by the teeth, upon the destruction of the prior composite, from a special conjunction of those [constituent] parts, in the resulting composite, a red color arises that did not exist in the [individual] parts — [it arose] from the special conjunction of those [parts] alone. Thus there is deviation [from the rule] in that case. This is the purport. He raises an objection with 'carvaṇe' and so on. The purport of the objector is: through the crushing by the teeth, upon the destruction of the prior composite down to the level of dyads, when the atoms become independent, through baking by the principal fire produced in the mouth through chewing — the red color arises [from baking], and hence the red color in the resulting composite is indeed preceded by a quality of the cause — so there is no deviation. He resolves this with 'na pramāṇābhāvāt' and so on. The special conjunction alone should be accepted as the cause of a different color in some cases. Just as in the case of turmeric powder, a red color is observed from the conjunction of the powder with water alone. Similarly here too, since that is possible, there is no evidence for postulating baking. This is the purport. Even if, in the case of chewing, the different color is [held to arise] only through <s>pīlupāka</s>, he states deviation in other cases with 'sitāsite' and so on. For in the case of a variegated cloth, baking in the parts is not possible. Nor is there a variegated color in the [individual] parts. And thus, the rule that a particular quality of a composite is preceded by a quality of the same kind in the parts is inconclusive in the case of variegated color. This is the purport. The 'same kind' is intended with respect to the sub-universal such as color-ness (<s>rūpatva</s>). For a white cloth is not produced from blue threads. But if the 'same kind' is intended with respect to color-ness and the like, then that [counter-example] too would apply. [Objection:] But variegated [color] is not accepted as a distinct color. Nor should it be said that a variegated cloth made from threads of various colors would then be colorless — because there is a rule that color and the like have only pervading occurrence, and since the non-pervading occurrence of possessing various colors cannot be accepted in it. And even if the variegated cloth is colorless, there is no harm, because its being visible is explained by the color of the [individual] parts alone. If it is held that a color that has arisen through one or the other relation — inherence or inherence in what inheres — serves as the cause of the visibility of a substance, then to this he replies with 'sarvam eva' and so on. The meaning is: since visibility is thus explained by the color of the parts alone, let it not be accepted that any composite at all possesses color. [Objection:] It is indeed accepted in this very way, by parsimony. To this he replies with 'anubhave' and so on. The meaning is: since the direct experience and convention of possessing color [in composites] are both uncontradicted, the expedient of making the composite colorless cannot be accomplished. And because the uncontradicted experience and convention of 'the cloth is variegated' [exist], variegated color too should be accepted. This is the purport. [Objection:] But it is accepted, on the strength of the cognition, that the variegated cloth has a variegated color that occurs in a non-pervading manner due to the various colors of the parts. And thus there is no deviation in that [example]. To this he replies with 'viśeṣaguṇaś ca' and so on. The hard touch (<s>kaṭhinasparśa</s>) perceived in a hailstone (<s>karaka</s>), which is watery, [arises] from a special conjunction of parts and from the diversity of cooperating causes at the time of formation, and is devoid of fluidity — this is not preceded by a quality of the cause. Because hard touch does not exist in the atoms of water. And thus there is deviation from the rule of being preceded by a quality of the cause in [the case of] hailstone-touch. This is the purport. [Objection:] Let hardness be a special conjunction of parts. And thus there would be no inconclusiveness. To this he replies with 'na ca saṃyoge' and so on. The purport is: if hardness were a form of the special conjunction of parts, then since that [conjunction] does not inhere in the composite, the experience and convention 'the hailstone is hard' would not arise. And even if that were somehow accounted for, since conjunction that inheres in a visible substance is itself visible, the absurd consequence would follow that hardness too would be perceived by the eye. 'Sparśaviśeṣataye' means: since it is a quality graspable only by the skin, hardness is properly a special kind of touch. And it has been accepted as a special kind of touch by the <s>Kāṇāda</s> experts in the categories of reality. This is the purport.
Having raised the objection of the contradiction of the agent-object relation in the body-is-the-self view, he resolves it with 'dṛśyasya' and so on. 'What contradiction?' means: 'how' is [a question asked] regarding what is contradictory. The purport is: since there is no contradiction in the seer being also the seen, what exactly is this 'how'? He states the contradiction with 'ayam eva' and so on. In one and the same action, the agent-hood and object-hood of one and the same [entity] is not proper. For the object is of the nature of what is to be accomplished (<s>sādhya</s>) — the most desired thing to be obtained through the action. And the agent is of an already-accomplished nature (<s>siddha</s>) — the locus of the action. Since what is already accomplished and what is to be accomplished cannot be identical, there is a contradiction between agent-hood and object-hood. This is the purport. In order to have the resolution spoken through the mouth of the objector himself, he states the counter-objection with 'yady evam' and so on. The objector states the resolution with 'rūpabhedāt' and so on. The body-is-the-self proponent states the equal applicability of the resolution with 'samānam' and so on. The purport is: just as, in the view of a distinct self, non-contradiction is stated because of a distinction in aspect — object-hood through being struck (<s>hantvā</s>) and the like, and agent-hood through conjunction with the mind and the like in the action of knowing — the same principle is not barred from the body-is-the-self view. In reality, the kind of object-hood that contradicts agent-hood is not the kind of object-hood that knowledge has. Hence too there is no fault — he says this with 'api ca pare' and so on. 'Svasamavetajñānaphalabhāgin' means: to the extent of the object-hood (<s>viṣayatā</s>) determined by the knowledge inhering in oneself. Since object-hood is determined by the possessor-of-object, the designation 'fruit of knowledge' is figurative. 'Object-hood itself does not exist' means: primary object-hood does not exist. The purport is this: primary object-hood is being the locus of the fruit [that is] the product of an action inhering in another — as in the object-hood of the village with respect to going. But the object-hood of knowledge and the like, characterized by the object-possessor relation, is merely secondary. For the convention of the logicians (<s>tārkika</s>) is: in the combination of a transitive verbal root with a [grammatical] object, object-hood is in the form of object-hood [i.e., viṣayatā]. Since knowledge-agency is also accepted for this [self], the [cognitions] 'he knows himself' and the like are not untenable. But it is only with primary [object-hood] that there is a contradiction with agent-hood. Nor should it be said that this secondary object-hood is not established by grammar — because the validity [of the grammar] is accepted in this [context] too through the same principle as the [sūtra] 'the most desired [thing] to be obtained by the agent is the object.' For the agent — the knower; through the action — through knowledge; the most desired thing to be obtained — what is intended as the thing to be known — is the object: this is the literal meaning to be stated in this position. And for what is undesired but known, through the [sūtra] 'and likewise what is undesired is appropriate' — [it means:] what is connected with the action, i.e., related to knowledge as its object, and even though it is an object of desire as something to be known, [it is] also an object — this too is the meaning in the position of secondary object-hood. Even though the convention is the fruit of knowledge, since [the object] is not the locus of that [convention], the object does not have primary object-hood. And even though the self is the locus of its own convention, since the knowledge — which is the cause of that [convention] and has that [self] as its scope — does not inhere in another, it is not that [primary object-hood either]. But if the intention is that the object is the fruit of knowledge in the sense of conformity with convention, then the knowledge-object-hood of a pot and the like would be primary — [but] we will discuss this further on. He concludes the established body-selfhood with 'ataḥ' and so on. The <s>Bārhaspatyas</s> are the <s>Cārvākas</s> who adhere to the <s>Lokāyata</s> system composed by <s>Bṛhaspati</s>. And it is well-known that <s>Bṛhaspati</s>, the guru of the gods, compelled by his solicitude for the lord of the <s>Asuras</s>, composed a deluding treatise to undermine the Vedic faith and destroy the glory of sovereignty of the <s>Asuras</s>. He cites the sūtra as authority for the consciousness of the body with 'tathā ca' and so on. The four elements — earth and the like — alone are the realities (<s>tattva</s>). From those, when combined to produce the body, consciousness arises in the composite even though it did not exist in each individually — just as the unprecedented intoxicating power [arises] in the liquor produced from ferment (<s>kiṇva</s>) and the like. This is the meaning of the sūtra.

body.text: rbhāgatrasareṇuvyatirekeṇa paramāṇusvīkāre kāraṇābhāvāt / pratyakṣayogyāvayavasya tathā pratibhāsaniyamādvā na vyabhicāraḥ / na cāvayavini bahirandriyagrāhya evāyaṃ niyama ityutprekṣyam / pramāṇābhāvāt / antaḥkaraṇasya ca kevalasyāvayavini vṛttyasambhavācca / vāyostu rūpādyabhāvāt kevalasparśādhāratayopalambhaḥ / tatrāpi tādṛśānekāvayavapratibhāso 'styeva spṛśyamāna iva ghaṭādāviti na tena vyabhicāraḥ /
body.translated_text: Or, because a part that is capable of being perceived must necessarily appear as such, there is no counter-example. And one should not conjecture that this rule [of parts appearing with the composite] applies only to composites perceptible to the external sense organs, because there is no evidence [for such a restriction]. And because the internal organ (<s>antahkarana</s>) alone cannot have an operation regarding a composite [without its parts being manifest]. But air (<s>vayu</s>) is perceived solely as the substrate of touch, due to the absence of color and the like. Even there, the appearance of multiple such parts [i.e., touch-sensations] does exist when something like a pot is being touched — hence there is no counter-example from that.

body.text: yattu sthūlo 'haṃ kṛśo 'hamiti śarīre 'haṃpratyayo dṛśyata iti ; tadapi paryālocanīyam / tatrāpyantaḥśarīramahamākārameva kimapi vastu ahaṅkāro gocayati, na punaścākṣuṣa iva dehapratyayaḥ sthaulyabālyādiyogidehamātram / ata eva mamedaṃ gṛhamitivāt mamedaṃ śarīramiti bhedapratibhāso vyavahāraśca / na hyasau sākṣātpratītabhedanimittaḥ pratāyamānaḥ śilāputrakaśīravyapadeśavadaupacāriko yukta āśriyituṃ mamātmetivat / tatrā'tmaśabdasyātmani vṛttairaikārthyādavivādācca yuktaṃ tathā'śrayaṇam / na caivamatra / ato dehavyatirekiṇaḥ cetanasya pratyakṣasiddhatvāccatsaṃbandhini lākṣaṇiko dehe 'haṃśabdaprayogaḥ /
body.translated_text: As for [the objection that] the 'I'-cognition is observed directed at the body in [experiences like] 'I am stout' or 'I am thin' — that too must be examined. Even there, the 'I'-cognition has as its object something within the body whose form is 'I' — [the 'I'-cognition] does not, like a visual cognition of the body, have as its object merely the body endowed with stoutness, youth, and the like. For this very reason, there is the appearance and usage of difference: 'this body is mine,' just as 'this house is mine.' And it is not proper to treat that [usage], which is perceived as occasioned by a directly apprehended difference, as figurative, like the designation of milk as 'my son' [referring to something nourished by it], unlike 'this is my self,' [where the word 'self'] is used in its primary sense regarding the self, since there is no dispute about the usage of the word 'self' for the self, [the primary meaning being established] through agreement with other uses. But that is not the case here. Therefore, since the conscious [self] distinct from the body is established through direct perception (<s>pratyaksa</s>), the use of the word 'I' regarding the body — which is connected [with the self] — is figurative (<s>laksanika</s>).

body.text: bāhyaviṣayeṣu parasparaviruddharūpaparimāṇasaṅkhayāsanniveśagrahaṇena vyatirekasya sphaṭatvāt ātmani tādṛśarūpāntarāgrahaṇena dehābhedapratibhāsabhramo 'vivekinām / itaśca - icchānuvidhāyisvavyāpāro 'yamātmā / icchayaiva hi saṅkalpayati smaratyabhyūhati ca / śarīramapi tadicchānuvidhāyiśayanāsanotthānādiceṣṭamiti bhavatyabhedabhramaḥ; śuktirajatādāviva / praṇihitamanasastu jñātṛtayā siddhyantamahamākāramarthamanavayavamidamiti parisphurataḥ sthūlādavayavinaḥ śarīrāt pṛthagaparokṣayantyeva /
body.translated_text: Because in the case of external objects, the distinction [between self and body] is clear due to the apprehension of mutually contradictory forms, dimensions, numbers, and configurations — [whereas] in the case of the self, due to the non-apprehension of such a different form, there is an error of non-distinction from the body for the undiscriminating. And for this further reason: this self has its own operations conforming to desire. For it is by desire alone that [the self] resolves, remembers, and deliberates. The body too, with its activities of lying down, sitting, rising, and the like, conforms to that desire — hence the error of non-difference arises, as in [the case of] nacre and silver. But for one whose mind is concentrated, the self — established as the knower, having the form of 'I,' and without parts — is directly perceived (<s>aparoksa</s>) as distinct from the body, which is a gross composite that manifests as 'this.'

children.text: bhavanti ca - jānāmīti pratyayaḥ śarīraviṣayo na bhavati ; arthāntaraviṣayo vāyam ; aprakāśamānatadavayavapratibhāsatvāt ; ya evaṃprakāraḥ sa tathā, yathāyamiti pratibhāsaḥ / yaccharīraviṣayaṃ, na tat
children.translated_text: And [the following arguments] are [advanced]: the cognition 'I know' does not have the body as its object; or this [cognition] has a different object — because the appearances of the parts of that [body] do not manifest [in the 'I'-cognition]. Whatever is of such a character is so, as is the appearance 'like this.' And what has the body as its object is not
so — as is the cognition of the body agreed upon by both [parties].

body.text: mataṃ śarīrajñānam / tathā - śarīramahaṃpratyayagocaro na bhavati, idamiti gṛhyamāṇatvāt, bāhyendriyagrāhyatvādvā, ghaṭādivaditi /
body.translated_text: Likewise: the body is not the domain of the 'I'-cognition, because it is apprehended as 'this,' or because it is perceptible to the external sense organs — like a pot and the like.

body.text:
atha dehātmavādamirāsaḥ 'atra pratividhi'rityādinā / atra - dehasyātmatve, pratividhiḥ - pratividhānam, bādhakapramāṇam / bādho vā / upanyasyata iti śeṣaḥ / 'pratyakṣabādhataḥ' iti / idantvena grahaṇameva hastagehāderiva dehasyātmabhedagrahalakṣaṇaṃ tasyātmatve bādhakamityarthaḥ / etadevopapādayati 'na khalu' iti / ahamidaṅkārau - ahamidaṃpratyayau / svātmagocaro 'haṃpratyayaḥ, svānyagocaraścedaṃpratyayaḥ ekasya puṃsa ekasminnevārthe na ghaṭata ityarthaḥ / vivṛṇotyetat 'ahaṃ jānāmī'tyādinā / pratyagvṛttiḥ - pratyagarthātmaviṣayiṇī / niṣkṛṣṭaṃ - vilakṣaṇam / parāgvṛttiḥ ātmānyaviṣayā / ahaṅkāragocarāt - ahaṃpratyayaviṣayāt svātmanaḥ / śiṣṭaṃ spaṣṭam / 'itarathe'ti / itarathā - ahamidaṃpratītyorvilakṣaṇārthaviṣayakatvābhāve / ayaṃbhāvaḥ - ahamiti svasmai bhāsamānaḥ pratyagarthaḥ svātmā / svasmā idantvenaṃ bhāsamānaśca parāgarthaḥ para iti svaparavibhāgo hi ahamidaṃbuddhiśabdābhyāmeva nirūpyaḥ / arthavailakṣaṇyābhāve tayorayaṃ na ghaṭata iti / ahamarthasyaiva bhavatvākārāntareṇa bhānamidantvenetyatrāha 'nahī'ti / pratyaktvenāhamiti bhāsamānasyaiva svātmanoḥ daṇḍitvenedamiti bhānaṃ syāddaṇḍyayamitītyarthaḥ /
nanvayamahasmītyādipratyayo bhavatyeva svātmani / satyam / tatrāpapīdaṃśabdena parāgrūpadharmollekhaḥ / ātmasvarūpasyollekho 'hamiti / tathā ca pratyagvṛttirahaṅkāraḥ, parāgvṛttiridaṅkāra iti vyavasthāyāṃ nānupapattiriti hārdam /
nanu mamedaṃ vapuriti mamāyamātmetivatsyādityarucerāha

children.translated_text: 'anyacca'

children.text: ti / hetvantaraṃ ca dehasyānātmatve 'stīti yāvat / tadevāha
children.translated_text: ('moreover') — meaning that there is another reason too for the non-selfhood of the body. He states that very [reason] with
'niyamita' ('when restrained')

children.text:
ti / nivāritabahirindriyapravṛttermānasamahamiti svātmānusandhānaṃ na dehagocaram, karacaraṇādya
viṣayakatvāt / avayavinaḥ sthūlam grahaṇe katipayatadavayavabhānasyāvarjanīyatvāditi bhāvaḥ / avahitamanasaḥ - ātmagrahaṇedaṃparamanasaḥ / avayataḥ - jānataḥ / sthavīyān - atiśayena sthūlaḥ / pratyakṣagrāhyāvayavasamaveta iti vivakṣitam / avayavigrahamasya tadavayavagocaratvamiti niyamasya tryaṇukagrahaṇe 'naikāntyaṃ vārayati 'vātāyane'ti / jālarandhrapraviṣṭaravikaragrāhyaniravayavatryaṇukātirekeṇa tadavayavāvayavaparamāṇukalpanāyāṃ pramāṇābhāvādityarthaḥ / trasareṇorniravayavatvānna tadgrūhaṇe niruktaniyamasya vyabhicāra iti bhāvaḥ / paramāṇukalpanāmupagamyāpyāha 'pratyakṣe'ti / pratyakṣayogyā avayavā yasya, tasyāvayavinaḥ avayavabhānavyāpyabhānavattvaniyamānna tryaṇukapratyakṣe vyabhicāraḥ / tadavayavasyātīndriyatvāditi bhāvaḥ / 'na cāvayavinī'ti / bāhyendriyajapratyakṣa evāvayavibhānaniyatatvamavayavabhānasyeti kalpanaṃ svoptekṣaṇamātram / avayavipratyakṣatvavyāpakatvasyāvayavabhāne svīkāre bādhakopalambho hi bāhyatatpratyakṣamātraviṣayakatayā niyamasaṅkoce mānam / tadabhāvāditi bhāvaḥ / nanu manasā kevalamavayavi gṛhyate vināvayavamityata eva niyamaḥ saṅkocanīya iti cettatrāha 'antakaraṇasye'ti / advārīkṛtabahirindriyasya manasaḥ kevale 'vayavaviśeṣṭa vā śarīrādau bāhyārthe grahaṇapravṛtterasaṃbhavāccetyarthaḥ / bāhyārthe svāntasyāsvātantryamiti hi tārkikāḥ / ato na manasā śarīrasya grahaṇaṃ ghaṭeta kevalena / caitanyavattvena tasyābāhyatvānmanasā grahaṇaṃ bavedvināvayaveneti tu na kalpanīyam / taccaitanya eva vigānāditi bhāvaḥ / niruktaniyamasya vāyuspārśane 'naikāntyaṃ pariharati 'vāyostu' iti / rūpādimadavayavipratyakṣasya tadavayavagocaratvamiti niyame naiva doṣaḥ nīrūpatvādvāyoḥ sparśavattvamātreṇa tasya spārśanopagame 'pīti bhāvaḥ / vastutaḥ vāyuspārśanasyāpi tadavayavagocaratvamityāha 'tatrāpī'ti / avayavisannikarṣe tadavayavasannikarṣasyāvarjanīyatvādyogyasannikṛṣṭāvayavabhānasyāvayavibhānaniyatatvenāvayavavipratyakṣasya tadavayavagocaratvamiti niyame 'pi na vāyuspārśane
vyabhicāraḥ / tatra tadavayavasyāpi bhānāt, ghaṭaspārśana iva ghaṭāvayavasyeti bhāvaḥ / dehātmatvasādhikāṃ pratyakṣapratītaṃ 'yattuṃ' ityādinānūdya samādhatte 'tadapī'tyādinā / śarīrāntarvartamānamahamākāram - ahantālakṣaṇaṃ
pratyagātmānamevāhaṃpratyayo viṣayīkaroti / sthūlo 'haṃ jānāmītyahaṃpratyayo dehadvārā sthaulyānvitāntarātmagocara eveti bhāvaḥ / mānase pratyaye dehabhānaṃ tūpanayamaryādayā / sthūlo 'haṃ jānāmīti vyavahāre 'pi śarīravācī sthūlaśabdastatsabandhinyantarātmanyaupacārikaḥ / siddhānte tu mukhya eva / śarīrasya cetanaṃ pratyapṛthaksiddhaprakāratvāt, apṛthaksiddhaprakāravācināṃ ca niṣkarṣakabhinnānāṃ śabdānāṃ dharmiṇi mukhyavṛtterupagamāt / abhrāntīyapratyayavyavahārayoritthaṃ gatirnirūpitā / samānādhikaraṇapratyayasya dehavadātmagocaratve vyadhikaraṇapratyayavyapadeśānugraho 'pyastītyāha 'ata eve'ti / mamedaṃ śarīramiti bhedavyapadeśasya śilāputrakasya śarīramitivadaupacārikatvamastvityāśaṅkāṃ vyudasyati 'na hyasā'viti / pratāyamānaḥ - pratanyamānaḥ vistāryamāṇaḥ / pracuraṃ prayujyamāno lokeneti yāvat / pracuravyapadeśasyaupacārikatvakalpanā na sādhīyasīti bhāvaḥ / 'mamāyamātme'tyasya tu matadvaye 'pi aupacārikatvamagatyā vācyamevetyāha 'tatre'ti / aikārthyāt - ahamātmaśabdayorabhinnārthakatvāt / avivādācca - ahamarthātmanauraikye vivādābhāvācca / 'na caivamatre'ti / śarīrāhaṃśabdayoraikārthyāsiddhestadarthaikye vivādācca 'mamedaṃ śarīraṃ'miti nopacaritārthaṃ kalpyam / kintu 'mamedaṃ gṛha'mitivanmukhyārthameva svīkāryamiti bhāvaḥ / dehe cāhaṃśabda aupacārika ityāha 'ata' iti / ahaṃ gacchāmītyādāvahaṃśabda ātmavati dehe lākṣaṇika iti yāvat / dehātmabhramavatāṃ tu śaktibhramamūlastathā prayoga iti bodhyam /
evaṃ tarkabalādahaṃ jānāmīti mānasapratyakṣasya sāvayavadehavyatiriktātmaparatvaṃ vyavasthāpitam / evaṃ dehavyatiriktasyātmano bhāne sati kathaṃ dehābhedabhrama udetītyatrāha 'bāhye'ti / sanniveśaḥ - ākṛtiḥ - avayava - saṃsthānam / sphuṭatvāditya
syānantaramabhedabhramasyānudaye 'pīti śeṣaḥ / dehābhedapratibhāsaścāsau bhramaśceti karmadhārayaḥ / bhedakākārāgrahādabhedabhramo dehātmanoravivekināṃ bhedakākāragraharahitānāmityarthaḥ / ayamāśayaḥ - yadyapi dehato vibhinnaparimāṇa ātmā / athāpi tatparimāṇaṃ na pratyakṣam / jñānasukhādi pratyakṣamapi na yāvaddehe tadasaṃbhavagrahaḥ, tāvattannabhedakam / rūpādyapyevamātmani tadasaṃbhavagrahamantarā na bhedakam /saṅkhyādistu sādhāramatvānna bhedaka iti / bādhakasya bhedakakāragrahasyābhāvamupapādya aikyabhrame sādhakaṃ sādṛśyajñānaṃ copapādayati
children.translated_text: [continued] — the self-investigation 'I am' of one whose external sense-organ activity has been restrained is not directed at the body, because it does not have hands, feet, and the like as its content. The sense is: in the apprehension of a gross composite, the appearance of some of its parts is unavoidable. 'Of one whose mind is concentrated' means: of one whose mind is focused on the apprehension of the self. 'Knowing' means cognizing. 'Very stout' means exceedingly gross. It is intended that [the composite] inheres in parts that are perceptible to direct perception. He wards off the inconclusiveness [of the rule] — that the apprehension of a composite entails the appearance of its parts — in the case of the tryaṇuka (triad of atoms), with 'vātāyane' (through the window aperture). The meaning is: because there is no evidence for positing atoms as parts of the part-less tryaṇuka that is apprehensible through the sun's rays entering through a lattice window, beyond that [visible tri-atomic dust-mote]. The sense is: because the trasareṇu (visible mote) is part-less, there is no deviation of the stated rule in its apprehension. Even granting the postulation of atoms, he says 'pratyakṣe' — because of the rule that the appearance of a composite whose parts are capable of being perceived is pervaded by the appearance of those parts, there is no deviation [of the rule] in the perception of the tryaṇuka — because its parts are beyond the senses. This is the sense. 'Na cāvayavinī' — the conjecture that the appearance of parts is invariably confined to perception produced by external sense organs alone is mere wishful thinking. For the evidence for the restriction [of the rule] to external perception alone is [in fact] a sublating cognition (bādhaka) that arises when accepting [the rule's application] in the appearance of parts — and that is absent. The sense is: because of the absence of such [evidence]. [Objection:] But if the composite alone is apprehended by the mind without its parts, then the rule [about parts appearing] should be restricted — to address this, he says 'antakaraṇasya.' The meaning is: because it is impossible for the mind, which has not employed the external sense organs as its instruments, to operate in apprehending the body and the like — bare external objects or composites possessing specific parts. For the logicians hold that the internal organ is not independent regarding external objects. Therefore, the apprehension of the body by the mind alone cannot be accomplished. Nor should it be conjectured that because the body possesses consciousness, it is not external, and hence it could be apprehended by the mind without [apprehending] its parts — because precisely that consciousness [of the body] is what is being disputed. This is the sense. He resolves the inconclusiveness of the stated rule in the case of touching wind with 'vāyostu.' In the rule that the apprehension of a composite possessing parts that have color and the like involves those parts as its content — there is indeed no fault, because wind is colorless; even though it is accepted as touchable merely by possessing touch, [the rule is not violated]. This is the sense. In reality, even in the touch of wind, [the apprehension] involves the content of its parts — he says 'tatrāpi.' Because in the contact with a composite, the contact with its parts is unavoidable, and because the appearance of parts that are in contact and capable [of being perceived] is invariably connected with the appearance of the composite — even in the rule that the apprehension of a composite whose parts are perceptible involves those parts as its content, there is no deviation in the touch of wind — because even there, the parts too appear, just as in touching a pot, the parts of the pot [appear]. This is the sense. Having restated the perception-based argument for the body being the self with 'yattu' and so forth, he resolves it with 'tadapi' and so forth. The 'I'-cognition, having the form of 'I' and located within the body, takes as its object the inner self (<s>pratyagātman</s>) itself, which has the characteristic of 'I'-ness (ahantā). Even in the usage 'I am stout, I know,' the 'I'-cognition has as its object the inner self endowed with stoutness through the instrumentality of the body. This is the sense. The appearance of the body in mental cognition, however, is in accordance with the standard of inference (upanaya). Even in the usage 'I am stout, I know,' the word 'stout,' which denotes the body, is figurative (aupacārika) with respect to the inner self that is connected with [the body]. But in the established doctrine [of the Siddhāntin], it is indeed primary. Because the body has the status of being an inseparable mode (apṛthaksiddhaprakāra) of the conscious self, and because words that denote inseparable modes — when not used in a restrictive sense — are accepted as having primary meaning with respect to the substance (dharmin). The manner of unerring cognition and usage has been explained thus. He says 'ata eva' to indicate that when the co-referential cognition has the self as its object just like the body, there is also support from the cognition and designation of difference. He dispels the doubt — 'Let the designation of difference "this body is mine" be figurative, like "the body of Śilāputraka"' — with 'na hyasāv.' 'Pratāyamānaḥ' means: being extended, being expanded. That is: being employed abundantly in the world. The sense is: the conjecture that an abundantly used designation is figurative is not sound. He says 'tatra' to indicate that 'mamāyamātmā' ('this is my self') is figurative in both doctrines. Because of the identity of meaning of 'I' and 'self' (ātman) — and because there is no dispute about the unity of the referents of 'I' and 'self.' 'Na caivam atre' — because the identity of meaning of 'body' and 'I' is not established, and because there is dispute about the unity of their referents, 'this body is mine' should not be construed as figurative. Rather, it should be accepted in its primary sense, just like 'this house is mine.' This is the sense. He states that the word 'I' regarding the body is figurative with 'ata.' That is: in [usages like] 'I go' and the like, the word 'I' is figurative (lākṣaṇika) with respect to the body that possesses a self. But for those who have the error of identifying body and self, such usage is based on an error regarding linguistic convention (śakti) — this should be understood. Thus, by the force of reasoning, the fact that the mental perception 'I know' has as its object a self distinct from the composite body has been established. Having thus established the appearance of a self distinct from the body, he addresses 'How does the error of non-difference from the body arise?' with 'bāhye.' 'Sanniveśa' means configuration — the arrangement of parts. [The supplement] 'even though the error of non-difference does not arise immediately after [the appearance of the distinct form]' is to be understood. 'The appearance-of-non-difference-from-the-body, which is an error' — this is a karmadhāraya compound. The error of non-difference [between body and self] is due to the non-apprehension of a differentiating form — [it arises] for those who do not discriminate between body and self, who lack the apprehension of a differentiating form. The purport is this: although the self has a dimension different from the body, nevertheless that dimension is not perceptible. Knowledge, pleasure, and the like, though perceptible, are not [recognized as] differentiating [the self from the body] until there is the apprehension that they are impossible in the body. Form and the like [of the body] similarly, without the apprehension of their impossibility in the self, are not differentiating. Number and the like, being common [to both], are not differentiating. Having thus justified the absence of a sublating cognition — the differentiating form — he also justifies the facilitating similarity-cognition for the error of identity.
And for this further reason
— the body's having its own activities conforming to the self's desire constitutes similarity with the self — this is the meaning.
'Conjectures'
— thus
— by a vārttika (grammatical supplement), the optionally parasmaipada [conjugation] of the verb 'ūha' with the prefix 'abhi' is stated.

children.text: siti vārtikeṇa vaikalpikaṃ parasmaipadam / abhyūhanam-vitarkaṇamutprekṣaṇaṃ vā / samānadharmadarśanātprasaktasyaikyabhramasya bhedakākāradarśanato nivṛttiṃ darśayati
children.translated_text: 'Abhyūhana' means speculation or supposition. He shows that the error of identity, which has arisen due to the observation of similar properties, ceases upon the observation of differentiating forms,
with 'praṇihite'

children.text:
ti / praṇidhānam-avadhānam / jñātṛtayā siddhyantaṃ-jñātṛtvaikākāreṇa prakāśamānam / anavayavam-niravayavam / ātmā hi manogocaraḥ, sa cet sāvayavaḥ, tathā gṛhyate / na ca tathā gṛhyate / kintu jñātṛtvaikākāraḥ / ato niravayavaḥ / ekarūpatayānavayavatayā graha eva ca bhedakākāragrahaḥ / avahitamanaso niruktaparāmarśavataśca manasā dehavailakṣaṇyenātmanaḥ pratyakṣaṃ bhavatyeveti bhāvaḥ / praṇihitetivākyaṃ yogipratyakṣaviṣayatayāpi yojayituṃ śakyate / evamahaṃ jānāmīti pratyakṣasya dehātiriktātmaviṣayatvaṃ tarkabalena vyavasthāpitam /
idameva prayogārūḍhaṃ pradarśayati
children.translated_text: ('when concentrated'). 'Praṇidhāna' means close attention. 'Established as the knower' means manifesting solely with the form of knower-hood. 'Without parts' means part-less. For the self is an object of the mind; if it were a composite, it would be apprehended as such. But it is not so apprehended. Rather, [it appears] solely with the form of knower-hood. Therefore, it is part-less. And the very apprehension [of the self] as having a single form and as part-less is the apprehension of the differentiating form. The sense is: for one whose mind is concentrated and who possesses the stated discernment, the self is indeed directly perceptible through the mind as different from the body. The sentence 'praṇihite' can also be construed with reference to yogic perception. Thus, by the force of reasoning, the fact that the perception 'I know' has as its object a self beyond the body has been established. He shows this very [conclusion] in the form of a formal argument (prayoga),
with 'bhavanti ca'

children.text: ti / prayogā iti śeṣaḥ / prathamaprayoge śarīraviṣayakatvābhāvaḥ, anantaraprayoge śarīrātiriktaviṣayakatvaṃ cāhaṃ jānāmītyaparokṣasya pradidarśayiṣitam / ubhayatrāpi hetureka eva śarīrāvayavāviṣayakapratibhāsatvarūpaḥ / anvayyudāharaṇamubhayatra
children.translated_text: — 'the arguments [are as follows]' is to be supplied. In the first argument, the absence of having the body as its object [is demonstrated]; in the next argument, the having of an object different from the body — both are shown for the immediate [cognition] 'I know.' In both [arguments], the reason is one and the same — namely, having the character of an appearance in which the parts of the body do not appear. The example of positive concomitance in both [arguments] is:
'whatever is of such a character'
— 'this' refers to the appearance — the appearance 'this is a pot' and the like. In the first [argument], the example of negative concomitance
'what has the body [as its content]'
is shown with this and so forth. Having stated the [argument with] the perception thesis, he states the positive-concomitant [argument] with the body thesis:
'Likewise — the body'

children.text:
iti / idamiti
gṛhyamāṇatvaṃ-bāhyatvena gṛhyamāṇatvam / bāhyatvamiti phalito hetuḥ /
children.translated_text: — 'being apprehended as "this"' means being apprehended as external. Externality is the resultant reason.
Moreover: one who knows one's own self — which is for its own sake — as the object of 'I,' and who knows other things as for the self's sake,
[recognizes that] because of being a composite (<s>saṅghāta</s>), this body — which is for another's sake — how can there be the cognition of selfhood in it?

children.text: sarvasya bāhyābhyantarabhogyavargasya śabdasukhāderātmārthatāṃ, bhoktuścātmano 'nanyārthatāṃ, sarvasya śeṣitāṃ pratyakṣataḥ pratipadyāmahe / na ca śarīramananyārtham ;saṅghātatvāt / saṅghātā hi sarve parārthā dṛṣṭāḥ śayanāsanarathādayaḥ /
children.translated_text: We directly perceive: the purposiveness-for-the-self (ātmārthatā) of the entire range of external and internal objects of enjoyment such as sound, pleasure, and the like; the non-purposiveness-for-another of the enjoying self; and the principal-hood (śeṣitā) of everything [with respect to the self]. But the body is not purposive-for-itself (ananyārtha) — because it is a composite. For all composites are observed to be for the sake of another — beds, seats, chariots, and the like.

children.text: na ca saṅghātāḥ saṃhataśarīrādyarthā dṛśyanta ityātmano 'pi saṃhatatvamāpadyata iti vācyam / tathā sati tasyāpi parārthatvaprasaṅgāt / aparārthaścāyamātmā pratyakṣataḥ prakāśata ityuktam / yogyānupalambhabādhitaṃ cātmani saṅghātatvam /saṅghātāntarārthatve ca tasyāpi tathā, tato 'nyasyāpi tatheti na vyavatiṣṭheta / na ca vyavasthāyāṃ satyāmavyavasthā yuktā / na ca saṅghātasya parārthatve parasya saṃhatatvamapi prayojakam ; bhoktṛtayaivātmanaḥ svārthasaṅghātaṃ prati paratvopapatteḥ / vyāptyanupayogino 'pi dṛṣṭāntadṛṣṭadharmamātrasyānurodhenānumānamicchataḥ sarvānumānocchedaprasaṅgaḥ /
children.translated_text: Nor should it be said that composites are seen [to exist] for the sake of a composite body and the like, so the self too would incur the status of being composite — because in that case, it too would have the consequence of being for another's sake. And it has been said that this self is manifest through perception as not being for the sake of another. And the composite-ness of the self is contradicted by the non-apprehension of what is fit to be perceived (yogyānupalambha). And if the composite [body] were for the sake of another composite, then that [second composite] too would be so, and another beyond that likewise — so there would be no settled conclusion. Nor, when a settled conclusion exists, is the absence of a settled conclusion tenable. Nor, when the composite is for the sake of another, is the composite-ness of the other even relevant — because the other-hood of the self with respect to the composite that is for its own sake is explicable simply through [the self's] being the enjoyer (bhoktṛ). For one who desires an inference that follows merely the property observed in the example — without [the property's] contributing to the pervasion — there would follow the consequence of the destruction of all inferences.
In the argument with the body-thesis proving non-selfhood, he introduces the third reason — namely the form of being a composite —
with 'kiṃ ca'
('moreover').
'Aparārtham'

children.text: iti / aparārthaṃ-svapradhānam, svamātmānam-ahamarthabhūtamātmānam, ātmārthe-bhoktṛbhūtāhamarthātmārthe, anyacca-parāgarthajātaṃ ca, jānataḥ-vidataḥ, saṅghātatvāt-avayavasanniveśavattvāt, parārthe-svabhinnabhoktṛbhogārthe, dehe 'smin, ātmabuddhiḥ kathaṃ jāyeteti ślokārthaḥ // atrāyaṃ prayogaḥ-deho nātmā parārthatvādrathādivat / na ca svarūpāsiddhiḥ / saṅghātatvāddehasya pārārthyasiddheriti bhāvaḥ //5//
children.translated_text: — 'aparārtham' means: having oneself as the principal. 'svam ātmānam' — the self that constitutes the referent of 'I.' 'Ātmārthe' — for the sake of the self that is the enjoyer, the referent of 'I.' 'Anyac ca' — and other things as well. 'Jānataḥ' — of one who knows. 'Saṅghātatvāt' — because of possessing the arrangement of parts. 'Parārthe' — for the sake of the enjoyment of an enjoyer distinct from itself. 'In this body' — how can the cognition of selfhood arise? — this is the meaning of the verse. Here is the argument: the body is not the self, because of being for the sake of another, like a chariot and the like. And there is no unestablished-ness of the thesis. Because the body's being-for-another is established from its being a composite — this is the sense.

body.translated_text: Now he presents the refutation of the body-self doctrine with [the words] 'atra pratividhih' and so forth. 'Atra' means: when the body is [held to be] the self. 'Pratividhih' means a counter-measure, a sublating means of valid cognition (<s>badhaka pramana</s>). Or [it means] sublation. [The verb] 'is presented' is to be supplied. 'Pratyaksabadhatah' — the meaning is: the very apprehension [of the body] as 'this,' just like a hand, house, and the like, constitutes the apprehension of the body's difference from the self, and that [apprehension] is the sublating [evidence] against its being the self. He substantiates this very [point] with 'na khalu.' 'Aham-idankarau' means the 'I'-cognition and the 'this'-cognition. The 'I'-cognition has one's own self as its domain, and the 'this'-cognition has what is other than oneself as its domain — these two do not occur together for one and the same person regarding one and the same object — this is the meaning. He elaborates this with 'aham janami' and so forth. 'Pratyagvrtti' means directed toward the inner object, the self. 'Niskrsta' means distinct. 'Paragvrtti' means directed toward what is other than the self. 'Ahankaragocarat' means from one's own self, which is the object of the 'I'-cognition. The rest is clear. 'Itaratha' — [means] if the 'I'-cognition and the 'this'-cognition do not have distinct objects. The purport is: the inner object — the self — that appears to oneself as 'I' [is one thing], and the outer object — the other — that appears as 'this' to oneself [is another]. For the distinction between self and other is to be determined only through the 'I'-cognition and the 'this'-cognition and [their corresponding] words. In the absence of a difference in their objects, this [distinction] would not be tenable. [The objection that] the very object of 'I' may appear in another form as 'this' is addressed with 'na hi.' The meaning is: the very self that appears as 'I' in its inward-facing aspect — the designation 'this one to be beaten with a stick' would [absurdly] apply to it in its aspect of carrying a stick. But one who says 'I am this' [uses 'this'] even regarding one's own self. True. But even there, the word 'this' involves the mention of an outward-facing property. The mention of the self's own form is through 'I.' And thus, when the inward-directed cognition is 'I' and the outward-directed cognition is 'this,' there is no difficulty in maintaining the distinction — this is the inner meaning. [Objection:] But 'this body is mine' might be like 'this is my self.' To address this hesitation, he says

body.text: ātmatvāparārthatvayoḥ parārthatvānātmatvayośca vyāpyavyāpakabhāvaṃ śloke pūrvārdhoktaṃ vivṛṇoti

children.translated_text: with 'sarvasya'
('of all'). 'Ātmārthatām' — being a means whose fruit is the enjoyment of the enjoying self. The result [of this] is stated as
'the principal-hood (śeṣitā) of all'

children.text:
iti / sarvasya bhogyasya bhoktṛtvena
svāmitāṃ pradhānatāmityarthaḥ / śarīrasyātmatvavyāpikāmananyārthatāṃ vārayati
children.translated_text: — the meaning is: the lordship, the primacy, of all objects of enjoyment by virtue of being the enjoyer. He negates the non-purposiveness-for-another — which pervades the selfhood — of the body, with
'na ca śarīram'
('and the body is not [so]'). He cites the instance for grasping the invariable concomitance of being-a-composite with being-for-another:
'saṅghātā hi'

children.text: ti / parārthāḥ-bhoktaparabhogārthaḥ / saṅghātaparasya saṃhatatvadṛṣṭeḥ śarīraparatvenānumitasyā'tmano 'pi saṅghātatvaṃ syādityāśaṅkāmanūdya pratikṣipati
children.translated_text: ('for composites indeed'). 'For the sake of another' — for the enjoyment of another who is the enjoyer. Having restated and refuted the objection — that since composites are observed [to be] for the sake of the composite body and the like, the self too, being inferred as the other [for whose sake the body exists], would incur composite-ness — he says:
'na ca saṅghātāḥ'
('and composites [are not so]').
'Tathā sati'

children.text: ti / ātmā saṅghātarūpaṃ saṃhataparatvādityanumāne pratitarko 'tra vivakṣitaḥ ātmā yadi saṅgātaḥ syāttarhiparārthaḥ syāditi / ātmā na saṅghātaḥ aparārthatvāditi pratyanumānaṃ vā / saṅghātadehaparatvenānumitasyā'tmanaḥ saṅghātarūpatve pratyakṣabādhamapyāha
children.translated_text: [The word] 'ti' [completes the previous]. The counter-argument (<s>pratitarka</s>) intended here against the inference 'the self has the form of an aggregate because of being for the sake of what is combined' is: if the self were an aggregate, then it would be for the sake of another. Or [it may be understood as] a counter-inference: the self is not an aggregate, because it is not for the sake of another. He also states the perceptual contradiction against the aggregate-nature of the self, which was inferred through the being-for-the-sake-of-another of the aggregate-body, with [the word]
'yogyanupalambhe' ('in the non-apprehension of what is fit [to be perceived]').

children.text: ti / yadvā anumānabalātprasaktamapi saṅghātatvamātmanaḥ pramāṇāntaraviṣayīkārato nivartsyatītyāha
children.translated_text: Or alternatively, [the meaning is that] even the aggregate-nature of the self, which is entailed by the force of inference, will be negated through the domain of another means of valid cognition — thus he says
'yogyanupalambhe.'

children.text: ti / śarīraṃ saṃhataparārtham, saṅghātatvāt khaṭvādivadityatra śarīrabhinnatvamupādhiśca / na ca pakṣabhinnatvasyopādhitve 'numānavilopaprasaṅga iti vācyam / yatra pakṣe sādhyābhāvaḥ pramāṇāntareṇa niścitaḥ tatra vahneranuṣṇatvānumāna iva pakṣabhinnatvasyopādhitvasaṃbhavāt / prakṛte 'pi śarīrātmavādināṃ tadatiriktātmavādināṃ vā saṃhataparārthatvābhāva evopeyate śarīrasyeti tadbhinnatvasyopādhitve na doṣa ityabhimatam / saṅghātatvasya saṃhataparārthatvena na vyāptiḥ / anavasthāpādakatvādityāha
children.translated_text: [In the inference:] 'The body serves the purpose of what is combined, because it is an aggregate, like a bedstead and the like' — here, 'being different from the body' is the limiting condition (<s>upadhi</s>). And one should not say that if being different from the thesis were a limiting condition, there would follow the consequence of the destruction of all inference. Because in a thesis where the absence of the provable is ascertained through another means of valid cognition — as in the inference of non-heat in fire — it is possible for being-different-from-the-thesis to be a limiting condition. In the present case too, whether for those who hold the body-self view or for those who hold the view of a self distinct from the body, it is accepted that the body lacks being-for-the-sake-of-what-is-combined — hence there is no fault in its being different [from the thesis] being a limiting condition — this is the intended [meaning]. The pervasion of being-an-aggregate by being-for-the-sake-of-what-is-combined does not hold, because of leading to an infinite regress — thus he says
'sanghataantare' ('in another aggregate').

children.text: ti / tasyāpi-sādhyaghaṭakasyāpi saṅghātasya, tathā- saṅghātāntarārthatvam / tato 'nyasyāpi-sādhyaghaṭakasaṅgātānumitasya / saṅghātāntarasyāpi, tathā-saṅghātāntarārthatvam /
children.translated_text: Of that too — of the aggregate that is a component of the provable — likewise, being for the sake of another aggregate. Of yet another too — of the one inferred through the aggregate that is a component of the provable — of another aggregate too, likewise, being for the sake of another aggregate.
'Na ca vyavasthayam'

children.text: iti / saṅghātatvasya parārthatvena vyāptau iṣyamāṇāyāṃ vyavasthāyāṃ saṃbhavatyāṃ saṃhataparārthatvena tasya vyāpterāśrayaṇamanavasthāprayojakatvānna yuktamiti bhāvaḥ / nanu bhūyaḥsahacāradarśanādhīno hi vyāptigrahaḥ / sa ca saṃhataparārthatvenaiva saṅghātatvasya bhavet, khaṭvādau tathā darśanādityata āha
