children.translated_text: ('Nor [is there a way to establish] a fixed determination'). When the pervasion of being-an-aggregate by being-for-another is being asserted, and when a fixed determination is possible, the resort to the pervasion of that [aggregate-nature] by being-for-the-sake-of-what-is-combined is not justified, because it leads to an infinite regress — this is the purport. [Objection:] But the grasp of pervasion depends on the observation of repeated co-occurrence. And that [co-occurrence] would be of being-an-aggregate with being-for-the-sake-of-what-is-combined, since it is so observed in bedsteads and the like. To this he says
'na ca sanghatasyah' ('nor of the aggregate').

children.text:
ti / parasya saṃhatatvamantaraiva saṅghātaprayojyaniyatabhogarūpātiśayabhāktvena taṃ prati śeṣitvalakṣaṇaṃ paratvaṃ -prādhānyaṃ saṃbhavatīti parārthatvaniyamasya saṅgāta upapatteḥ sapakṣadṛṣṭamapi parasya saṃhatatvaṃ nāvinābhāvagrahopayogi
/ saṃhataparārthatve sādhye saṅghātatvahetoraprayojakatvamiti ca bhāvaḥ / sapakṣe darśanamātreṇa vyāptyanupayogi-sarvagharmoparāgeṇa sādhyasya pakṣe 'numāne 'numānāprāmāṇyaprasaṅgaśvetyāha
children.translated_text: Even without the other being combined, the aggregate serves [another] by partaking of a specific enjoyment in the form of an invariable experience that is produced by the aggregate — and thus being-for-another, characterized by the <s>sesitva</s> (accessory-relation), i.e., subordination to that [enjoyer], is possible. Therefore, the pervasion with being-for-another [holds].
'vyaptyanupayogino 'pi'

children.text: ti / pakṣe parvate sapakṣadṛṣṭamahānasīyatvakārīṣatvādyuparaktahneranumāne 'prāmāṇyaprasaṅga iti bhāvaḥ / dharmamātrasyakṛtsnasya dharmasya / anurodhena-vyāpakatāvacchedakakoṭighaṭanena / anumānam-pakṣe tāvadākāroparaktasādhyānumānam / sarvānumānocchedaprasaṅgaḥ- anumānamātraprāmāṇyavilopaprasaṅgaḥ / śiṣṭaṃ spaṣṭam / evamahaṃ jānāmītyāderahaṃpratyayasya pratyakṣarūpasya dehātiriktaviṣayatvaṃ vyavasthāpitaṃ tarkeṇa / tathā cāhaṃpratyaya eva dehabhedapratyayarūpa itīdaṅkāragocare dehe ātmabhedo 'pi pratyakṣasiddha ityavarṇi /
children.translated_text: ('even of what is not useful for the pervasion'). The purport is: in the inference of fire on the mountain (the thesis), when the fire is affected by [accidental properties] such as being-in-a-kitchen or being-from-cowdung, which are observed in the similar example — there would follow the consequence of invalidity [of all inferences]. 'Dharmamtrasya' — 'of the property alone,' i.e., of the complete property. 'Anurodhe' — [means] in conformity [with what is required].
Even when the distinction [of the self from the body] is unclear, [consciousness] is impossible in the body.
And from the dissimilarity of knowledge from the other qualities of that [body], knowledge is not a quality of that [body].

children.text: sarva eva kāryadravyagataviśeṣaguṇaḥ kāraṇaguṇapūrvaka iti kathamatatpūrvakaḥ śarīre caitanyaguṇaḥ saṃbhavet? /
children.translated_text: Every specific quality in a produced substance is preceded by a quality of the cause — so how could the quality of consciousness arise in the body without being preceded [by a quality of the cause]?

children.text: yattu bārhaspatya vacanam - pṛthivyāpastejo vāyuriti tattvāni, tebhyaścaitanyam, kiṇvādibhyo madaśaktivat iti; tadanupapannam / śakteraviśeṣaguṇatvena tathopapatteḥ / sarvadravyeṣu tattatkāryasamadhigabhyaḥ tatpratiyogī śaktayākhyo guṇaḥ sādhāraṇaḥ / naivaṃ caitanyam, dehaikaguṇatvābhyupagamāt / kāryatve satyekavidhapratyakṣasiddhatayā ca viśeṣaguṇatvāt / dravyāntarasaṃyogasamāsāditamadaśaktibhirakāryabhūtaiḥ paramāṇubhirnijaguṇapuraskāreṇa svakāryadravyeṣu madaśaktayutpādo 'pi nānupapannaḥ / tāmbūlarāgastu pūrvadravyāvayavavibhāgānantaraṃ dravyāntarasaṃyogajanitaraktimaguṇaiḥ kāraṇaiḥ kriyate / dṛśyate hi tatrāvayaveṣvapi pratyekaṃ raktimaguṇaḥ / naca śarīrāvayaveṣu pratyekaṃ caitanyaguṇaḥ prajñāyate pratijñāyate vā / tadupagame ca ekaśarīra evānekacetanāpātādaṅgāṅgitvābhāvaḥ, pratisandhānavyavahāralopaśca
children.translated_text: As for the statement of the <s>Barhaspatya</s> [materialist]: 'Earth, water, fire, and air — these are the realities; from these [arises] consciousness, like the power of intoxication from fermented ingredients (<s>kinva</s>) and the like' — that is untenable. Because power (<s>sakti</s>) is a general quality (<s>samanyaguna</s>),

body.translated_text: He elucidates the pervaded-pervader relation (vyāpyavyāpakabhāva) between selfhood and being-for-no-other, and between being-for-another and non-selfhood, as stated in the first half of the verse,

body.text: ; devadattadṛṣṭa iva yajñadattādeḥ /
body.translated_text: like the [unseen] merit (<s>drsta</s>) of <s>Devadatta</s> [which is inferred to exist similarly] in <s>Yajnadatta</s> and others.

body.text: yattu- akāraṇaguṇapūrvakaṃ citrarūpaṃ paṭe iti ; tanna / nānārūpatā hi citratā / sā ca nānārūpaiḥ tantubhiḥ kriyata iti kimanupapannamiti / pratyekamavidyamānamapi taccitrarūpaṃ tantuṣu saṃhateṣu dṛśyata eva citrā ime tantava iti /saṃbhūya ca teṣāṃ paṭārambhakatvam / evaṃ tatkāraṇeṣvapi taditi na kvacivdyabhicāraḥ / na caikarūpaniyamābhāvenāvayavino 'cākṣuṣatvam ; mahacvaikārthasamavāyinā rūpavattvenaiva cākṣuṣatvasiddheḥ / astu vā citraṃ nāmaiko rūpaviśeṣaḥ / sa tu rūpaireva kāraṇagatairnānāvidhairārabhyata iti dṛṣṭam / na caivamavayavavartibhireva caitanyairavayavini śarīre caitanyaviśeṣārambhaḥ / cititanmātrasyaiva teṣvasaṃbhavāt / ato na dehaguṇaḥ caitanyam / etena sukhādayo 'pi śarīraguṇāḥ pratyuktāḥ /
body.translated_text: As for [the objection]: 'Variegated color in cloth is not preceded by a quality of the cause' — that is not [valid]. For variegation is simply the possession of multiple colors. And that is produced by threads of various colors — so what is untenable? [The variegation] is indeed preceded by [qualities of] the individual [threads].

body.text: api ca dṛḍha eva śarīre virodhiguṇāpātamantareṇa kusumavilepanagandha iva nivartamānaḥ caitanyasukhādirna tadguṇo bhavitumarhati / na khalu tadviśeṣaguṇā rūpādayastathā nivartante / ātmanaḥ pareṣāṃ ca śarīraguṇāḥ pratyakṣayogyāḥ, bāhyendriyagrāhyāśca; na ca tathā jñānādiriti nāso tadguṇaḥ /
body.translated_text: Moreover, consciousness, pleasure, and the like — which firmly exist in the body and depart only when opposed qualities intervene, like the fragrance of flower-ointment — cannot be qualities of that [body]. For a specific quality of that [substance]

body.text: atha deha ātmabhedasyāpratyakṣatve 'pi tasyānātmatvamacetanatvalakṣaṇamanu- mānāt setsyatītyāha

children.translated_text: 'asphutatve 'pi' ('even when unclear').

children.text: ti / yadvā-nanu saṅghātarūpo 'pi deha evātmopeyate lāghavāt / dehabhinnasaṅghātatvameva bhavatu parārthatvavyāpyamityatrāha
children.translated_text: Or alternatively — [objection:] let the body itself, even though having the form of an aggregate, be accepted as the self, due to parsimony. Let being-an-aggregate-different-from-the-body be what is pervaded by being-for-another. To this he says
'asphutatve' ('when unclear').

children.text:
ti / prathamāvataraṇikāyāṃ bhedasyā'tmabhedasya śarīre 'sphuṭatve-apratyakṣatve 'pītyarthaḥ / dvitīyasyāṃ ca parārthatvena śarīra ātmabhedasyāprasiddhatve 'pītyarthaḥ / tadasaṃbhavāt - tasmin-śarīre asaṃbhavaḥ-udayāyogaḥ tadasaṃbhavaḥ tasmāt / yadvā śarīra iti madhyamaṇinyāyenobhayānvayi / tadasaṃbhavāt-jñānasyāsaṃbhavādityarthaḥ / atra ca tacchabdayoravairūpyaṃ sahyam / tadguṇāntare tyatra tadruṇa ityatra ca tacchabdena śarīrasya
parāmarśanīyatvāt / śarīre jñānaguṇasyotpatterayogāccharīraviśeṣaguṇāntaravaidharmyācca na jñānaṃ śarīraviśeṣaguṇa iti kārikārthaḥ //6//
children.translated_text: In the first introductory statement, the meaning of 'even when the distinction — the distinction of self [from body] — in the body is unclear' is: even when not [established through] perception. And in the second, [the meaning is:] even when the distinction of self from the body is not established through being-for-another.

body.translated_text: Now, even if the distinction of the self from the body is not [established] through perception, its non-selfhood — characterized by non-consciousness — will be established through inference. Thus he says

body.text: śarīre jñānasyāsaṃbhavaṃ tāvadupapādayati

children.translated_text: 'sarva eva' ('every [specific quality] indeed').
'Preceded by a quality of the cause' means: having as its non-inherent cause a quality of the same kind inhering in its own substrate through inherence (<s>samavaya</s>).
'sambhaved'

children.text: diti / śarīrāvayaveṣu jñānasyābhāvāt, bhāve vā ekasminneva dehe 'nekacetanaprasaṅgāt na kāraṇaguṇapūrvakaṃ śarīre caitanyaṃ bhavet / viśeṣaguṇatvādakāraṇaguṇapūrvakatvamapi dehe jñānasyāsaṃbhavīti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: ('could arise'). Since knowledge is absent in the parts of the body — or, if present [in the parts], there would follow the consequence of multiple conscious beings in a single body — consciousness in the body cannot be preceded by a quality of the cause. Because it is a specific quality and not preceded by a quality of the cause.
'sakteh'

children.text: riti / sāmānyaguṇatvena śakterakāraṇaguṇapūrvakatvamupapadyate / sarvadravyavṛttitvācca sāmānyaguṇatvam / dṛśyatattatkāryeṇānumeyaḥ tatprati- yogī- tattatkāryeṇa nirūpyasvarūpaḥ prayojakatvena śaktayākhyo guṇaḥ sarvasminnapi dravye tattatkāryapratiniyato 'stīti ca
children.translated_text: ('of power'). Being a general quality, the non-precedence of power by a quality of the cause is accounted for. And it is a general quality because it exists in all substances. Its counter-correlate — that which is inferred by seeing the particular effects — is [understood through]
'The powers of all entities are objects of inconceivable knowledge'
— thus it is understood from the words of the jewel among <s>Puranas</s> — this is the purport.
'naivam'

children.text:
iti / naivaṃ-na sāmānyaguṇo jñānam / kintu śarīra evopagamādviśeṣaguṇaḥ / dravyatvanyūnavṛttiguṇatvaṃ ca tattvam / siddhāntaprakriyayedam / siddhānte paratvādi ca na guṇāntaram / kṣaṇasaṃbandhādhikyādinaiva
paratvādivyavahāranirvāhāditi bhāvaḥ / vaiśeṣikaprakriyayāpyāha
children.translated_text: ('not so'). 'Not so' — knowledge is not a general quality. Rather, since it is accepted as [residing] only in the body [on the opponent's view], it is a specific quality. And being a quality whose occurrence is not less than [that of] substance-hood is its true nature. This is according to the established system (<s>siddhanta</s>). In the established system,
'karyatve sati'

children.text:
ti / jñānaṃ viśeṣaguṇaḥ kāryatve sati ekavidhapratyakṣaviṣayatvādrūpādivat / saṅkhyāderdvīndriyagrāhyatvāttatra vyabhicāravāraṇāya ekavidheti pratyakṣaviśeṣaṇam / prabhābhittisaṃyoge vyabhicāravāraṇāya ekavidhapratyakṣaviṣayajātimattvaṃ vaktavyam / saṃyogatvajāterdvīndriyagrāhyatvānna doṣaḥ / ātmano mānasapratyakṣaviṣayatvāttatra vyabhicāravāraṇāya kāryatve satīti / evamapi prabhātvajātisvīkāre prabhāyāṃ, vāyoḥ spārśanopagame vā vāyau vyabhicāravāraṇāya ekavidhapratyakṣagrāhyajātīyaguṇatvāditi vaktavyam / guṇatvapraveśe ca kāryatve satīti cintyaprayojanamiti bodhyam / viśeṣaguṇalakṣaṇe ca jñānādibhinnatvaṃ na dātuṃ śakyaṃ jñānāderviśeṣaguṇatve prāmāṇike satīti ca bhāvaḥ / saṅghātaviśeṣāvayavivāde tu avayaveṣu caitanyābhāvādeva dehasya
caitanyaṃ na saṃbhavatīti cānusandheyamatra / nanu rasaviśeṣo gandhaviśeṣo vā mādako madaśabdavācyaḥ / sa ca viśeṣaguṇo na kāraṇaguṇapūrvaka iti kāryadravyaviseṣaguṇasya kāraṇaguṇapūrvakatvaniyamo durvaca ityatrā'ha
children.translated_text: ('when being an effect'). Knowledge is a specific quality because, being an effect, it is an object of a single type of perception — like color and the like. To exclude deviation in the case of number and the like, which are grasped by two sense organs, [the qualification] 'of a single type' [is added to] perception.
'dravyadinam'

children.text: mīti / kiṇvādīnāṃ sammardanādināvdyaṇukaparyantanāśe svatantraiḥ paramāṇubhirdravyāntarāvayavasaṃśleṣajanitamadairārabdhe surādravye kāraṇaguṇapūrvaka eva guṇa iti bhāvaḥ / atha tāmbūlarasarāge 'naikāntyamuktaniyamasya pariharati
children.translated_text: ('of substances and the like'). When the fermented ingredients (<s>kinva</s>) and the like are destroyed up to the dyad through processes like grinding, and when a liquor-substance is produced through the conjunction of the independent atoms with parts of other substances, and the intoxicating [powers] therein are produced — [these are] preceded by a quality of the cause.
'tambule'
('in the betel'). The meaning is clear.
'na ca sarire'

children.text: ti / prajñāyate-upalabhyate / pratijñāyate-sādhyate / dehāvayaveṣu caitanye sādhakābhāvamuktvā bādhakamapyāha
children.translated_text: ('nor in the body'). 'Prajnayate' means 'is perceived.' 'Pratijnayate' means 'is to be proved.' Having stated the absence of a proof for consciousness in the parts of the body, he also states the sublating [evidence] with
'tadupagama'

children.text: iti / aṅgāṅgitvābhāvaḥ - niyāmyaniyāmakabhāvalakṣaṇaguṇapradhānabhāvābhāvaḥ / ekacetananiyāmyatve hi śarīrāvayavānāṃ vyavahārāvisaṃvādo ghaṭate / teṣāmeva cetanatve tu parasparāniyamyatayā parasparavārtānabhijñatayā ca vyavahāravisaṃvādaḥ prasajyata iti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: ('acceptance of that'). 'Absence of the part-whole relation' means the absence of the relationship characterized by the controlled-controller relation, i.e., the absence of the principal-subordinate relation among qualities. For when the parts of the body are controlled by a single conscious [self], conventional practice is not contradicted. If those [parts]
'pratisandhane' ('in reconnection')

children.text: ti / yamadrākṣaṃ taṃ spṛśāmītyādipratisandhānasya tanmūlavyavahārasya ca vilopaḥ prasajyate / avayavacaitanye draṣṭuḥ spraṣṭuścānyānyatvāditi bhāvaḥ / aniṣṭāpattiriṣṭahāniścātrokte padadvayena / nānārūpatā-vibhinnajātīyarūpasamavīyitā / vijātīyarūpeṣu tantuṣu saṃhateṣu citrapratītimāha
children.translated_text: — the recognition 'What I saw, I now touch' and the conventional practice based on it would be destroyed. The purport is: if consciousness belonged to [individual] body-parts, the seer and the toucher would be different [persons]. The undesired consequence and the loss of the desired [consequence] are stated here by the two words. 'Manifold form' (<s>nānārūpatā</s>) — being constituted by forms belonging to different classes. When threads of heterogeneous forms are combined, he describes the variegated cognition [that arises] with
'each' (<s>pratyekam</s>)
and so forth.
'Thus' (<s>evam</s>)
and so forth. 'Even in its causes' — even in the threads, which are the causes of the variegated cloth. 'That' — the variegated form.
'Because of the absence of restriction to a single form'
— the meaning is: because of the absence of a single form that pervades [all of it] in the variegated cloth, which possesses manifold forms that do not pervade [it entirely].
'For the sole purpose of [the quality of] magnitude' (<s>mahattvaikārtha</s>)

children.text: ti / laukikaviṣayatayā dravyacākṣuṣe sāmānādhikaraṇyena mahattvaviśiṣṭodbhūtarūpasya samavāyena hetutvasaṃbhave hetutāvacchedakakoṭau vyāpyavṛttitvaviśeṣaṇe prayojanābhāvaḥ / tathā ca citrapaṭasya na cākṣuṣatvānupapattiriti bhāvaḥ / rūpasya vyāpyavṛttitvaniyame 'pyāha-
children.translated_text: and so forth. When, as a worldly object, the visual perception of a substance has the possibility of the manifested color, qualified by magnitude, serving as a cause through inherence in the [substance characterized by] co-referentiality [with magnitude] — there is no purpose in adding the qualification 'pervading' (<s>vyāpyavṛttitva</s>) to the condition for causal delimitation. And thus, the impossibility of the variegated cloth being perceptible to the eye does not follow — this is the purport. Even when the restriction of color to being pervading [is maintained], he says —
'Let it be' (<s>astu</s>)
and so forth.
'And not in this way' (<s>na caivam</s>)

children.text:
iti / tantugatavividharūpaiḥ paṭe citrarūpārambhavadavayavagatairanudbhūtacaitanyairdehe udbhūtacaitanyārambho 'stviti ca na śaṅkyam / cititanmātrasyaiva-caitanyasāmānyasyaiva mānābhāvena dehāvayaveṣvasaṃbhavāt / śarīrasya caitanyetadavayaveṣu caitanyakalpanā, tatkalpa
nāyāmeva śarīre caitanyasiddhirityanyo 'nyasaṃśrayāśceti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: and so forth. Just as with the diverse colors residing in the threads, a variegated form arises in the cloth — so too, one should not suspect that, from the unmanifested consciousness residing in the parts of the body, manifested consciousness arises in the body. Because consciousness as such (<s>cititanmātra</s>) — consciousness in general — has no means of valid knowledge [to establish its existence] in the parts of the body, and thus is impossible [there]. If consciousness [is posited] in the body [on the basis of] consciousness in its parts, then [the establishment of] consciousness in the body [depends on] the very assumption of consciousness in the parts — and thus there is circular reasoning (<s>anyonyāśraya</s>). This is the purport.
'By this' (<s>etena</s>)

children.text: ti / jñānasyeva sukhāderapi viśeṣaguṇasya na śarīradharmatvasaṃbhava iti bhāvaḥ / evaṃ
children.translated_text: and so forth. The purport is: just as with knowledge, the possibility that pleasure and the like — which are also specific qualities (<s>viśeṣaguṇa</s>) — are properties of the body is [equally] denied. 'Thus',
'the impossibility of those [qualities] in the body'

— has been explained.
Now he elucidates 'because of the dissimilarity with other qualities of that [body]' with
'even if' (<s>api ca</s>)

and so forth. 'Without the onset of an opposing quality' — without the consequence of a quality that would remove the prior quality. 'The fragrance of floral unguent' — the fragrance of garlands and sandalwood.
'Indeed, that is not' (<s>na khalu ta</s>)
and so forth.
This is the purport:

children.text: agnisaṃyogena rūpaparāvṛttāvapi tadaprasaṅge rūpasya yāvaddravyabhāvitvaṃ dṛṣṭam / na ca jñānādi sthiramevam / na cottarottaraviśeṣaguṇa eva pūrvapūrvajñānādivirodhīti vācyam / evamapi antyasya ciramavasthānaprasaṅgāditi / ayāvaddravyabhāvittvaṃ jñānādeḥ śarīraviśeṣaguṇāntarato vaidharmyamityuktaṃ bhavati / atha vaidharmyāntaraṃ dvidhā'ha
children.translated_text: Even when a change of color [occurs] through contact with fire, it is observed that color persists for the entire duration of the substance — and the absence of such a consequence [for knowledge is noted]. And it should not be said that only the next specific quality is the contradictory of the prior knowledge and the like — because even so, the consequence that the last [quality in a series] would persist for a long time [would follow]. The fact that knowledge and the like do not persist for the entire duration of the substance has been stated as their dissimilarity from the other specific qualities of the body. Now he states another [kind of] dissimilarity in two ways with
'of the self' (<s>ātmana</s>)

children.text: iti / svātmamātragrāhyatvaṃ manomātragrāhyatvaṃ ca jñānādeḥ śarīraviśeṣaguṇāntaravaidharmyamiti phalitam / rūpādayo hi śarīraguṇāḥ svaparagrāhyā bahirindriyagrāhyāśca /
children.translated_text: and so forth. The result is: being apprehensible solely by oneself, and being apprehensible solely by the mind — these are the dissimilarities of knowledge and the like from the other specific qualities of the body. For color and the like, which are qualities of the body, are apprehensible both by oneself and by others, and are apprehensible by the external sense organs.
'But knowledge and the like are not so' (<s>na ca tathā jñānādī</s>)

children.text: ti / atra prayogaḥ-jñānaṃ na śarīraviśeṣaguṇaḥ ayāvaddravyabhāvitvānmanomātragrāhyatvādvā yannaivaṃ tannaivaṃ yathā rūpādīti / evaṃ jñānasya śarīradharmatvābhāvasādhanena śarīrasyātmatvaṃ pratikṣiptaṃ bhavati / yathā-deho nātmā ājñātṛtvāddhaṭādivaditi /
children.translated_text: and so forth. Here the formal argument is: knowledge is not a specific quality of the body, because it does not persist for the entire duration of the substance, or because it is apprehensible solely by the mind — whatever is not of such a character is not of such a character, like color and the like. Thus, by establishing the absence of knowledge as a property of the body, the selfhood of the body has been refuted. Namely: the body is not the self, because it lacks knower-hood — like a pot and the like.
Moreover: 'because of being produced; because of [arising from] a specific configuration;
because of possessing color and the like; because of being material — the body is not the self, like a pot and the like.' (Verse 7)
'Because of having apertures; because of not being an embodied being; because of being a body — like a dead body;'
'by such proper reasonings, the consciousness of the body should be denied.' (Verse 8)

children.text: evaṃ pratyakṣavirodhāt, anvayamukhena sādhyamupasthāpadbhirudīritasādhanairapahṛtaviṣayatayā indriyāśrayatvādivyatirekihetavo na sādhyamupasthāpayitumīśate /
children.translated_text: Thus, because of the contradiction from direct perception, [the arguments] by those who present the provable through the positive method (<s>anvaya</s>) — [their] stated reasons, whose subject-matter has been removed [by the counter-arguments], namely reasons based on negative concomitance (<s>vyatireka</s>) such as 'because of being the substrate of the sense organs' and the like — are unable to present the provable.
(Thus ends the section on the refutation of the body-self doctrine.)

children.text: santu tarhīndriyāṇyevātmā / na ca tānīdantayā prathante; yena dehavadaha
children.translated_text: Then let the sense organs themselves be the self. And they do not shine forth as 'this' [i.e., as objects], so that — like the body — they would be excluded from the domain of the I-cognition.

body.translated_text: He first establishes the impossibility of knowledge in the body with

body.text: ṅkāragocarādbahiṣkrriyeran / nāpi tathodbhūtarūpādiguṇāni sthūlāni; yena tatpratibhāsa ivendriyagocaratve 'haṃpratyayasya rūpāvayavādipratītiḥ prasajyeta / tavdyāpāraphalaṃ ca jñānaṃ tadgāmi yuktaṃ snānādhyayanādiphalavat / ata eva satyapatāḥ draṣṭuścakṣuṣaḥ iti /
body.translated_text: Nor are they gross, possessing manifest qualities such as color and the like, so that — as in the case of the appearance of the body — if [the sense organs] were the object of the I-cognition, there would follow the consequence that the 'I'-awareness would be accompanied by the cognition of their component forms and parts. And knowledge, which is the fruit of their operation, appropriately belongs to them — like the fruits of bathing, study, and the like. For this very reason [it is stated]: 'The faculty of seeing is the seer, and of the eye' and so forth.

children.translated_text: (Thus ends the section on the preliminary argument for the sense-organs as self.)

body.text: tanna / vikalpāsahatvāt / tathā hi-kiṃ pratyekamindriyāṇi cetanāni, saṃbhūya vā? / yadi pratyekam, indriyāntaradṛṣṭasyendriyāntareṇa pratisandhānaṃ na syāt / asti ca tat- yamahamadrākṣaṃ tamahaṃspṛśāmīti / ata eva na saṃbhūyāpi cetanatvam / na hi pañcabhirindriyaiḥ saṃbhūyaikaṃ vastvanubhūyate 'nusandhīyate vā / ekendriyavigame ca prāyaṇaprasaṅgaśca / indriyacaitanye ca tattadindriyāpāye tattadindriyārthasmaraṇamapi na bhavet / na ca tavdyāpāraphalatayā tatsamavāyitvaṃ jñānasya / śastrādivyāpārajanmano 'pi pāpādeḥ parasamavāyitvāt / anyathā ca praṣṭurmṛtyupapattiṃ śaraṇāgataparityāgasya nṛśaṃsatāṃ cā'locya satyatapasastathā vacanam /
body.translated_text: That is not so, because it cannot withstand analysis. For thus: are the sense organs individually conscious, or collectively? If individually, then the recognition of what is seen by one sense organ through another would not be possible. But it does exist: 'What I saw, that I now touch.' For this very reason, there is no consciousness even collectively. For five sense organs do not collectively experience or recognize a single object. And if one sense organ were lost, there would be the consequence of death. And if consciousness belonged to the sense organs, then upon the loss of each sense organ, even the memory of the object of that sense organ would not occur. Nor does knowledge [simply] inhere in them because it is the fruit of their operation — because even sin (<s>pāpa</s>) and the like, which arise from the operation of weapons and the like, inhere in another [i.e., the agent, not the instrument]. Otherwise, considering that the questioner's death could result [from the weapon's operation], and considering the cruelty of abandoning those who have taken refuge — <s>Satyatapas</s> [made] his statement accordingly.

children.translated_text: (Thus ends the section on the refutation of the sense-organ-self doctrine.)

body.text: astu tarhi mana eva cetanam / tathā sati hi pūrvoktā doṣāḥ parihṛtā bhavanti / taddhi sarvendriyādhyakṣaṃ prajñāyate pratijñāyate ca / upapadyate cendriyāntareṇa pratisandhānam ; darśanānusandhānādhārasya manasa ekatvāt / tattadindriyāpāye 'pi smaraṇamapyupapadyata eva, manaso nityatvāt /
body.translated_text: Then let the mind itself be the conscious [self]. For in that case, the previously stated faults would be resolved. For it is understood and proclaimed as the superintendent of all the sense organs. And the recognition through one sense organ [of what was perceived by another] is also explained — because the mind, which is the substrate of observation and recognition, is one. And memory, even when a particular sense organ is lost, is also explained — because of the eternality of the mind.

children.translated_text: (Thus ends the section on the preliminary argument for mind as self.)

children.text: tadapi na; karaṇatvāccakṣurādivat / bāhyāntarasakalaviṣayasaṃvedanakaraṇatayā hi manaḥ prakalpyate / bāhyendriyeṣu yathāyathaṃ nijaviṣayasannikarṣabhāgiṣvapi yato na yugapadeva sarve viṣayāḥ pratīyante, ato 'vagacchāmaḥ-asti
children.translated_text: That too is not [correct], because [the mind] is an instrument (<s>karaṇa</s>), like the eye and the like. For the mind is posited as the instrument of cognition of all objects, both external and internal. Even when the external sense organs are each in contact with their respective objects as appropriate, since all objects are not cognized simultaneously, we understand: there exists

body.text: kiñcidaparamapi sādhanam, yatsāhāyakavirahānna sarve prakāśante, kaścidevaikaḥ pratīyate iti / tathā sukhādisaṃvedanānyapi karaṇavanti, kriyātvāt, saṃvedanatvādvā, rūpādijñānavaditi / tadevaṃ jñānakaraṇatayāvagatasya manasaḥ kathamiva jñāne kartṛtvam ?/ svātantryalakṣaṇaṃ hi tat / tacca svacchandānurodhena sādhyasiddhyanuguṇopakaraṇasaṃpādanasāmarthyam ; svasamavetameva vā guṇāntaraṃ tantrīkṛtya pravṛttiḥ / karaṇatvaṃ tu parādhiṣṭhānādhīnavyāpāratārūpapāra tantryaniyataṃ sādhakatamatvamiti kathamivaikatra manasi parasparaviruddha tadubhayadharmasaṃbandhaṃ pratipadyemahi ? / atha tadapi manaḥ karaṇāntareṇa smaraṇādiṣu kartṛbhāvamanubhavati, tathā sati saṃjñāmātre vivādaḥ / ya eva hi cakṣurādibhī rūpādin āntarakaraṇena ca sukhādīṃścetayate, sa evā'tmā / tasminneva cet manaḥsaṃjñā niveśyate, kāmaṃ niveśyatām / na naḥ kiñciddhīnam / kintu tadā sarvalaukikavyavahāro bādhyetetyalamanena /
body.translated_text: some further instrument, without whose assistance not all [objects] are manifest and only some particular one is cognized. Likewise, even the cognitions of pleasure and the like must have instruments, because they are actions — or because they are cognitions — like the cognition of color and the like. Thus, how could the mind — which is understood as an instrument of knowledge — have agency (<s>kartṛtva</s>) in knowledge? For agency is characterized by independence. And that [independence] is the capacity to accomplish the intended end by arranging the appropriate instruments according to one's own will; or activity by taking control of (<s>tantrīkṛtya</s>) some other quality inherent in oneself. But instrumentality (<s>karaṇatva</s>) is the most effective facilitation — determined by being other-directed (<s>pāratantrya</s>) — whose operation depends on being governed by another. So how could we accept both these mutually contradictory properties in a single [entity], the mind? Now if that mind too, by means of another instrument, experiences agency in memory and the like — then the dispute is merely about terminology. For the very one who cognizes colors and the like through the eyes and pleasure and the like through the internal instrument — that one is the self. If the designation 'mind' is to be assigned to that very one, let it be assigned — nothing is lost for us. But then all ordinary worldly convention would be violated — enough of this.

children.translated_text: (Thus ends the section on the refutation of the mind-self doctrine.)

children.text: āha- kimidaṃ mano nāma ? / nanūktamāntaraṃ jñānakaraṇaṃ dravyamiti / kiṃ punarasya sādhanam ? / nanuktaṃ yugapajjñānānutpattirmanaso liṅgamiti / uktaṃ nāma; tathāpi kathaṃ tattvāntarasiddhiḥ ?/ kalpayitvāpi hi tat yugapatsmaraṇānutpattyupapattaye 'vaśyāśrayaṇīyameva nimittāntaram / santi hi yugapadasya smartṛrnānārthānubhavabhāvitāḥ saṃskārāḥ / atha ca na sarve smaryante / kiñcideva kadācit smaryate / saṃskāronmeṣahetūpanipātakramāttathātvamiti cet, evamapi praṇidhānamātrodbodhanīyasaṃskārasya smṛtiyaugapadyamāpadyeta / yāvadanubhūtasakalaviṣayasusmūrṣayā sarvataḥ pratyāhṛtacetasaḥ sādhāraṇyena praṇidadhayo 'pi na sarva evārthāḥ smṛtimadhirohanti / yadi tu śubhāśubharūpatayā smaraṇānāmadṛṣṭavaśāvdyavasthā, kramajñānasvābhāvyādvā
children.translated_text: He says: What is this thing called 'mind'? [Reply:] Was it not stated — an internal substance that is an instrument of knowledge? [Objection:] But what is the evidence for it? [Reply:] Was it not stated — the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions is the mark (<s>liṅga</s>) of mind? [Objection:] Stated it may be; but still, how is the existence of a separate category established? For even if one postulates it, some other cause must necessarily be resorted to in order to explain the non-simultaneous arising of memories. For one who intends to remember numerous objects has latent impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>) conditioned by the experience of various objects, all [occurring] simultaneously. And yet not all are remembered — only something particular is remembered at some [particular] time. [Reply:] If [one says] this is due to the sequence of the arising of the causes that activate the latent impressions — even so, the simultaneous arising of memories would result, because the latent impressions to be activated by mere attentiveness (<s>praṇidhāna</s>) [would all be activated at once]. Even when one who has withdrawn the mind from all [other objects] — desiring to remember the totality of previously experienced objects — focuses attentively in a general manner, not all objects ascend to memory. But if the arrangement of memories — whether auspicious or inauspicious in form — is due to unseen merit (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>), or due to the natural character of sequential cognition

children.text: ātmanaḥ ; tathā sati bahirindriyeṣu ca yathā
children.translated_text: belonging to the self — then, in that case, even with regard to the external sense organs, when each

body.text: yathaṃ svaviṣayasaṃprayukteṣu tathaiva yugapajjñānānutpattirupapadyata iti kṛtamindriyāntareṇa /
body.translated_text: is in contact with its own object as appropriate, the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions is explained in the very same way — so the postulation of an additional instrument [viz., the mind] is superfluous.

body.text: syānmatam- kādācitkasya sukhāderātmasamavāyino bāhyaviṣayādṛṣṭādinimittakāraṇasyāsamavāyikāraṇena bhāvyam / taccātmamanaḥ- sannikarṣa iti manodravyasiddhiriti / tadasat / sukhaduḥkhādipūrvakālajanmano 'bhimatānabhimataviṣayasaṃparkajajñānasyā'tmasamavāyina evāsamavāyikāraṇatvāt / tasya ca viṣayasaṃprayuktendriyasaṃprayoga evā'tmasamaveto 'samavāyikāraṇam / taddheturapīndriyavyāpāraḥ prayatnamadṛṣṭaṃ cā'tmasamavetamapekṣamāṇādātmendriyasānnikarṣādasamavāyikāraṇāt / prayatnasya tu svapūrvakṣaṇavarti kartavyatājñānam / prayatna eva tvadṛṣṭasyāpīti nātmaviśeṣaguṇānāṃ buddhisukhaduḥkhecchādīnāmasamavāyikāraṇasāpekṣatayāpi dravyāntaraparikalpanaṃ nyāyyam /
body.translated_text: [Objection:] One might think: for an occasional [quality] like pleasure and the like, which inheres in the self, there must be a non-inherent cause (<s>asamavāyikāraṇa</s>) — [namely,] an external object, <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen merit/demerit), and other efficient causes. And that [non-inherent cause] is the contact of the self with the mind — and thus the existence of the mind-substance is established. [Reply:] That is wrong. Because the cognition — which arises prior to pleasure and pain and is itself inherent in the self — generated by the contact with a desired or undesired object, is itself the non-inherent cause. And the contact with a sense organ that is in contact with the object is itself the non-inherent cause inherent in the self. The operation of the sense organ, which is the cause of that [contact], and effort (<s>prayatna</s>) and <s>adṛṣṭa</s> — which are inherent in the self — are required by the non-inherent cause, namely the contact of the self with the sense organ. And the cause of effort is the cognition of what is to be done, residing in the immediately preceding moment. And effort alone [is the cause] even of <s>adṛṣṭa</s> — so it is not proper to postulate an additional substance as required by the non-inherent cause of the self's specific qualities such as cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, and the like.

children.text: yattu-nityadravyaviśeṣaguṇasya dravyāntarasaṃyoga evāsamavāyikāraṇam, pārthivaparamāṇuṣvagnisaṃyogādasamavāyikāraṇādrūpotpatteriti; tadapi sthavīyaḥ / pārthivaparamāṇuṣu rūpādayo dahanasaṃyogāditi kṛto 'vagatam ? / kāryadravye tathā darśanāditi cet, iha vā tahri kiṃ na dṛśyate iṣṭāniṣṭaprāptyavagamānantaraṃ sukhādirjāyata iti ?/ dṛṣṭakāraṇavyabhicāre hi kāraṇāntarānumānāvasaraḥ / na cehāsti vyabhicāraḥ / ataḥ prasiddhakāraṇabhāveṣveva yatra kāryasamavāyaḥ tat samavāyikāraṇam, yattu tatpratyāsannaṃ tadasamavāyi, yadanyat tannimittimiti vyavasthāśrayaṇamucitam / na tvanapekṣitāprasiddhadravyāntarasaṃyogābhyupagamena tasyāsamavāyikāraṇatvāśrayaṇam / kāraṇāntarānupalabdheḥ, dṛṣṭānusārāccāṇugatarūpādau tathābhyupagamaḥ / iha tu tadviparyayaḥ pradārśita eva / evamapi vyāptibalena yadi dravyāntarasaṃyogo 'numātavyaḥ, sa tarhi sparśavaddravyasamaveto bhautika eva copalabdha iti prasiddhadehādisaṃyoga evānumānaparyavasānānna navama
children.translated_text: As for [the objection] that 'the non-inherent cause of a specific quality of an eternal substance is exclusively the conjunction with another substance — as in the case of color arising in earthy atoms from conjunction with fire as the non-inherent cause' — that too is too hasty. How has it been ascertained that in earthy atoms, color and the like [arise] from conjunction with heat? [Reply:] If [one says] 'because in an effect-substance, such [color arising from fire-conjunction] is observed' — then here too, why is it not observed that pleasure and the like arise after the apprehension of a desired or undesired [object]? For the occasion for inferring another cause arises when there is deviation from the observed cause. And here there is no deviation. Therefore, it is proper to resort to the following determination: among the established causal factors, that in which the effect inheres is the inherent cause (<s>samavāyikāraṇa</s>); that which is proximate to it is the non-inherent [cause]; and what is other [than these two] is the efficient cause (<s>nimitta</s>). But it is not proper to accept as non-inherent cause the conjunction with an additional, undemanded, and unestablished substance. Because of the non-apprehension of another cause, and following what is observed, such an acceptance [is made] regarding color and the like in atoms. But here, the opposite has been demonstrated. Even so, if by the force of pervasion a conjunction with another substance is to be inferred, then — since that [substance must be] endowed with touch and therefore material, and since it is perceived only as inherent in [physical substances] — the terminus of inference is [merely] the conjunction with the already-established body and the like — so the establishment of a ninth

body.text: dravyasiddhiḥ /
body.translated_text: substance is not [achieved].

body.text: athocyeta-bhautikatve hi manasaḥ pṛthivyādyanyatamatvena bhavitavyam / taccānumānāntarairvyatirekamāpādayadbhiḥ pratyāsiddham / tathā hi-na pārthivaṃ manaḥ rasāvagamanimittendriyatvādrasanāvat / na pāthasīyam, gandhagrahaṇanimittondriyatvāk ghrāṇavat / evamataijasatvādyapi tattadindriyāgocaragrahaṇanimittatayā śakyādhyavasānamityabhautikatvaṃ manasa iti / tadanupapannam / dharmiviśeṣaviparītasādhanāt / rasāvagamanimittendriyatvamapārthivatvamiva pāthasīyatvamapi samarthayati / evaṃ sādhanāntarāṇyapi bhūtāntaravyatikeramivā'mīyabhūtabhāvamāpādayanti / atha śabdasparśarūparasagandheṣu yadguṇagrāhi yadindriyam, tadeva tadguṇakabhūtārabdham; hanta tarhi tadeva taditarabhūtavyatirekitayāpyavagatamiti na tadavagamakatāmātreṇābhimatavyatirekasiddhiḥ / api ca śabdādiguṇāvagamasādhāraṇasādhanatayā śarīramiva pāñcabhautikam, ekadvitrādimayaṃ vā itarabhūtasaṃsṛṣṭamastu manaḥ / yathā'mnāyate annamayaṃ hi somya mana iti / tanna tatprakṛtitvapratipādanaparam, apitu tadadhīnavṛttitāmātrapradarśanārtham āpomayaḥ prāṇaḥ ityādivat / ata evāpavargadaśāyāmapi mano 'nuvṛttiḥ / darśitaṃ hi tatraivāṣṭame manasaitān kāmān paśyan ramate mano 'sya daivaṃ cakṣuriti / tathā parasyāśca devatāyāḥ so 'nyaṃ kāmaṃ manasā dhyāyīteti mahopaniṣadi / manasaiva jagatsṛṣṭimiti ca purāṇe / ucyate-satyamevam / dravyāntaraparikalpanāto varamevaṃ vā'śrayaṇamityuktam / paramārthatastu na bhautikam, nāpi navamaṃ dravyam / kva tarhīdānīṃ manaḥśabdaḥ ?/ buddhāveva / ata eva hi buddhimān manasvīti vyapadiśyate / manaso 'vasthābhaidāśca drāgevāparokṣyante kṣubhitaṃ me manaḥ, prasannaṃ me mana iti / evaṃ ca manasaḥ karaṇatayā vyapadeśo buddhyahaṅkārayoriva vṛttibhedapradarśanaparaḥ pūrveṣāmiti /
body.translated_text: Now if it is said — if <s>manas</s> (mind) were <s>bhautika</s> (elemental), it would have to be identical with one of the elements such as earth and so on. And that is contradicted by other inferences establishing its distinctness from each. For instance — <s>manas</s> is not made of earth (<s>pārthiva</s>), because it is a sense organ whose function is the apprehension of taste, like the tongue. It is not made of water (<s>pāthasīya</s>), because it is a sense organ whose function is the apprehension of smell, like the nose. Similarly, its non-fiery nature and so on can be inferred from its being the instrument of apprehending what is beyond the range of each respective sense organ — thus <s>manas</s> is non-elemental (<s>abhautika</s>). That is untenable, because the proof establishes the opposite of the intended property-distinction. The property of being a sense organ whose function is the apprehension of taste establishes not only non-earthiness but also its being made of water. Likewise, the other proofs establish not merely distinctness from one element but also identity with another element. Now, if the rule is that whichever sense organ apprehends a particular quality among sound, touch, form, taste, and smell is itself composed of the element possessing that quality — well then, that very sense organ is also known as distinct from other elements, so mere apprehension of a quality does not establish the intended distinctness. Moreover, since it is a common instrument for apprehending qualities like sound and so on, <s>manas</s> may be made of all five elements like the body, or made of one, two, three, or more elements mixed with other elements. As the scripture declares: "<s>manas</s> is indeed made of food (<s>annamaya</s>), O <s>Somya</s>." But that statement is not intended to teach that food is its material cause; rather, it is meant to show merely that its functioning depends on food, just as in "<s>prāṇa</s> is made of water (<s>āpomaya</s>)" and similar passages. For this very reason, <s>manas</s> continues to exist even in the state of <s>apavarga</s> (liberation). For it has been shown in that very eighth [chapter]: "Seeing these desires with <s>manas</s>, he rejoices; <s>manas</s> is his divine eye." And in the <s>Mahopaniṣad</s>: "He should meditate on other desires with <s>manas</s>" — this regarding the Supreme Deity as well. And in the <s>Purāṇa</s>: "The world was created by <s>manas</s> alone." It is replied — this is indeed true. It has been said that rather than postulating a separate substance, it is better to resort to this view. But in ultimate truth, <s>manas</s> is neither elemental nor a ninth substance. Where then does the word '<s>manas</s>' apply? To <s>buddhi</s> (intellect) itself. For this very reason, one who has <s>buddhi</s> is designated as '<s>manasvī</s>' (wise/spirited). And the states of <s>manas</s> are directly perceived without any difference — 'my <s>manas</s> is agitated,' 'my <s>manas</s> is serene.' Thus, the designation of <s>manas</s> as an instrument, like <s>buddhi</s> and <s>ahaṅkāra</s> (ego-sense), is intended by the earlier teachers to indicate different modes of functioning.

body.text: ucyate-yadi buddhireva manaḥ ; yadi vā dravyāntaram; ubhayadhāpi tasya na cetanatvamiti kimanenāpratijñātasvarūpavimarśena /
body.translated_text: It is replied — whether <s>buddhi</s> itself is <s>manas</s>, or whether it is a separate substance, in either case it is not conscious (<s>cetana</s>) — so what is the point of this examination of a nature that has not been asserted?

children.translated_text: (Thus ends the incidental section examining the nature of <s>manas</s>)

children.text: astu tarhi prāṇa evā'tmā, tathā sati tadanvayini śarīre sātmakatvapratītiḥ, tadvirahiṇi nirātmakatvapratītiścopapadyeyātām / dehādutkrāntirlokāntaragamanaṃ dehāntarasañcāraścopapadyantetarām,
children.translated_text: Then let <s>prāṇa</s> (vital breath) itself be the <s>ātman</s> (self). In that case, the perception that a body possessing <s>prāṇa</s> has a self, and the perception that a body devoid of <s>prāṇa</s> is without a self — both would be explained.

body.text: gatvarasvābhāvyāt prāṇasya / itarathā paramamahato mahataśca sparśavirahiṇaḥ parispandānupapatterutkrāntigatyāgatiśrutayo bhāktāḥ syuḥ /
body.translated_text: Departure from the body, travel to other worlds, and passage into another body would also be explained, since <s>prāṇa</s> is by nature capable of movement. Otherwise — since for something supremely great and great yet devoid of touch, movement would be impossible — the scriptural statements about departure, going, and coming would have to be taken in a figurative sense.

children.translated_text: (Thus ends the section presenting the prima facie view of <s>prāṇa</s> as <s>ātman</s>)

body.text: idamapyasat; vāyutvādeva bāhyavāyuvat prāṇasya caitanyānupapatteḥ / vṛttihīne 'pyātmani suṣuptau prāṇasya vṛttimattvācca / tadvṛttyā hi suptasyāpi saptadhātubhāvenāśitapītadravyapariṇāmaḥ ; śvāsapraśvāsau ca / tanutaratejobannānuviddhaḥ kauṣṭhyamāruto hi prāṇaḥ / sa ca kaṇṭhamukhanāsābhyantare bahiśca recitaḥ tvacā spṛśyamāno ghaṭādiriva sphuṭamanātmatayā cakāsti /
body.translated_text: This too is untenable; because <s>prāṇa</s>, being air (<s>vāyu</s>), cannot possess consciousness (<s>caitanya</s>), just like external air. And because even when the <s>ātman</s> is without activity in deep sleep (<s>suṣupti</s>), <s>prāṇa</s> continues to function. For through its activity, even in a sleeping person, the consumed food and drink are transformed through the seven bodily constituents (<s>saptadhātu</s>); and inhalation and exhalation continue. For <s>prāṇa</s> is the internal air (<s>kauṣṭhya mārutaḥ</s>), pervaded by the subtlest fire and food. And this <s>prāṇa</s>, exhaled through the throat, mouth, and nostrils and externally, being tangible to the skin, clearly manifests as non-self, like a pot and similar objects.

body.text: atraiva sādhye sādhanāntarāṇi cāha

children.translated_text: Because of being originated —

children.text: dityādikārikādvayena / pārārthyaṃ bhrotrkrantarārthatvam / tacca saṅghātatvāt / bhūtatvambahirindriyagrāhyaviśeṣaguṇavattvam / etairhetubhiḥ śarīre cetanabhinnatvaṃ sādhyam / nyāyyaiḥ-pratijñādyavayavapañcakātmakanyāyapratipādyarūpapañcakopapanneḥ / varṣmaṇaḥ- śarīrasya / citiḥ jñānam //7//8//
children.translated_text: this is said through the pair of <s>kārikā</s>s beginning with this. <s>Pārārthya</s> means being for the sake of another, i.e., for the sake of another entity. And that follows from being an aggregate (<s>saṅghāta</s>). <s>Bhūtatva</s> means possessing specific qualities that are apprehensible by the external senses. Through these reasons, distinctness from the conscious entity (<s>cetana</s>) in the body is established. 'By valid means' (<s>nyāyyaiḥ</s>) — endowed with the five forms that are demonstrable through a valid inference consisting of the five members beginning with the thesis (<s>pratijñā</s>). Of the body (<s>varṣmaṇaḥ</s>). <s>Citi</s> means knowledge. //7//8//

body.translated_text: He now states additional proofs for this same proposition.

body.text: samarthitametāvatā dehasyānātmatvaṃ pratyakṣānumānābhyām / etadvādhitatvamāha dehe ātmatvaṃ sādhayatāṃ kevalavyatikeriṇām

children.translated_text: Thus —

By means of positive concomitance (<s>anvaya</s>) — through the invariable co-presence; as having a refuted thesis — as having the proposition contradicted; to establish — to settle.
Now he introduces the view that the senses (<s>indriya</s>) are the self.
Then let —

children.text:
ti / dehātmatvapakṣoktāni dūṣaṇāni
nātra pakṣe prasajyanta ityāha
children.translated_text: The refutations stated against the view that the body is the self do not apply in this position, he says.
And those [objections] do not —
through this pair of statements. Having stated the absence of refutation, he also states something positive in favor of the position.
In its operation —

children.text: ti / jñānamindriyadharmaḥ, indriyavyāpāraphalatvāt, yavdyāpāraphalaṃ yat tattanniṣṭham, yathā snānādhyayanādivyāpāraphalaṃ śaucākṣararāśigrahaṇādi snātradhyetṛsamavetamiti prayogo bodhyaḥ / indriyasya vyāpāraḥ- arthasannikarṣārthendriyapravṛttiḥ, arthenendriyasya sannikarṣa eva vā / hetau dravyabhinnabhāvatve satīti viśeṣaṇaṃ deyam / tena ghaṭataddhvaṃsānukūlavyāpāravato daṇḍāderghaṭavattvādyabhāve 'pi na kṣatiḥ / indriyātmatve 'numānamuktvā'ptavākyamapi saṃvādarūpaṃ nirdiśati
children.translated_text: Knowledge is a property of the sense organ (<s>indriya</s>), because it is the result of the operation of the sense organ. Whatever is the result of whatever operation inheres in that [agent of the operation], just as the results of the operations of bathing, studying, and so forth — such as purity, grasping collections of syllables, and so on — inhere in the bather, the student, and so on. This is the form of the inference to be understood. The operation of the sense organ is the activity of the sense organ directed toward contact with its object, or the very contact of the sense organ with the object. The qualification 'when there is non-difference from the substance as the locus' must be added. Thereby, even though a stick and such things, whose operation is conducive to a pot and its destruction, do not possess pot-hood and so on, there is no difficulty. Having stated the inference for the selfhood of the senses, he also points out the corroborating authoritative statement (<s>āptavākya</s>).
For this very reason —
He refutes the selfhood of the senses (<s>indriya</s>).
That is not so —

children.text: ti / vikalpāsahatvaṃ nāma vikalpadharmiṇaḥ saṃbhāvitayāvatkoṭivikalpena vikalpitayāvatkoṭyanyatamakoṭisaṃbandhasyāpyanarhasvarūpatvam / kṣodakṣamatvābhāva iti yāvat / pratyakṣabādhābhāve 'pi yauktikabādho 'stīndriyātmatva iti hārdam / pratyekendriyacaitanyapakṣe nānāsvāmika iva grāma ekasminneva dehe nānācetanādhiṣṭānānnityakalahādi prasajyate iti dūṣaṇaṃ hṛdi nādhāya dūṣaṇāntaramāha
children.translated_text: The inability to withstand the dilemma (<s>vikalpāsahatva</s>) means that the entity subject to the dilemma, when examined through the alternatives of the possible options, has a nature that is incompatible with any of those alternatives — that is, it lacks the capacity to withstand scrutiny. The purport is that even in the absence of direct perceptual refutation, there is logical refutation of the selfhood of the senses. In the view that each individual sense is conscious, the objection is that — like a village with many owners — in a single body with many conscious entities presiding over it, there would be perpetual conflict and so on. Without dwelling on this objection, he states another objection.
In another sense organ —
This objection is also common to the view that the self is the aggregate of senses. He states this.
For this very reason —
For this very reason — precisely because of the impossibility of the aforementioned recognition (<s>pratisandhāna</s>). He now establishes that very point.
For it is not the case that —

children.text: ti / indriyasaṅghāto nānubhavitā, nāpyanusmartā / tathā hi - saṅghāto yadi saṃyogo bahutvasaṅkhyā vā, tarhi guṇatvādeva na jñātṛtvasaṃbhavaḥ / yadi saṃyuktānāṃ bahūnāmeva saṅghātatvena vivakṣā, tadāpi na bahūnāmindriyāṇāṃ cākṣuṣāśrayatā spārśanāśrayatā vā / tathā ca draṣṭuḥ spraṣṭuścānyānyatvāduktapratisandhānānupapattireveti bhāvaḥ / indriyasaṅghātasyā'tmatve doṣāntaramāha
children.translated_text: The aggregate of senses (<s>indriyasaṅghāta</s>) is neither the experiencer nor the one who remembers. For — if the aggregate is conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>), or the number plurality (<s>bahutva</s>), then being a quality (<s>guṇa</s>), the possibility of being a knower does not arise. If the intention is that the aggregate means just the many conjoined [senses] themselves, even then, the many senses do not serve as the locus of visual [cognition] or the locus of tactile [cognition]. And thus, since the seer and the toucher are different from each other, the aforementioned impossibility of recognition follows. He states another defect in the selfhood of the aggregate of senses.
When one sense organ [is destroyed] —

children.text: ti / saṅghātasya tāvataiva vinaṣṭatvānnirātmakatvena dehasya maraṇaprasaktiriti bhāvaḥ / pratyekasaṅghātapakṣadvayasādhāraṇaṃ doṣāntaramāha
children.translated_text: Since the aggregate would be destroyed by just that much [loss], the body would become without a self, and death would follow. He states another defect common to both the individual and aggregate positions.
When a sense organ —

children.text:
ti / draṣṭuścakṣuṣo vināśe mayedaṃ dṛṣṭamiti smṛteranupapattiḥ / vidyamānasyādraṣṭṛtvāt / anyadṛṣṭasyānyena smṛtyayogāditi bhāvaḥ / indriyacaitanye
bādhakānyuktāni / atha tatsādhakamanumānaṃ dūṣayati
children.translated_text: Upon the destruction of the eye which was the seer, the memory 'I saw this' would be impossible — because the existing [sense organ] was not the seer [at that time]; and because what was seen by one cannot be remembered by another. He states the refutations of sense-consciousness. Now he refutes the inference that supports it.
And it is not the case that in its operation —

children.text: ti / pāpāderityādipadena dvaidhībhāvo 'pi grāhyaḥ / tayośchettṛcchaidyagatatayā śastre 'samavetatvāvdyabhicāra iti bhāvaḥ / atra vipakṣe bādhakavirahādaprayojakatvamapi bodhyam / atha satyatapaso vacanaṃ karaṇe kartṛtvopacāreṇa pravṛttamanyaparaṃ nendriyacaitanye pramāṇamityāha
children.translated_text: The word '<s>ādi</s>' after '<s>pāpa</s>' (sin) should be understood to include bifurcation as well. The <s>vyabhicāra</s> (deviation/inconclusiveness) consists in the fact that both [results, namely sin and merit] belong to the cutter and the cut respectively, and thus do not inhere in the instrument. Here it should also be understood that there is ineffectiveness due to the absence of a counter-proof in the opposing instance. Now, the statement of <s>Satyatapas</s> is applied to the instrument through figurative attribution of agency (<s>kartṛtva</s>) to the instrument (<s>karaṇa</s>), and has a different purport; it is not a valid authority for sense-consciousness. He says —
Otherwise —
The statement of <s>Satyatapas</s> takes the form of a reply to a question posed by a hunter who had entered his hermitage in pursuit of a forest deer.
"The eye that sees does not have a tongue —"
and so on. On this subject, the following verse was endorsed by our revered teacher (<s>gurucaraṇa</s>):

children.text: yā paśyati na sā brūte sā na paśyati / dṛṣṭirvakti kathaṃ vyādha vāṇī vā vīkṣate katham //
children.translated_text: "That which sees does not speak, and that [which speaks] does not see. How can sight speak, O hunter, or how can speech see?"

children.text:
iti / anena praṣṭā vyādha iti gamyate / akathane 'śanāyāpīḍitasya vyādhasya maraṇaprasaṅgaṃ, kathane ca śaraṇāgataparityāganibandhanaṃ mahatpāpaṃ paryālocya evaṃ
vaktoktiḥ kṛtā maharṣiṇeti bodhyam /
atha mana ātmatvapakṣamupakṣipati
children.translated_text:
By this, it is understood that the questioner was a hunter. It should be understood that the great sage made this statement after reflecting that if he did not speak, there would be the danger of death for the hunter tormented by hunger, but if he did speak, there would be great sin arising from the abandonment of one who had taken refuge.
Now he introduces the view that <s>manas</s> (mind) is the <s>ātman</s> (self).
Then let —
[this be the case].
Its —

children.text: ti / mano hi pradhānāṃ sarvendriyaprerakaṃ ca gamyate pramāṇato, vyavahliyate ca tathetyarthaḥ / indriyātmatvapakṣoktānāṃ smṛtipratisandhānānupapattinānātmaprasaṅgādidoṣāṇāṃ nātra pakṣe prasaṅga ityāha
children.translated_text: For <s>manas</s> is understood from authoritative sources to be the chief [inner organ] and the impeller of all sense organs, and it is also commonly spoken of as such — this is the meaning. The defects stated against the view that the senses are the self — such as the impossibility of memory and recognition (<s>pratisandhāna</s>), the consequence of multiple selves, and so on — do not apply in this position, he says.
And it is explained —

through this pair of statements.
He refutes the selfhood of <s>manas</s>.
That too is not —
[acceptable].
Because of being an instrument (<s>karaṇa</s>) —

children.text: diti sarvatra jñāne karaṇatvānmanaso na tatra kartṛtvamāśrayatvaṃ saṃbhavati / mano hi na pratyakṣaviṣayaḥ / kintu yugapajjñānānutpattiliṅgena sakalajñāne karaṇaviśeṣatayānumīyate / tasya ca na jñātṛtvaṃ cakṣurāderiva saṃbhavatīti bhāvaḥ / etadevopapādayati
children.translated_text: since <s>manas</s> is an instrument in all cognition, agency (<s>kartṛtva</s>) and being the locus [of cognition] are not possible for it. <s>Manas</s> is indeed not an object of direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>). Rather, it is inferred as a specific instrument in all cognition through the inferential mark that simultaneous cognitions do not arise. And for this [<s>manas</s>], knower-hood (<s>jñātṛtva</s>) is not possible, just as it is not for the eye and other [sense organs]. He now establishes this very point.
When the external senses —

children.text: ti / yatsāhāyakavirahāt-yatsahakāravirahāt / (sahāyasya karma-sāhāyakam) yatsannikarṣavirahāditi yāvat / tattadarthagrāhakendriyasyeti śeṣaḥ / evaṃ bāhyārtheṣu yugapajjñānānāmanutpattiliṅgena sarvendriyasahakāritvenāṇubhūtasya manasaḥ karaṇaviśeṣasyānumānamuktvā āntarasukhādisākṣātkāreṣu karaṇatayāpi manaso 'numānamāha
children.translated_text: In the absence of whose assistance — in the absence of whose cooperation (the action of an assistant is assistance); in the absence of whose contact — this is the meaning. The remainder is: of the sense organ that apprehends the respective object. Thus, having stated the inference for <s>manas</s> as a specific instrument through cooperation with all sense organs, based on the inferential mark that simultaneous cognitions of external objects do not arise, he now states the inference for <s>manas</s> as an instrument also in the direct apprehension of internal [states] such as pleasure and so on.
Similarly, pleasure and so on —

children.text:
ti / nanu karaṇatayānumitasyaiva manaso jñānādau kartṛtvamapyastu lāghavā
diti cettatrāha
children.translated_text: Now, if one objects: let that very <s>manas</s> which has been inferred as an instrument also have agency in cognition and so on, for the sake of parsimony — to this he replies:
That being so —

children.text: iti / karaṇasya kartṛtvaṃ na saṃbhavati / karaṇatvakartṛtvayorvirodhāt svātantryapāratantryalakṣaṇayoriti bhāvaḥ / kartṛtvakaraṇatvasvarūpabhedaṃ vivṛṇoti
children.translated_text: Instrumentality (<s>karaṇatva</s>) and agency (<s>kartṛtva</s>) are not compatible in the same entity, because of the mutual opposition between instrumentality and agency, which are characterized respectively by dependence (<s>pāratantrya</s>) and independence (<s>svātantrya</s>). He elaborates the essential distinction between agency and instrumentality.
Independence (<s>svātantrya</s>) —

children.text: tyādinā / kartṛtvaṃ nāma svecchādhīnasvapravṛttikatvarūpasvātantryaniyataṃ svecchayaiva sādhyasiddhyaupayikasāmagrīsaṃpādanasāmarthyam / karaṇatvaṃ ca parecchāprayātnādhīnasvavyāpṛtīkatvalakṣaṇapāratantryaniyataṃ parasya ripsitakriyāniṣpattau prakṛṣṭopakārakatvalakṣaṇam / na caitayorekatra samāveśaḥ saṃbhavatīti bhāvaḥ / yadyapi cetanasyaikatra kartṛtvaṃ karaṇatvaṃ ca saṃbhavennāmā'kārabhedataḥ / athāpi manasaścaitanye dṛḍhatarapramāṇābhāvāt lokasiddhavyāptyā ca cakṣurādivatparasya cetanasya sukhādyanubhavakaraṇatayaiva siddherna manaso jñātṛtvam / vastutastu atyantātīndriyeṣvartheṣu śāstrameva pramāṇam / tataśca mano vijñānamayasya jīvasyopakaraṇatayaiva siddhyatīti hārdam / nanu rūpasukhādibāhyāntarapadārthānubhaveṣu mana eva kartṛ / āntarasukhādyanubhave karaṇaṃ tvāntaramanyatkalpyata iti śaṅkate
children.translated_text: and so on. Agency (<s>kartṛtva</s>) is the capacity to accomplish the requisite aggregate of means for achieving the desired end, characterized by the independence (<s>svātantrya</s>) of having one's own activity depend on one's own will. Instrumentality (<s>karaṇatva</s>) is the characteristic of being preeminently helpful in the accomplishment of the action desired by another, characterized by the dependence (<s>pāratantrya</s>) of having one's own activity depend on another's will and effort. And these two cannot coexist in a single entity. Although for a conscious being (<s>cetana</s>), agency and instrumentality might coexist in one entity in different respects, nevertheless, since there is no strong proof for the consciousness of <s>manas</s>, and since by commonly established invariable concomitance, <s>manas</s> is established merely as an instrument for the experience of pleasure and so on by another conscious entity — like the eye and other [sense organs] — knower-hood does not belong to <s>manas</s>. In truth, regarding matters entirely beyond the senses, scripture alone is the valid authority. And from scripture, <s>manas</s> is established only as an instrument of the individual self (<s>jīva</s>) who is of the nature of consciousness (<s>vijñānamaya</s>). Now, if one objects: <s>manas</s> alone is the agent in experiences of external and internal objects such as form, pleasure, and so on, and some other internal [organ] should be postulated as the instrument for the internal experience of pleasure and so on —
Now, if that too —
He replies:
In that case —

children.text: tī / evaṃ sati asmadiṣṭasya jñātaryantaḥ- karaṇabhedasya na kāpyanupapattiḥ / saṃjñā tu aicchikīti nārthe vivāda ityarthaḥ / jñāturātmano manaḥsaṃjñāyāṃ vyavahāravirodhamāha
children.translated_text: [The word ends with] '-tī.' This being so, there is no impossibility whatsoever regarding the distinction of the internal organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>) from the knower, which is our accepted [position]. The designation is merely conventional — the meaning is that there is no dispute about the substance. He states the conflict with common usage when the designation <s>manas</s> (mind) is applied to the knower, the self.
'However' (<s>kintu</s>) —

children.text:
iti / mana iti nātmano vyavahāro laukikānāṃ vaidikānāṃ ca / ato manaḥsaṃjñā'tmani vyavahāravisaṃvādādapārtheti bhāvaḥ /
athātra paramācāryo 'yaṃ vimarśakabhūmikāmāsthitaḥ prasaṅgāt manasastattvavicāraṃ prakramate
children.translated_text:
thus. The designation 'mind' (<s>manas</s>) is not used for the self in either worldly or Vedic [usage]. Therefore, applying the designation <s>manas</s> to the self is pointless because it contradicts established usage — this is the purport.
Now here, the supreme teacher [<s>Yāmuna</s>], having assumed the role of an examiner, incidentally undertakes an investigation into the true nature of <s>manas</s> (mind).
He says —

children.text: ti / kaścidvimarśaka ityādiḥ / vimarśaścāyaṃ tārkikābhimatānāṃ manaḥsādhakayuktīnāṃ kṣodakṣamatvābhāvapradarśanārthaḥ /
children.translated_text: thus. 'A certain examiner' and so forth. And this examination is for the purpose of demonstrating that the arguments adduced by the logicians (<s>Tārkikas</s>) to establish <s>manas</s> are incapable of withstanding scrutiny.
'What is this' —

children.text: iti / kimiti svarūpapraśnaḥ / kiṃpunariti pramāṇapraśnaḥ / manasi pramāṇamākṣipati
children.translated_text: thus. 'What' is a question about the essential nature (<s>svarūpa</s>). 'What, moreover' is a question about the means of valid cognition (<s>pramāṇa</s>). He challenges [the opponent to provide] a <s>pramāṇa</s> for <s>manas</s>.
'It has been stated, has it not' —

children.text: tyādinā /yugapajjñānānutpattiliṅgena dravyāntaramāntaraṃ karaṇaṃ na siddhyati / adṛṣṭādisahakāraviraheṇaiva yugapajjñānānutpattyupapatteriti bhāvaḥ / yugapatsmaraṇānāmanutpattaye 'dṛṣṭasahakāraviraho 'vaśyameva śaraṇīkaraṇīyaḥ svīkṛte 'pyāntarakaraṇa ityāha
children.translated_text: and so forth. Through the inferential mark (<s>liṅga</s>) of the non-arising of simultaneous cognitions (<s>yugapat-jñāna</s>), a separate substance — an internal instrument (<s>āntara karaṇa</s>) — is not established. The purport is that the non-arising of simultaneous cognitions can be accounted for merely by the absence of the cooperation of <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen force) and the like. He states that even if one accepts an internal organ, the absence of the cooperation of <s>adṛṣṭa</s> must necessarily be resorted to in order to [explain] the non-arising of simultaneous recollections —
'Even after postulating' —
thus. 'Conditioned by the experience of various objects' means 'produced by the experience of various objects.'
'The <s>saṃskāra</s> (mental impression)' —

children.text: ti / saṃskārasyonmeṣaheturudbodhakaḥ / saṃskārodbodhakasamavadhānakramāt smṛtīnāmayaugapadyam /udbuddhasaṃskārasyaiva smṛtihetutvāt / udbodhasya kramabhāvitvācceti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: thus. The awakener (<s>udbodhaka</s>) is the cause of the <s>saṃskāra</s>'s arising. The non-simultaneity of recollections is due to the sequential co-occurrence of the <s>saṃskāra</s> and its awakener. Because only an awakened <s>saṃskāra</s> is the cause of recollection, and because the awakening occurs sequentially — this is the purport.
'Even so' —

children.text: ti / praṇidhānaṃ-manaso 'vadhānena cintanam / yeṣāmarthasaṃskārāṇāṃ sādhāraṇamudbodhakaṃ praṇidhānaṃ kṛtamanubhūtayāvadarthasmṛtīcchayaikadaiva tadāpi na yāvadarthasmṛtayo yugapat jāyante / tatsatyapi nānārthasmṛtiṣu dṛṣṭakāraṇe 'dṛṣṭasahakāravirahādeva na smṛtiyaugapadyam, kintu ekasyaivaikadā bhavati smṛtiradṛṣṭasahakārādityeṣitavyamiti bhāvaḥ / śubhāśubharūpatayā-sukhaduḥkhajanakatayā / nanvevamapi sukhahetvarthānāṃ śubhādṛṣṭabalādyugapatsmaraṇāni syuriti cettatrāha
children.translated_text: thus. <s>Praṇidhāna</s> (attentive contemplation) is the mind's thinking with focused attention. Even when attentive contemplation — which is the common awakener of the <s>saṃskāras</s> of [various] objects — has been applied at one and the same time, with the desire to remember all the objects one has experienced, even then recollections of all those objects do not arise simultaneously. Even granting that, since there is an observed cause for the recollections of various objects, it is due to the absence of the cooperation of <s>adṛṣṭa</s> alone that there is no simultaneity of recollections; rather, only one recollection occurs at a time due to the cooperation of <s>adṛṣṭa</s> — this should be understood as the purport. 'In the form of auspicious and inauspicious' means 'in the capacity of producing pleasure and pain.' [Objection:] Even so, there might be simultaneous recollections of objects that cause pleasure, by the force of auspicious <s>adṛṣṭa</s>. To this he responds —
'In sequence' —

children.text:
ti / kramikajñānabhāktvalakṣaṇātmasvabhāvabalādadṛṣṭasahakāravirahācca smṛtiyaugapadyasyeva bāhyārthajñānayaugapadyasyāpi pariharaṇasaṃbhavāt nāṇubhūtaṃ manobāhyendriyasahakāri karaṇāntaramāntaraṃ kalpanīyamiti samuditāśayaḥ /
manasi pramāṇāntaramupakṣipati
children.translated_text:
thus. Since it is possible to account for the non-simultaneity of cognitions of external objects as well — just as [one accounts for] the non-simultaneity of recollections — by the inherent nature of the self, characterized by sequential cognition, and by the absence of the cooperation of <s>adṛṣṭa</s>, there is no need to postulate an additional internal instrument (<s>manas</s>) as a minute [substance] that cooperates with the external sense organs as a separate instrument. This is the combined purport.
He introduces another means of valid cognition regarding <s>manas</s> —
'It might be held' —

children.text:
iti / atra prayogaḥ- sukhādi sāsamavāyihetukaṃ bhāvakāryatvātkāryarūpādivaditi / asamavāyihetuśca sukhādāvātmamanaḥsaṃyoga eva, anyasyāsaṃbhavāditi hṛdayam /
ātmetyādi bāhyetyādi ca ṣaṣṭhyantaṃ padadvayaṃ bahuvrīhivṛttaṃ sukhāderviśeṣaṇam / padadvayena ca sukhādāvātmanaḥ samavāyikāraṇatvamadṛṣṭādernimittahetutvaṃ coktam / etannirasyati
children.translated_text:
thus. Here the argument [runs]: Pleasure and the like have a non-inherent cause (<s>asamavāyi-hetu</s>), because they are effects that are positive entities — like the color of an effect such as [a pot]. And the non-inherent cause of pleasure and the like is precisely the conjunction of the self with <s>manas</s>, since no other [cause] is possible — this is the gist.
'Of the self' and 'of the external' — these two words ending in the sixth case are a <s>bahuvrīhi</s> compound qualifying pleasure and the like. By the two words, it is stated that the self is the inherent cause (<s>samavāyi-kāraṇa</s>) of pleasure and the like, and that <s>adṛṣṭa</s> and the like are the efficient cause (<s>nimitta-hetu</s>). He refutes this —
'That is not' —
and so forth.
'In [the case of] pleasure' —

children.text:
ti / anukūlaviṣayasya pratikūlaviṣayasya ca jñānasyaivātmani niyatapūrvavṛtteḥ sukhe duḥkhe ca kāraṇasya tatrāsamavāyihetutvaṃ yuktam / na tu ātmamanassaṃseyogasyāprasiddhasya / tattadviṣayasannikṛṣṭendriyātmasaṃyoga eva ca tattajjñāne 'samavāyikāraṇam / kṛtisādhyatājñānameva prayatne tathā cikīrṣādvārā / kāryatājñāne ca smṛtirūpe udbuddhasaṃskāraḥ, anubhavarūpe ca liṅgajñānādi tathā / saṃskāre cānubhavaḥ tathā / prayatna evādṛṣṭasyāpyasamavāyihetuḥ / idamupalakṣaṇam / icchāṃ prati iṣṭajātīyatvasyeṣṭasādhanatvasya vā
jñānaṃ tathā / dveṣaṃ prati cāniṣṭatvasya tatsādhanatvasya vā jñānaṃ tathā / ātmaviśeṣaguṇānāṃ kutrāpyasamavāyihetutvaṃ nāstīti pravādastu na śraddheya iti manuditāśayaḥ / icchādīnāmityādipadena dveṣaprayatnādṛṣṭasaṃskārāṇāṃ grahaṇam / atra viṣayendriyasaṃyogahetubhūtasyendriyavyāpārasya prayatnavadātmasaṃyogāsamavāyihetukatvakathanaṃ prasaṅgāt / kutrāpi jñānādau ātmaviseṣaguṇe mano 'pekṣā nāstīti hārdam /
sādhanāntaraṃ manasi śaṅkate
children.translated_text:
thus. Since cognition of a favorable object or an unfavorable object alone invariably precedes [the arising of] pleasure or pain in the self, it is proper that [such cognition] is the non-inherent cause of pleasure and pain respectively. But not the conjunction of the self with <s>manas</s>, which is unestablished. And the conjunction of the self with the sense organ that is in contact with the respective object is itself the non-inherent cause of the respective cognition. In the case of effort (<s>prayatna</s>), the cognition of what is to be accomplished through action is [the non-inherent cause], and that [operates] through desire (<s>cikīrṣā</s>). In the case of cognition of what is to be done — which is in the form of recollection — the awakened <s>saṃskāra</s> [is the non-inherent cause]; and in the case of [cognition] in the form of experience, inferential cognition (<s>liṅga-jñāna</s>) and the like are so. And in the case of <s>saṃskāra</s>, experience [is the non-inherent cause]. In the case of effort alone, <s>adṛṣṭa</s> too [has] the non-inherent cause [role]. This is illustrative [not exhaustive]. With respect to desire (<s>icchā</s>), the cognition of [something] being of a desired kind or being a means to what is desired is so [i.e., the non-inherent cause]. With respect to aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>), the cognition of [something] being undesired or being a means to what is undesired is so. The doctrine that the particular qualities of the self have no non-inherent cause anywhere is not to be credited — this is the combined purport. By the word 'and the like' after 'desire,' aversion, effort, <s>adṛṣṭa</s>, and <s>saṃskāra</s> are included. Here, the statement that the operation of the sense organs — which is the cause of the conjunction of [the self with] the object and the sense organ — is, like effort, a non-inherent cause dependent on conjunction with the self, is incidental. The essential point is that in no case — in cognition and the like, which are particular qualities of the self — is there any need for <s>manas</s>.
He raises an alternative argument for <s>manas</s> —
'But with regard to an eternal [substance]' —

children.text: ti / atra prayogaḥ- sukhādirdravyasaṃyogāsamavāyihetukaḥ kāryatve sati nityadravyaviśeṣaguṇatvāt pākajaparamāṇurūpavaditi / dravyāntarasaṃyogasya sukhādau asamavāyihetutvāsaṃbhavānmanaḥsaṃyogasyaiva tathātvena pariśeṣānmanasaḥ siddhiriti bhāvaḥ / etaddūṣayati
children.translated_text: thus. Here the argument [runs]: Pleasure and the like have a conjunction with a [separate] substance as their non-inherent cause, because they are particular qualities of an eternal substance that are effects — like the color of an atom transformed by heat (<s>pākaja-paramāṇu-rūpa</s>). Since a conjunction with any other substance cannot be the non-inherent cause of pleasure and the like, by the process of elimination (<s>pariśeṣa</s>), it is the conjunction with <s>manas</s> alone that is so — thus <s>manas</s> is established. This is the purport. He refutes this —
'That too' —
thus. 'More gross' (<s>sthavīyaḥ</s>) means 'cruder still' — that is, [it is] a statement made without due reflection.
The purport is this —

children.text: anvayavyatirekasahacāradarśanādeva hi sarvatra kāraṇatvādhyavasāyaḥ / pārthivāṇurūpādau dahanasaṃyogasya hetutvamapi tato dehāvayavādau rūpādiparāvṛtterddaṣṭatvāddṛṣṭānusārādeva kalpyate / iha cānukūlajñānādereva sukhādau hetutvaṃ dṛṣṭam / samavāyikāraṇa ātmani pratyāsannatvāttasyaivāsamavāyihetutvaṃ ca yuktaṃ tatreti nādṛṣṭadravyāntarasaṃyogasya tathātvena kalpanāvasara iti /
children.translated_text: It is only from observing the co-presence and co-absence [of two things] that causality is determined in every case. Even the causality of conjunction with fire for the color and the like of earthy atoms — since the transformation of color and the like in bodily parts and the like is observed — is postulated only in accordance with what is observed. But here, it is cognition of a favorable [object] and the like alone that is observed as the cause of pleasure and the like. Since it is proximate to the self, which is the inherent cause (<s>samavāyi-kāraṇa</s>), it is proper that [cognition] itself is the non-inherent cause of [pleasure and the like]. Therefore, there is no occasion for postulating the conjunction of an unobserved separate substance as having that role.
'When there is an observed cause' —

children.text: ti / dṛṣṭahetorabhāve 'pi kāryotpatterdarśane hi kāraṇāntarakalpanāvasaraḥ / na ca dṛṣṭahetorvyabhicāra ityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: thus. It is only when one observes the arising of an effect even in the absence of an observed cause that there is occasion for postulating another cause. But there is no deviation (<s>vyabhicāra</s>) of the observed cause — this is the meaning.
'Therefore' —

children.text: iti / dṛṣṭahetuṣveva tattallakṣaṇayogena samavāyihetutvādi vyavasthāpyam / jñānādidṛṣṭahetubhinnasyānapekṣitasyāprasiddhasya dravyāntarasaṃyogasya hetutvakalpanāyāṃ tu kḷptatyāgo 'kḷptaparikalpanā ca / jñānāderasamavāyihetutve bādhakasyānupalabdheḥ tadbhinnatvasyāsamavāyihetulakṣaṇe niveśo 'narthakaśceti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: thus. Among the observed causes themselves, the status of inherent cause and the like should be determined by the fulfillment of the respective defining characteristics. But in postulating the causality of a conjunction with a separate substance that is different from the observed causes such as cognition and the like, that is not needed, and that is unestablished — [this involves] abandoning what is established and fabricating what is not established. Since there is no sublating evidence against cognition and the like being the non-inherent cause, and since introducing the condition of being different from [cognition] into the definition of non-inherent cause is purposeless — this is the purport.
'Here' —

children.text: ti/ sukhādau tu tadviparyayaḥ- kāraṇāntaropalambharūpaṃ dṛṣṭāntato vaiṣamyaṃ prādarśīti yāvat / etāvatā pūrvoktānumāne 'prayojakatvāvdyāpyatvāsiddhirūktā / vyāptisvīkāre cārthāntaramityāha
children.translated_text: thus. But in the case of pleasure and the like, the opposite [holds] — [the opponent] showed the dissimilarity from the cited example, in the form of the perception of another cause. By this much, the defect of the aforementioned inference being inconclusive (<s>aprayojakatva</s>) — [i.e.,] the unestablished pervasion (<s>vyāpti</s>) — has been stated. He states that even if the pervasion is accepted, [the conclusion] is beside the point (<s>arthāntara</s>) —
'Even so' —
thus.
'Then that [conjunction]' —

children.text:
ti / tarhī sa ityanvayaḥ / dṛṣṭānte saḥ dravyāntarasaṃyogaḥ bhautikaḥ- bhūtārabdhaḥ bhautikapratiyogika
eva dṛṣṭa iti prakṛte 'pi bhautikadehādipratiyogikātmānuyogikasaṃyoga evānumānaparyavasānānna kāṇādābhimatanavamadravyarūpābhautikamanaḥsiddhipratyāśetyarthaḥ / sparśavaddravyasamaveta iti nidarśanābhiprāyeṇa / sparśavannityadravyaviśeṣaguṇaṃ pratyevakāryabhūtaṃ dravyāntarasaṃyogasya hetutvaṃ dṛṣṭānusārātkalpyam / na tvasparśanityadravyaviśeṣaguṇaṃ pratyapīti vyajyate 'nena / evaṃ sukhādāvasamavāyihetutvena dravyāntasaṃyogasya sādhanaṃ na saṃbhavatītyuktam /
atha tatsādhanābhyupagame 'pi vivakṣitamabhautikaṃ manastattvāntaraṃ na setsyatīti prapañcayati / tatra śaṅkā
children.translated_text:
thus. The construction is: 'then that.' In the cited example, that conjunction with a separate substance is observed only as physical (<s>bhautika</s>) — i.e., constituted of gross elements — and having a physical counterpart. Therefore, the inference in the present case too culminates only in a conjunction that has a physical [entity] such as the body as its counterpart and the self as its co-relatum. Hence there should be no expectation of establishing a non-physical <s>manas</s> as a ninth substance (<s>navama-dravya</s>) as conceived by the <s>Kāṇādas</s> (Vaiśeṣikas) — this is the meaning. 'A substance possessing touch' is said with illustrative intent. The causality of conjunction with a separate substance is to be postulated, in accordance with observation, only with respect to a particular quality of an eternal substance that possesses touch — not also with respect to [a quality of] a substance that is devoid of touch and eternal. This is indicated [by the passage]. Thus it has been stated that the establishment of a conjunction with a separate substance as the non-inherent cause of pleasure and the like is not possible.
Now, even if one concedes that proof, [the author] elaborates that the desired non-physical <s>manas</s> as a separate category will not be established. There [follows] an objection —
'Now it is said' —

children.text: ti / pratyāsiddham-pratiṣiddham / pāthasīyaṃ-jalīyam / śakyādhyavasānaṃ-śakyaniścayam / mano na pārthivaṃ taijasādi vā rasāvagamanimittendriyatvādrasanāvat / mano na jalīyaṃ gandhagrāhakendriyatvādghrāṇavaditi bhautikatvaniṣedhaḥ / yugapajjñānānutpattiliṅgenāṇutvena siddherna vibhudravyāntarbhāvaḥ / ato navamadravyatvasiddhirmanasa ityabhimānaḥ / pariharati
children.translated_text: thus. 'Refuted' (<s>pratyāsiddham</s>) means 'prohibited.' 'Aqueous' (<s>pāthasīya</s>) means 'of the nature of water.' 'Capable of being ascertained' (<s>śakyādhyavasāna</s>) means 'capable of being determined.' [The argument:] <s>Manas</s> is not earthy, nor fiery and the like, because it is a sense organ that apprehends taste — like the tongue (<s>rasanā</s>). <s>Manas</s> is not aqueous, because it is a sense organ that apprehends smell — like the nose (<s>ghrāṇa</s>). Thus [there is] the negation of [its] being elemental (<s>bhautika</s>). Through the inferential mark of the non-arising of simultaneous cognitions, [<s>manas</s>] is established as atomic, so there is no inclusion among all-pervading substances (<s>vibhu-dravya</s>). Therefore, <s>manas</s> is established as a ninth substance — this is the [opponent's] claim. He resolves [this] —
'That is untenable' —
and so forth.
'The subject' (<s>dharmī</s>) —

children.text: ti / manasi pakṣe 'bhimato yo viśeṣo 'bhautikatvarūpaḥ, tadviparītasādhakatvāduktahetunāmityarthaḥ / rasagrāhakendriyatvaṃ jalīyatvaṃ gandhagrāhakendriyatvādi pārthivatvādi ca manasaḥ sādhayediti bhāvaḥ / atra śaṅkate
children.translated_text: thus. The particular property of <s>manas</s>, which is the intended subject — namely, its being non-elemental (<s>abhautikatva</s>) — [is undermined] because the stated reasons would prove the opposite of that. The meaning is that the stated reasons would establish that <s>manas</s> is aqueous because it is a sense organ that apprehends taste, earthy because it is a sense organ that apprehends smell, and so on — this is the purport. Here he raises an objection —
'Now, in the case of sound' —

children.text: ti / rūpādiṣu madhye gandhamātragrāhakatvaṃ pārthivatvasādhakam / evaṃ rasamātragrāhakatvādi ca jalīyatvādeḥ / tathā ca manasaḥ pārthivatvādisādhakahetorasiddhiriti bhāvaḥ / atrottaraṃ
children.translated_text: thus. Among [the qualities] such as color and the like, it is the apprehension of smell alone that establishes earthiness. Likewise, the apprehension of taste alone [establishes] aqueousness, and so on. And thus, the reason [adduced] to establish earthiness and the like of <s>manas</s> is unestablished — this is the purport. To this, the reply [is] —
'Well then!' —
