children.text:
ti / yadbhūtaguṇamātragrāhakaṃ yadindriyaṃ tadeva bhūtāntaravyatiriktatvena saṃpratipannamiti bhūtāntaraguṇagrāhakatāmātreṇa na tattadbhūtaguṇagrāhakasya manasaḥ tattadbhūtavyatirekasiddhirityarthaḥ /
gandhādyagrāhakatvamevāpārthivādisādhakam / tacca manaso 'bhautikānumāne pakṣe manasyasiddhamiti bhāvaḥ / apārthivatvādyanumāne tattadbhūtaguṇāgrāhakatvamupādhiriti coktaṃ bhavati / evamabhautikatvānumānaṃ pradūṣya manaso bhautikatvānumānamupasthāpayati
children.translated_text:
thus. Whatever sense organ apprehends only the quality of a [single] element — that alone is acknowledged as being distinct from other elements. Hence, merely because [<s>manas</s>] apprehends the quality of another element, the distinctness of <s>manas</s> — which apprehends the qualities of each and every element — from each and every element is not established. This is the meaning.
The non-apprehension of smell and the like [by a given sense organ] is itself what establishes its being non-earthy and the like. And that [non-apprehension] is unestablished in the subject, namely <s>manas</s>, in the inference for [its] being non-elemental — this is the purport. It is also thereby stated that the non-apprehension of the qualities of each respective element is a limiting condition (<s>upādhi</s>) in the inference for [<s>manas</s>] being non-earthy and the like. Having thus refuted the inference for [<s>manas</s>'] being non-elemental, he presents an inference for the elementality of <s>manas</s> —
'Moreover, sound and the like' —

children.text:
ti / manaḥ pāñcabhautikaṃ pañcabhūtaguṇāvagamasādhanatvāddeha
vaditi prayogaḥ / pañcabhūtopādanakatve gauravājjātisāṅkaryabhītyā ca pakṣāntaramāha
children.translated_text: thus. The argument [is]: <s>Manas</s> is constituted of the five elements (<s>pāñcabhautika</s>), because it is an instrument for apprehending the qualities of the five elements — like the body. If [one objects to] the heaviness of [it being constituted of] five elements, or out of fear of an intermixture of categories (<s>jāti-sāṅkarya</s>), he states an alternative thesis —
'One or two' —

children.text: ti / dehasyevaikabhautikasya bhūtāntaropaṣṭabdhatvādbhūtāntaraguṇopalambhasādhanatvopapattirmanasa iti bhāvaḥ / asya pārthivatve śrutimapi saṃvādarūpeṇodāharati
children.translated_text: thus. Since even a body that is constituted of a single element is supported by other elements, the capacity of <s>manas</s> to serve as an instrument for apprehending the qualities of other elements is accounted for — this is the purport. In support of [<s>manas</s>'] being earthy, he also cites a <s>śruti</s> (Vedic text) as corroboration —
'Made of food (<s>annamaya</s>) indeed' —
thus. He raises the possibility of an alternative interpretation of the <s>śruti</s> —
'That [is] not' —
thus. 'But' (<s>nanu</s>) and so forth [is the objection]. 'That' refers to the aforementioned Vedic statement.
'Dependent on that' —

children.text: ti / annarasāpyāyitasyaiva manasaḥ saṅkalpanādivyāpārakṣamatayānnamayatvaṃ śrūyate 'nnarasaparipoṣitatvalakṣaṇam, vāyuviśeṣasya prāṇasyevāmmayatvaṃ jalarasāpyāyitatvāditi bhāvaḥ / mano 'bhautikatve śrutyarthāpattimapyāha
children.translated_text: thus. The <s>śruti</s> declares <s>manas</s> to be <s>annamaya</s> (made of food) because only when nourished by the essence of food does <s>manas</s> have the capacity for operations such as willing (<s>saṅkalpana</s>) and the like — [the term <s>annamaya</s>] has the character of being sustained by the essence of food, just as <s>prāṇa</s> (vital breath), which is a modification of air, is [called] <s>āpomaya</s> (made of water) because it is nourished by the essence of water — this is the purport. He also states an <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption) from <s>śruti</s> for the non-elementality of <s>manas</s> —
'For this very reason' —

children.text: ti / yadi bhautikaṃ manaḥ, tarhi muktau nānuvarteta dehādivaditi / muktau mano 'nuvṛttau śrutimāha
children.translated_text: thus. If <s>manas</s> is elemental, then it would not persist in <s>mukti</s> (liberation), just like the body and the like. He cites a <s>śruti</s> for the persistence of <s>manas</s> in <s>mukti</s> —
'In that very [text]' —
thus. In the eighth <s>prapāṭhaka</s> (chapter) of the <s>Chāndogya</s> [Upaniṣad] itself.
'Made of food indeed' —

children.text: ti tu ṣaṣṭhe / muktasya manoyogamuktvā nityamuktasvabhāvasyeśvarasyāpi tatra pramāṇamudāharati
children.translated_text: is in the sixth [<s>prapāṭhaka</s>]. Having mentioned the connection of <s>manas</s> with the liberated [soul], he also cites a <s>pramāṇa</s> (authoritative source) regarding <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord), who is by nature eternally free —
'Likewise' —
thus. 'In the <s>Purāṇa</s>' — in the fifth <s>aṃśa</s> (section) of the <s>Śrī Vaiṣṇava</s> [Purāṇa, i.e., the Viṣṇu Purāṇa].
'That [is] not' —
and so forth — he resolves the objection raised [earlier] by partially conceding [it] —
'It is replied' —

children.text: iti / satyamityardhāṅgīkāre / śruterānyaparye 'bhyupagamaḥ / manaso 'tiriktatattvatve 'nupagamaḥ / evaṃ vā'śrayaṇam-bhautikatvāśrayaṇaṃ vā / vākāro 'nāsthāyām / ata eva svāśayaṃ prakaṭīkaroti manoviṣaye
children.translated_text: thus. 'True' [indicates] the partial concession. [There is] acceptance of an alternative interpretation of the <s>śruti</s>. [But there is] non-acceptance of <s>manas</s> being a separate category. Or alternatively, 'taking recourse' means 'taking recourse to [the view that <s>manas</s> is] elemental.' The particle 'vā' [indicates] non-commitment. For this very reason, he reveals his own considered view regarding <s>manas</s> —
'But in ultimate reality' —
and so forth.
'In cognition (<s>buddhi</s>) alone' —

children.text: ti / buddhāveva manaḥśabdo vācakatvena vartata ityarthaḥ / muktasyeśvarasya ca buddhimattvādeva samanaskatvavācoyuktiḥ / tayoramanaskatvavacanaṃ tu karmakṛtabuddhivṛttiniṣedhābhiprāyamiti bhāvaḥ / buddhereva manastve laukikavyavahāramuktvā laukikapratyakṣamapi pradarśayati
children.translated_text: The word '<s>manas</s>' (mind) functions as denoting <s>buddhi</s> (intellect) itself — this is the meaning. Since the liberated soul and <s>Īśvara</s> (God) possess <s>buddhi</s>, it is fitting to speak of them as possessing <s>manas</s>. The statement that they lack <s>manas</s> is intended to deny the mental modifications (<s>buddhi-vṛtti</s>) produced by <s>karma</s> — this is the purport. To show that <s>buddhi</s> itself is <s>manas</s>, he presents, beyond ordinary usage, direct perception as well.
Of <s>manas</s> (the mind) —

children.text: iti / manaḥ prasannamityādyadhyakṣaṃ pratyakṣabuddhyālambanameva saṃbhavati, na tvatīndriyamanogocaramiti bhāvaḥ / buddhiśabdena jñānaṃ vivakṣitam / nanu buddherjñānasyaiva manastve 'ntaḥkaraṇatvoktistasya kathaṃ saṅgacchata ityatrāha
children.translated_text: Thus: The direct experience (<s>adhyakṣa</s>) such as 'the mind is calm' is possible only as something grounded in perceptual cognition (<s>pratyakṣa-buddhi</s>), not as something apprehended by a supersensory mind — this is the purport. By the word '<s>buddhi</s>' (intellect), <s>jñāna</s> (knowledge) is intended. To the objection — if <s>manas</s> is indeed <s>buddhi</s> or <s>jñāna</s>, how is the designation of it as an internal organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>) consistent? — to this he says:
If so —

children.text: ti / viṣayasmṛtyādihetubhūtavyāpāravattvapradarśanārthaṃ buddherantaḥkaraṇatvavyapadeśaḥ, adhyavasāyādihetuvyāpāravattvapradarśanārthaṃ buddhyādivyapadeśa iva manaso 'tirekavāde 'pīti bhāvaḥ / atra vimarśakena sukhādisākṣātkārakaraṇatvena manaso 'numānaṃ tārkikābhimataṃ na vimṛṣṭam /
children.translated_text: The designation of <s>buddhi</s> as an internal organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>) is for the purpose of showing that it possesses the function of being the cause of memory of objects and so forth; just as the designation as '<s>buddhi</s>' and the like is for showing its function as the cause of determination (<s>adhyavasāya</s>) — even on the view that <s>manas</s> is distinct, this is the purport. Here the examiner has not critically assessed the <s>Tārkika</s> (Naiyāyika) inference of <s>manas</s> as the instrument for the direct apprehension of pleasure and the like.
The intention here is as follows —

children.text: - indriyasauṣṭhavopaghātayoreva sukhaduḥkharūpatvāttayoścātīndriyatvānna tatsākṣātkārakāraṇatayā mano 'numeyam / yadvā jñānaviśeṣarūpatvāttayorjñānasvayaṃ- prakāśatvabalādeva tatpratibhāsopapattiriti /
children.translated_text: Since pleasure and pain are of the nature of the excellence or impairment of the sense organs, and since these are supersensory, <s>manas</s> cannot be inferred as the instrument for their direct apprehension. Alternatively, since pleasure and pain are of the nature of specific cognitions, by the force of the self-luminosity of cognition itself, their manifestation is accounted for.
He says —
By means of these words, after the examiner has refuted a separate <s>manas</s>, the proponent (<s>siddhāntin</s>) reveals his own position.
It is said —
By means of this and what follows.
Not having been asserted —

children.text: ti / manaso 'nātmatvameva pratijñātam-prakṛtam / manaḥsvarūpatattvavicārasyāprakṛtatvānnāsmābhiridānīmatiriktamanaḥsādhane pravartyata ityāśayaḥ / astu vā muktānāmīśvarasya ca mano buddhirūpameva / baddhānāṃ tu mana āhaṅkārika mantaḥkaraṇaṃ śrutibalādabhyupagantavyameva / smṛtyādikaraṇatayā ca tadabhyupagamārham / paraṃ tu tasya na cetanatvaṃ śakyamadhyavasitumiti hārdam //
children.translated_text: The non-selfhood (<s>anātmatva</s>) of <s>manas</s> alone was asserted — this is the subject under discussion. Since the investigation of the true nature of <s>manas</s> is not the topic at hand, we do not presently undertake to establish a separate <s>manas</s> — this is the intention. Granted, for the liberated and for <s>Īśvara</s>, <s>manas</s> may indeed be of the nature of <s>buddhi</s>. But for bound souls, <s>manas</s> — the <s>āhaṅkārika</s> (ego-derived) internal organ — must be accepted on the strength of <s>śruti</s> (scripture). And it deserves acceptance as the instrument of memory and the like. However, the essential point is that consciousness cannot be attributed to it.

body.translated_text: Thus far, the non-selfhood of the body has been established through perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) and inference (<s>anumāna</s>). He states that this refutes those who establish selfhood of the body through mere negative concomitance (<s>vyatireka</s>) alone.

body.text: prāṇātmavādamupakṣipati

children.translated_text: Let it then be —

children.text: ti / prāṇavati dehe jīvatīti, tadrahite ca mṛta iti vyavahārātprāṇa eva jīvanakartṛtvājjīva iti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: Since when the body possesses <s>prāṇa</s> (vital breath), there is the convention 'it lives,' and when devoid of it, 'it is dead,' <s>prāṇa</s> alone, being the agent of life, is the <s>jīva</s> (individual self) — this is the purport.
Otherwise —

children.text:
ti / paramamahataḥ, amahataśca, iti padacchedaḥ / amahattvamaṇutvam / niḥsparśatvādātmani na kriyā vibhutve 'ṇutve vā saṃbhavatīti bhāvaḥ /
pratikṣipati vādamenam
children.translated_text: The word-division is: 'of the supremely great' and 'of the non-great.' Non-greatness means atomicity (<s>aṇutva</s>). Since the self is without touch (<s>niḥsparśa</s>), action is not possible in it whether it is all-pervading (<s>vibhu</s>) or atomic (<s>aṇu</s>) — this is the purport. He refutes this doctrine:
This too is not valid —

children.text: diti / atra prayogatrayam- prāṇo nātmā, suṣuptau vyāpāravattvarūpādātmavaidharmyāt / prāṇo nātmā, tvācapratyakṣagrāhyatvāddhaṭādivat / prāṇo nātmā vāyutvāvdyajanapavanavaditi /
children.translated_text: Here there are three arguments: (1) <s>Prāṇa</s> is not the self, because it differs from the self in having activity during deep sleep (<s>suṣupti</s>). (2) <s>Prāṇa</s> is not the self, because it is perceptible to touch, like a pot. (3) <s>Prāṇa</s> is not the self, because it is a form of wind (<s>vāyu</s>), like a fan or breeze.
By its activity —
The activity of <s>prāṇa</s> is the cause of the transformation of consumed food and drink.

children.text: ahaṃ vaiśvānaro bhūtvā prāṇināṃ dehamāsthitaḥ / prāṇāpānasamāyuktaḥ pacāmyannaṃ caturvidham
children.translated_text: "Becoming <s>Vaiśvānara</s> (the digestive fire), I dwell in the bodies of living beings; joined with <s>prāṇa</s> and <s>apāna</s>, I digest the four kinds of food" —
This is established by the <s>Gītā</s> scripture.
In a more subtle manner —

children.text: ti / alpatarapṛthivījalatejoṃśottambhito jaṭharagato vāyuviśeṣaḥ prāṇa ityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: The meaning is: <s>prāṇa</s> is a particular form of wind (<s>vāyu</s>) situated in the stomach, sustained by smaller portions of earth, water, and fire.
Moreover — from the standpoint of the refutation of the doctrine that the body is conscious (<s>dehacaitanya</s>), which has already been negated,
The <s>prāṇātmavāda</s> (doctrine that the vital breath is the self) does not separately call for refutation. (verse 9)

children.text: avibhutvenāsyā'tmanaḥ sparśavirahiṇo 'pi prayatnādṛṣṭapreraṇānuguṇyena manasa ivotkrāntigatyādayo yujyanta iti na tannirdeśānāmamuravyārthatā / parimāṇanirūpaṇe 'pyetadbhaviṣyatītyalamadhunā /
children.translated_text: Even though the self is non-pervading and devoid of touch, activities such as departure and movement are possible for <s>manas</s> through the impulsion of effort (<s>prayatna</s>) and unseen merit (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>) — therefore the scriptural references to these are not purposeless. This will also be relevant when determining the size (<s>parimāṇa</s>) of the self. Enough for now.
(Thus concludes the section on the refutation of the <s>prāṇātmavāda</s>.)

body.translated_text: He introduces the <s>prāṇātmavāda</s> (the doctrine that <s>prāṇa</s> is the self) —

body.text: bhavatu tarhī saṃvidevā'tmā, ajaḍatvāt / jaḍatvapratibaddhaṃ hyanātbhyaṃ ghaṭādiṣu dṛṣṭam / jaḍatvaṃ ca saṃvido nivartamānaṃ tadapi nivartayati / ajaḍatvaṃ ca saṃvidaḥ sattayaiva prakāśamānatvāt / nahisatī saṃviddhaṭādirivāprakāśamānāvatiṣṭhate, yena parāyattasiddhirāsthīyeta /
body.translated_text: Let consciousness (<s>saṃvid</s>) then be the self, since it is non-insentient (<s>ajaḍa</s>). For non-selfhood is observed to be bound up with insentience (<s>jaḍatva</s>) in things like pots. And when the insentience of consciousness is removed, that non-selfhood is also removed. The non-insentience of consciousness consists in the fact that it shines forth by its very existence. For consciousness, when present, does not remain unmanifest like a pot, such that one would need to resort to establishment dependent on something else.

children.translated_text: (Thus the presentation of the thesis that consciousness is the self.)

body.text: syānmatam-jātāyāmapi saṃvidi viṣayamātraṃ prathate / na khalunīlamidamiti pratiyantaḥ tadaivānīlamanidaṃrūpamapi saṃvedanaṃ pratīmaḥ / ataḥ svarūpasatyaiva saṃvidā indriyasannikarṣeṇeva viṣayaḥ prakāśyate / tataśca tadgatāgantukaprakāśātiśayadarśanena paścāt saṃvidanumāsyate iti /
body.translated_text: One might think: even when consciousness has arisen, only the object is manifest. Indeed, when we cognize 'this is blue,' we do not at that very moment cognize the cognition itself as 'not-blue' and 'not-this' in nature. Therefore, consciousness, which is real in its own nature, illuminates the object through sense-contact; and then, observing the adventitious excess of illumination belonging to the object, one subsequently infers consciousness.

children.translated_text: (Thus the objection to the non-insentience of consciousness through the thesis that consciousness is inferable.)

children.text: tanna / jñānavyatirekiṇor'thadharmasya prakāśasya nipuṇamapi nirīkṣamāṇānāṃ rūpādivadanupalabdheḥ / ubhayābhyupetasaṃvidaiva sakalavyavahāropapattau ca tatkalpanānupapatteḥ / vittiveditṛpratibhāsaśūnyāyāṃ ca viṣayavittāvabhyupagamyamānāyāṃ ghaṭastāvadayam, ahaṃ tu jānāmi na veti, na jñāyate iti ca kadācitpratibhāsaḥ syāt / nacaivamasti / atītānāgataviṣayagrahaṇasmaraṇeṣu vyāhāravyavahārayorabhāve, bhāve 'pi, tataḥ prāgeva viditatvapratīteḥ nānumānikī tatra viṣaya(prakāśa)siddhiḥ, natarāṃ tatpūrvikā tatra buddhisiddhiḥ / tathāhi- kenacitpreritaḥ praṇidhāya smṛtvānantarameva prativadati smṛtamadya mayeti / na cāya
children.translated_text: That is not so. Because even upon the most careful examination, the property of illumination (<s>prakāśa</s>) belonging to the object — which would be distinct from cognition — is not apprehended, just as color and the like are not. And because, since consciousness accepted by both parties accounts for all practical activity, there is no justification for postulating such an additional entity. Moreover, if object-cognition were admitted to be devoid of the appearance of a knower (<s>veditṛ</s>), then sometimes the thought would arise: 'This is indeed a pot, but do I know it or not? It is not known' — but this never happens. In cases of grasping and recollecting past and future objects, whether verbal expression is absent or present, since the awareness of 'already known' arises even prior to that, the establishment of illumination in the object is not inferential; still less is the establishment of cognition based upon it. For instance: someone, when prompted, after concentrating and remembering, responds immediately, 'I have remembered it today.' And this

body.text: meva vyāhārastatra liṅgam; tatpūrvakatvāt, anyonyāśrayaṇāpatteśca / svavyāhāreṇa svajñānānumānaṃ ka iva nirapatrapaḥ pratijānīta? /
body.translated_text: very utterance is not the inferential mark there, because it presupposes the cognition, and because mutual dependence would result. Who would shamelessly claim that one infers one's own knowledge through one's own utterance?

children.translated_text: (Thus the refutation of the thesis that consciousness is inferable.)

body.text: anyacca-yatsaṃbandhādarthāntare yo vyavahāraḥ dharmabhedo vā, sa tasminnupalabhyamānastatsvarūpaprayuktaḥ; na tu tatsaṃbandhanibandhanaḥ / yathā sattāsaṃbandhāt pṛthivyādiṣu sadvyavahāraḥ,rūpasaṃbandhācca cākṣuṣatvaṃ sattāyāṃ rūpe ca / evaṃ saṃvitsaṃbandhātpravartamāno ghaṭādiṣu prakāśata iti vyavahāraḥ prakāśamānatvaṃ vā dharmaḥ saṃvidi tu paridṛśyamāno na saṃvitsaṃbandhāpekṣaḥ, api tu tatsvarūpaprayukta iti svayaṃprakāśatvāt saivā'tmeti / kiñca yo 'pi saṃvido 'nyaṃ saṃveditāramabhyupagacchati, abhyupagacchatyevāsau saṃvidam / nahyasatyāmeva saṃvidi saṃvettītyupapadyate / evaṃ cet, ubhayavādisaṃpratipannatayā saiva varaṃ veditrī bhavatu; kimanyena kalpitena? /
body.translated_text: Furthermore: whatever practical activity or distinguishing property arises in something else by virtue of a relation — when that is observed in that thing, it is caused by the thing's own nature, not occasioned by that relation. For example, the designation 'existent' (<s>sat</s>) applies to earth and the like by virtue of their relation to existence (<s>sattā</s>), and visual perceptibility applies by virtue of the relation to color — both in the case of existence and of color. Similarly, the practical activity of 'being illuminated' (<s>prakāśa</s>) or the property of 'being manifest' that operates in pots and the like by virtue of their relation to consciousness (<s>saṃvid</s>) — when observed in consciousness itself — does not depend on a relation to consciousness, but is caused by its own nature. Therefore, since consciousness is self-luminous (<s>svayaṃprakāśa</s>), it alone is the self. Moreover, even one who posits a knower other than consciousness nonetheless accepts consciousness itself. For without consciousness being real, the notion of a knower is untenable. This being so, since consciousness is accepted by proponents of both views, let it alone be the knower; what need is there for another postulated entity?

children.translated_text: (Thus the establishment of selfhood through the self-luminosity of consciousness.)

children.text: nanu ahaṃ jānāmīti jñānātiriktastadāśrayabhūto 'yamātmā pratīyate / satyam
children.translated_text: Objection: In the cognition 'I know,' a self distinct from knowledge and serving as its substrate is cognized. True —

children.text: sa tu vikalparūpatayā sākṣātpratyakṣa iti na śakyaḥ saṃśrayitum / bhedajñānasiddhavatkāreṇa pṛthagvastutayā gṛhītāvyabhicāreṇa sahopalambhaniyamena, aprakāśātmanaśca svabhāvavirodhādeva prakāśāyogāt, prakāśasvābhāvye ca saṃvedanatvamityādinā vā prakāśātmano 'hamityaṃśasya tattvameva durupagamam / grāhyavikalpapratyuddhāre 'pyeṣa eva prakāraḥ / ato vāsanābhidhānasamanantarapratyayasāmarthyādanādyavidyāvaśācca samāropitāvāstavagrāhyagrāhakavikalpollekhinī svayaṃprakāśā saṃvideva paramārthasatī / saivā'tmeti saugatāḥ prakaṭāḥ pracchannāśca /
children.translated_text: But since that appears in the form of a conceptual construction (<s>vikalpa</s>), it cannot be relied upon as direct perception. By the invariable rule of co-perception (<s>sahopalambhaniyama</s>), which is not violated — established by the cognition of difference appearing as if it were a separate entity — and because something whose nature is non-luminous (<s>aprakāśa</s>) is by its very nature incapable of being illuminated, and because if it lacked the nature of illumination then the designation 'cognition' (<s>saṃvedanatva</s>) and the like would apply — by such reasoning, the reality of the 'I' component as something with the nature of illumination is itself difficult to establish. Even upon eliminating the conceptual construction pertaining to the apprehended object, this same analysis applies. Therefore, by the power of latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>), designation, immediately preceding cognition, and beginningless <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), consciousness (<s>saṃvid</s>) alone — self-luminous, bearing the superimposed and unreal conceptual constructions of apprehended and apprehender, ultimately real — is the self. This is the position of both the open (<s>prakaṭa</s>) and the crypto (<s>pracchanna</s>) Buddhists.
As the open [Buddhists] say: "
Though the cognizing self (<s>buddhyātman</s>) is undivided, to those with distorted vision it appears as if possessing the distinctions of apprehended, apprehender, and cognition."
Thus.
And as the crypto [Buddhists] say: "

children.text: śuddhaṃ tattvaṃ prapañcasya na heturanivṛttitaḥ / jñātṛjñeyavibhāgasya māyaiva jananī tataḥ
children.translated_text: The pure principle (<s>tattva</s>) is not the cause of the phenomenal world, since it does not cease. <s>Māyā</s> alone is the mother of the division into knower and known."
Thus.
(Thus concludes the section presenting the <s>pūrvapakṣa</s> [prima facie view] of consciousness as the self.)

children.text: atrāha-kṣaṇabhaṅginī prativiṣayamanyānyā ca saṃviccakāsti / saiva cedātmā, pūrvedyurdṛṣṭamaparedyurahamidamadarśamiti kathamiva pratyabhijānīyāt ? / na ca nīrālambanapratibhābhedamātratayeha samādheyam nirālambanatvapratijñāyāḥ pratyakṣādisaka
children.translated_text: To this he responds: Consciousness, being momentary (<s>kṣaṇabhaṅginī</s>) and different for each object, how could it effect recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>) such as 'I saw this on a previous day'? Nor can this be resolved by treating it as merely a difference in contentless appearances, since the thesis of contentlessness (<s>nirālambana</s>) is contradicted by all cognitions including perception and the like.

body.text: lapratītibādhitaviṣayatvāt / sādhanasya ca sālambanatve tadaviśeṣādaśeṣaśemuṣīṇāṃ tathātvāpatteḥ; nirālambanatve ca sādhanābhāvādeva sādhyāsiddheḥ / prapañcitaśca pūrvottaramīmāṃsābhāgayornirālambanatvapratiṣedhaḥ ; yathārtharavyātisamarthanena ca śāstra iti na vyāvarṇyate /
body.translated_text: And if the means of proof (<s>sādhana</s>) has content (<s>sālambana</s>), then since there is no difference from the thesis, it would follow that all cognitions are likewise contentless. If the means of proof is contentless, then since the means of proof itself is absent, the thesis remains unestablished. The refutation of contentlessness has been elaborated in both the <s>Pūrvamīmāṃsā</s> and <s>Uttaramīmāṃsā</s> portions; and since it has been vindicated in the <s>śāstra</s> by establishing the veridicality of cognition, it need not be discussed further here.

body.text: ata eva na santānāśrayaṇenāpi pratyabhijñopapādanaṃ sādhīyaḥ / vijñānakṣaṇavyatiriktasya sthāyino 'nusandhāyinaḥ santānasyābhyupagame svasiddhāntatyāgaḥ, parasiddhāntābhyupagamaśca / anabhyupagame pratyabhijñānupapattiḥ / na hyanyenānubhūte 'nyasya pratisandhānasaṃbhavaḥ / na ca susadṛśatayā bhedāgrahaṇena pradīpādāviva pramātari pratyabhijñābhrāntiḥ / yujyate hi tatraikasyaiva pūrvāparavyaktidarśinaḥ tulyasaṃsthānatayā vyaktīnāṃ bhedamaviduṣaḥ tathā bhramaḥ / iha tu saṃvidvyaktayaḥ parasparavārtānabhijñā niranvayavināśinyaśca sugatamata iti na tāsvekatvabhramasyā'śrayatā viṣayatā vā saṃbhavinī / na ca susadṛśatve 'pi anyena kṛtamātmakṛtatayānyo 'nusandhātumalamityāgamāpāyisaṃvitsantānāśrayaḥ pratyabhijñānakṣaṇasthāyī cetano 'bhyupagantavyaḥ /
body.translated_text: For this very reason, even the attempt to account for recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>) by resorting to a continuum (<s>santāna</s>) is not tenable. If one admits a continuum that is distinct from the momentary cognition-instants, enduring and capable of connecting experiences, one abandons one's own doctrine and accepts the opponent's. If one does not admit it, recognition remains unaccounted for. For it is impossible for one entity to reconnect what was experienced by another. Nor is the error of recognition in the case of the cognizer analogous to the case of a lamp and similar objects, where non-apprehension of difference occurs due to close resemblance. For in that case, such error is possible for a single observer who sees successive instances and, due to similarity of form, fails to discern their difference. But here, according to the Buddhist view, the instances of consciousness are mutually unaware of each other and perish without remainder — so neither the substrate nor the object of the illusion of unity is possible among them. Nor can one, even given close resemblance, reconnect as one's own what was done by another. Therefore, one must accept a conscious entity that endures through the moment of recognition, having as its basis a continuum of consciousness that arises and perishes.

children.translated_text: (Thus concludes the section on the refutation of the doctrine of momentary consciousness as the self.)

children.text: kaścidāha-na saṃvidanityā, prāgabhāvādyasiddheḥ / tadasiddhiśca tasyāḥ svataḥsiddhatvāt / nahi svataḥsiddhasya prāgabhāvādayaḥ svato 'nyato vā
children.translated_text: Someone says: Consciousness is not non-eternal, because prior non-existence (<s>prāgabhāva</s>) and the like cannot be established with respect to it. And the non-establishment of these is because consciousness is self-established (<s>svataḥsiddha</s>). For the prior non-existence and the like of something self-established cannot be established

children.text: siddhyanti / svayaṃ hi svābhāvamavagamayat sadvā asadvā sādhayet / sattve 'bhāv eva nāstīti kathaṃ sādhayet ? / asattvādeva sādhakasya pakṣāntare natarāṃ sādhakatvamiti na svataḥ tāvattatsiddhiḥ / nāpyanyataḥ ; ananyagocaratvādanu- bhūteḥ / anubhāvyatve ca ghaṭādivadananubhūtitvaprasaṅgāt / ataḥ sā na jāyate / janmābhāvādevetare 'pi bhāvavikārāḥ nirākāryāḥ, tatpratibaddhatvātteṣām / ata eva nānātvamapi saṃvidi pratyuktam ; utpattimattvavyāpakanivṛttyā tadvyāpyabhūtanānātvasyāpi nivṛttisiddheḥ / nahyajaṃ vibhāgyasti / cetyatvācca bhedetaretarābhāvādayo na taddharmāḥ, rūpādivat / ato 'syā na meyaḥ kaścidapi dharmo 'sti / ato nirdhūtanikhilabhedavikalpanirdharmaprakāśamātraikarasā kūṭasthanityā saṃvidevā'tmā paramātmā ca / yathā'ha "
children.translated_text: either by itself or by another. For that which reveals its own non-existence would establish it as either existent or non-existent. If existent, then non-existence simply does not exist — so how could it be established? If the establishing cognition is non-existent, then a fortiori it cannot establish anything in the other case — so it is not established by itself. Nor by another, because experience has no object other than itself. And if it were made an object, then like a pot and the like, it would become something not directly experienced. Therefore, consciousness is never born. And since birth is absent, the other modifications of being are also to be rejected, since they are dependent on birth. For this very reason, plurality (<s>nānātva</s>) in consciousness is also refuted, since by the removal of the pervader — namely, being subject to origination — the pervaded, namely plurality, is also removed. For what is unborn cannot be divided. And since it is not an object of cognition (<s>cetya</s>), mutual absence, difference, and the like are not its properties, just as color and the like are not. Therefore, no property whatsoever is to be predicated of it. Hence, consciousness alone — of a single essence that is pure luminosity, free from all distinctions and conceptual constructions, eternally unchanging (<s>kūṭastha</s>) — is the self and the supreme self. As it is said: "
That experience which is unborn, immeasurable, and of infinite self —"
Thus. And this alone is the ultimate import of the <s>Vedānta</s> statements —
Such is their doctrine. As the author of the <s>Vārttika</s> says: "

children.text: parāgarthaprameyeṣu yā phalatvena saṃmatā / saṃvit saivaiha meyor'tho vedāntoktipramāṇataḥ // aprāmāṇyaprasaktiśca syādito 'nyārthakalpane / vedāntānāmatastasmānnānyamarthaṃ prakalpayet
children.translated_text: [Verse:] The awareness (<s>saṃvit</s>) that is accepted as the fruit with regard to objects known (<s>prameya</s>) through other [means of knowledge] — that very [awareness] is here the object to be known (<s>meya</s>), on the authority of the <s>Vedānta</s> statements. And if one were to postulate a different object, there would be the consequence of the invalidity of the <s>Vedānta</s> [texts]; therefore one should not postulate a different object.
Thus.
(Thus ends the section establishing the view that the self is qualityless, eternal consciousness.)

body.text: tadidamalaukikamavaidikaṃ ca darśanamityātmavidaḥ / tathāhisaṃviditi svāśrayaṃ prati sattayaiva kasyacitprakāśanaśīlo jñānāvagatyanubhūtyādipadaparyāyanāmā sakarmakaḥ saṃvediturātmano dharmaḥ prasiddhaḥ / tathaiva hi sarvaprāṇabhṛtpratyātmasiddho 'yamanubhavaḥ 'ahamidaṃ saṃvedmī'ti / tasyāsyotpattisthitinirodhāśca sukhaduḥkhāderiva pratyakṣāḥ prakāśante / svāpamadamūrcchādaśāsu ca yogyānupalambhanirākṛtaḥ tatsadbhāvo nābhyupagamamarhati / yadi hi tāsvapi daśāsu saṃvedanamavartiṣyata, tataḥ prabodhasamaye 'nusamadhāsyata / na cānusandhīyate / ata eva hi 'iyantaṃ kālaṃ na kiñcidahamajñāsiṣa'miti prabuddhaḥ pratyavamṛśati /
body.translated_text: This is an extraordinary and non-Vedic view — so say the knowers of the self. For thus: awareness (<s>saṃvit</s>), designated by the synonymous words 'cognition' (<s>jñāna</s>), 'apprehension' (<s>avagati</s>), 'experience' (<s>anubhūti</s>), and the like, is well-known as a transitive property of the experiencing self — one whose nature is to illuminate something for its own substrate by its very existence. For this experience, established in each and every living being's own self, is [of the form] 'I am aware of this.' And its origination, persistence, and cessation — like those of pleasure and pain — are manifest through perception. And in the states of sleep, intoxication, and fainting, its existence — negated by the non-apprehension of what is fit [to be perceived] (<s>yogyānupalambha</s>) — should not be accepted. For if awareness had existed in those states too, then at the time of waking, one would have recollected [it]. But it is not recollected. For precisely this reason, upon waking, one reflects: 'For this much time, I knew nothing.'

children.text: yāvadanubhūtapadārthasmaraṇaniyamābhāve 'pi saṃskāravicchedanimittaprāyaṇādiprabalahetuvirahe 'pi nityavadasmaraṇamanubhavābhāvameva sādhayati / na ca satyapi saṃvitprakāśe viṣayāvacchedavirahādahaṅkāragocarāpāyādvā tatsmṛtyanudayaḥ ; arthāntarābhāvasya tadagrahaṇasya cārthāntaraprakāśaprayuktakāryapratibandhakatvāyogāt / tritayāvabhāse 'pi yathāsvamavabhāsānāṃ svagocarasmaraṇahetutvāt / naca pratyabhijñābalalabdhasthemāhamarthaḥ svāpādidaśāsu nidhanamupagata iti śakyo 'bhidhātum / ata eva hi 'iyantaṃ kālamahasvāpsa'miti prabodhe parāmarśaḥ / naca nirviṣayā nirāśrayā vā saṃvinnāma kācit saṃbhavati, atyantānupalabdheḥ / saṃbandhiśabdāśca saṃvidanubhūtijñānaprakāśādiśabdā iti śabdārthavidaḥ
children.translated_text: Even in the absence of a rule that everything experienced is remembered, and even in the absence of a powerful cause such as the severance of latent impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>) occasioned by death and the like, the non-remembering — as in the case of what is eternal — establishes precisely the absence of experience. Nor [can one say that] even though the light of awareness exists, there is no arising of that memory because of the absence of object-delimitation or because of the departure of the referent of the ego-sense — because the absence of another object, or the non-apprehension of that [object], cannot obstruct the effects produced by the illumination of another object. Because even when all three [self, awareness, and object] appear, each appearance [individually] is a cause of memory of its own object. Nor can it be said that the 'I'-referent — whose stability is gained through the strength of recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>) — perishes in the states of sleep and the like. For precisely this reason, upon waking there is the reflection: 'I slept for this much time.' And there is no such thing as an awareness (<s>saṃvit</s>) that is without an object or without a substrate, because of its complete non-apprehension. And the words 'awareness,' 'experience,' 'cognition,' 'illumination,' and the like are relational words — so say those who know the meaning of words.

body.text: / na hyakarmakasya jānātyāderakartṛkasya vā prayogo loke vede vā /
body.translated_text: For there is no usage, in ordinary language or in the <s>Veda</s>, of [the verb] 'jānāti' ('knows') and the like without an object or without an agent.

children.text: yattu svataḥsiddhasya sattve tadvirodhādeva prāgabhāvādeḥ tadānīmavasthānāsaṃbhavānna tataḥ siddhiriti, tadatisthavīyaḥ / nahi saṃvidāsvakālavartina evārthāḥ siddhyantītyasti niyamaḥ / atītānāgatayorasaṃvedyatvaprasaṅgāt / atha saṃvitprāgabhāvādeḥ siddhyataḥ tatsamakālatayā bhavitavyamiti; kimevaṃ kvaciddṛṣṭam ? hantaivaṃ
children.translated_text: As for [the objection] that since what is self-established (<s>svataḥsiddha</s>) exists [always], the prior absence (<s>prāgabhāva</s>) and the like of that [awareness], being contradictory to it, cannot exist at that time, and therefore its establishment [as non-existent in sleep] does not follow — that is exceedingly crude. For there is no rule that awareness establishes only those objects that exist at its own time — because otherwise, the past and the future would be unknowable. And if one says that the prior absence of awareness, since it is established [by awareness], must be contemporaneous with it — has anything like this ever been observed? Indeed, thus —

children.text: sati tatsiddherna prāgabhāvādyasiddhiḥ / tatprāgabhāvaḥ tatsamakāla ityunmattavacaḥ / aindriyikapratyakṣasvabhāvo hyayaṃ svasamakālapadārthaprakāśakatvaṃ nāma / na jñānamātrasya, pramāṇamātrasya vā / etena tadapi parākṛtam- "
children.translated_text: if [prior absence] is established only when [awareness] exists, then there is no establishment of prior absence and the like. 'The prior absence of that is contemporaneous with that' — this is the speech of a madman. For this nature of illuminating objects contemporaneous with itself belongs to sensory direct perception — not to cognition in general, nor to <s>pramāṇa</s> in general. By this, the following [verse] too is refuted:

children.text: mānaṃ svayaṃprakāśatvātsvataḥsaccetsadāstyataḥ / tanmeyaṃ ca sadāstyeva mānaṃ meyayugeva hi
children.translated_text: [Verse:] 'If the means of knowledge (<s>māna</s>), being self-luminous, always exists as self-established, then its object (<s>meya</s>) too always exists, for the means of knowledge is always conjoined with its object.'

children.text: " //iti / nahi mānasya svasattākāler'thāvinābhāvo meyayogaḥ / kintu yaddeśakālādimattayā meyamavabhāsate tādṛśatadrūpamithyātvavirodhitvam / ata eva 'smṛtirnabāhyaviṣayā, naṣṭe 'pyarthe smṛtidarśanā'dityapi pralāpaḥ /
children.translated_text: Thus. For the conjunction of the means of knowledge with its object does not mean that the object is inseparable from the time of the [means of knowledge's] own existence. Rather, it means: that [object] which appears as possessing [specific] place, time, and the like is of such a form, and [the means of knowledge's conjunction means] being incompatible with the falsity of that form. For precisely this reason, the prattle that 'memory does not have an external object, because memory is observed even when the object has perished' [is also refuted].

children.text: atha saṃvitprāgabhāvāderavartamānatayā na pratyakṣatvam / liṅgādyabhāvācca na pramāṇāntarataḥ siddhiriti / yadyevam, akāraṇaṃ tarhi svataḥsiddhatvaṃ prāga
children.translated_text: Now, [objection:] since the prior absence of awareness does not exist [in the present], it is not an object of perception. And since there is no inferential mark and the like, there is no establishment through another means of knowledge either. [Reply:] If so, then self-establishedness is groundless, since the prior absence and the like [of awareness] are not established.

body.text: bhāvādyasiddheḥ / pramāṇābhāva eva hīdānīṃ vācyaḥ / na ca tadabhāvaḥ śakyo 'bhidhātumityuktameva / yogyānupalabdhyaivābhāvasya samarthitatvāt /
body.translated_text: For what should now be stated is simply the absence of a <s>pramāṇa</s> [for establishing the prior absence]. And it has already been said that that absence [of the <s>pramāṇa</s>] cannot be maintained — because the absence [of awareness in sleep] has been established through the non-apprehension of what is fit [to be perceived] (<s>yogyānupalabdhi</s>) alone.

body.text: apica pratyakṣasaṃvit svasattākāle svaviṣayasya sadbhāvaṃ sādhayantī yattasya na sarvadā sattāṃ sādhayati, tadavasīyate ahamidānīmevāsmi nānyadeti kālaviśeṣāvacchinnaiva sā cakāstīti / itarathā ghaṭāderapi nityatvaprasaṅgāt / evamanumānādisaṃvido 'pi / naca pratyakṣānumānādibhedaśūnyā nirviṣayā nirāśrayā dhīḥ saṃbhavatītyuktameva /
body.translated_text: Moreover, perceptual awareness, while establishing the existence of its object at the time of its own existence, does not establish its existence at all times — this is understood from the fact that it shines forth as delimited by a specific time alone: 'I exist only now, not at another [time].' Otherwise, even a pot and the like would be eternal. The same applies to awareness through inference and the like. And it has already been said that there is no cognition that is devoid of the distinctions of perception, inference, and the like, or that is without an object, or without a substrate.

body.text: na cānyāviṣayatvāt saṃvido 'nyataḥ tatprāgabhāvādyasiddhiḥ / ajñāsiṣamiti prāktanasaṃvido 'dyatanadhiyā viṣayīkriyamāṇatvāt / pratikūlānuviṣayaniyatahānopādānādiliṅgāvagamyatvācca parasaṃvidaḥ / tadanabhyupagame ca śabdārthagrahaṇāsaṃbhavena vaidikalaukika samastavyavahārābhāvaprasaṅgaḥ / gurūpasarpaṇādyanupapattiśca ; jñānavattvena tasyāpratīteḥ /
body.translated_text: Nor does the prior absence and the like of awareness become established through another [means], just because awareness has another [thing] as its object. Because the former awareness [that existed before sleep] is made an object by the present cognition [as in the recollection] 'I did not know.' And because the awareness of another [person] is knowable through inferential marks such as the invariable adoption and avoidance [of actions] conforming to favorable and unfavorable [objects]. And if that [awareness of others] were not accepted, there would follow the consequence of the absence of all Vedic and worldly convention, due to the impossibility of grasping the meaning of words. And the untenable consequence of approaching a teacher and the like [would follow], since one would have no cognition of his being a knower.

children.text: na cānyaviṣayatve 'nanubhūtitvam / svāśrayasya svasattayaiva prakāśamānatvaṃ, svaviṣayasādhanatvaṃ vā hyanubhūtitvam / te ca saṃvidantara viṣayabhāve 'pi svānubhavasiddhe na bhraśyata iti kathamananubhūtitva prasaṅgaḥ? / ghaṭādestu tathāsvābhāvyābhāvādevānanubhūtitvaṃ, nānubhāvyatvāt / api cānanubhāvyatve 'pi samānaḥ tatprasaṅgaḥ, gaganakusumavat / na cātmano 'nubhūtitvam, anubhavitṛtvāt / nāpyasāvananubhāvyaḥ,
children.translated_text: Nor does being the object of another [awareness] entail not being an experience. For being an experience means: shining forth to one's own substrate by one's very existence, or being the means of establishing one's own object. And these [properties], even when [awareness] becomes the object of another awareness, are established through one's own experience and do not lapse — so how can there be the consequence of not being an experience? But for a pot and the like, it is precisely because they lack such a natural [self-luminosity] that they are not experiences — not because they are incapable of being experienced. Moreover, even if [the pot] were incapable of being experienced, the same consequence [of non-selfhood] would apply equally, like a sky-flower. And the self is not an experience [in that absurd sense], because it is the experiencer. Nor is it incapable of being experienced,

body.text: anubhavasyeva svataḥsiddhyato 'pyasya svaparasaṃvedyatvābhyupagamāt / vedyatve 'nātmatvāpādanamavedyatve 'pi samānaṃ pūrvavat / yadi tu gaganakusumasyāsattvamevānātmatvānanubhūtitvaprayojakamāsthīyeta; āsthīyatāṃ tarhī ghaṭāderapi asaṃvidāśrayatvājñānāvirodhitvayoreva tatprayojakatvam / atha te api viṣayatve syātāmiti cet, aviṣayatve 'pi tathaivetyalamapratiṣṭhitakṛtarkāpahasanena /
body.translated_text: because, even though it too is self-established like experience [itself], it is accepted as being knowable to itself and to others. And the reduction to non-selfhood when [the self is] knowable — the same [applies] even when [it is said to be] unknowable, as before. But if it is maintained that the very non-existence of the sky-flower is what causes its non-selfhood and non-experiencehood — then let it be maintained that for a pot and the like too, their not being a substrate of awareness, and their non-contradiction with ignorance, are precisely the causes of that [non-selfhood]. [Objection:] But those [pots] too, when they become objects, would become [selves]. [Reply:] Even when they are not objects, it would be the same — so enough with the laughter provoked by this groundless sophistry.

body.text: yadapi jananavirahādanubhūtervikārāntaranirasanam, vyabhicarati tadapi prāgabhāve / janmābhāve 'pi tasya vināśadarśanāt / bhāvaviśeṣaṇopādāne 'pi bhavadabhimatāvidyayānaikāntyam / sā hyanādirapi vividhavikāravatī vināśavatī ca tattvajñānodayāt / aparamārthāstadvikārāḥ santīti cet, paramārthāśca te kiṃ vikārāḥ santi?, janmavanto vā paramārthāḥ; yena pāramārthyena viśeṣaṇaṃ sādhyasya sādhanasya vār'thavattāmaśnuvīta / tathāca sati sādhu samarthitaṃ tarkakuśalenetyamanena /
body.translated_text: As for [the argument] that because experience (<s>anubhūti</s>) is unoriginated, other transformations are negated — that too deviates in [the case of] prior absence. Because even though origination is absent for it [i.e., prior absence], its destruction is observed. Even if [the qualification] 'of a positive entity' is added, there is inconclusiveness due to the <s>avidyā</s> accepted by your [Advaita] school. For that [<s>avidyā</s>], though beginningless, is possessed of various transformations and is subject to destruction upon the arising of knowledge of reality. [Objection:] Its transformations are not ultimately real. [Reply:] Then are those [transformations] ultimately real modifications? Or are they ultimately real [things] that are originated? [The question is:] by virtue of what ultimate reality could the qualification of the provable or the reason attain meaningfulness? And this being so, it has been well argued by the one skilled in reasoning with [the verse beginning] 'and with this.'

body.text: yadapi nahyajaṃ vibhāgyastīti; tadapi na; ajasyaivātmano dehendriyādibhyo vibhāgasya samarthitatvāt / anāditvenābhyupagatasyājñānasyā'tmano vyatiriktatayāvaśyāśrayaṇīyatvāt / aparamārthaḥ sa vibhāga iti cet, paramārthabhedaḥ kiṃ janmapratibaddhaḥ kvaciddṛṣṭaḥ? nirbādhapratītisiddhaśca dṛgdṛśyabhedaḥ paramārtha evetyanantaramevopapādayiṣyāmaḥ /
body.translated_text: As for [the statement] 'the unborn cannot be separated' — that too is not [valid]. Because the separation of the unborn self from the body, sense-organs, and the like has been established. Because the ignorance (<s>ajñāna</s>) accepted as beginningless must necessarily be resorted to as distinct from the self. [Objection:] That separation is not ultimately real. [Reply:] Has a real difference that is bound to origination ever been observed anywhere? And the difference between the seer and the seen, which is established through uncontradicted experience, is indeed ultimately real — we shall establish this immediately hereafter.

children.text: yadapi nāsyā meyo dharmo 'pyasti; cetyānāṃ na ciddharmatvamiti ca; tadapi śāstrānumānādipramāṇasiddhaiḥ svayaṃprakāśatvanityatvādidharmaiḥ svayamabhyupagatairanaikāntikam / na ca te citimātramiti vācyam; tatsiddhāvapi teṣu
children.translated_text: As for [the statement] 'it has no knowable property either,' and 'consciousness does not have consciousness as a property' — that too is inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>), due to properties such as self-luminosity, eternality, and the like, which are established through scripture, inference, and other <s>pramāṇas</s> and are accepted by [the Advaitin] himself. Nor should it be said that those [properties] are merely consciousness — because even when their identity with consciousness is established, disagreement regarding them

children.text: vimatidarśanāt / abhyupagamyaiva hi saṃvidaṃ tadanumeyatvakṣaṇikatvādi pratijānate vādinaḥ / svarūpabhedācca / svāśrayaṃ prati sattayaiva kasyacit prakāśanaṃ hi saṃvedanam / svayaṃprakāśatā tu sattayaivā'tmane prakāśamānatā / prakāśaśca cidacidaśeṣapadārthasādhāraṇo dharma iti saṃvitsiddhāveva sādhitam / tadanabhyupagame tu vyavahārānuguṇyavacanaḥ prakāśaśabdaḥ / nityatā tu sarvakālavartamānatā / ekasaṅkhyāvaccheda ekatvamiti / naca jaḍatvakāladeśanānātvādyavaccheda- śūnyatārūpatvātteṣāṃ na yathoktadoṣa iti yuktam / tathābhūtairapi taiḥ citidharmabhūtairanaikāntyasyāparihāryatvāt / saṃvidi ca niṣedhyatvābhimataja
children.translated_text: is observed. For disputants, having accepted awareness, nevertheless assert its inferability, momentariness, and the like. And [the properties are distinct from consciousness] because of the difference in essential nature. For awareness (<s>saṃvedana</s>) is the illumination of something for one's own substrate by its very existence. But self-luminosity (<s>svayaṃprakāśatā</s>) is shining forth to oneself by [one's] very existence. And illumination (<s>prakāśa</s>) is a property common to all entities, sentient and insentient — this has been established in establishing awareness itself. But if that [identity] is not accepted, the word 'illumination' [is used] in the sense of conformity with convention. Eternality (<s>nityatā</s>) means existing at all times. Oneness is delimitation by the number one. And it is not proper [to say] that because those [properties] lack delimitation by insentience, time, space, plurality, and the like, and because their nature is such, the stated fault does not apply — because the inconclusiveness is unavoidable even with such [properties] that are properties of consciousness. And when, in awareness, the various contrary properties — such as insentience, non-eternality, plurality, and the like — which are the intended objects of negation, are absent, the negation-statement is a mere statement,

body.text: ḍatvānityatvanānātvādivirūddhavividhadharmābhāve niṣedhoktiruktimātrameva / cetyaṃ cājñānamātmani dṛṣṭamiṣṭaṃ ca bhavatām / api cāsyā iti ṣaṣṭhyānubhūteḥ saṃbandhamabhidhāya nirdharmatvaṃ pratijñāyamānaṃ vandhyātvamiva jananyā viruddhārthamāpadyeta /
body.translated_text: without [real] content. And the knowable (<s>cetya</s>) and ignorance (<s>ajñāna</s>) are both seen and accepted by you [Advaitins] as [existing] in the self. Moreover, by the genitive 'of this' [in 'it has no property'], having stated a relation [between the self and its properties] for experience, the assertion of propertylessness would lead to a contradictory meaning — like [asserting] barrenness of one's own mother.

body.text: prāṇātmavāde dehātmavādadūṣaṇajātamatidiśannāha nirasta iti / anirasto 'dūṣito hi pratipakṣitayāvasthitaḥ prāṇātmavādaḥ nirāsakayuktayantarāpādana- prayojakībhāvamāpadyeta / na tu dehātmavādadūṣaṇaireva dūṣito 'satprāya iti bhāvaḥ //9//
body.translated_text: In [the section on] the <s>prāṇātmavāda</s> (the view that the vital breath is the self), he says 'nirasta' ('refuted'), extending the refutations [already given] of the <s>dehātmavāda</s> (body-self view). For the <s>prāṇātmavāda</s>, which stands as the opposing position unrefuted — that is, not countered — would occasion the introduction of reasoning for its refutation. But it is not [the case] that it stands as an independent position requiring separate refutation, since it is mostly refuted by the very refutations of the body-self view. This is the purport.

body.text: ātmano gatyanupapattiṃ pariharati

children.translated_text: 'Avibhutvena' ('because of non-omnipresence').

children.text: ti / vibhutve gatirnopapadyeteti yuktam / aṇutve tu manasa iva niḥsparśasyāpi gatirātmana upapadyata eva / na ca sparśasya gatau hetutvaṃ prayatnādṛṣṭādipreraṇamantareti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: If [the self] were omnipresent (<s>vibhu</s>), motion would indeed be untenable. But when [the self is] atomic (<s>aṇu</s>), like the mind, even for the self that is intangible (<s>niḥsparśa</s>), motion is perfectly tenable. And it is not the case that touch (<s>sparśa</s>) is the cause of motion without the impulse from effort (<s>prayatna</s>), unseen merit (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>), and the like. This is the purport.
'Parimāṇe' ('regarding measure').

children.text:
ti / etadātmano gatimattvamātmanaḥ parimāṇanirūpaṇaprakaraṇe 'pi nirūpitaṃ bhaviṣyatīti adhunaitāvatā gatimattvavarṇanenālamityarthaḥ / alamamuneti pāṭhāntaram /
atra saṃvidātmavādī samuttiṣṭhate
children.translated_text:
This — the possession of motion by the self — will be examined in the section on determining the measure (<s>parimāṇa</s>) of the self too. Hence for now, this much description of the possession of motion suffices — this is the meaning. 'Alam amunā' ('enough with this') is an alternative reading.
Here the proponent of the consciousness-self view (<s>saṃvidātmavādin</s>) rises [to object]:
'Bhavatu tarhi' ('let it be then').
The self is consciousness, because it is non-insentient (<s>ajaḍa</s>) — this is the inferential formulation. He states the negative concomitance (<s>vyatirekavyāpti</s>):
'Jaḍatve' ('if insentient').

children.text: ti / pratibaddhaṃ-vyāpyam / anātmyam-anātmatvam / ātmano bhāva ātmyaṃ tasyābhāva iti vyutpatteḥ / vyatirekopanayanigamane āha
children.translated_text: 'Pratibaddha' means: pervaded (<s>vyāpya</s>). 'Anātmya' means: non-selfhood (<s>anātmatva</s>) — derived as: <s>ātmya</s> is the state of being a self, and its absence is [<s>anātmya</s>]. He states the application and conclusion of the negative concomitance:
'Jaḍatvaṃ ca' ('and insentience').

children.text: ti / tadapi-anātmyamapi / vyāpakanivṛttervyāpyanivṛttyākṣepakatvāt vyāpaka jaḍatvanivṛttyā vyāpyānātmyanivṛttiḥ siddhyatīti bhāvaḥ / ajaḍatvahetorasiddhiṃ pariharati
children.translated_text: 'That too' — non-selfhood too [is negated]. Because the cessation of the pervader necessitates the cessation of the pervaded, through the cessation of the pervader, namely insentience, the cessation of the pervaded, namely non-selfhood, is established. This is the purport. He resolves the unestablishedness of the reason of non-insentience:
'Ajaḍatvaṃ ca' ('and non-insentience').

children.text: ti / svasattāmātrataḥ prakāśamānatvāt parāyattaprakāśatvalakṣaṇajaḍatvābhāva iti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: Because [the self] shines forth by its mere existence, there is the absence of insentience, which is characterized by dependence on another for illumination. This is the purport.
'Na hi' ('for not').

children.text:
ti / parāyattasiddhiḥ-parādhīnaprakāśā / jaḍeti yāvat /
atra saṃvidanumeyatvavādināṃ bhāṭṭānāṃ matamanuvadati
children.translated_text:
'Parāyattasiddhi' means: one whose illumination depends on another — that is, insentient (<s>jaḍa</s>).
Here he states the view of the <s>Bhāṭṭa</s> [<s>Mīmāṃsakas</s>], who hold that awareness is inferable (<s>anumeyatva</s>):
'Syān matam' ('the view would be').
Thus.
'Viṣayamātram' ('merely the object').

children.text: iti / na hi nīlo 'yaṃ ghaṭa iti jñāne jñānasya viṣayatvaṃ saṃbhavati paṭāderiveti bhāvaḥ / nanu ghaṭamahaṃ jānāmīti jñānaprakāśastarhi katham ? tatrāha
children.translated_text: For in the cognition 'this is a blue pot,' it is not possible for the cognition [itself] to be an object — just as cloth and the like [which are not the object of that cognition]. This is the purport. [Objection:] But then how does the cognition become manifest [as in the cognition] 'I know the pot'? To this he says:
'Tataś ca' ('and therefore').
'Tataḥ' means: thereafter — this is the syntactical connection. 'Ca' is in the sense of 'tu' (however).
The purport is this —

children.text:
jñānādviṣaye jñātatā nāma dharmo jāyate / sa eva prakāśa ityucyate / sa eva jñānakṛtor'thasyātiśayo nāma / sa ca pratyakṣo jñātuḥ / tena cārthaprakāśarūpaliṅgenātmani taddhetuṃ jñānamanuminoti / ānumānikajñānālambanaśca ghaṭamahaṃ jānāmīti niruktapratyayaḥ / anumānaprakāraśca iyaṃ ghaṭatvaprakārakajñātatā ghaṭatvaprakārakajñānajanyā tathā vidhajñātatātvāditi / taddharmaprakārakajñānajñātatayoḥ
kāryakāraṇabhāvācca vyāptisiddhiḥ /
etadbhāṭṭamataṃ pratikṣipati
children.translated_text: From knowledge, a property called 'being-known' (<s>jnatatva</s>) arises in the object. That itself is called 'illumination' (<s>prakasa</s>). That itself is the 'excellence' (<s>atisaya</s>) that the object acquires through knowledge. And that [being-known] is perceptible to the knower. And through that — the inferential mark having the form of the illumination of the object — one infers knowledge as its cause in the self. And the cognition 'I know the pot,' which is an inferential cognition having knowledge as its object, is an analyzed cognition. And the form of the inference is: this being-known-as-possessing-pot-hood is produced by knowledge having the form of pot-hood, because it is a being-known of that type. And the establishment of pervasion is from the cause-effect relation between knowledge having that property as its form and being-known [as having that property]. This is the <s>Bhatta</s> view, which he refutes with
'tanna'
('that is not so').
'jnane'

children.text: ti / jñānaviṣayatā hi jñātatā / tadviṣayatayār'thasaṃbaddhajñānavyatiriktatayā viṣayadharmasyātiśayaviśeṣasyāsiddhiḥ / mama ghaṭajñānaṃ jātam, jñāto mayā ghaṭa iti pratītyordharmidharmabhāvavyatyāsamantarār'thabhedasyānānubhāvikatvāditi bhāvaḥ / pratyakṣāsiddhimuktvā jñātatārūpātiriktaprakāśe kalpanāsiddhimāha
children.translated_text: ('in knowledge'). For being-known (<s>jnatatva</s>) is being the object of knowledge. Since it is not distinct from knowledge that is connected with the object through being its object, the alleged specific excellence that is a property of the object is not established. Because the difference in meaning between the two cognitions 'knowledge of the pot has arisen in me' and 'the pot is known by me' — despite the interchange of property and property-bearer — is not experientially given. This is the purport. Having stated the non-establishment through perception, he states the non-establishment through postulation regarding an illumination distinct from the form of being-known with
'ubhaye'

children.text: ti / jñānaviṣayatayaivārthe jñātavyavahāropapattestadanupapattilakṣaṇaṃ jñātatāyāmatiriktāyāṃ kalpakamasiddhamiti bhāvaḥ / arthajñāneṣu jñānasya jñāturahamarthasyātmanaśca niyataṃ bhānamiti prābhākaraprakriyayā samarthayati
children.translated_text: ('in both'). Since the convention of 'known' regarding an object is justified merely through being an object of knowledge, the postulator [i.e., the need to postulate] being-known as something additional is not established — this is the purport. He justifies through the <s>Prabhakara</s> method that in cognitions of objects, the appearance of knowledge, the knower (the 'I'-object), and the self is invariable, with
'vitti'

children.text: ti / jñānajñātranavagāhinyāṃ jñeyapratītāvupagatāyāṃ jāte 'pi ghaṭajñāne 'haṃ tajjñānavān na veti saṃśayaḥ, tajjñānābhāvavānahamityādiviparītaniścayaśca kadācidbhavet,svasya jñānavattvenāpratibhāsāt / tantritayaviṣayakatvaṃ jñānasyaṣitavyamiti bhāvaḥ / tathāca svaprakāśatvasiddherjñānasya tata eva viṣayavyavahāravat jñātatāvyavahāro 'pi ghaṭata iti nārthāntarajñātatākalpanāvasara iti hārdam / athātītānāgateṣvartheṣu jñātatāyā utpattyasaṃbhavāttatra jñānenaiva jñātatāpratītirupapādyā, samaiva ceyaṃ rītiḥ pratyakṣe 'pītyāśayenā'ha
children.translated_text: ('awareness'). When the cognition of the knowable is accepted [as occurring] without knowledge and the knower being involved [in its content], then even when knowledge of the pot has arisen, the doubt 'am I possessed of that knowledge or not?' and even the contrary certainty 'I am not possessed of that knowledge' could sometimes arise — because [the knower] does not appear as possessing knowledge. Therefore, knowledge must be accepted as having a threefold object [knowable, knowledge, and knower] — this is the purport. And thus, from the self-luminosity of knowledge being established, from that alone the convention of being-known is justified, just like the convention regarding the object — hence there is no occasion for postulating a separate being-known. This is the inner meaning. Now, since in the case of past and future objects, being-known cannot arise [at the present time], the cognition of being-known there must be accounted for through knowledge alone — and this same method applies even in perception. With this intention he says
'atite' ('in the past').

children.text:
ti / atra grahaṇamanumānādilakṣaṇam / vyāhāraḥ-śabdo vyavahāraḥ/ vyavahāraḥ kāyikohānopādānādiḥ / ubhau viditatvapratītimūlāvatra grāhyau / viditapratītimūlayostayoḥ sadbhāve 'sadbhāve vā viditatvavyavahārātpūrvameva viditatvapratītestanmūlabhūtāyā udaya iti na tatra vyāhāraliṅgena viditatvamanumāya tato vedanānumā
nam / kintu svayaṃprakāśavedanabalādeva viditatvapratītiḥ atha ca tanmūlavyavahāra iti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: Here 'apprehension' (<s>grahana</s>) refers to [cognition through] inference and the like. 'Vyahara' means verbal expression, [and also] conventional usage. 'Vyavahara' means bodily [activity such as] taking up and setting aside. Both should be understood here as rooted in the awareness of being-known. When both — which are rooted in the awareness of being-known — either exist or do not exist, the awareness of being-known arises prior to the convention of being-known itself. Therefore, it is not the case that one first infers being-known through the inferential mark of convention and then infers the awareness [of being-known]. Rather, from the very force of self-luminous awareness itself, the awareness of being-known [arises], and then the convention rooted in it [follows] — this is the purport.
'Inferential in that case'
'is the establishment of the object'
— in some readings this is the meaning: the establishment of the object is [merely] ascertained through the means of valid cognition that is inference in the form of illumination.
'visayaprakasasiddhih'

children.text: riti pāṭhe tu anumānapramāṇajanitā viṣayaprakāśānumitirityarthaḥ / vyavahārātpūrvameva jñātatvapratītiṃ smṛtisthale udāharati
children.translated_text: — in this reading, the meaning is: the inference of the illumination of the object, generated by the means of valid cognition that is inference. He gives an example from the domain of memory for the awareness of being-known arising prior to convention with
'kenacid' ('by someone').
Having understood the remembered-ness of the object through memory itself, one expresses [it]:
'It has been remembered by me today.'

children.text: ti / yadi laiṅgikī smṛtatvapratītiḥ, tarhyanenaiva vyāhāreṇa liṅgena svasyārthe smṛtatvapratītirānumānikīti vācyam / tatra cānyonyāśrayaṇaṃ prasajyate / smṛtatvapratītyā tadvyavahāraḥ, tenaiva ca sā svasyeti / tathā ca jñānasvaprakāśatvanibandhanaiva jñātatvapratītireṣṭavyeti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: If the awareness of remembered-ness were inferential, then it would have to be said that through this very verbal expression as the inferential mark, the inferential awareness of remembered-ness regarding one's own object [arises]. And in that case, mutual dependence (<s>anyonyasraya</s>) would follow: the convention [depends on] the awareness of remembered-ness, and that [awareness depends] on the convention itself. And thus, the awareness of being-known should be accepted as grounded in the self-luminosity of knowledge alone — this is the purport.
'svavyaharenaiva'

children.text:
ti / nirapatrapa iva ka ityanvayaḥ / nirapatrapaḥ-nirlajjaḥ / svavyāhāreṇa-ahaṃ
jānāmīti svaniṣṭhajñānavyavahāreṇa, svajñānānumānam-svaniṣṭhajñānapratītiṃ laiṅgikīm / vyavahāre vyavahartavyajñānasya hetutvāt svakīyajñānavyavahāreṇaiva svasya svakīyajñānānumānamiti pratijñānupapannātyantamiti yāvat / parakīyena parātmano jñānavyavahāreṇa tadanyasya parātmaniṣṭhajñānānumānasaṃbhavāt
children.translated_text: ('through one's own verbal expression alone'). The construction is: 'who, like a shameless [person]?' 'Nirapatrapa' means shameless. 'Through one's own verbal expression' — through one's own convention of knowledge, i.e., 'I know.' 'Inference of one's own knowledge' — inferential awareness of knowledge residing in oneself. Because in conventional usage, knowledge of what is to be conventionally dealt with is the cause — [therefore,] inferring one's own knowledge through one's own knowledge-convention is absolutely untenable [as a thesis]. Since the inference of knowledge residing in another self is possible through another's verbal expression of knowledge,
'inference of one's own knowledge through one's own verbal expression'

children.text:
iti nirdiṣṭam / evaṃ jñātatāyā asiddhiḥ; jñāta iti pratītivyavahārayoḥ svaprakāśajñānata evopapatteḥ / jñānasya svaprakāśatvaṃ cajāte jñāne svātmani jñānasaṃśayajñānābhāvaniścayānudayabalāt niśceyamiti varṇitam /
idānīmabhyupagamyāpi viṣayaniṣṭhaṃ dharmāntaraṃ prakāśaṃ tadavaṣṭambhenaiva jñānasya svayaṃprakāśatvaṃ samarthayati prakāśānumeyajñānavādanirāsārtham
children.translated_text: was specified [as the problematic case]. Thus, being-known is not established [as a separate entity], since both the awareness and the convention of 'known' are justified from self-luminous knowledge alone. And the self-luminosity of knowledge has been demonstrated from the fact that, when knowledge arises, [no] doubt about knowledge regarding itself, [no] certainty of the absence of knowledge [about itself], ever arises — [hence self-luminosity] is to be ascertained. Now, even granting a property called 'illumination' distinct from the object [i.e., jnatatva], he justifies the self-luminosity of knowledge on the basis of that very [illumination], in order to refute the view that knowledge is to be inferred from illumination, with
'anyasca'

children.text:
tyādinā / atra prayogadvayam-anubhūtirananyādhīnataddharmā svasaṃbandhādarthāntare taddharmahetutvāt yathā rūpam, taddhi svasaṃbandhāddhāṭādau cākṣuṣatve hetuḥ svasmin rūpāntarānapekṣataddharmavat; anubhūtiḥ ananyādhīnasvavyavahārā svasaṃbandhādarthāntare vyavahārahetutvāt / yathā sattā / sā hi svasaṃbandhāddhaṭādau saditi vyavahārahetuḥ svīyasadvyavahāre sattāntarā
napekṣā iti / ādyaḥ prayogo 'tra jñātatārūpaṃ dharmāntaramabhyupetya, dvitīyastu tadanupagamena / hetusādhyaniṣkarṣaḥ śrutaprakāśikādito 'nusandheyaḥ / anena jñānaniṣṭhaprakāśasya jñānāntarānapekṣatvasiddhyā jñānasya svayaṃprakāśatvopapattiḥ / tathā ca tasyaivātmatvamityāha
children.translated_text: ('and another') and so forth. Here there are two formal arguments: (1) Awareness (<s>anubhuti</s>) possesses its own property independent of anything else, and is the cause of that property in another thing through its own connection — just like form (<s>rupa</s>). For form, through its own connection, is the cause of being visible in a pot and the like, and it itself possesses that property without depending on another form. (2) Awareness has its own convention independent of anything else, and is the cause of convention in another thing through its own connection — just like existence (<s>satta</s>). For existence, through its own connection, is the cause of the convention 'it exists' regarding a pot and the like, and it does not depend on another existence for its own convention of 'existent.' The first argument is on the assumption of a separate property called being-known; the second, without that assumption. The extraction of the reason and the provable should be investigated from the <s>Srutaprakasika</s> and so forth. By this, through establishing that the illumination residing in knowledge does not depend on another knowledge, the self-luminosity of knowledge is justified. And since that [knowledge] is the self — he says
'svayamprakasatvad'
('because of self-luminosity'). The purport here is: the self-luminosity of the self is established through <s>sruti</s> (scripture) such as
'This person is self-luminous'

children.text: tyādiśrutisiddham / jñānasya svayaṃprakāśatvaṃ ca niruktānumānataḥ / atastasyaivātmatvaṃ nyāyyamiti / saṃvida ātmatve lāghavamapyāha
children.translated_text: and the like. And the self-luminosity of knowledge is [established] through the analyzed inference [stated above]. Therefore, it is fitting that that [knowledge] itself is the self. He also states the parsimony in [accepting] awareness (<s>samvid</s>) as the self with
'kim ca' ('moreover').
'Veditri' means: of the nature of the knower — that is, the self. This is the meaning.
'bhavatu'

children.text:
ti loṭū kāmacārābhyanujñāyām / itipadamanuṣañjanīyam / saṃvida eva prakāmamātmatvamityabhyanujñānaṃ śreṣṭhamityarthaḥ /
saṃvida ātmatve bādhakamāśaṅkate
children.translated_text: — the imperative mood [is used] in the sense of willing permission. The particle 'iti' should be connected [with the previous]. The meaning is: the unrestricted acceptance of awareness itself as the self is the best [view]. He raises an objection against awareness being the self with
'nanu aham' ('but I').

children.text: iti / prādhānyādahamarthasyaivātmatvaṃ pratīyate, natu dharmatayā bhāsamānāyāḥ saṃvida iti bhāvaḥ / ardhāṅgīkāreṇa pariharati
children.translated_text: The purport is: it is the 'I'-object that is primarily understood as the self, not awareness, which appears as a property [of the self]. He answers with partial acceptance:
'satyam' ('true').
There is acceptance regarding the cognition of the knower-self. But non-acceptance regarding its being a [separate] valid cognition. He states the reason for its non-validity with
'sa tu' ('that, however').

children.text:
iti / jñātā tu bhedarūpatayā nasākṣāt pratyakṣapramāṇasiddhaḥ, kintu bhrāntisiddhaḥ / svalakṣaṇavastumātrāvagāhi nirvikalpakameva hi pramāṇam / dharmadharmibhāvādikalpitabhedāvagāhi savikalpakaṃ tu
bhramalakṣaṇamati hārdam / jñātṛbhedapratīteḥ yauktikabādhamapyāha
children.translated_text: The knower, however, is not directly established by the means of valid cognition that is perception as having the form of difference; rather, it is established through error. For only non-conceptual [cognition] that apprehends mere particular realities is a valid means of cognition. But conceptual cognition that apprehends fabricated distinctions such as the property-property-bearer relation is of the nature of error — this is the inner meaning. He also states the rational sublation of the cognition of the knower as different with
'bhedajnane' ('in the cognition of difference').
The [phrase] 'as if established' should be connected with what follows too.
'aprthagvastutaye'

children.text: ti pāṭhaḥ saṃbhāvyate / vā aprakāśātmana iti padacchedaḥ / tathā cāyamarthaḥ-bhedajñānasiddhavatkāreṇāpi-kvacidbhedajñānasya prāmāṇyopagamenāpi / saṃvedanānāṃ bhedasya saugataiḥ tattvataḥ iṣyamāṇatvāt / apṛthagvastutayā-abhinnavastutvena sādhyena, gṛhītāvyabhicāreṇa-gṛhītavyāptikena, sahopalambhaniyamena-jñānajñātroḥ mahopambhaniyamarūpahetunā, jñāturaprakāśasvabhāvatve prakāśāyogaḥ svabhāvavirodhādeva, prakāśasvabhāvatve ca saṃvedanatvamevetyādinā vā saṃvidabhedasādhakena saṃvidbhedavādhakena hetunā aprakāśātmanaḥ saṃvidbhinnasya jñāturahamarthasyātmanaḥ tattvaṃ-svarūpaṃ durupagamam-upagantumaśakyamityarthaḥ / tṛtīyāntadvayaṃ durupagamamityanenānvitam / jñātā saṃvidabhinnaḥ saṃvidā sahaivopalabhyamānatvāt prakāśasvabhāvatvādvā iti prayogo 'tra bodhyaḥ / yadvā pṛthagvastutayenatvāt syātpāṭhaḥ / avyabhicāranirūpakasyābhedarūpasādhyasyopasthitistvarthāt / prakāśātmana ityeva cāstu padacchedaḥ / sahopalambhaniyamena, prakāśasvābhāvye ca saṃvedanatvamityādinā vā hetunā prakāśātmanaḥ saṃvidabhinnasya siddhyata ātmanaḥ, bhedajñānasiddhavatkāreṇa-bhādajñānaprāmāṇyasiddhavadaṅgīkaraṇena, pṛthagvastutayā-saṃvidbhinnatvena tattvam astitvaṃ, durupagamamityarthaḥ / nirukprakāraṃ grāhakabhedanirāsahetuṃ grāhyabhedanirāse 'pyatidiśati
children.translated_text: is a possible reading. Or the word-division is 'aprakasatmanah.' And thus the meaning is: even with the acceptance ('as-if-established') of the validity of the cognition of difference in some cases — since the Buddhists accept the difference of cognitions as ultimately real — [nevertheless,] through the provable of non-separate-entity-hood, i.e., non-difference, through the invariable concomitance that has been grasped — through the reason that is the rule of co-perception (<s>sahopalambhaniyama</s>) of knowledge and the knower — if the knower has a non-luminous nature, illumination is impossible due to the very incompatibility of natures; and if it has a luminous nature, then it is itself awareness. By this or similar reasons that prove the non-difference of awareness, which sublate the difference of awareness — the reality, i.e., the essential nature, of the knower — the 'I'-object — the self — which is different from awareness and of non-luminous nature, is difficult to accept (i.e., cannot be accepted). This is the meaning. The two instrumentals [in the verse] are to be construed with 'difficult to accept.' The formal argument to be understood here is: the knower is non-different from awareness, because it is always apprehended together with awareness, or because it has a luminous nature. Or alternatively, the reading may be 'prthagvastutayenatvat.' The presence of the provable in the form of non-difference, which determines the non-deviation, is [understood] from the context. And let the word-division be simply 'prakasatmanah.' Through the reason of the rule of co-perception, or through [the argument that] if it has a luminous nature then it is awareness, and the like — [the self that is] of a luminous nature, established as non-different from awareness — [yet] its reality, i.e., existence, as a separate entity from awareness, even with the acceptance ('as-if-established') of the validity of the cognition of difference, is difficult to accept — this is the meaning. He extends the stated method — the reason for negating the difference of the apprehender — to the negation of the difference of the apprehended too with
'grahye' ('regarding the apprehended').

children.text: ti / sahopalambhaniyamāt prakāśasvabhāvye ca saṃvedanatvamityādito vā saṃvidabhinnatvaṃ nīlāderviṣayasyeti jñānabhinnatvena nīlādyarthabhedasyāpyasattvamityarthaḥ / nanu grāhyagrāhakayoḥ saṃvidabhede jñātṛjñeyabhedānāṃ jñānatobhedenāvabhāsaḥ kathamityatrāha
children.translated_text: From the rule of co-perception, or from [the argument that] if it has a luminous nature then it is awareness, and the like — the non-difference from awareness of blue and the like, which are objects — hence the non-existence even of the difference of objects such as blue and the like as different from knowledge — this is the meaning. [Objection:] If both the apprehended and the apprehender are non-different from awareness, how does the appearance of the distinctions of knower and known, as different from knowledge, [arise]? To this he says
'atah' ('therefore').

The appearance of the difference of apprehended and apprehender, rooted in a defect, is false; only the mere appearance as awareness is real — this is the purport. For the overt Buddhists, the <s>Yogacaras</s>, the defect is latent impression (<s>vasana</s>). For the covert [Buddhists], the <s>Mayavadins</s> [i.e., Advaitins], the defect is beginningless <s>avidya</s> (ignorance). 'The conceptual construction of apprehended and apprehender' — the distinction of known and knower, characterized by being-the-object-of-knowledge and being-the-locus-of-knowledge. He presents the assent of the overt Buddhists to the stated doctrine with
'avibhago 'pi' ('even though undivided').

children.text: ti / buddhirevā'tmā / sā ca nirbhedāpi bhrāntijñānaiḥ nīlabhedādigrāhyabhedacaitramaitrādigrāhaka bheda- pratyakṣatvānumānatvādilakṣaṇajñānabhedavatīva pratīyata iti kārikārthaḥ / māyināṃ saṃmatimupadarśayati
children.translated_text: Cognition (<s>buddhi</s>) itself is the self. And it, even though without [internal] division, through erroneous cognitions, appears as if possessing the division of blue and the like (the apprehended), <s>Caitra</s>, <s>Maitra</s>, and the like (the apprehender), and the division of cognitions characterized as perception, inference, and the like — this is the meaning of the verse. He presents the assent of the <s>Mayavadins</s> [Advaitins] with
'suddham' ('pure').

children.text:
iti / bheda prapañcasya śuddhaṃ tattvaṃ nopādānam / tathā sati paramārthatvāpattyānivṛttiprasaṅgāt / tatastasya prapañcasya māyaiva-vividhavicitramithyārthapratibhāsahetuḥ mithyābhū
tānādyavidyaiva jananī upādānamiti kārikārthaḥ / nirviśeṣasanmātraṃ cidrūpaṃ paramārthaḥ / tatrādhiṣṭhāne aparamārthanānābhedapratibhāso māyayeti bhāvaḥ /
ātmanaḥ svayaṃprakāśatvaṃ śrautam / saṃvidastathātvaṃ ca yuktisiddham / tattasyā evātmatvam / tadbhinnasya tu sarvasya doṣamūlatvādābhāsamātratvamiti saṃvidātmatvaṃ pūrvapakṣitam / tatra cāsti matadvayam / kṣaṇikavijñānamātmā, nityavijñānamātmeti ca / tatra kṣaṇikavijñānātmatvamataṃ prakaṭasaugatānāṃ tāvannirasyati
children.translated_text: The pure reality is not the material cause of the manifold of differences. If it were, there would follow the consequence of [those differences] being ultimately real, and hence the impossibility of their cessation. Therefore, <s>maya</s> alone — the cause of the appearance of manifold and variegated false objects — beginningless <s>avidya</s> (ignorance) alone, which is a false entity, is the mother, the material cause, of that manifold. The ultimate reality is mere undifferentiated being, of the nature of consciousness. The appearance of manifold non-ultimate differences upon that substratum is through <s>maya</s> — this is the purport. The self-luminosity of the self is scriptural. And the self-luminosity of awareness is established through reasoning. Therefore, that [awareness] itself is the self. But everything other than it, being rooted in defect, is mere appearance — thus awareness being the self has been presented as the prima facie view (<s>purvapaksa</s>). And there are two sub-views within this: momentary consciousness is the self, and eternal consciousness is the self. Of these, he first refutes the view that momentary consciousness is the self — [the view] of the overt Buddhists — with
'atra ahe'
and so forth. The meaning is: the proponent of an eternal self states the refutation against the view that momentary consciousness is the self.
'ksanabhangini' ('that which perishes every moment')

children.text: ti / kṣaṇarūpāvināśasvabhāvā viṣayabhedena nānā ca saṃvidupalabhyate / tasyāścedātmatvaṃ pratyabhijñādikaṃ nopapadyate / anusandhāturātmanaḥ sthiratva eva tadupapatteriti bhāvaḥ / atha pratibhāyā iva nirviṣayatvaṃ pratyabhijñāyāḥ śaṅkate
children.translated_text: and so forth. Cognition is apprehended as momentary in nature — without destruction of its form — and as manifold due to the difference in objects. If that [cognition] is the self, then recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>) and the like cannot be explained. The purport is: recognition is explained only if the self — who reconnects [past and present experience] — is stable. Now he raises the doubt that recognition might be objectless, like imaginative fancy (<s>pratibhā</s>), with
'nor [is it the case that] without an object' (<s>na ca nirālambana</s>)

children.text: ti / pratyabhijñā nirviṣayā pratibhātvāt mānasakalpanāvilāsavaditi prayogaḥ / atra bādhitatvamāha
children.translated_text: and so forth. The formal argument is: recognition is objectless, because it is a fancy (<s>pratibhā</s>) — like the play of mental imagination. Regarding this, he states its sublation with
'if [it were] without an object' (<s>nirālambanatva</s>)

children.text: ti / jñānasāmānyasya saviṣayakatvaniyamānnirviṣayakatve jñānatvāyogāt jñānaviśeṣe nirviṣayakatvasādhanaṃ bādhitaviṣayamityarthaḥ / pratibhāyāmapi nātyantāya nirviṣayatvam / anyatra sata evānyatra bhānāt / kvacidyāthārthyasyāpi dṛṣṭeriti bhāvaḥ / jñānasāmānyasya nirviṣayakatvamiti pakṣe svapravṛttivyāghātamapyāha
children.translated_text: and so forth. The meaning is: since cognition in general is necessarily object-directed, the proof of objectlessness in a specific [type of] cognition has a sublated subject — because if [cognition] lacked an object, it would not qualify as cognition at all. Even in the case of imaginative fancy (<s>pratibhā</s>), objectlessness is not absolute — because what exists somewhere appears somewhere else. And because veridicality is also observed in some [instances of fancy]. The purport is clear. He also states the self-defeating nature [of the argument] if cognition in general were objectless, with
'and of the proof' (<s>sādhanasya ca</s>)

children.text: ti / nirviṣayakatvasādhakānumānasya saviṣayakatve tadaviśeṣeṇāśeṣajñānānāṃ saviṣayakatvaṃsyāt / tasya nirviṣayakatve ca na nirviṣayakatvarūpasādhyasiddhiriti sādhanārthapravṛttivaighaṭyamiti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: and so forth. If the inference that proves objectlessness is itself object-directed, then without any distinction [between it and other cognitions], all cognitions would be object-directed.
