And if that [inference] itself is objectless, then the provable — namely objectlessness — is not established. So the functioning of the proof toward its purpose is incoherent. This is the purport.
'And it has been elaborated' (<s>prapañcitaśca</s>)

children.text:
ti / pūrvamīmāṃsāprathamādhyāyaprathamapāde uttaramīmāṃsādvitīyādhyāyacaraṇe ca jñānanirālambanatvamatanirākaraṇaṃ sūtratadvyākhyākartṛbhiḥ kṛtam / śāstre ca nyāyatattāvakhye sarvavijñānayāthārthyasamarthanena kṛtamityarthaḥ / atra pūrvottaramīmāṃsābhāgayorityanena mīmāṃsāyā viṃśatilakṣaṇyā aikaśāstrayaṃ tatpūrvottarabhāgarūpatvaṃ ca karmabrahmavicārayorabhimatam /
nanu vijñānaṃ dvividhaṃ pravṛttivijñānamālayavijñānaṃ ceti / tatrā'dyaṃ nīlapītādijñānam / antyaṃ cāhamākāramātmarūpam / kṣaṇikatve 'pyubhayavidhavijñānasyā'layavijñānadhārānuvṛttyā pratyabhijñopapadyata ityatrāha-
children.translated_text:
and so forth. The refutation of the doctrine that cognition is objectless has been carried out by the authors of the <s>sūtras</s> and their commentators in the first section of the first chapter of the <s>Pūrvamīmāṃsā</s> and in the fourth quarter of the second chapter of the <s>Uttaramīmāṃsā</s>. And in the treatise called <s>Nyāyatattvā</s> [i.e., <s>Nyāyatattvākhya</s>], it has been done through the vindication of the veridicality of all cognitions — this is the meaning. Here, by the expression 'in the two portions of the Pūrva- and Uttara-Mīmāṃsā,' the unity as a single <s>śāstra</s> of the <s>Mīmāṃsā</s> with its twenty chapters, and [the fact that] the inquiry into action (<s>karmavicāra</s>) and the inquiry into <s>Brahman</s> (<s>brahmavicāra</s>) are its earlier and later portions, is intended.
[Objection:] Cognition is of two kinds: active cognition (<s>pravṛttivijñāna</s>) and store-consciousness (<s>ālayavijñāna</s>). Of these, the former is the cognition of blue, yellow, and the like. The latter has the form of 'I' and is of the nature of the self. Even though both types of cognition are momentary, recognition is explained by the continuity of the stream of <s>ālayavijñāna</s>. To this he says:
'for this very reason' (<s>ata eva</s>)
and so forth.
'In a moment of cognition' (<s>vijñānakṣaṇa</s>)

children.text:
ti / vijñānameva kṣaṇo vijñānakṣaṇaḥ / anusandhāyinaḥ-pūrvānubhūtārthapratisandhānakartṛḥ kṣaṇikavijñānavyatiriktasya sthirasyopagame sarvaṃ kṣaṇikamiti siddhāntatyāgaḥ / prakārāntareṇa jñānavyatiriktajñātrabhyupaga
maprasaṅgaśceti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: and so forth. 'Cognitive moment' (<s>vijñānakṣaṇa</s>) — cognition itself is a moment, hence 'cognitive moment.' If one accepts a stable [entity] other than momentary cognition — one that reconnects previously experienced objects — then [the Buddhist] would abandon the established doctrine (<s>siddhānta</s>) that everything is momentary. And by another mode of reasoning, there would follow the consequence of accepting a knower distinct from knowledge. This is the purport.
'Without accepting' (<s>anabhyupagama</s>)

children.text: iti / kṣaṇikakramikavijñānasamudāyalakṣaṇaṃ santānaṃ samudāyyanatiriktaṃ cetpratyabhijñānupapattireva, santānāntargatasya pūrvasyānubhaviturvinaṣṭatvāt, uttarasya cānanubhavitṛtvena pratisandhānāyogāditi bhāvaḥ / atredamanusandheyam-kṣaṇikānāṃ samudāyabhāvo 'pi na ghaṭate, sthiraikadeśakālādyupādhikroḍīkārāsaṃbhavāt saugate naye / ekabuddhikroḍīkārastvatiprasaktaḥ / bhinnasantānivijñānānāmapi tathātvena santānaniyamānupapattyāpatteḥ / pūrvapūrvavijñānopādānakottarottaravijñānaparamparā santānamiti cenna / vinaṣṭasya kāryakāle 'sata upādānatvāyogāt / pūrvatvamātrasyātiprasaktatvācca / tatsantānaniyamānupapattireveti / nanvālayavijñānasya sausādṛśyena aikyabhrāntyā pratisandhānaṃ bhramātmakaṃ ghaṭata iti śaṅkate
children.translated_text: and so forth. If the continuum (<s>santāna</s>) — characterized as an aggregate of successive momentary cognitions — is not distinct from the aggregate, then recognition is simply impossible, because the prior experiencer within the continuum has perished, and the subsequent [cognition] — not being the experiencer [of the prior object] — cannot reconnect [past experience]. This is the purport. Here the following should also be considered: for momentary [entities], even the state of being an aggregate does not hold, because in the Buddhist system, there is no possibility of being encompassed by a stable temporal location or other limiting adjunct (<s>upādhi</s>). And being encompassed by a single cognition is over-extended — because even cognitions belonging to a different continuum (<s>bhinnasantāna</s>), being similarly [momentary], would [have to be included], and thus the restriction to a [particular] continuum would be inexplicable. [Objection:] The continuum is the succession of subsequent cognitions having the preceding cognitions as their material cause (<s>upādāna</s>). [Reply:] No, because something that has perished cannot be a material cause at the time of its effect, being non-existent [then]. And because mere priority [in time] is over-extended. So the restriction to a [particular] continuum is simply inexplicable. Now he raises the doubt that recognition — being of the nature of erroneous cognition — could occur through the similarity of the <s>ālayavijñāna</s> [moments], with
'nor' (<s>na ca</s>)

children.text: ti / bhrāntirūpā ca pratyabhijñā na ghaṭata ityarthaḥ / ghaṭate iti śeṣaḥ / dṛṣṭāntavaiṣamyamupapādayati
children.translated_text: and so forth. The meaning is: recognition of the nature of error does not hold [either]. 'Does not hold' is to be supplied. He demonstrates the dissimilarity of the example with
'it is appropriate' (<s>yujyata</s>)

children.text:
iti / dṛṣṭānte bhinnakālikadīpakalikayoḥ susadṛśayoḥ sākṣātkartā sthiraścetanaḥ prasiddho bhrāntibhāktvayogyaḥ / tattatra bhrāntirūpā pratyabhijñā ghaṭate / na ca tathā prakṛte saṃvidāṃ draṣṭātiriktaḥ sthiro 'bhyupeyate / ataḥ saṃvidevātmānyenātmanābhedaṃ svātmani bhāvayediti vācyam / parasparavārtāmabhijñatvānnānyasmādbhedamabhedaṃ vā svātmani gṛhītumalam / niranvayavināśācca pūrvadharmānuvṛttibalādapi pūrvānubhūtapratisandhānādi na ghaṭate iti samuditāśayaḥ / parasparavārtānabhijñatvaṃ-jñānāntaratadviṣayāgrāhitvam / niranvayavināśitvaṃ-samūlavināśitvaṃ- svarūpato dharmataśca / uttarottarakṣaṇeṣu pūrvapūrvavijñānakṣaṇato vāsanodayātpratisandhānopapattirityapi na / anantavāsanotpattivināśādikalpanāyāmatigauravāditi dik / śiṣṭaṃ spaṣṭam /
atra nityātmavādinā kenaciduktaṃ saṃvida āgamāpāyitvādikamamṛṣyamāṇo 'dvaitī pratyavatiṣṭhate / taducyate
children.translated_text:
and so forth. In the example, there is a well-known stable conscious being who directly perceives the two closely similar lamp-flames at different times — and who is capable of being subject to error. Therefore, recognition of an erroneous nature is appropriate there. But in the present case, no stable [entity] other than the cognitions themselves is accepted as their perceiver. Hence the objection: 'cognition itself, as the self, should apprehend in itself non-difference with another self' — [but this is impossible] because [momentary cognitions,] being unaware of each other's affairs, cannot apprehend difference or non-difference with another in themselves. And because of perishing without any trace (<s>niranvayavināśa</s>), even by the force of the continuity of prior properties, the reconnection of what was previously experienced and the like does not hold. The combined purport is [as follows]. 'Being unaware of each other's affairs' — means: not apprehending other cognitions and their objects. 'Perishing without trace' — means: perishing root and all — both in own-nature and in properties. [Objection:] Through the arising of latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>) from prior cognitive moments at subsequent moments, the reconnection is explained. [Reply:] Even that does not [work], because of the extreme prolixity (<s>atigaurava</s>) in postulating the origination and destruction of infinite latent impressions — this is the direction [of the argument]. The rest is clear.
Here, a certain proponent of the eternal self, unable to accept the arising and passing away and the like of cognition, takes the Advaita position. That is addressed with
'someone says' (<s>kaścidāha</s>)

children.text: ti / svasyāsattve grāhakābhāvāt svasya svattve grāhyābhāvāśca na svataḥ saṃvidaḥ prāgabhāvagrahaḥ / saṃvido jñānāntarāgocaratvenānyajñānatastajjñānaprāgabhāvagraho 'pi na saṃbhavati / jñānaviṣayīkāramantarā taduparaktaprāgabhāvagrahaṇāyogāt / jñānāntaragocaratve ca ghaṭādivajjaḍatvaprasaṅgāt / tatpramāṇābhāvātprāgabhāvaḥ saṃvido nāstīti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: and so forth. If it [cognition] does not exist [at a given time], there is no apprehender — so the prior absence (<s>prāgabhāva</s>) of cognition cannot be grasped through cognition itself. If it does exist, there is no object to be grasped [viz., its own absence] — so again, cognition's prior absence cannot be grasped through itself. And since cognition is not an object of another cognition, the apprehension of its prior absence through another cognition is also not possible — because without making cognition an object [of that other cognition], the prior absence connected with it cannot be grasped. And if [cognition] were the object of another cognition, there would follow the consequence of its being inert (<s>jaḍa</s>), like a pot and the like. Since there is no means of valid knowledge for it [the prior absence], the prior absence of cognition does not exist — this is the purport.
'Therefore' (<s>ata</s>)
and so forth. Because of the absence of prior absence, cognition has no origination. The meaning is: because prior absence is itself included among the factors that produce [origination].
'Because of the absence of birth' (<s>janmābhāva</s>)

children.text:
diti / itare bhāvavikārāḥ-astitvavṛddhipariṇāmāpakṣayavināśāḥ / astitvamatra svopā dānāvacchinnasthitilakṣaṇam / utpattipratibaddhatvāt-u
tpattivyāpyatvāt / vyāpakanivṛttyā vyāpyanivṛttiriti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: and so forth. The other modifications of existence [are]: being (<s>astitva</s>), growth (<s>vṛddhi</s>), transformation (<s>pariṇāma</s>), decay (<s>apakṣaya</s>), and destruction (<s>vināśa</s>). 'Being' (<s>astitva</s>) here has the defining characteristic of continued existence delimited by one's own material cause (<s>svopādāna</s>). Because of being connected with — i.e., pervaded by — origination [which has been negated]. The purport is: the negation of the pervader entails the negation of the pervaded.
'For this very reason' (<s>ata eva</s>)
and so forth. The meaning is: because of the very absence of origination, multiplicity too — characterized by the difference among cognitions of the same class — is also negated.
'What is pervaded by having origination' (<s>utpattimattvavyāpaka</s>)

children.text: ti / karmadhārayo 'yam / vibhāgi-nānā, bhinnam / atra saṃvinna nānā, nāpi vikāravatī, ajatvādyannaivaṃ tannevaṃ yathā ghaṭa iti vyatirekiprayogaḥ / saṃvidi bhedādiniṣedhe dharmapakṣakamanvayi ca pradarśayati cetyatvācce ti / bhedādayo na saṃvidi anubhāvyatvādrūpādivat / atra bhedapadaṃ vikārātmakotpattyādyavasthābhedaparaṃ prakaraṇāt / itaretarābhāvaḥ-sajātīyabhedaḥ / vijātīyasvāgatabhedāvādipadagrāhyau / yadvā bhedo vijātīyabhedaḥ / itaretarābhāvo yathoktarūpaḥ / ādipadagrāhyāḥ-utpattyādyavasthāḥ svagatabhedāśca / etanmataṃ kroḍīkaroti
children.translated_text: and so forth. This is a <s>karmadhāraya</s> compound. '<s>Vibhāgin</s>' — manifold, differentiated. Here the negative concomitance argument (<s>vyatireki prayoga</s>) is: cognition is not manifold, nor does it undergo modification — because it is unborn (<s>aja</s>) — whatever is not so is not so, like a pot. He also shows the positive concomitance argument (<s>anvaya</s>) regarding the negation of difference and the like in cognition, with 'and because' (<s>cetyatvāt</s>) and so forth. Differences and the like do not belong to cognition, because it is [an object of] experience — like color and the like. Here, the word 'difference' (<s>bheda</s>) refers, from the context, to the stage-differences (<s>avasthābheda</s>) consisting of origination and the like, which are of the nature of modification. 'Mutual absence' (<s>itaretarābhāva</s>) — difference within the same class (<s>sajātīyabheda</s>). The heterogeneous and internal differences are to be understood from the word 'ādi.' Or alternatively: 'difference' is heterogeneous difference; 'mutual absence' is as described [i.e., intra-class difference]; what is to be understood from the word 'ādi' are the stages of origination and the like, and internal differences. He consolidates this doctrine with
'therefore' (<s>ata</s>)

children.text: iti / nirastanikhilabhedāsattvaprakāśatvādidharmarahitā prakāśaikasvarūpā saṃvidevāvikāranityā paramātmā jīvātmā ca / jīvabhedo 'pi kalpita iti bhāvaḥ / uktārthe saṃvādamudāharati
children.translated_text: and so forth. Cognition alone — having removed all difference, devoid of properties such as existence [as a separate thing], manifestation, and the like — having a single essential nature as pure manifestation — is the unchanging, eternal <s>Paramātman</s> (supreme self) and <s>jīvātman</s> (individual self). The distinction of <s>jīvas</s> too is [merely] imagined. This is the purport. He cites a supporting passage for the stated thesis with
'that experience' (<s>yānubhūti</s>)

children.text: riti / ajatvam-anutpattimattvam / ameyatvaṃ-jñānāgocaratvam / anantatvaṃ-vināśarāhityam / ātmatvam-jīvātmaparamātmarūpatvam / niruktarūpaikā saṃvideva sarvavyāpikā paramātmarūpopādhibhedena nānājīvātmarūpā ceti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: and so forth. 'Birthlessness' (<s>ajatva</s>) — not having origination. 'Immeasurability' (<s>ameyatva</s>) — not being an object of [another] cognition. 'Infinitude' (<s>anantatva</s>) — absence of destruction. 'Selfhood' (<s>ātmatva</s>) — having the form of both the individual self and the supreme self. Cognition alone — of the nature described — is all-pervading, and in the form of the supreme self; through the difference of limiting adjuncts (<s>upādhi</s>), it assumes the form of the manifold individual selves. This is the purport.
'And that itself' (<s>saiva ca</s>)

children.text: ti / na vācyaśaktayeyaṃ vedānteṣu pratipādyate / avācyaiva satī tātparyavṛttyā teṣu gamyata ityarthaḥ / bhāṣā-paribhāṣā, saṅketa iti yāvat / saṅketabalādeva śraddheyatvametanmatasyeti hārdam / vedāntānāmevaṃbhūtāyāṃ saṃvidyeva tātparyamadvaitavārtikakāravacanena saṃvādayati
children.translated_text: and so forth. It is not by the power of words that this [cognition] is conveyed in the <s>Vedānta</s> texts. Rather, being in itself inexpressible, it is understood in those [texts] through the intended purport (<s>tātparyavṛtti</s>) — this is the meaning. '<s>Bhāṣā</s>' — convention (<s>paribhāṣā</s>), i.e., stipulation. The essential point is: the credibility of this doctrine rests solely on the force of [scriptural] stipulation. He corroborates the claim that the purport of the <s>Vedānta</s> texts lies precisely in such a cognition, with a statement from the author of the <s>Advaitavārttika</s>, with
'regarding an external object' (<s>parāgartha</s>)

children.text:
ti / ghaṭapaṭādiṣu parāgartheṣu yā pramāṇajanyām iti #ḥ phalarūpeṣyate tāntrikaiḥ saiva mitirvedānteṣu prameyabhūtā / ito 'nyasmin parāgarthe tātparyakalpane ca vedāntānāmaprāmāṇyameva syāt / parāgarthasyāsatyatvāditi ślokadvayārthaḥ / nirviśeṣanityacaitanyamātrasyaiva tattatpramāṇādhīnāntaḥkaraṇavṛttipratibimbitatayā tattadvṛttyavacchinnatayā vā tattadarthaprakāśakatvātpramāṇaphalatvopacāra iti bodhyam /
prakrāntaṃ māyāvādimataṃ tāvadvistareṇa pratikṣeptumupakramate
children.translated_text:
and so forth. That cognition which the <s>Tāntrikas</s> [i.e., the Advaitins following <s>Sureśvara</s>] consider to be the result (<s>phala</s>) of valid cognition — arising from valid means of knowledge directed at external objects such as pots and cloths — that very cognition (<s>miti</s>) is, in the <s>Vedānta</s> texts, the object of knowledge (<s>prameya</s>). And if the purport [of the <s>Vedānta</s> texts] were construed as referring to some other external object, then the <s>Vedānta</s> texts would simply lack authority — because external objects are unreal. This is the meaning of the two verses. It should be understood that because the undifferentiated eternal consciousness alone, being reflected in the modifications of the internal organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇavṛtti</s>) — which depend on the respective means of valid knowledge — or being delimited by those modifications, illuminates the respective objects, there is a figurative designation (<s>upacāra</s>) of it as the result of valid cognition.
He now begins the detailed refutation of the <s>Māyāvāda</s> (illusionist) doctrine that was introduced, with
'this' (<s>tadidam</s>)

children.text: ityādinā / alaukikam-laukikapratyakṣādipramāṇaviruddham, avaidikaṃvedādisacchāstraviruddham,lokavedānanuguṇaṃ cedaṃ māyāvādināṃ darśanamityātmatattvasākṣātkartāro vadantīti bhāvaḥ / saṃvidadvaite parābhimate 'dhyakṣavirodhamādau nirūpayati
children.translated_text: and so forth. 'Unworldly' (<s>alaukika</s>) — contradicted by worldly means of valid knowledge such as perception and the like. 'Non-Vedic' (<s>avaidika</s>) — contradicted by the <s>Veda</s> and other authoritative scriptures. The purport is: those who have directly realized the truth of the self declare that this doctrine of the <s>Māyāvādins</s> is neither in conformity with the world nor with the <s>Veda</s>. He first examines the contradiction with perception regarding the non-duality of cognition advocated [by them], with
'for thus' (<s>tathāhi</s>)
and so forth. For the author of the <s>Vārttika</s> stated that the cognition directed at external objects has the nature of the self. That it is clearly not the self, he says with
'cognition' (<s>saṃvid</s>)

children.text:
diti / jñānādipadaṃ praryāyanāmekārthavācakaṃ yasyai
vaṃbhūtaḥ ātmadharmaḥ kaścidviṣayaprakāśakaḥ saṃvicchabdita ityarthaḥ/
children.translated_text: and so forth. The words '<s>jñāna</s>' and the like are synonyms denoting a single meaning. That which is a property of the self, which illuminates some object, [and which] is designated by the word '<s>saṃvit</s>' (cognition) — this is the meaning.
'Of that' (<s>tasyāsya</s>)

children.text: ti / anyadharmatvenānityatvena ca pratyakṣasiddhasyāsya pramāṇaphalasya viṣayavedanasya na nityātmasvarūpatvaṃ saṃbhavatīti bhāvaḥ / pramāṇaphalasya sakarmakasyānubhavasyānityatvaṃ prakārāntareṇa sādhayati
children.translated_text: and so forth. The purport is: this result of valid cognition — the apprehension of the object — which is established by perception as being a property of something else [i.e., the self] and as being non-eternal, cannot be the very nature of the eternal self. He establishes the non-eternality of the result of valid cognition — the experience that takes an object — by another mode of reasoning, with
'in sleep' (<s>svāpa</s>)

children.text: ti / svāpādau sattve yogyatvādvedanasyopalabdhiḥ syāt / anupalabdheśca na tadā tasya sattvamiti bhāvaḥ / suṣuptikālikaṃ vedanābhāvaṃ suptotthitasya parāmarśenāpi draḍhayati
children.translated_text: and so forth. If [cognition] existed in sleep and the like, there should be apprehension of it, because of its fitness [to be apprehended]. And from the non-apprehension, its non-existence at that time [follows]. This is the purport. He further confirms the absence of cognition during deep sleep through the reflection of one who has just awakened, with
'for this very reason indeed' (<s>ata eva hi</s>)

children.text: ti / nanu saṃvidaḥ svaprakāśatvātsvāpe 'pyastyevopalambhaḥ / anubhūtamavaśyaṃ smartavyamiti niyamābhāvācca tadananusandhānaṃ ghaṭate prabodhe / iyantaṃ kālaṃ na kiñcidahamavediṣam iti parāmarśastu viṣayaprakāśakatvaviśiṣṭajñānābhāvagocaraḥ / svāpe sato 'pi hi vijñānasya na viṣayaprakāśakatvamiti codyamanūdya pariharati
children.translated_text: and so forth. [Objection:] Since cognition is self-luminous, even in sleep there is indeed apprehension [of it]. And because there is no rule that 'what has been experienced must necessarily be remembered,' its non-recollection upon waking is consistent. The reflection 'For this entire time I did not cognize anything' is directed at the absence of cognition qualified by the capacity to illuminate objects. For even though cognition exists in sleep, it does not have the capacity to illuminate objects. — Having reproduced this objection, he resolves [it] with
'as long as' (<s>yāvat</s>)

children.text: diti / niyamābhāve 'pītyantena codyānuvādaḥ / agre parihāraḥ / prāyaṇādeḥ saṃskāravicchedakaratvaṃ saṃvitsidvāvabhihitaṃ
children.translated_text: and so forth. Up to 'even in the absence of the rule' is the reproduction of the objection. What follows is the resolution. It has been stated in the <s>Saṃvitsiddhi</s> that death and the like are agents that sever latent impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>):
'Experiences from former births — long elapsed through death, hell's torments, the suffering of [re]birth, and calamity — are not within the range of memory.'

children.text: // iti/ prāyaṇam-maraṇam / nityavat-sārvadikam / yadvā niyamavat / niyatamiti yāvat / nikhilasaṃskārapramoṣahetuprabaladuḥkhahetuvirahe 'pi niyamenāsmaraṇaṃ saṃvidaḥ svāpe 'prakāśameva sādhayet / svayaṃprakāśasvabhāvāyāśca tasyā aprakāśastadā tadabhāvaparyavasanna iti bhāvaḥ / siddhānte tu viṣayaprakāśanavelāyāmeva dharmabhūtajñānasya svayaṃprakāśatvopagamāt svāpesato 'pi tasyāprakāśo na kṣatikara iti bodhyam / atra śaṅkate
children.translated_text: Thus. '<s>Prāyaṇa</s>' — death. 'As if eternal' (<s>nityavat</s>) — perpetual. Or alternatively: 'with a rule' (<s>niyamavat</s>) — necessarily, without exception. Even in the absence of a powerful cause of suffering that would erase all latent impressions, the invariable non-remembering [of cognition during sleep] would establish precisely the non-manifestation of cognition in sleep. And since that [cognition] is of the nature of self-luminosity, its non-manifestation at that time amounts to its non-existence — this is the purport. But in the established doctrine [of Viśiṣṭādvaita], since the self-luminosity of essential-attribute-knowledge (<s>dharmabhūtajñāna</s>) is accepted only at the time of illuminating objects, the non-manifestation of that [knowledge] even when it exists in sleep is not damaging — this should be understood. Here he raises a doubt with
'nor' (<s>na ca</s>)
'even when existing' (<s>satyapi</s>)

children.text: ti / viṣayāvacchedavirahāt-viṣayasaṃbandhavirahāt / ahaṅkāragocarābhāvāt-ahaṃbuddhibodhyasya jñāturahamarthasya vilayāt / ahamarthopaśliṣṭāyā viṣayānvayavatyā eva saṃvidaḥ saṃskārādhāyakatvam / svāpetadubhayavaidhuryātsvaprakāśasyāpi caitanyamātrasya na saṃskārādhāyakatvamiti na tasya prabodhe 'nusandhānaprasaṅga iti bhāvaḥ / atrottaramāha
children.translated_text: Because of the absence of delimitation by an object — because of the absence of connection with an object. Because of the absence of the domain of the 'I'-cognition — because of the dissolution of the knower, the 'I'-object, which is revealed by the 'I'-cognition. Only awareness that is connected with the 'I'-object and accompanied by connection with an object has the capacity to deposit latent impressions (<s>samskara</s>). In deep sleep, due to the loss of both [object-connection and I-object], even though mere consciousness is self-luminous, it does not deposit latent impressions — hence there is no consequence of recognition upon waking. This is the purport. To this he replies with
'arthantare' ('regarding another object').
'Of the non-apprehension of that' means of the non-apprehension of another object.
'tritaye'

children.text: ti / jñānajñeyajñātṛtritayāvabhāse 'pi yathāyathaṃ tattadanubhavasyaiva tattatsaṃskāraṃ prati hetutvādekāgratayā saṃvidanubhave sati svāpe tataḥ tatsaṃskārotpāde 'hamarthavilayaghaṭapaṭādyarthāntarānanubhavayorapratibandhakatvātsaṃvinmātrapratyavamarśaprasaṅgo durvāro bhavanmate prabodhasamaya iti bhāvaḥ / nanu jñāturvinaṣṭatvātsvāpekaḥ smaredityatrāha
children.translated_text: ('in the triad'). Even when the triad of knowledge, knowable, and knower appears, since only the experience of each respectively is the cause of the respective latent impression, when awareness is experienced in a focused manner in deep sleep, and from that the latent impression of that [awareness] arises — the non-experience of the 'I'-object and of other objects such as pot, cloth, and the like not being an impediment [to the arising of the latent impression of awareness] — the consequence of the recollection of mere awareness upon waking is unavoidable on your view. This is the purport. [Objection:] Since the knower has perished [in deep sleep], who would remember? To this he says
'na ca pratyabhijne' ('nor in recognition').

children.text:
ti / pūrvadine kṛtasyāparadine pratisandhānātpūrvāparadinasthāyitvena sidhyato jñāturahamarthasya madhyakāle svāpe vilayo na ghaṭata iti bhāvaḥ / evaṃ svāpe 'pyahamarthasya
sadbhāvamupapādya tadā tadbhānamapi vartata ityupapādayati
children.translated_text: Because of the reconnection on the following day of what was done on the previous day, the knower — the 'I'-object — which is established as persisting across the previous and following days, cannot have its dissolution in deep sleep in the intervening period. This is the purport. Having thus established the existence of the 'I'-object even in deep sleep, he further establishes that its appearance also continues at that time with
'ata eva hi' ('for this very reason indeed').

children.text: ti / svāpakālikāhamarthapratisandhānamidaṃ tātkālikatatpratibhāsasamarthakam / na cānumitasvāpatatsukhatvātmasvarūpasattāgocaramidamastu, tathā cedaṃ na svāpe 'hamarthaprakāśasyopapādakamiti vācyam / svāpāṃśe 'numitilakṣaṇatve 'pi ahamarthe pratisandhānarūpatvasya prātastatrāhaṃ (na) āsa mityādāviva svarasasiddhasyānapodyatvāt / prātaḥkālānubhūtātmasvarūpa- parāmarśitvādasyātmasvarūpe pratisandhānarūpatvopapattiryathā, evaṃ svāpe 'nubhūtātmasvarūpaparāmarśitvādātmāṃśe pratisandhānarūpatvopapattiriti bhāvaḥ / na ca nityātmaprakāśasya saṃskārajanakatve mānābhāvātkathamahamartha ātmani pratisandhānarūpatvamasyeti vācyam / svajanyasaṃskāravattvenānubhavasya pratisandhāne ekahetutvanirvāhāya nityānubhavasyāpi saṃskārahetutvopagamāt / spaṣṭaṃ cedaṃ siddhāntasiddhāñcane / svāpe 'nubhūtātmāṃśaprakāśanarūpatvādvā pratisandhānavāco yuktiḥ / adhikamanyatra / nanu saviṣayajñānasya nityatvaṃ māstu śuddhasaṃvido nityatvādyupapannamevetyatrāha
children.translated_text: This reconnection of the 'I'-object during the time of deep sleep confirms its appearance at that time. And it should not be said that this [reconnection] may have as its domain merely the existence of the essential nature of the self, the pleasure of that [state], which are inferred from the sleep [state] — for if so, this would not serve to establish the appearance of the 'I'-object in deep sleep. Because even if the sleep-portion has the character of being inferential, the character of being a reconnection regarding the 'I'-object — which is spontaneously established, as in 'I was there in the morning' and the like — cannot be set aside. Just as the justification for this [reconnection] having the character of reconnection regarding the essential nature of the self arises from its grasping the essential nature of the self experienced in the morning — similarly, from its grasping the essential nature of the self experienced in sleep, the justification for its having the character of reconnection regarding the self-portion [in sleep] is established. This is the purport. And it should not be said: since there is no evidence for the eternal self-illumination producing latent impressions, how can this have the character of reconnection regarding the self? Because, for the purpose of maintaining the single-cause-hood of experience in reconnection through its possessing [its own] latent impressions, even eternal experience is accepted as a cause of latent impressions. And this is clearly [explained] in the established system's definitive interpretation. Or, because [the reconnection] has the character of illuminating the self-portion experienced in sleep, the justification for [its being called] 'reconnection' is [established]. Further [details] elsewhere. [Objection:] Let the eternality of consciousness with objects not hold; the eternality and the like of pure awareness alone is well-established. To this he says
'na ca nirvisaye' ('nor regarding the objectless').

children.text: ti / svayaṃprakāśasaṃvidanubhavo hi viṣayāśrayopaśliṣṭasaṃvidviṣaya eva lokaviditaḥ idamahaṃ jānāmī ti / kevalasaṃvidanubhavastu na kasyāpi svato 'nyato vā prasiddha iti bhāvaḥ / nanu siddhānte jñānasvarūpasyātmano nirviṣayatvaṃ nirāśrayatvaṃ cābhyupagataṃ kathaṃ saṅgacchate? / ucyate / saṃvidādiśabdānāṃ saviṣayakajñāna eva rūḍhatvāttadarthasya nirviṣayatvādiniṣedhoktirupapannaiva / dharmabhūtasya jñānasya ca viṣayaprakāśakasya na nirāśrayatvaṃ nityātmasvarūpāśritatvāt /ātmasvarūpajñānasyāpi pratyaktvānukūlatvaikatvaprakārataḥ svarūpaprakāśakatvānna nirviṣayatvaṃ nirdharmakatvaṃ vā / ātmanyekatvānekatvāhantvānahantvādisaṃśayasya kadāpyanudayācca pratyaktavādinā bhānameṣṭavyam / nirupādhikapremāspadatvācca sukhatveneti siddhānte 'bhimato viśeṣaḥ / saṃvidaḥ saviśeṣatvaṃ saṃvidādiśabdānāṃ saṃbandhiśabdatvaprasiddhyāpyupapādayati
children.translated_text: For the experience of self-luminous awareness is known by all as having as its object awareness connected with an object and a substrate — as in 'I know this.' But the experience of bare awareness is not known to anyone, whether from one's own [experience] or from others. This is the purport. [Objection:] But in the established system (<s>siddhanta</s>), it is accepted that the essential nature of the self, which is knowledge, is objectless and substrateless — how is this consistent? We reply: Since the words 'awareness' (<s>samvid</s>) and the like are conventionally established only in reference to knowledge that has objects, the denial of objectlessness and the like regarding that meaning is well-justified. And <s>dharmabhutajnana</s> (attributive knowledge), which illuminates objects, is not substrateless, because it rests on the eternal self as its substrate. And even the essential knowledge of the self (<s>atmasvarupajnana</s>) is not objectless or propertyless, because it illuminates its own form through the modes of inwardness, suitability, and unity. And because doubt regarding oneness, multiplicity, I-ness, non-I-ness, and the like never arises regarding the self, the proponent of inwardness (<s>pratyaktva</s>) must accept [its] appearance. And because it is the object of unconditional love, it is [also] blissful — this is the specific [view held] in the established system. He also establishes the qualified nature of awareness through the well-known status of words like 'awareness' as relational words with
'sambandhi' ('relational').

children.text: ti / niyatasaṃbandhyākāṅkṣāśālitvaṃ saṃbadhiśabdatvam / jñānaṃ, saṃvedanamityukte hi kasya kiṃviṣayakamiti viṣayāśrayākāṅkṣā niyatā / etadeva vyatireka niṣedhena draḍhayati
children.translated_text: Being a relational word means having the characteristic of invariably expecting a determinate relatum. When one says 'knowledge' or 'awareness,' the expectation regarding 'whose?' and 'of what object?' — i.e., regarding the substrate and the object — is invariable. He strengthens this very [point] through the negation of the contrary with
'na hi' ('for it is not the case').

children.text:
ti / jānātyādeḥ jñādhātuprabhṛteḥ / nanu jñānasvarūpa mityādiṣu kevalasyaiva prayogo dṛśyata iti cenna / āśayānabhijño hi bhavān / atratyasya dharmivācino jñānaśabdasya svayaṃprakāśatvapravṛttinimittakasya saṃbandhiśabdāddharmabhūtajñānavācinaḥ śabdācchabdāntaratvāt catuṣpādvācina iva gośabdātkiraṇādivācinastasya / asmākaṃ saṃbandhiśabdatvaprasiddhiḥ
dharmabhūtajñānavācini sāvakāśā / bhavatāṃ tu dharmiṇaḥ svarūpajñānasya dharmabhūtasya ca viṣayajñānasya bhedābhāvāt ekasyaiva caitanyasyātmarūpasya nirviśeṣatvasiddhāntāt saṃbandhiśabdatvaprathānopapannā saṃvidādiśabdasyeti / nirviśeṣajñaptimātrasya parvṛttinimittāyogenaiva dharmivācijñānaśabdavācyatvamapi na saṃbhavatītyapyanusandheyam /
evaṃ parairātmatayābhimatasya pramāṇaphalasyāgantukatvādātmadharmatvācca nātmatvamityaktam / atha tasya prāgabhāvāsiddhiṃ paroktāmanuvadati
children.translated_text: 'From janati and the like' — from the root 'jna' and so forth. [Objection:] But in [expressions like] 'the essential nature of knowledge' and the like, the bare [unqualified] usage is observed. [Reply:] No. You are ignorant of the intention. Here, the word 'knowledge' that denotes the property-bearer, whose ground of application is self-luminosity, is a different word from the relational word that denotes <s>dharmabhutajnana</s> (attributive knowledge) — just as the word 'go' meaning 'cow' is a different word from [the same word] meaning 'ray' and the like. For us, the well-known status of [these words] as relational words has scope with reference to the word denoting attributive knowledge. But for you, since there is no difference between the essential knowledge of the property-bearer and the attributive object-knowledge, and since the doctrine is that the single consciousness of the nature of the self is without qualifications — the fame of words like 'awareness' as relational words is well-justified. And it should also be considered that since mere undifferentiated consciousness (<s>nirvisesajnaptimatra</s>) cannot be the ground of application [of any word], it cannot even be denoted by the word 'knowledge' that denotes the property-bearer. Thus it has been stated that the result of valid cognition (<s>pramanaphalah</s>), which is held by others to be the self, is not the self because it is adventitious and because it is a property of the self. Now he restates the opponent's statement about the non-establishment of the prior absence [of consciousness] with
'yat tu svata' ('but that which, by itself').
[This is] indicative of the absence of establishment from another [source].
'svatahsiddhasya' ('of what is self-established').

children.text: iti / anubhavasyeti viśeṣyapadamadhyāhāryam / tadvirodhādeva-pratiyoginā yaugapadyāvasthānāsaṃbhavalakṣaṇādvirodhādeva / prāgabhāvādeḥ- saṃvitprāgabhāvādeḥ / śiṣṭaṃ spaṣṭam / dūṣayati
children.translated_text: The qualificand 'of experience' (<s>anubhavasya</s>) should be supplied. 'From that very contradiction' — from the contradiction characterized by the impossibility of co-existence with its counter-correlate. 'Of the prior absence and the like' — of the prior absence of awareness and the like. The rest is clear. He refutes [this] with
'tad'
and so forth. He states the defect in the rule that knowledge in general apprehends only objects contemporaneous with itself with
'atite' ('regarding the past').
Restatement of the objection:
'atha'

children.text: ti / itītyanantaraṃ matamiti śeṣaḥ / saṃvitprāgabhāvasya svasamānakālikagrahagrāhyatvameveti niyama iti śaṅkāgranthārthaḥ / niyamamupagamyā'ha
children.translated_text: ('now'). After 'iti,' the word 'matam' ('it is held') should be supplied. The meaning of the objection-passage is: the prior absence of awareness is graspable only by what is contemporaneous with itself — this is the rule.
'kimevam'

children.text: iti / tatsiddheḥ-saṃvitprāgabhāvagrahasiddheḥ / na prāgabhāvādyasiddhiḥ-na saṃvitprāgabhāvādyasiddhiḥ / ayaṃ ca niyamo yadyapi siddhānte yuktaḥ,vidyamānayatkiñcajjñānaprāgabhāvasya vidyamānenaiva jñānāntareṇānumānādinā grahaṇāt / ahamidānīṃ cākṣuṣābhāvavān unmīlitacakṣuṣkatvādityādyanumānasaṃbhavāt / athāpi paramate 'yaṃ niyamo 'nupapanna ityāha
children.translated_text: ('is it so?'). 'Of the establishment of that' — of the establishment of the apprehension of the prior absence of awareness. 'There is no non-establishment of prior absence and the like' — there is no non-establishment of the prior absence of awareness and the like. And although this rule is justified in the established system — because the prior absence of whatever knowledge exists is grasped by another existing knowledge through inference and the like — and because inferences such as 'I now lack visual [cognition], because my eyes are closed' are possible — nevertheless, this rule is untenable in the opponent's view. Thus he says
'tatpragabhava' ('the prior absence of that').

children.text: iti / bhavatā hi jñānaṃ jñānāntarāgrāhyamiṣyate / evaṃ sati tajjñānaprāgabhāvastenaiva samānakālikenagrāhyaḥ syādbhavaduktaniyamānusārāt / taccānupapannamiti bhāvaḥ / nanvata evāsmābhiḥ saṃvitprāgabhāvāsiddhirucyata iti cettatrāha
children.translated_text: For you accept that knowledge is not graspable by another knowledge. This being so, the prior absence of that knowledge would not be graspable by the very same contemporaneous [knowledge], according to the rule you stated. And that is untenable. This is the purport. [Objection:] It is precisely for this reason that we say the prior absence of awareness is not established. To this he says
'aindriyike' ('in sensory [perception]').

children.text: ti / laukikapratyakṣa eva samānakālikapadārthagrāhitvamiti niyamaḥ / na tu jñānasāmānyasya, pramitisāmānyasya vā / tathā ca prākkālikasya svaprāgabhāvasya tenaiva vartamānena jñānena grahaṇe nānupapattiriti hārdam / agrecaitadvyaktībhaviṣyati / pramāṇasya prameyāvinābhūtatvātpramāṇajñānasya svayaṃprakāśatvena nityatvāttatprameyamapi nityamiti mataṃ nirākaroti
children.translated_text: The rule that [cognition] grasps only contemporaneous objects [applies] only to ordinary perception. Not to knowledge in general, or to valid cognition in general. And thus, there is no difficulty in the apprehension of one's own prior absence, which belongs to an earlier time, by that very present knowledge. This is the inner meaning. This will become clearer later. He refutes the view that since the means of valid cognition is inseparable from the knowable, and since the knowledge that is the means of valid cognition is eternal due to its self-luminosity, the knowable too is eternal, with
'etena' ('by this').
'By this' — by [the fact that] the rule that mere knowledge-as-means-of-valid-cognition grasps only contemporaneous objects does not hold. Restatement of the view to be refuted:
'manam' ('the means of valid cognition').

children.text:
iti / svayaṃprakāśatvāt, mānaṃ-pramitiḥ, svataḥsat-ananyāpekṣasattākaṃ sadāstyeva / evaṃ cet, ato vakṣyamāṇāddhetoḥ tanmeyaṃ ca vastu sadāstyeva / hi-yataḥ, mānaṃ-pramāṇajñānaṃ, meyayugeva- prameyāvinābhāvyevetyarthaḥ / svayaṃprakāśasyāpi pramāṇajñānasya pramāṇajanyatvādevānitya
tvam / tatprāgabhāvagraho 'pi svataḥ parato vā saṃbhavedeva / ato mitinityatvamupajīvya meyanityatvavyavasthāpanamayuktam / pramāṇajñānasya samānakālārthagrāhakatvaniyamābhāvācceti parākaraṇaprakārobodhyaḥ / nanvasadarthagrāhitve miteḥ kathaṃ prameyāvinābhāvo ghaṭate ?/ tatrāha
children.translated_text: Because of its self-luminosity, the means of valid cognition (<s>pramiti</s>) exists inherently — having existence independent of anything else — it always exists. If so, then from the reason to be stated, the knowable too always exists. 'Hi' — because. 'Manam' — the cognition that is the means of valid cognition. 'Meyayugeva' — is inseparable from the knowable. This is the meaning. Even though the cognition that is the means of valid cognition is self-luminous, it is non-eternal precisely because it is produced by a means of valid cognition [i.e., a sense-object contact, etc.]. The apprehension of its prior absence too is possible either from itself or from another. Therefore, establishing the eternality of the knowable by relying on the eternality of cognition is unjustified — because the rule that the cognition that is the means of valid cognition grasps only contemporaneous objects does not hold. This is the manner of refutation to be understood. [Objection:] If valid cognition grasps non-existent objects, how can the inseparability of the knowable [from the means of cognition] hold? To this he says
'na hi' ('for it is not the case').

children.text: ti / yadā prabhitistadā prameyamiti na prameyāvinābhāvaḥ pramiteḥ / kintu yaddeśakālasaṃbandhitvena yādṛśākāravattvena ca yadbhāsate pramitau, tasya tatprakārābhāvābhāvaparyavasitaṃ prameyayogitvam / atadrūpānavagāhitvaṃ meye, tadvati tatprakārakatvameva ca taditi bhāvaḥ / smṛteraprāmāṇyamatamapi pratikṣipati prasaṅgataḥ
children.translated_text: The inseparability of the knowable from valid cognition is not [that] whenever there is valid cognition, there is a knowable. Rather, the knowable-connection [means]: whatever appears in valid cognition as connected with a particular place and time and as having a particular form — the absence of the absence of that thing having that form [at that place and time] is its being connected with the knowable. Non-apprehension of a different form in the knowable, and cognition having that very form regarding what possesses that [form] — that is [the inseparability]. This is the purport. He also refutes, incidentally, the view that memory is not a valid means of cognition with
'ata eva' ('for this very reason').

children.text: ti / pralāpaḥ- pralāpamātram / nirarthakaṃ vacanamiti yāvat / atītamapi bāhyamarthaṃ tathātvenaivāvagāhinyāḥ smṛterna nirviṣayatā, meyavyabhicāro vā / prameyayogitvasya tadvati tatprakārāvagāhitvarūpatvādeveti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'Pralapa' — mere prattle. Meaningless statement — this is what is meant. Even an external object that is past, since memory apprehends it as having that very [past] form, [memory] is not without an object, nor is there deviation from the knowable. Because the connection with the knowable has the form of apprehending what possesses that [form] through that form. This is the purport.
'atha'
and so forth is a restatement of the objection.
'utyete'
or alternatively,
'matam'
('it is held') should be supplied to complete [the sentence]. The answer [begins with]
'yadyevam' ('if so').

children.text: mityādiḥ / svataḥsiddhatvāt saṃvidaḥ prāgabhāvādyasiddhiriti vadatā pramāṇābhāvasyedānīṃ taddhetutvenābhidhāne hetvantaram / pramāṇābhāvo 'pyasiddha iti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: When [the opponent] says that because awareness is self-established, the prior absence and the like [of awareness] are not established — now, when the absence of a means of valid cognition is stated by [the opponent] as the reason for that [non-establishment], this is another reason [being offered]. [But] the absence of a means of valid cognition is itself not established. This is the purport.
'samarthitatvad'
('because of having been demonstrated'). For it has already been stated previously:

'In the states of deep sleep, intoxication, and fainting, the existence of that [consciousness] has been negated through the non-apprehension of what is fit to be perceived (<s>yogyanupalambha</s>) and does not deserve to be accepted.'
Thus.
Here this should be understood:

children.text:
aprakāśe 'pi saṃvidaḥ svāpe 'haṃ na jānāmīti tadabhāvapratyakṣamātmani tadā na ghaṭate yadyapi / svāpasya vyāghātāt / saviṣayakajñānasāmānyābhāvo hi saḥ / athāpi svayaṃprakāśasvabhāvāyāḥ saṃvido 'prakāśātsvāpe 'bhāvaḥ siddhaḥ / tatpratītitsvānumānikī prabodha evāsmaraṇaniyamānumitena svāpakālikasaṃvidananubhavaliṅgena yogyānupalabdhilakṣaṇena / idameva cānumānaṃ jñānatvasāmānyena svāpe svasyāpyabhāvaṃ viṣayīkarotīti siddhaṃ svaprāgabhāvagrahaḥ svenaiveti /
prakārāntareṇāpyanityatvaṃ saṃvidāṃ sādhayati
children.translated_text: Even though awareness does not shine in deep sleep, the direct perception 'I do not know' — [as evidence for] the absence of that [awareness] — does not occur regarding the self at that time, because of the contradiction with [the very state of] deep sleep. For that [perception 'I do not know'] is the absence of object-directed knowledge in general. Nevertheless, from the non-shining of awareness, whose nature is self-luminosity, in deep sleep, the absence [of awareness then] is established. And its cognition is inferential, occurring only at the time of waking — through the inferential mark of non-experience of awareness during sleep, inferred from the invariable non-remembering [of any awareness upon waking], which has the character of non-apprehension of what is fit to be perceived (<s>yogyanupalabdhi</s>). And this very inference, through the generality of knowledge-hood, encompasses even the absence of its own [cognition] in deep sleep. Thus it is established that the apprehension of one's own prior absence is by [knowledge] itself.
'api ca' ('moreover').

children.text: ti / na sādhayatina prakāśayati / tat -tasmāt / kālaviśeṣāvacchinnaiva-kādācitkaiva / kādācitkatayā pratyakṣaprakāśasyābhinayaḥ
children.translated_text: 'Does not establish' — does not illuminate. 'Tat' — therefore. 'Delimited by a particular time alone' — merely occasional. The demonstration of the direct perception of [its] occasionality:
'I exist only now, not at another time.'

children.text: iti / cetanasamādhyāropeṇaivaṃ vyapadeśaḥ / yadvā pramāṇaphalasyaivātmatvasvaprakāśatvayoḥ parairupagamāttanmata evameva prakāśaḥ pramiteḥ syādityākūtam /
children.translated_text: Such a designation is through the attribution of meditative concentration (<s>samadhi</s>) upon the conscious [self]. Or alternatively, since the opponents accept both selfhood and self-luminosity of the result of valid cognition (<s>pramanaphalah</s>), on their own view, the illumination of valid cognition would be exactly thus. This is the purport.
'itaratha' ('otherwise')

children.text:
ti / pratyakṣasya samānakālīnārthaprakāśakatvasvābhāvyena tasya nityatve tadviṣayasya ghaṭāderapi nityatvaprasaṅga iti yāvat / yāvatsvasattaṃ ghaṭādirnādhyakṣyate, kintu sannapi kadācideva, tathāca ghaṭādyadhyakṣasya kādācitkatvaṃ na viṣayāsattvaprayuktam,
kintu svasya kādācitkatva prayuktameveti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: [continued] — because of the natural capacity of perception to illuminate an object contemporaneous with it, if [awareness] were eternal, there would follow the consequence of even its objects — pots and the like — being eternal. That is: a pot and the like is not perceived for as long as it exists; rather, even when existing, [it is perceived] only sometimes. Accordingly, the occasionality of the perception of a pot and the like is not caused by the non-existence of the object, but rather is caused solely by the occasionality of [the awareness] itself — this is the sense.
Here is the formal argument:

children.text: pratyakṣasaṃvit svaviṣayakālāvyāpinī, samānakālīnārthabhāsakatve sati yāvadarthasattaṃ tadaprakāśakatvāditi / pratyakṣavadanumānādisaṃvidāmapyanityatvaṃ sādhayati
children.translated_text: Perceptual awareness does not pervade the time of its object — because, while having the nature of illuminating a contemporaneous object, it does not illuminate that [object] for as long as the object exists. He establishes the non-eternality of inferential and other awarenesses as well, just like perception, with
'evam'

children.text: iti / kādācitkatayaiva cakāsatī ti śeṣaḥ / liṅgaparāmarśādisāpekṣāṇāṃ tāsāṃ na hi nityatvaṃ saṃbhavati / anvaminavam, aśādbayamityādipratītayaśca kādācitkatāṃ gamayanti / samānakālārthagrāhitvaniyamarahitānāmapyetāsāṃ pratītaṃ kādācitkatvaṃ na viṣayāsattvaupādhikam, kintu svarūpaprayuktameveti bhāvaḥ / nanu saviṣayakajñānānāmanityatve 'pi nirviṣayaṃ jñānamātraṃ nityamiti cettatrāha
children.translated_text: ('likewise'). The supplement is: '[they] shine forth only occasionally.' For those [awarenesses], which depend on the apprehension of the inferential mark and the like, eternality is simply not possible. And cognitions such as 'I inferred,' 'I heard,' and the like convey [their] occasionality. The experienced occasionality of even these [awarenesses], which are not restricted to apprehending a contemporaneous object, is not conditioned by the non-existence of the object, but is caused solely by [their] essential nature — this is the sense. [Objection:] Even if awarenesses that have objects are non-eternal, mere objectless knowledge is eternal — to this he says
'na ca'

children.text: ti / pratyakṣānumānapade bhāvapradhāne / dhīsaṃvidādipadānāṃ saviṣayakajñāna eva svārasikaḥ prayogaḥ / tadarthasya ca sāśrayatvaniyama eva / upalambhabalācchāstrabalācca svarūpajñānasyāpi na nirviśeṣatvamiti bhāvaḥ / etena caitanyamātraṃ nityanirviśeṣasvaprakāśarūpaṃ sat / tasyaivāntaḥ- karaṇavṛttyavacchinnasya viṣayaprakāśakatvam / vṛttyavacchedakādācitkatayā viśiṣṭasya tasyānityatvapratītiḥ / antaḥkaraṇāvacchinnaṃ tadeva jñātrityapi parāstam / antaḥkaraṇasya vṛttiḥ kiṃ vyāpāralakṣaṇā uta pariṇāmalakṣaṇā / nādyaḥ, tāvanmātreṇa jñānavyāpāramantarā viṣayaprakāśābhāvāt /
children.translated_text: ('nor'). The words 'perception' and 'inference' [here are used] with prominence on the abstract state [i.e., as perceptual-ness, inferential-ness]. The natural usage of terms like 'cognition' (<s>dhī</s>), 'awareness' (<s>saṃvid</s>), and the like pertains only to cognition that has objects. And that object necessarily has a substrate. From the force of experience and from the force of scripture, even the cognition of essential nature is not without qualification — this is the sense. By this, [the following view is] also set aside: that mere consciousness (<s>caitanyamātra</s>) is eternal, without differentiation, and of the nature of self-luminosity; that it is only when delimited by a modification (<s>vṛtti</s>) of the internal organ that it illuminates objects; that because of the occasionality of the delimitation by the modification, the cognition of the qualified [awareness] is perceived as non-eternal; and also [the view] that consciousness delimited by the internal organ is the knower. [Reply:] Is the modification of the internal organ an operation (<s>vyāpāra</s>) or a transformation (<s>pariṇāma</s>)? Not the first, because by that much alone — without the operation of knowledge — there would be no illumination of objects.

children.text: indriyāṇāṃ hi caratāṃ yanmano 'nuvidhīyate / tadasya harati prajñām tenāsyakṣarati prajñā
children.translated_text: 'For when the mind conforms to the wandering senses, it carries away one's wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>), just as the wind [carries away] a boat on water'

children.text:
ityādiṣu manaindriyadvārakajñānaprasaraṇata
evārthaprakāśavyavasthāpanāt / kvacitprajñāmanasorabhedopadeśastu jñānavyāpārānuguṇavyāpāravattvānmanaso bhākto jñeyaḥ / na dvitīyaḥ, manaso viṣayākāraparimāṇe dṛḍhatarapramāṇābhāvāt / caitanyasya nirviśeṣatve ca na pramāṇam; yena tasyaivaupadhikabhedarūpatvakalpanaṃ jñātrādeḥ sādhīyo bhavet / nirūpādhikajñātṛjñeyajñānabhedapratipādakābādhitapratyakṣaśāstrādipramāṇabādhitaṃ cedamityalamadhunā /
evaṃ svenaiva svaprāgabhāvasiddhimuktvānyato 'pi tāmāha
children.translated_text:
— because in such [passages] and the like, the illumination of objects is established as being precisely through the spreading forth of knowledge through the instrumentality of the mind and the senses. The occasional teaching of the non-difference of wisdom and mind is to be understood as figurative, because the mind possesses an operation that conforms to the operation of knowledge. Nor [is] the second [alternative tenable], because there is no firm evidence for the mind's transformation into the form of an object. And there is no evidence for consciousness being without differentiation — on the basis of which the conjecture that the distinctions of knower and the like are merely adventitious qualifications [of consciousness] would be more sound. And this [view] is contradicted by the unsublated perception, scripture, and other means of valid knowledge that establish the unconditional distinction of knower, known, and knowledge — so enough of this for now.
Having thus stated the establishment of the prior non-existence (<s>prāgabhāva</s>) of awareness through [awareness] itself, he states that [establishment] from other [sources] as well, with
'na cānye'

children.text: ti / atītasya svakīyajñānasya smṛtyādigrāhyatvamuktvā parakīyajñānasyāpi jñānāntaragrāhyatvamāha
children.translated_text: ('nor others'). Having stated the apprehendability of one's own past knowledge through memory and the like, he states the apprehendability of another's knowledge too by another knowledge, with
'pratikūle'

children.text: ti / parakīyasya viṣayaviśeṣe 'nukūlatvajñānasya pratikūlatvajñānasya vā tadīyahānopādānādipravṛttirūpadarśanānumeyatvāditi yāvat / jñānasya jñānāntaragrāhyatvānupagame bādhakamāha
children.translated_text: ('unfavorable'). That is: because the knowledge of another person's favorableness or unfavorableness toward a particular object is inferable from the observed behavior of that person's avoidance, acquisition, and the like. He states the defeating consequence if the apprehendability of knowledge by another knowledge is not accepted, with
'tadanupagame ca'

children.text:
ti / parajñānānupagame vyavahārācchaktigrahasya parajñānānumānasāpekṣatvācchaktigrahasyaivāsaṃbhavena tanmūlasya vyavahārasya vilopaprasaṅga ityarthaḥ / yadvā śabdārthasaṃbandhasya bodhyabodhakabhāvasya bodhaghaṭitasya jñānasya jñānāntaragrāhyatvānupagame vyākaraṇādinā
pratipādanāsaṃbhavātsamastaśābdavyavahāravilopaprasaṅga ityarthaḥ / śabdārthagrahaṇāsaṃbhavena-śabdārthasaṃbandhagrahaṇāsaṃbhavena / parakīyajñānānumānānupagame gurūpasarpaṇāderapyanupapattirityāha
children.translated_text: ('and if that is not accepted'). The meaning is: if another's knowledge is not accepted, then since the apprehension of [linguistic] convention (<s>śakti</s>) from usage depends on the inference of another's knowledge, the very apprehension of convention would be impossible, and the conventional usage rooted in it would be destroyed. Or alternatively, the meaning is: if the apprehendability of knowledge by another knowledge is not accepted — since knowledge, which constitutes the relation of expression and meaning (<s>śabdārthasaṃbandha</s>), i.e., the relation of what instructs and what is instructed, and which is composed of understanding — cannot be established through grammar and the like, there would follow the consequence of the destruction of all verbal usage. 'Because of the impossibility of the apprehension of the relation of word and meaning' — because of the impossibility of the apprehension of the relation of word and meaning [when knowledge cannot be apprehended by other knowledge]. He states that if the inference of another's knowledge is not accepted, even approaching a teacher would be unjustified, with
'gurūpasarpaṇe'

('in approaching a teacher'). 'Of him' — of the teacher.
Then he rejects [the objection] that being-apprehendable-by-another is contradictory to being-an-experience, with
'na ca anyaviṣayatva'

children.text: iti / svāśrayasyetyubhayatra saṃbadhyate / svāśrayāya svayameva prakāśamānatvam, svāśrayāya svaviṣayaprakāśakatvaṃ vā svasattākāle saṃvido vidyata eva / ubhayavidhaṃ cedamanubhūtitvaṃ svasattākāle svāśrayāyāprakāśamānatve svaviṣayāprakāśakatve vā na ghaṭeta / na tadasti / atītatvadaśāyāṃ svāśrayāya vartamānadaśāyāṃ vā puruṣāntarāya jñānāntareṇa bhāsamānatve 'pi tasyā na niruktānubhūtitvabhaṅgaprasaṅga iti bhāvaḥ / anubhāvyatvasyānanubhūtitve 'prayojakatvaṃ cāha
children.translated_text: ('nor is being-the-object-of-another [contradictory]'). 'Of its own substrate' connects with both [clauses]. Awareness at the time of its own existence indeed possesses: self-luminosity for its own substrate, or the capacity to illuminate its own object for its own substrate. And this twofold experiential nature would not be possible if, at the time of its own existence, it were not luminous for its own substrate or did not illuminate its own object. But that [situation] does not obtain. Even when, in the past state, [the awareness] appears through another knowledge to its own substrate or, in the present state, to another person — there is no consequence of the destruction of the stated experiential nature — this is the sense. He also states that being-apprehendable does not entail being a non-experience, with
'ghaṭādeḥ'

('of a pot and the like'). 'Precisely because of the absence of such essential nature' — precisely because of the absence of the stated twofold experiential nature. 'Non-experiential-ness' means being different from experience, or not being denotable by the word 'experience.' He raises the objection that if apprehendability could entail non-experiential-ness merely through co-occurrence, then [the following consequence arises], with
'api ca'

children.text: ti / tatprasaṅgaḥ-ananubhūtitvaprasaṅgaḥ / asatodṛṣṭāntatayā nirdeśaḥ paraprakriyayā / evaṃ saṃvido 'nubhāvyatvaṃ samarthyā'tmano 'pi tat, saṃvidbhinnatvaṃ ca samarthayate
children.translated_text: ('moreover'). 'That consequence' — the consequence of being a non-experience. The citation as an unreal example is from the opponent's own framework. Having thus justified the apprehendability of awareness, he also justifies the same [apprehendability] for the self, and [its] being different from awareness, with
'na ca ātmanaḥ'
('nor of the self'). 'Experiential nature' means having the form of object-cognition. 'Because of being the experiencer' — because of being the locus of object-cognition.
'Nor is it the case that [the self] is'

children.text: viti / jñānāntaranirapekṣaprakāśasyāpi nijātmasvarūpasya śravaṇādijñānagrāhyatvāt, parātmano 'pi taccharīragataceṣṭādinānumeyatvādātmano 'nanubhāvyatvaṃ śrutiyuktiviruddhamanupapannamityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: non-apprehendable — because even the self's own essential nature, which is luminous independently of another knowledge, is apprehendable through knowledge [arising] from hearing (<s>śravaṇa</s>) and the like; and because the supreme self too is inferable through the movements and the like of its body — the meaning is: the non-apprehendability of the self is untenable as it contradicts scripture and reasoning.
'Let it be accepted'

children.text: iti / ghaṭādeḥ jñānānāśrayatvamevānātmatve 'jñānāvirodhitvamevānanubhūtitve prayojakamiṣyatāṃ nānubhāvyatvamityarthaḥ / śaṅkātra
children.translated_text: — the meaning is: let the very non-substrate-hood of knowledge [serve as the ground] for non-selfhood, and the very non-opposition to knowledge [serve as the ground] for being a non-experience — not apprehendability. The objection here [is]:
'atha'
('but'). 'Those two' — non-substrate-hood of knowledge and non-opposition to knowledge. 'In being-an-object' — in being apprehendable. The resolution [is]:
'aviṣayatve 'pi'

children.text: ti / tathaiva te syātāṃ gaganakusumavaditi yāvat / asattvameva tayoḥ prayojakaṃnānanubhāvyatvamiti cet ananubhāvyatve 'sattvamapi prāptaṃ tadvadeva / aprayojakatmavamiti cettulyamanubhāvyatve 'pīti hārdam /
children.translated_text: ('even if not an object'). That is: even then, those two would obtain — like a sky-flower. [Objection:] If non-existence itself is the cause of those two, not non-apprehendability — [Reply:] But if non-apprehendability [were the cause], then non-existence too would follow, just like that. [Objection:] If [non-existence] is not the cause either — [Reply:] the core point is: the same [applies] even in the case of apprehendability.
'ityalam'

children.text:
iti / vyāptyābhāsamūlatvātkutarkatvam / ata evāpratiṣṭhitatvaṃ siṣādhayiṣitārthasiddhiparyavasānaviraha iti bodhyam / eva manubhāvyatvasamarthanena parato 'pi saṃvidaḥ prāgabhāvasiddhirabhimatā / siddhānte dharmabhūtajñānasya nityatve 'pi viṣayaprakāśopayogyavasthāviśeṣaviśiṣṭasyānityatvādīṣṭameveti dhyeyam /
svaprakāśatvātsaṃvido na prāgabhāvasiddhiḥ / prāgabhāvābhāvāccānutpannatvaṃ, tata eva
bhāvavikārarahitatvaṃ coktamanyaiḥ / tatra saṃvitprāgabhāvasiddhisamarthanenānutpannatvahetoḥ svarūpāsiddhaṃ siddhavatkṛtya vikārāntaranirāsakānumāne 'naikāntyamāha
children.translated_text:
('enough'). Because it is based on mere semblances of pervasion, it is sophistical reasoning (<s>kutarka</s>). For this very reason, 'being ungrounded' means the absence of culmination in the establishment of what is sought to be proved — this should be understood. Thus, through the justification of apprehendability, the establishment of the prior non-existence of awareness from other [sources too] is intended. In the established doctrine, even though attributive knowledge (<s>dharmabhūtajñāna</s>) is eternal, since [the awareness] qualified by a specific state useful for illuminating objects is non-eternal, this is quite acceptable — this should be reflected upon.
[Objection:] Because of the self-luminosity of awareness, the prior non-existence [of awareness] is not established. And because of the absence of prior non-existence, [there is] non-originatedness; and from that alone, freedom from [other] modifications of existence — so say others. Against this, having established the prior non-existence of awareness and thereby treating the reason of non-originatedness as though its formulation is unestablished, he states the inconclusiveness in the inference that negates other modifications, with
'vyabhicarati'

children.text: ti / saptamyā avacchedakatvamarthaḥ / tasya vyabhicārapadārthe 'nvayaḥ / anutpannatvaṃ prāgabhāvāvacchedenāvināśitvarūpasādhyavyabhicārītyarthaḥ / tadadhikaraṇasyaiva tanniṣṭhadharmāvacchedakatvātprāgabhāvasya hetuniṣṭhavyabhicārāvacchedakasya hetumattvaṃ sādhyābhāvavattvaṃ ca siddhyati /
children.translated_text: ('it deviates'). The locative [case] has the sense of being a delimiting condition. Its connection with the meaning of the word 'deviation' [is as follows]: non-originatedness, delimited by prior non-existence, deviates [from] the provable characterized by non-destructibility — this is the meaning. Since the substrate of [prior non-existence] itself has the status of delimiting the property residing in it, the prior non-existence — which is the delimiting condition of the deviation residing in the reason — is established as both possessing a reason-bearer [i.e., being in the subject] and possessing the absence of the provable.
'bhāve'

children.text: ti / bhāvavṛttitvasyānutpannatvahetuviśeṣaṇatve 'pi parābhimatāyāmanādisāntāvidyāyāṃ vyabhicāra ityarthaḥ / vyabhicāre 'vacchedakasyā jñānasya taddhetutvavivakṣāto 'vidyayeti tṛtīyā / anaikāntyaṃ parihartuṃ śaṅkate
children.translated_text: — even when existence-in-positive-entities is a qualifier of the reason 'non-originatedness,' there is deviation in the beginningless-but-having-an-end <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) accepted by the opponent — this is the meaning. In the case of deviation, because the delimiting condition — namely <s>avidyā</s>, which is the intended cause — has the status of [being the reason for deviation], the instrumental case 'by <s>avidyā</s>' [is used]. He raises an objection to resolve the inconclusiveness:
'aparamārtha'

children.text: iti / paramārthavikārarāhityaṃ sādhyam / tadabhāvaśca paramārthavikāro nāvidyāyāmiti na vyabhicāra iti bhāvaḥ / prativakti
children.translated_text: ('non-ultimate'). The provable is: freedom from transformation in the ultimate sense. And the absence of that — namely ultimate transformation — does not exist in <s>avidyā</s> — so there is no deviation. This is the sense. He replies:
'paramārthāś ca'

children.text: ti / te-tava / mate iti pūraṇīyam / sādhyasya-sādhyaghaṭakavikārādeḥ / sādhanasya vā-sādhanaghaṭakotpattervā / arthavattāmaśruvīta-anvitārthakaṃ bhavet; vyabhicārasyāsiddheśca vārakatayā saprayojanaṃ vā / saṃvido 'pi kalpitotpattimattvasaṃbhavena svarūpāsiddhivāraṇāya sādhanasya vetyuktam /
children.translated_text: ('and ultimate'). 'Your' — in your view — is to be supplied. 'Of the provable' — of the modification and the like that constitute the provable. 'Or of the reason' — or of the origination that constitutes the reason. '[Would it] have meaningfulness' — would it become meaningful in its connected sense? And [would it] also have the capacity to ward off the deviation, so as to be purposeful? Because the view that awareness can have a constructed origination, [the phrase] 'or of the reason' was said to ward off the [objection of] formulation-unestablishedness of the reason.
The purport is this:

children.text:
paramārthavikārādeḥ paramārthotpattervānupagamādbhavatāṃ sādhyahetvoḥ pāramārthyaviśeṣaṇaṃ na ghaṭate /
sādhyasādhanavyatirekavyāptīnāmaprasiddhiprasaṅgāt / aviśeṣaṇe ca vyabhicārasya svarūpāsiddhervā na parihārasaṃbhava iti /
children.translated_text: Because you do not accept ultimate modification or ultimate origination, the qualification 'ultimate' cannot apply to your provable and reason. Because the well-knownness of the negative concomitance of provable and reason would be [thereby rendered] impossible. And without the qualification, there is no possibility of resolving the deviation or the formulation-unestablishedness.
'tathā ca sati'

children.text:
ti / upahāsagarbhamupālambhavacanamidam / tathā ca sati-viśeṣaṇadāne sati ca / vyabhicāravārakaṃ viśeṣaṇaṃ vivakṣatāsiddhau dṛṣṭirna vidhīyata iti bhāvaḥ /
anutpannatvānnirbhedatvaṃ saṃvida iti cānūdya pratikṣipati
children.translated_text:
('and in that case'). This is a censuring remark tinged with mockery. 'In that case' — when the qualification is given. The sense is: for one who wishes to give a qualification that wards off the deviation, 'the eye is not directed' — [i.e.,] the unestablishedness [of the qualification itself] is not heeded.
Having restated the [argument] — that from non-originatedness, the non-differentiatedness of awareness [follows] — he refutes it:
'yad api'
('even that which').
'tad api na'

children.text: ti / sajātīyavijātīyasvagatabhedānāmabādhitādhyakṣādisiddhatvādbādhitaviṣayaṃ tanniṣedhānumānamiti bhāvaḥ / vibhāgi- bhedayogi / vijātīyabhedaniṣedhe 'nutpannatvena siṣādhayiṣite 'naikāntyamāha
children.translated_text: ('that too is not [valid]'). Because the differences — of the same class (<s>sajātīya</s>), of a different class (<s>vijātīya</s>), and internal (<s>svagata</s>) — are established through unsublated perception and the like, the inference that negates them has a sublated subject-matter — this is the sense. 'Vibhāgi' — possessing divisions, i.e., possessing differences. He states the inconclusiveness in the [inference] seeking to prove the negation of vijātīya (cross-class) difference through non-originatedness:
'ajasyaiva'
('of the unborn alone'). Even in <s>ajñāna</s> (ignorance) accepted by the opponent, he states this [problem]:
'anāditvena'

('through beginninglessness'). With the notion that — since the difference of self and non-self is non-ultimate, in the negation of ultimate difference there is no inconclusiveness — he raises the objection:
'aparamārtha'
('non-ultimate'). He refutes the notion:
'paramārthabheda'

children.text:
iti / janmapratibaddhaḥ- utpattimattvavyāpyaḥ / yatparamārthabhedavattadutpannamiti hi vyatirekavyāptirvācyā / sā ca na; paramārthabhedasyaiva bhavannaye 'prasiddheḥ / tathā ca viśeṣaṇadāne 'siddhiprasaṅgaḥ / viśeṣaṇādāne cānaikāntyaṃ duṣpariharamiti bhāvaḥ / naca paramārthatvarūpavyadhikaraṇadharmāvacchinnabhedaniṣṭhapratiyogitākābhāvaḥ sādhyate, tathā ca na
doṣa iti vācyam / evamapi bhavanmate hetusādhyayoḥ / sāhacaryagrahopayogipakṣātiriktasthalāntarābhāvādvyāpyatvāsiddhireva / vyaghikaraṇādharmāvacchinnapratiyogitākābhāvasya kevalānvayitayā vyatirekavyāpterapi durvacatvāt / naca śāstrata eva saṃvinmātrasya nityatvaṃ nirbhedatvaṃ ca sidhyatīti vācyam / śāstrasyāpi bhavanmatavipratīpatvāt / nityānāṃ cidacidīśvarādīnāṃ paramārthato bhedo hi śāstreṣu varṇyata ityanyatra vistaraḥ / agre ca vyaktībhaviṣyati / saṃvidi sajātīyabhedaniṣedhe sādhyamāne pratyakṣabādhamāha
children.translated_text: ('ultimate difference'). 'Bound to origination' — pervaded by possessing origination. For the negative concomitance to be stated is: 'Whatever possesses ultimate difference is originated.' And that [concomitance] does not [hold] — because, in your doctrine, ultimate difference itself is not established [anywhere]. Accordingly, when the qualification [of 'ultimate'] is given, there follows the consequence of unestablishedness [of the negative concomitance]. And without the qualification, the inconclusiveness is irresolvable — this is the sense. Nor should it be said that what is proved is: the absence of the counter-positive-ness residing in a difference delimited by a property that is a different-substratum-property [from the form of] being-ultimate — and thus there is no fault. Even so, in your doctrine, for the reason and the provable — because of the absence of any locus other than the subject where both the co-occurrence of [reason and provable] can be grasped — there is simply unestablishedness of the pervasion. Because the absence delimited by a counter-positive-ness delimited by a different-substratum-property, being a <s>kevalānvayin</s> (universally positive [property]), makes the negative concomitance itself difficult to state. Nor should it be said that the eternality and non-differentiatedness of mere awareness are established from scripture alone — because scripture too is contrary to your doctrine. For in the scriptures, the difference of the eternal [entities] — conscious selves, non-conscious matter, and <s>Īśvara</s> — is described as ultimately real. The elaboration is elsewhere. And it will become clear further on. He states the perceptual contradiction when the negation of sajātīya (same-class) difference within awareness is sought to be proved:
'nirbādhe'

children.text:
ti / dṛgdṛśyabhedaḥ-dṛśāṃ, dṛśyānāṃ, dṛgdṛśyānāṃ ca mitho bhedaḥ /
saṃvidaḥ svagatabhedaniṣedhānumāne 'pi dūṣaṇamāha
children.translated_text:
('when there is no sublation'). 'The difference of seer and seen' — the mutual difference of seers, of things seen, and of seers and things seen.
He states the fault even in the inference negating svagata (internal) difference within awareness:
'tad api'

children.text: ti / saṃviddharmāṇāṃ pramāṇasiddhatvakathanena saṃvidi dharmaniṣedhasādhanasya kālātyayāpadiṣṭatvaṃ phalitam / ata eva saṃvitpakṣake vyatirekiṇi dharmapakṣake cānvayini saṃviddharmaniṣedhānumāne pakṣa eva vyabhicārodbhāvanaṃ ghaṭate / nanu saṃviddharmāṇāṃ saṃvidabhinnatayā bhinnadharmaniṣedhānumāne na kṣatirityatrāha
children.translated_text: By stating that the properties of <s>saṃvid</s> (consciousness) are established through <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge), the result is that any means of proving the denial of properties in <s>saṃvid</s> is rendered belated (<s>kālātyayāpadiṣṭa</s>). Therefore, in the inference denying properties of <s>saṃvid</s>—where <s>saṃvid</s> is the subject (<s>pakṣa</s>) possessing the negative concomitance (<s>vyatirekin</s>) and the property-side possesses positive concomitance (<s>anvayī</s>)—the deviation (<s>vyabhicāra</s>) arises in the very subject itself. To the objection that since the properties of <s>saṃvid</s> are non-different from <s>saṃvid</s>, the inference denying distinct properties is not harmed, he says—
"Even if that is established"—

children.text: ti / vivādaviṣayāṇāṃ dharmāṇāṃ saṃpratipannasaṃvitsvarūpatā na ghaṭata iti bhāvaḥ / ghaṭapaṭayorivākārabhedācca saṃvittaddharmayornaikyamityāha
children.translated_text: The sense is that for the properties under dispute, identity with the accepted nature of <s>saṃvid</s> does not hold. And because of the difference in form, just as with a pot and a cloth, <s>saṃvid</s> and its properties are not identical—he says—
"Because of the difference in essential nature"—
He substantiates the very difference in essential nature—
"Its own substrate"—

children.text: mityādinā / kasyacit-kiñcidarthasya / prakāśanaṃ-prakāśāpādanam / saṃvedanamiti bhāvapradhāno nirdeśaḥ / saṃvedanatvamiti yāvat / yadvā prakāśanaṃ-prakāśakam / ātmane-svasmai, svāśrayāya vā / svāśrayāya svaviṣayaprakāśakatvaṃ saṃvedanasya saṃvedanatvam; svayaṃbhāsamānatvaṃ ca saṃvedanasya svayaṃprakāśatvamityenayordharmayoḥ svarūpabhedo bodhyaḥ / saṃvedanatvasvayaṃprakāśatvaśarīrānupraviṣṭaṃ prakāśapadārthamāha
children.translated_text: with the words beginning "its own substrate" and so forth. "Of something for some purpose"—<s>prakāśana</s> (illumination) means causing to shine forth (<s>prakāśāpādana</s>). "<s>Saṃvedana</s>" (cognition)—this designation has the sense of a state or activity; it means "the nature of being cognition" (<s>saṃvedanatva</s>). Alternatively, <s>prakāśana</s> means "that which illuminates" (<s>prakāśaka</s>). "For itself" (<s>ātmane</s>)—for its own sake, or for its own substrate. The <s>saṃvedanatva</s> (nature of cognition) of <s>saṃvedana</s> is its capacity to illuminate its own object for its own substrate; and the <s>svayaṃprakāśatva</s> (self-luminosity) of <s>saṃvedana</s> is its shining by itself. The difference in essential nature between these two properties should be understood. He states the meaning of the term <s>prakāśa</s> as pervading the nature of both <s>saṃvedanatva</s> and <s>svayaṃprakāśatva</s>—
"And <s>prakāśa</s> (luminosity)"—

children.text: ti / prakāśo 'yaṃ jñātatāpararyāyo dharmaviśeṣaḥ / ayaṃ ca na jaḍamātrasya, kintu citpadārthasyāpi / taducyate
children.translated_text: This <s>prakāśa</s> is a specific property synonymous with <s>jñātatā</s> (the state of being known). And this belongs not merely to insentient things (<s>jaḍa</s>), but also to the conscious entity (<s>cit</s>). That is stated—
"Common to all entities, both sentient (<s>cit</s>) and insentient (<s>acit</s>)"—
thus.
"In the <s>Saṃvitsiddhi</s> itself"—

children.text: ti / saṃvidaḥ svaprakāśatvasādhana ityarthaḥ / yadvā saṃvitsiddhināmake prakaraṇa evetyarthaḥ / etenā'tmasiddheḥ pūrvameva saṃvitsiddheḥ kṛtatvaṃ jñāyate / yadyapi upalabhyamāne saṃvitsiddhigranthabhāge prakāśapadārthanirūpaṇaṃ nopalabhyate / athāpi saṃvitsiddhaubhūyāṃso bhāgā ādāvante madhye ca viluptāḥ / tatraitatsaṃbhavatīti dhyeyam / dharmāntaraprakāśānabhyupagame 'pyāha
children.translated_text: The meaning is: in the proof of the self-luminosity of <s>saṃvid</s>. Alternatively, the meaning is: in the very treatise named <s>Saṃvitsiddhi</s>. From this it is known that the <s>Saṃvitsiddhi</s> was composed even before the <s>Ātmasiddhi</s>. Although in the extant portion of the <s>Saṃvitsiddhi</s> text, an examination of the meaning of <s>prakāśa</s> is not found, nevertheless many portions of the <s>Saṃvitsiddhi</s>—at the beginning, end, and middle—have been lost. It should be considered that this could have been contained therein. Even if one does not accept <s>prakāśa</s> as a separate property, he says—
"Even without accepting that"—

children.text: iti / vyavahārānuguṇyameva jñānādhīnaṃ prakāśaśabditam / avyavahliyamāṇasyāpi jñānatovyavahārayogyatākṣuṇṇaiveti bhāvaḥ / ekasaṅkhyāvacchedaḥ- ekatvasaṅkhyāvattvam / śaṅkate
children.translated_text: What is called <s>prakāśa</s> is precisely the fitness for practical activity (<s>vyavahāra</s>) that depends on knowledge (<s>jñāna</s>). The sense is that even for what is not currently being dealt with in practice, the fitness for practical activity through knowledge remains unimpaired. "Delimitation by the number one" means possessing the numerical property of oneness. He raises an objection—
"And not in the case of insentience"—

children.text:
ti / jaḍatvābhāvaḥ svapra
kāśatvam, deśakālāparicchinnatve vibhutvanityatve / bahutvābhāva ekatvam / na tvetānibhāvarūpāṇi / abhāvasya cādhikaraṇātmakatvānna saṃvidaḥ sadharmatvaṃ prasajatīti bhāvaḥ / pariharati
children.translated_text: The absence of insentience (<s>jaḍatva</s>) is self-luminosity (<s>svaprakāśatva</s>); non-delimitation by space and time constitutes omnipresence (<s>vibhutva</s>) and eternality (<s>nityatva</s>); the absence of multiplicity is oneness (<s>ekatva</s>). But these are not positive entities—they are of the nature of absence (<s>abhāva</s>). And since absence is of the nature of its locus (<s>adhikaraṇātmaka</s>), the objection is that <s>saṃvid</s> would not thereby possess properties (<s>sadharmatva</s>). He resolves this—
"Even by those of such nature"—

children.text: ti / abhāvānāmatiriktatvamadhikaraṇavṛttidharmāntararūpatvaṃ vā / ādhārādheyabhāvapratītisvārasyādityabhāvarūpairapi sadharmatvamavarjanīyamityarthaḥ / yasmin pratīte niṣedhyabuddhirnodeti tasyaivābhāvarūpatvam / pratīyamānāyāmapi saṃvidi anityatvādisaṃśayodayācca na tadabhāvarūpatvaṃ tasyāḥ / kintu sarvakālasaṃbandhitvādivirodhidharmāntaralakṣaṇameva nityatvādīti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: Absences either have a separate existence or have the nature of properties different from those residing in the substrate. Due to the natural force of the cognition of the substrate-superstratum relation, even through properties of the nature of absence, the possession of properties (<s>sadharmatva</s>) is unavoidable—this is the meaning. That whose cognition does not give rise to the notion of what is to be negated is alone of the nature of absence. But since <s>saṃvid</s>, even while being cognized, gives rise to doubts such as non-eternality and the like, it is not of the nature of their absence. Rather, eternality and such are defined as counter-properties opposed to those, such as being related to all times—this is the purport.
"Of <s>saṃvid</s>"—

children.text:
ti / virodhidharmavattābodhanamantarā jaḍatvādiniṣedhakatvānupapattiḥ pratijñāyāḥ ; tadbodhane ca sadharmatvasiddhiravarjanīyeti bhāvaḥ / naca jaḍatvādivirodhisvarūpatvameva pratijñayā bodhyate saṃvido na virodhidharmavattvamiti vācyam / sarvādhyāsādhiṣṭhānabhūtāyāstasyāḥ sarvavirodhitvāsiddheḥ / naca śuddhā sā tatheti vācyam / tasyāḥ sarvaviśeṣapratyanīkatvopagame jaḍatvādipratyanīkatevājaḍatvādipratyanīkatāpīti jaḍājaḍavilakṣaṇatvādiprasaṅgāt / ajaḍatvādyabhāve 'pi ajaḍādisvarūpaiva seti ceddharmatvābhāve 'pi dharmasvarūpaiva sā kiṃ na syāditi dik /
bhedādidharmapakṣakacitsaṃbandhitvābhāvasādhane 'naikāntyamapyāha
children.translated_text: Without cognizing the possession of opposing properties, the negation of insentience and the like in the thesis cannot be sustained; and if such is cognized, then the possession of properties (<s>sadharmatva</s>) becomes unavoidable—this is the purport. Nor can one say that what the thesis conveys is merely the nature of being opposed to insentience and the like, not the possession of opposing properties. For <s>saṃvid</s>, being the substratum of all superimpositions (<s>adhyāsa</s>), its opposition to everything cannot be established. Nor can one say it is pure (<s>śuddha</s>) and therefore so. For if one accepts that it is opposed to all particularities (<s>viśeṣa</s>), then being opposed to insentience would also entail being opposed to non-insentience, leading to the absurd consequence of being different from both the insentient and the non-insentient. If one says that even without the absence of non-insentience, it is of the very nature of non-insentience—then why should it not also be of the very nature of properties even without the absence of properties? This is the direction of the argument. He also states the fallacy of inconclusive reasoning (<s>anaikāntya</s>) in proving the absence of any connection of <s>cit</s> with the property-side of difference and the like—
"The object of cognition"—

children.text: iti / cetyam-anubhāvyam / ātmani-cinmātra ātmani / kiñca ciddharmatvābhāvasādhanamanupapannam / pratiyogyaprasiddheḥ / dharmā na cita ityapi na sādhīyaḥ / ṣaṣṭhyarthasya saṃbandhasya citpadārthenānanvayādbhavatāsityāha
