atha svāpe muktau cāhamarthasya bhānaṃ nāsti, tannāhamarthasyātmatvaṃ yuktamiti paramatamanūdya nirasyati
children.translated_text:
('therefore'). Because the cognition of knower-hood cannot be erroneous in the manner stated, the self is precisely the 'I'-object that is established as the knower — not mere cognition (<s>jñaptimātra</s>). This is the sense. Here is the formal argument: knowledge is not the self, because it is apprehended as a property — like form and the like. Thus the selfhood of the 'I'-object, which is the knower, has been justified.
Now, having restated the opponent's view — that the 'I'-object does not appear in deep sleep and in liberation, and therefore the selfhood of the 'I'-object is not tenable — he refutes it, with
'yat tu suṣuptī'

children.text:
tyādinā / tatra-suṣuptimuktayoḥ / ghaṭakatvaṃ saptamyarthaḥ / tasya suṣuptāva
nvayaḥ / tathāvasthitiḥ- ahaṃbhāvavigamena jñaptimātratayātmano 'vasthitiḥ, purastādeva nirastā, pratisandhānabalātsvāpe 'hamarthasadbhāvatatpratītisamarthanabalāditi bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: and so forth. 'There' — in deep sleep and liberation. 'Being a constituent' is the meaning of the locative. Its connection [is] with deep sleep. 'Such a state' — the state of the self as mere cognition through the departure of the I-sense — has already been refuted previously, through the force of the reconnection argument that justifies the existence and cognition of the 'I'-object in deep sleep. This is the sense.
'yadi'

children.text: ti / ucyeteti śeṣaḥ / tattatparāgarthānubhavitṛtvena sphuṭaṃ jñānajñeyato vivicyā'tmano bhānaṃ svāpe nāstīti paraṃ yadyucyetetyarthaḥ / parāgarthānanubhavādvivicya bhānaṃ na, tamoguṇābhibhavācca sphuṭaṃ tanneti anusandheyam / paramate 'pi tatsamānamityaha
children.translated_text: ('if'). The supplement is: 'it is said.' The meaning is: if what is said is merely that the clear appearance of the self — distinctly discriminated from knowledge and the known as the experiencer of the respective other objects — is not present in deep sleep. The reason the appearance is not [present] is that there is no experience of other objects to discriminate [it], and [the appearance is] not clear because of the overpowering by the <s>tamas</s> quality — this should be reflected upon. He says that the same holds in the opponent's view too:
'bhavadabhimate'

children.text: ti / viśadabhānābhāve 'pi sūkṣmatayāhamarthasya bhānaṃ parābhimatasaṃvida iva svāpe 'stīti ca hārdam /
children.translated_text: ('in your accepted [view]'). The core point is: even in the absence of vivid appearance, the appearance of the 'I'-object exists in deep sleep in a subtle form — just like the awareness accepted by the opponent.
'na aham aham'

children.text: iti / idānīmahantvena bhāsamāna ātmāsvāpe tathā nāstītyarthaḥ / ekamahamityadhikaṃ patitaṃ vā / etāvantamityādipratisandhānamajñānasākṣitayāhamarthasyaiva svāpe sattve 'nuguṇamiti bhāvaḥ / śaṅkate
children.translated_text: ('not I, I'). The meaning is: the self that currently appears as 'I' does not exist as such in deep sleep. Or the extra 'aham' ('I') is a scribal error. The reconnection 'for so long' and the like is compatible with the very existence of the 'I'-object in deep sleep as the witness of ignorance — this is the sense. He raises the objection:
'etāvantam'
('for so long'). 'Such-ness' — the state of mere awareness shining forth. The proponent of the established doctrine counters:
'katham'
('how?'). The objector replies:
'na kiñcit'
('nothing'). He presses the objection:
'nanu evam'

children.text: iti / kiñcidityahamarthasyevāsaṅkocātsaṃvido 'pi kroḍīkārāt saṃvinmātrasyāpi bhānaṃ bhavatāṃ tadābhimataṃ na siddhyedityarthaḥ / nanu kiñciditi jaḍamātrasya parāmarśa iti cettarhyahamarthasyāpi na niṣedhaḥ pratyaktvenājaḍatvāditi bhāvaḥ / yadvā jñeyamātrasya kiñciditi parāmarśo na jñānasyeti cettulyanayena jñāturapi na parāmarśa iti bhāvaḥ / parapakṣe pratisandhānavirodhamāha
children.translated_text: ('but in that case'). Because 'nothing' extends without restriction to the 'I'-object, and because it encompasses awareness too, even the shining forth of mere awareness — which is accepted by you [the opponent] at that time — would not be established. This is the meaning. [Objection:] If 'something' (<s>kiñcit</s>) refers only to inert [things] — [Reply:] then there is no denial of the 'I'-object either, because of its non-inert nature as inward-facing. This is the sense. Or alternatively: if 'something' refers only to what is knowable and not to knowledge — [Reply:] by the same reasoning, there is no reference to the knower either. This is the sense. He states the contradiction with the reconnection [argument] on the opponent's position:
'api ca'

children.text: ti / devānāṃ priyaḥ-murkhaḥ / tathāhi nipātanam / anubhavaprakārānabhijñatvaṃ ca maurkhyam / na hi bhūtale ghaṭo nāstītyasya ghaṭasadbhāvabhūtalaniṣedhaviṣayakatvaṃ kasyacinmatam / kintu ghaṭaniṣedhabhūtalāstitvaviṣayakatvameva / tattulyā caitāvantamitipratītirjñānaniṣedhajñātṛsadbhāvaviṣayaiveti bhāvaḥ / nanu saviṣayasaṃvinniṣedhe 'pi nirviśeṣasaṃvitprakāśe na virodha ityatrāha
children.translated_text: —the beloved fool of the gods. For indeed, falling (into error) and ignorance of the mode of experience constitute foolishness. For no one holds that the statement 'there is no pot on the ground' has as its content the affirmation of the pot's existence and the denial of the ground; rather, it has as its content precisely the denial of the pot and the affirmation of the ground's existence. Similarly, the cognition 'this much alone (was experienced)' has as its content precisely the denial of <s>jñāna</s> (knowledge) and the affirmation of the <s>jñātṛ</s> (knower)'s existence—such is the purport. Now, to the objection that even upon the denial of object-directed awareness, there is no contradiction in the shining of undifferentiated consciousness, he says—
'without an object'—

children.text:
ti / nirviṣayamapi sāśrameva jñānaṃ mataṃ svāpe / tacca dharmabhūtaṃ naiva tadā prakāśata iti tu siddhāntinaḥ /
svāpe 'hamarthānanubhave pratisandhānāntaraṃ pramāṇatvena śaṅkate
children.translated_text: Thus. Even objectless <s>jñāna</s> (knowledge) in deep sleep is admitted to be effortful (i.e., requiring a basis). And that <s>dharmabhūtajñāna</s> (attributive knowledge) does not manifest at that time—so hold the <s>Siddhāntins</s> (those maintaining the established doctrine). Regarding the non-experience of the <s>ahamartha</s> (I-referent) in deep sleep, he raises an objection by way of the subsequent recollection serving as a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge)—
'But me'—
Thus. He resolves it by partial concession—
'True'—
Thus. There is acceptance with regard to the recollection, but non-acceptance of the complete non-experience of the <s>ahamartha</s> (I-referent) in deep sleep in every respect.
'In deep sleep'—

children.text: ti / svāpakālikāviśadasvaprakāśaikāśrayasyetyarthaḥ / tena rūpeṇa-varṇāśramādiviśiṣṭaveṣeṇa / jñasvabhāvasya-jñātṛsvarūpasya / svāpe na jñānasya prakāśaḥ, kintu jñātṛsvarūpasyaiveti dyotanāyedamuktam / pratīterarthamabhilapati
children.translated_text: Thus. The meaning is: of that which has as its sole basis the indistinct self-luminous (awareness) pertaining to the time of deep sleep. 'In that form' means in a particularized guise such as <s>varṇa</s> (caste) and <s>āśrama</s> (stage of life). 'Of the nature of a knower' means of the essential nature of the <s>jñātṛ</s> (knower). In deep sleep, it is not <s>jñāna</s> (knowledge) that shines, but rather the essential nature of the <s>jñātṛ</s> (knower) itself—this is stated to make that clear. He expresses the meaning of the recollection—
'Just so'—

children.text: ti / ivaśabdo 'vadhāraṇe / ajñānasākṣitvenā'tmā svāpe prakāśata iti parapakṣarītyāpi tadāhamarthasya bhānamavarjanīyamityāha
children.translated_text: Thus. The word <s>iva</s> is used in the sense of emphasis (certainty). Even according to the opponent's position that the <s>ātman</s> (self) shines in deep sleep as the witness of ignorance, the appearance of the <s>ahamartha</s> (I-referent) at that time is unavoidable—so he says—
'Even if'—
Thus.
'In the designation of one who sees directly'—

children.text:
iti sākṣātkartaryeva hi
sākṣiśabdo 'nuśiṣṭaḥ / sa ca jñātṛtvena pratī
to 'hamartha eveti ahamajña ityajñānasākṣitayā svāpe 'hamarthabhānaṃ setsyatyeveti bhāvaḥ / pratyaktvasyāhaṃbuddhivyavasthāpyatvādapi ātmano 'hantvameṣitavyamevetyāha
children.translated_text: The word <s>sākṣin</s> (witness) is taught as applying only to a direct agent (one who acts directly). And that (witness) is cognized as the <s>jñātṛ</s> (knower), which is none other than the <s>ahamartha</s> (I-referent). Thus, by the witness-nature of ignorance, the appearance of the <s>ahamartha</s> in deep sleep will certainly be established—such is the purport. Since <s>pratyaktva</s> (inwardness/subjectivity) is established through the <s>ahambuddhi</s> (I-cognition), the selfhood (<s>ahantva</s>) of the <s>ātman</s> must be accepted—so he says—
'For oneself'—
Thus. He concludes the demonstration of the appearance of the <s>ahamartha</s> (I-referent) in deep sleep—
'Thus it is established'—

children.text:
iti / svāpādītyādipadena mohādyavasthā grāhyā /
atha muktāvahamarthanivṛttimanūdya dūṣayati
children.translated_text: Thus. By the word 'etc.' after 'from deep sleep,' states such as swoon and the like are to be included. Now he states and refutes the cessation of the <s>ahamartha</s> (I-referent) in <s>mukti</s> (liberation)—
'As for the view that'—

children.text: iti / ta dvārtam iti / vārtaṃ-phalgu / tadidaṃ mataṃ kṣudramityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: Thus. 'That is trifling'—<s>vārta</s> means paltry. The meaning is: that view is contemptible.
'Because'—
Thus. The <s>Vaināśika</s> (annihilationist) view means the Buddhist view. By another mode, through the manner of stating the non-continuation of <s>ahambhāva</s> (I-sense)—
'By which'—

children.text: ti / ātmana ityasyāgre ātmā iti pūraṇīyam / ahamarthasya dharmamātratve tannivṛttāvapi muktau ātmā anuvartate iti bhavatkathanaṃ sādhīyo bhavet / na tu dharmamātraṃ saḥ / kintu sa evātmeti piṇḍitārthaḥ / jñānamātrasyātmatvaṃ pratikṣipati
children.translated_text: Thus. After 'of the self,' the word '<s>ātmā</s>' (self) is to be supplied. If the <s>ahamartha</s> (I-referent) were a mere <s>dharma</s> (attribute), then even upon its cessation, the <s>ātmā</s> would continue in <s>mukti</s> (liberation)—your statement to that effect would be more cogent. But it is not a mere attribute; rather, it is the self itself—this is the condensed meaning. He rejects the selfhood of mere <s>jñāna</s> (consciousness)—
'Even knowledge'—

children.text: ti / dharmatayā pramīyamāṇasya jñānasya na svatantrātmatvaṃ saṃbhavatīti bhāvaḥ / antaraṅgasya jñānasyaivā'tmatvāsambhave bahiraṅgasyendriyādeḥ sutarāṃ na sambhāvitamātmatvamityāha
children.translated_text: Thus. The purport is that <s>jñāna</s> (knowledge), being cognized as a <s>dharma</s> (attribute), cannot be an independent self. If even <s>jñāna</s>, which is more intimately related (to the self), cannot be the self, then all the more so the senses and other external things have no claim to selfhood—so he says—
'What talk then'—

children.text:
ti / jñātṛtayā pramīyamāṇādahamarthādanyasya na kasyāpyātmatvaṃ yuktamiti bhāvaḥ /
muktāvahaṃbhāvanivṛttau dūṣaṇāntaramāha anyaśce ti / sukhaduḥkhabhoktṛtvaṃ duḥkhatrayābhighātāt mumukṣutvaṃ ca jñāturahamarthasyaiva, sa cet svasyaiva vināśaṃ muktau jānīyāt na tasyai spṛhayet / tathāca tasyā apuruṣārthatvaprasaktiḥ / nāpi mokṣasādhanajñānānuṣṭhānayoḥ pravartetaivaṃ jānan / tathāca jñāpakatayānuṣṭhāpakatayā ca prāmāṇyaṃ bhajatāṃ mokṣaśāstrāṇāṃ prāmāṇyaṃ bhajyeteti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: Thus. The purport is that nothing other than the <s>ahamartha</s> (I-referent), which is cognized as the <s>jñātṛ</s> (knower), can properly be the self. He states another refutation of the cessation of <s>ahambhāva</s> (I-sense) in liberation: 'And another...' The enjoyership of pleasure and pain, and the desire for liberation arising from affliction by the three kinds of suffering, belong to the <s>jñātṛ</s> (knower) who is the <s>ahamartha</s> (I-referent). If that (I-referent) were to know its own destruction in <s>mukti</s>, it would not aspire to it. And thus liberation would turn out to be not a <s>puruṣārtha</s> (human goal). Nor would one knowing thus engage in the <s>jñāna</s> (knowledge) and <s>anuṣṭhāna</s> (practice) that are the means to liberation. And thus the authority of the <s>mokṣaśāstras</s> (scriptures on liberation), which possess validity as informing and prompting action, would be undermined—such is the purport.
'For indeed not'—

children.text:
ti / yathā dehagehādyupalakṣitaḥ pṛthivībhāgaḥ sthāsyatīti svadehagehanāśe na pravarteta svayameva kaścit prekṣāpūrvakārī, evamahamarthopalakṣitaḥ prakāśaḥ sthāsyatīti buddhyā na svanāśāya mokṣāya jñātāhamarthaḥ pravarteteti bhāvaḥ /
cittvāt svayaṃprakāśatvam, tataḥ pratyaktvaṃ, tataścātmatvaṃ cito jñānasyaiva, na tu tadbhinnasyāhamarthasyeti pakṣaṃ pratikṣipati
children.translated_text: Thus. Just as no prudent person would himself undertake (action) if (told that) the portion of earth marked by his house, dwelling, etc. will remain (while he perishes)—thinking 'it will persist even after the destruction of my body and house'—similarly, the <s>jñātṛ</s> (knower), the <s>ahamartha</s> (I-referent), would not engage in his own destruction, i.e., <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation), with the thought 'the light marked by the I-referent will persist'—such is the purport. He refutes the position that self-luminosity belongs to <s>cit</s> (consciousness), i.e., <s>jñāna</s> (knowledge) alone, by virtue of being conscious, and from that inwardness (<s>pratyaktva</s>), and from that selfhood—but not to the <s>ahamartha</s> (I-referent) which is different from it—
'By this'—

children.text:
ti / ahaṃ jānāmīti pratyaye caitanyaikarūpaḥ parāgbhinnaḥ pratyak yaḥ jānāmīti pratīyate, saḥ prakāśa evātmā / tasminnadhiṣṭhāne bhāsamānaḥ tadadhīnaprakāśaḥ ahamartho yuṣmadarthalakṣaṇa eva-parāgarthasvarūpaṃ eva, tannātmetyarthaḥ/ tasminnityanena cidbhinnatvaṃ, tadbalanirbhāsitatayeti asvaprakāśatvaṃ, lakṣaṇato yuṣmadartha eveti parāktvaṃ cāhamarthasyānātmatve liṅgamuktam lakṣaṇataḥ-svarūpataḥ; yadvā asvayaṃprakāśatvaliṅgāt / jñānaṃ svaprakāśaṃ jñānatvāt, jñānaṃ pratyak svayaṃprakāśatvāt, jñānamātmā pratyaktvāditi prayogatrayam, ahamartho na svayaṃprakāśaḥcidbhinnatvāt, ahamarthaḥ parāk anyādhīnaprakāśatvāt, ahamartho nātmā parāktvā
diti prayogatrayaṃ cātragarbhitam / asya pratikṣevayuktiḥ
children.translated_text: Thus. In the cognition 'I know,' what is cognized as 'I know'—that which is of the sole nature of consciousness, undivided from the outward, inward (<s>pratyak</s>)—that light alone is the <s>ātman</s>. The <s>ahamartha</s> (I-referent), appearing upon that substratum and having its manifestation dependent on it, is of the nature of the <s>yuṣmadartha</s> (thou-referent) alone—i.e., its essential nature is that of an outward object—and therefore is not the self: such is the meaning. By (the word) 'always different from consciousness,' the difference from <s>cit</s> is stated; by 'manifested through its power,' non-self-luminosity is stated; by 'of the nature of <s>yuṣmadartha</s> from the standpoint of definition,' outwardness (<s>parāktva</s>) is stated—these are the marks (<s>liṅga</s>) cited for the non-selfhood of the <s>ahamartha</s>. 'From the standpoint of definition' means from the standpoint of essential nature; alternatively, from the mark of non-self-luminosity. Three inferences are implied: '<s>jñāna</s> is self-luminous because it is knowledge,' '<s>jñāna</s> is inward (<s>pratyak</s>) because it is self-luminous,' '<s>jñāna</s> is the self because it is inward.' And three counter-inferences: 'the <s>ahamartha</s> is not self-luminous because it is different from consciousness,' 'the <s>ahamartha</s> is outward (<s>parāk</s>) because its manifestation depends on another,' 'the <s>ahamartha</s> is not the self because it is outward.' The refutation of this is—
'Because of contradiction with perception'—

children.text: diti / cito jñānasyā'tmatve dharmigrāhakamānabādho 'tra vivakṣitaḥ / pratyakṣeṇa tasya dharmatvenaiva pramīyamāṇatvāt / ahamartho yuṣmadartha iti pratijñāvākye virodhamāha aham iti / mātā vandhyeti pratijñātulyeyamiti yāvat / nanu yuṣmadartha iti ḷ ākṣaṇikaṃ parāktvaparam / nāto virodhaḥ / parāktvaṃ cāhamarthasya cidadhīnaprakāśatvādityatrā'ha
children.translated_text: Thus. If <s>cit</s>, i.e., <s>jñāna</s> (knowledge), were the self, there would be contradiction with the means of knowledge that apprehends the <s>dharmin</s> (property-bearer)—this is what is intended here, since by perception it is cognized only as a <s>dharma</s> (attribute). Regarding the contradiction in the proposition 'the <s>ahamartha</s> is the <s>yuṣmadartha</s> (thou-referent),' he says: 'I'—this is like the proposition 'the mother is barren.' Now (the objection): '<s>yuṣmadartha</s>' is used figuratively, referring to <s>parāktva</s> (outwardness); hence there is no contradiction. To the argument that the <s>ahamartha</s>'s outwardness is due to its manifestation being dependent on consciousness, he says—
'Nor is that'—

children.text: viti / atra prayogaḥ- ahamartho 'nanyāpekṣaprakāśaḥ caitanyadharmakatvāt, yannaivaṃ yannaivaṃ yathā ghaṭa iti / prātyakṣikī dharmatvena pramitiścaitanyasyā'tmatve pūrvaṃ bādhakatvenoktā / athā'numānikīṃ tāṃ tathātvenā'ha
children.translated_text: Thus. Here the inference is: the <s>ahamartha</s> (I-referent) has manifestation independent of anything else, because it possesses the property of consciousness; whatever is not so is not so, like a pot. The perceptual cognition of consciousness as a <s>dharma</s> (attribute) was previously stated as a contradiction to its being the self. Now he states that inferential (cognition) too (contradicts it)—
'And light'—

children.text:
ti /
muktāvahamarthasya sadbhāve pūrvaṃ tarka uktaḥ/ atha tadā muktasyāhantvena bhāne 'numānaṃ samagrāṅgakanyāyamukhena prapañcayati
children.translated_text: Thus. The reasoning (<s>tarka</s>) for the existence of the <s>ahamartha</s> (I-referent) in liberation was stated earlier. Now he elaborates the inference for the liberated soul's being manifest with I-ness at that time, through the method of the full-membered syllogism (<s>samagrāṅgaka nyāya</s>)—
'If that'—
Thus.
'And not thus'—

children.text: iti / evaṃ bhāsamānatve- ahantvena bhāsamānatve muktasya saṃsāriṇa ivājñatvādi nāpādayituṃ śakyate, muktatvavirodhāt-śāstrasiddhamuktidaśābhāvyajñānanivṛttyādivirodhādityarthaḥ / muktātmā ajñānavān saṃsaraṇadharmavān vā ahantvena bhāsamānatvāt saṃsāryātmavaditi anumānaṃ muktaviśeṣa- pratipādakaśāstrabādhitamiti bhāvaḥ / nanu nāsmābhirajñatvādi muktasya sādhyate / kintu ahantvena bhāseta yadi muktātmā, tarhyajñānādimān syāditi prasañjanameva kriyata iti cettatrāpyāha
children.translated_text: Thus. Even when (the liberated soul) appears thus—i.e., appears with I-ness—ignorance and the like cannot be attributed to the liberated one as they are to the bound soul, because of contradiction with the state of liberation—meaning, because of contradiction with the cessation of ignorance and such, which characterize the state of liberation as established by scripture. The inference 'the liberated self possesses ignorance and is subject to transmigration because it appears with I-ness, like the bound self' is contradicted by the scriptures that teach the distinctive state of the liberated soul—such is the purport. Now, to the objection: 'We do not seek to prove ignorance etc. of the liberated soul; rather, we merely raise the <s>prasaṅga</s> (absurd consequence) that if the liberated self were to appear with I-ness, then it would have ignorance etc.'—to this too he says—
'Because (the I-cognition) is not conditioned by that'—

children.text: diti / tatpratyayasya-ahamitipratyayasya, atadupādhitvācca-ajñānakāraṇakatvābhāvaccetyarthaḥ / āpādyāpādakayorvyāpyavyāpakabhāve sati hyāpādanaṃ yujyate / nātra so 'sti tanniyāmakahetuhetumadbhāvādyabhāvāditi bhāvaḥ / ajñānopādhiriti bahuvrīhiḥ ajñānamupādhiḥ prayojakaṃ yasyeti / vāmadevādīnāmityādipadena mahādevādirgrāhyaḥ / atatpratyayetiprācīnamudritapāṭhastvaśuddhaḥ / etatpratyayeti vā, ahaṃpratyayeti vā pāṭhaḥ saṃbhāvyate /
children.translated_text: Thus. 'Of that cognition' means of the I-cognition (<s>aham iti pratyaya</s>); 'because it is not conditioned by that' means because there is no causal dependence on <s>ajñāna</s> (ignorance). For an attribution (<s>āpādana</s>) is valid only when there is a <s>vyāpya-vyāpaka</s> (pervaded-pervader) relation between what is attributed and that through which it is attributed. That relation does not exist here, due to the absence of such a determining cause—such is the purport. '<s>Ajñānopādhi</s>' is a <s>bahuvrīhi</s> compound: 'that of which <s>ajñāna</s> (ignorance) is the <s>upādhi</s> (conditioning adjunct), i.e., the instigating cause.' By the word 'etc.' after '<s>Vāmadeva</s> and others,' <s>Mahādeva</s> and the like are to be included. The printed reading '<s>atatpratyaya</s>' is corrupt; the correct reading is probably '<s>etatpratyaya</s>' or '<s>ahaṃpratyaya</s>'.
'I alone'—

children.text: ti rudravākyamatharvaśirasi / nivṛttasavāsanāvidyādoṣāṇāmapi ahaṃpratyayadarśanāt nāsyājñānopādhitvaṃ saṃbhavatīti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: This is the statement of <s>Rudra</s> in the <s>Atharvaśiras</s> (Upaniṣad). Since even those from whom <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) along with its residual impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>) and defects has been completely removed still exhibit the I-cognition, its being conditioned by ignorance is impossible—such is the purport.
'I am food'—

And similar statements of the liberated one's meditative experience should also be considered here. To the objection that in the case of these (liberated beings), the I-cognition is merely a persisting trace of what has been sublated, he says here too—
'Similarly'—

children.text: ti / avidyāsmitārāgadveṣābhiniveśāḥ pañca kleśāḥ / kleśagrahaṇaṃ karmavipākāśayānāmupalakṣaṇam /
children.translated_text: Thus. <s>Avidyā</s> (ignorance), <s>asmitā</s> (I-am-ness), <s>rāga</s> (attachment), <s>dveṣa</s> (aversion), and <s>abhiniveśa</s> (clinging to life) are the five <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions). The mention of <s>kleśa</s> serves as an indication (<s>upalakṣaṇa</s>) for <s>karma</s> (action), <s>vipāka</s> (fruition), and <s>āśaya</s> (latent deposit) as well.
'<s>Īśvara</s> (God) is a special <s>Puruṣa</s> untouched by <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions), <s>karma</s> (actions), <s>vipāka</s> (fruitions), and <s>āśayas</s> (latent deposits)'—

children.text:
iti hi yogatantre prasiddham / sarvadā sarvathāvidyārahitasyeśvarasyāhamiti svātmani pratyayo nāvidyādimūlaḥ saṃbhavediti hārdam / sṛṣṭiprākkāle 'haṅkārādyupādherabhāvāttadānīntano 'haṃpratyayoneśvarasya paropādhiprayuktaḥ, kintu svarūpaprayukta eveti pradarśanāya sṛṣṭisaṅkalpavākyopādānam / cidacidantaryāmisva
rūpapāmarśī
children.translated_text: This is indeed well known in the <s>Yoga-tantra</s> (Yoga-sūtras). The essential point is that for <s>Īśvara</s>, who is in every way and at all times free from <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), the I-cognition directed toward His own self cannot possibly be rooted in ignorance. Since before the time of creation, the <s>upādhis</s> (conditioning adjuncts) such as <s>ahaṅkāra</s> (ego-principle) did not exist, the I-cognition of <s>Īśvara</s> at that time is not caused by any external adjunct but is caused by His own essential nature alone—to demonstrate this, the statement of His will to create is cited. (His I-cognition) is an awareness of His own essential nature as the inner controller (<s>antaryāmin</s>) of <s>cit</s> (conscious beings) and <s>acit</s> (unconscious matter)—
'Let me, I'—
Thus the word '<s>aham</s>' (I). It denotes the supreme essential nature that is attained by the liberated.
'Because of whom'—

children.text: diti gītāvākyebhagavato 'haṃśabdaḥ / naca sopādhirīśvaro 'ntaryāmī muktaprāpyo vā bhavatīti bhāvaḥ / tathā mṛtyusaṃsārasāgaratārakaṃ śuddhameva svarūpaṃ bhagavato 'hamiti nirdiṣṭaṃ
children.translated_text: This is the word '<s>aham</s>' (I) of the <s>Bhagavān</s> (Lord) in the <s>Gītā</s> verses. And <s>Īśvara</s> (God) is not conditioned by adjuncts, nor is the inner controller (<s>antaryāmin</s>) or the one attained by the liberated so conditioned—such is the purport. Similarly, the Lord's own pure essential nature, which carries one across the ocean of death and <s>saṃsāra</s> (transmigration), is designated by '<s>aham</s>' (I)—
'For them, I'—

children.text: mityatra / nahi svayaṃ sopādhiritaropādhimocanasamartha iti bhāvaḥ / pitṛtvarakṣakatvādyabhiprāyaṃ ca
children.translated_text: —in this (verse). For indeed, one who is himself conditioned by adjuncts cannot be capable of freeing others from their adjuncts—such is the purport. And with the intention of (expressing) fatherhood, protectorship, and the like—
'I am the seed-giving father'—

children.text: ti / ahaṃśabditaṃ jagatkāraṇasvarūpaṃ nājñānopahitaṃ, na vā jñānamātram, kintu sarvajñamiti jñāpanāya copāttaṃ
children.translated_text: Thus. What is denoted by the word '<s>aham</s>' (I)—the essential nature that is the cause of the universe—is not affected by <s>ajñāna</s> (ignorance), nor is it mere <s>jñāna</s> (consciousness); rather, it is omniscient—this is cited to make that known—
'I know'—

children.text:
iti vacanam / na caiṣāṃ niṣkṛṣṭasvarūpaviṣayāṇāmahaṃśabdānāṃ bahūnāmamukhyatvaṃ yuktam / kintu pratyaktvapravṛttinimittakatvānmukhyatvamahantvena svarūpabhānaprayuktatvameva ceti bhāvaḥ /
nanvevamahambhāvasyā'tmasvarūpatve 'haṅkārasya kṣetrāntarbhāvavacanaṃ tyājyatvapratipādanaṃ ca gītāsthaṃ kathamityatrā'ha
children.translated_text: —this statement. And it is not proper that so many occurrences of the word '<s>aham</s>' (I) in these (passages), which refer to the essential nature in its pure form, should be taken as non-primary (figurative). Rather, since they have <s>pratyaktva</s> (inwardness/subjectivity) as the ground of their usage, their primary (literal) sense is established, and they are occasioned by the self's being manifest with I-ness—such is the purport. Now, if <s>ahambhāva</s> (I-sense) thus belongs to the essential nature of the self, then how does one account for the <s>Gītā</s>'s inclusion of <s>ahaṅkāra</s> (ego) within <s>kṣetra</s> (the field) and its teaching that it should be abandoned? To this he says—
'Thus'—

children.text: ti / āvyaktikapariṇāmabhedena- pradhānapariṇāmamahatpariṇāmenāhaṅkāreṇa / anahamahaṃ kriyate 'nenetyahaṅkāraḥ / karaṇaṃ ca mānasam / tathā cānahami dehe 'hamabhimānaheturanātmani ātmabhramaheturahaṅkāraḥ kṣetrāntargatatvenopadiṣṭa iti phalitam / atha
children.translated_text: Thus. 'As a modification in the series beginning from the <s>Avyakta</s> (unmanifest)'—that is, by the <s>ahaṅkāra</s> which is a modification of <s>Pradhāna</s> (primal matter) through <s>Mahat</s> (the great principle). The etymology is: '<s>ahaṅkāra</s>' is that by which <s>aham</s> (I) is imposed on what is not-I (<s>anaham</s>). And it is a mental instrument (<s>karaṇa</s>). Thus, <s>ahaṅkāra</s>—the cause of the false identification 'I am this' with respect to the body which is not-I, the cause of the delusion of selfhood in what is not the self—is taught as being included within the <s>kṣetra</s> (field of matter). This is the upshot. Now—
'<s>Ahaṅkāra</s> (ego), <s>bala</s> (strength), <s>darpa</s> (arrogance)'—

He states that the <s>ahaṅkāra</s> taught as something to be abandoned (in this verse) is of the nature of pride rooted in false self-importance arising from (factors such as) noble birth and the like—
'When one regards oneself as worthy of honor'—

children.text: ti / anahamahaṃ kriyata iti cātra vyutpattiḥ / praśastakulīnadehāvātmābhimāna ityarthaḥ / sacāyaṃ pūjyāvamānanahetugarvahetutvādgarva ityujyate iti bhāvaḥ / cvyarthamantarbhāvyobhayatra vyutpattiḥ / cvyarthamanantarbhāvya tu vyutpanno 'haṅkāra iti ātmani ahaṃ buddhivācīti vivekaḥ /
children.translated_text: Thus. The etymology here too is: 'that by which <s>aham</s> (I) is imposed on what is not-I.' The meaning is: the false identification with a body belonging to a distinguished family as being oneself. And this is called <s>garva</s> (pride) because it is the cause of the pride that leads to honoring and dishonoring others—such is the purport. In both cases the etymology involves the <s>cvi</s>-suffix sense. But when the <s>cvi</s>-suffix sense is not incorporated, the derived word '<s>ahaṅkāra</s>' denotes the I-cognition directed toward the self—this is the distinction.
'Therefore'—

children.text: diti / abādhitāhaṃbuddhirmukhyā'tmagocaraiva / dehādau tu sā bhrāntilakṣaṇaiveti bhāvaḥ / atra saṃvādipurāṇaratnavacanaṃ
children.translated_text: Thus. The unsublated <s>ahambuddhi</s> (I-cognition) has as its primary referent the self alone. But when directed toward the body and the like, it is of the nature of error—such is the purport. Here is a corroborating verse from the jewel among <s>Purāṇas</s>—
'Let it be heard'—
Thus.

children.text: ātmanyeṣa na doṣāya śabdo 'hamiti yo dvija / anātmanyātmavijñānaṃ śabdo vā bhrāntilakṣaṇaḥ
children.translated_text: This word 'I' (<s>aham</s>) when applied to the <s>ātman</s> (self) is not a fault, O <s>dvija</s> (twice-born one); but the cognition of self in what is not the self, or the word (I applied there), is of the nature of error.

children.text: // iti ca tatratyamatrānusandheyam / ātmavijñānam- ahambuddhiḥ / śabdo 'haṃśabdaḥ / vāsiṣṭhanandanena-vasiṣṭhaputrasya śakteḥ putreṇa bhagavatā parāśareṇa / dehātmabhramākāraparīkṣāto 'pi svīkāryamahamarthatvamātmana ityāha
children.translated_text: And this passage from that (text) should be considered here. '<s>Ātmavijñāna</s>' means the <s>ahambuddhi</s> (I-cognition). 'The word' means the word '<s>aham</s>' (I). 'By the son of <s>Vāsiṣṭhanandana</s>'—by the illustrious <s>Parāśara</s>, son of <s>Śakti</s> who was the son of <s>Vasiṣṭha</s>. Even from the examination of the form of the erroneous identification of the body as the self, the <s>ahamartha</s>-nature (I-referent nature) of the <s>ātman</s> must be accepted—so he says—
'Nor is mere apprehension'

children.text: ti / anātmabuddhiḥ- anātmanyātmabuddhiḥ / tathaiva pāṭhaḥ syāditi saṃbhāvyate / jñaptimātrasyātmatve sthūlāsaṃvidityeva dehātmabhramasyā'kāraḥ syāt / natu sthūlo 'hamiti / ato 'pyātmāhamartha eva / yasmin sati ahamiti buddhirdehe udeti / apakrānte ca na / so 'yamātmāhamartha eveti ca yuktamabhyupagantumiti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: and so forth. 'The cognition of non-self' (<s>anātmabuddhi</s>) — the cognition of the self in what is not the self. Such should be the reading, it is conjectured. If mere cognition (<s>jñaptimātra</s>) were the self, then the error of taking the body as the self would have the form 'the gross is not cognition' — and not 'I am gross.' Therefore, for this reason too, the self is the 'I'-referent alone. The purport is: the [entity] in whose presence the 'I'-cognition arises regarding the body, and in whose absence it does not — it is proper to accept that very [entity], the self, as the 'I'-referent, because no sublating cognition is apprehended.
'Therefore, because of being established by perception, because of conformity with the stated reasoning and scripture,
and because of the connection with <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) [in the case of error], the self — the knower — shines forth as 'I.'' (Verse 14)
(Thus ends the section establishing that the self, which is the knower, always shines forth as the 'I'-sense, even in liberation and the like.)

children.text: yaduktam-ajaḍatvādvittirevā'tmeti; tatredaṃ vācyaṃ kimidamajaḍatvaṃ nāmeti / yadyucyeta-sadapi yanna prakāśate tajjaḍam, tadviparītamavyabhicaritaprakāśasattākamajaḍamiti; tathā sati sukhādibhirvyabhicārī hetuḥ / na khalu sukhaduḥkhecchādayo vidyamānā api kadācidamavabhāsamānā bhavanti / svasattāprayuktaprakāśatvamapi dīpādibhiranaikāntikam / jñānavyatiriktaprakāśānaṅgīkārāccāsiddhatā, viruddhatā ca / yadi matam-avyabhicaritaprakāśo 'pi sukhādiranyasmai prakāśata iti ghaṭa iva jaḍatāṃ nātivartate, tenānātmeti; jñānaṃ vā kiṃ svasmai prakāśate? anyasyaiva hi tadapi jānato 'hamarthasya prathate 'haṃ jānāmīti, ahaṃ sukhītivat / tena svasmai prakāśamānatvamabhipretya prayujyamāno 'jaḍatvaheturasiddhaḥ saṃvidi / ataḥ sattayaiva svamātmānaṃ prati sidhyannajaḍo 'hamartha evātmā / tatsaṃbandhāyattā tu jñānasyāpi prakāśatā / ata eva hi svāśrayacetanaṃ prati prakaṭatā, itaraṃ pratyaprakaṭatā ca jñānasya sukhaduḥkhaderiva / nacaivamātmāntarasaṃbandhamarthāntaraṃ vāpekṣyāyamātmā'tmane prakāśate / etaccānantaramevopapādayiṣyate /
children.translated_text: As for what was said — 'because of non-inertness (<s>ajaḍatva</s>), cognition (<s>vṛtti</s>) alone is the self' — regarding this, the following should be said: what is this non-inertness? If it is said that what does not shine forth even when existing is inert (<s>jaḍa</s>), and the opposite — that whose existence is invariably accompanied by manifestation — is non-inert — then, this being so, the reason is vitiated by pleasure and the like. For pleasure, pain, desire, and the like, even when existing, never fail to shine forth. [Objection:] The [defining characteristic of non-inertness as] manifestation produced by one's own existence is also inconclusive because of lamps and the like. [Reply:] And because of the non-acceptance of manifestation other than knowledge, [the reason is] also unestablished, and contradictory. [Objection:] If you think: even though pleasure and the like have invariable manifestation, since they shine forth for another, they do not transcend inertness like a pot — and so they are non-self. [Reply:] Does knowledge too shine forth for itself? For that [knowledge] too manifests for the knower — the 'I'-referent — who knows [it]: 'I know,' just like 'I am happy.' Therefore, the reason of non-inertness, when deployed with the intention of 'shining forth for itself,' is unestablished in the thesis [viz., cognition]. Therefore, the 'I'-referent alone — who, being non-inert, establishes himself for himself by his very existence — is the self. And the manifestation of knowledge too depends on its connection with that [self]. For this very reason, knowledge has the character of being manifest to the conscious being that is its substrate, and of being non-manifest to others — like pleasure and pain. And it is not the case that this self shines forth for itself by depending on a connection with another self or with something else [like knowledge]. And this will be demonstrated immediately hereafter.
(Thus ends the refutation of non-inertness as a proof of the selfhood of cognition.)

children.text: na ca jñānena sahopalambhaniyamo 'hamarthasyārthāntaratāṃ vārayati, jñānasyāpi tathātvaprasaṅgāt / tadapi hi tena niyatena sahopalambhamityahamarthādanarthāntaraṃ mithyārūpamevā'padyeta / asiddhaśca saṃvidviśeṣaiḥ sahopalambhaniyamaḥ, pratyekaṃ vyabhicāradarśanāt / na ca viśeṣamātraṃ nirdhūtanikhilaviṣayaviśeṣopaśleṣaṃ vā vittimātramasti, yena sahopalambhaniyamaḥ
children.translated_text: Nor does the invariable co-apprehension (<s>sahopalambhaniyama</s>) of the 'I'-referent with knowledge preclude the 'I'-referent from being a different entity — because the same consequence would apply to knowledge too. For that [knowledge] too is co-apprehended with that [I-referent], which is invariably [present]. And so [by the same logic], it would turn out that [knowledge too] is not different from the 'I'-referent — [i.e.,] merely a false appearance. And the invariable co-apprehension with specific [types of] cognition is unestablished — because deviation is observed in each individual case. Nor is there any bare cognition-as-such, stripped of all connection with object-specific details, with which the invariable co-apprehension

children.text: saṃvediturabhidhīyeta / sāmānyaṃ tu sadapi saugaterna vastutayā'sthīyate / samastavṛttipratyastamaye 'pi svayañjyotirayamātmāvatiṣṭhata iti ca vakṣyāmaḥ / svavāgvighātaśca-ekaṃ dvāviti nirdeśāt / dvayorhyekakriyānupraveśe sahaśabdaḥ, śiṣyeṇa saha gacchatyācārya iti yathā / api ca nilataddhiyoriti dve upādāya abheda ityekatvavidhiḥ savitrīvandhyātvavidhiriva / anekāntaśca saṃvidi pratiṣidhyamānairjaḍatvādibhiḥ; sarvajñajñānena sahopalambhaniyamabhāgibhiḥ saṃsārijñānaiśca / teṣāmabhedābhyupagame jñānasya jaḍatvamūrtatvādi, buddhasya baddhatvamityāpadyeta / niyamenaikajñānasiddhatvamapyuktaprakāreṇa pratyu
children.translated_text: of the cognizer might be asserted. And the universal (<s>sāmānya</s>), even if it exists, is not accepted as a real entity by the Buddhists. And we will state: 'Even when all mental modifications have subsided, this self-luminous self persists.' And there is self-contradiction [in the opponent's position] — because of the statement 'the one, the two.' For the word 'together' (<s>saha</s>) is used when two [things] participate in a single action, as in 'the teacher goes together with the student.' Moreover, taking two — 'blue and the cognition of it' — and [then asserting] non-difference is [like] a prescription of unity — like a prescription that one's mother is barren. And [the reason of invariable co-apprehension] is inconclusive (<s>anekānta</s>) with respect to cognition, because of the things [that are co-apprehended with cognition but] from which [it should be distinguished] — namely inertness and the like, which are being negated [of cognition]; and because of the cognitions of worldly beings (<s>saṃsārijñāna</s>), which share the invariable co-apprehension with cognition [just as much as the self does]. If their non-difference [from cognition] were accepted, cognition would have inertness, corporeality, and the like; and the <s>Buddha</s> would be in bondage — this would follow. And if non-difference is not accepted in those cases, then the reason is inconclusive. This is the purport. He also refutes, by the same method, another reason adduced to prove non-difference [of cognition and knower], with

body.translated_text: Having thus negated the manifesting function [of ahaṅkāra], he also negates the essential nature of manifestor as claimed by the opponent, with

body.text: ktam / vipakṣavyatirekaścāsiddhaḥ / bhavatu niyamenaikajñānasiddhatvaṃ jñānajñeyajñātṛṇām, mā ca bhūdabhedaḥ; ko virodhaḥ? /
body.translated_text: and so forth. [Objection:] Let the invariable establishment of knower, knowledge, and the knowable in a single cognition [obtain]; but let there not be non-difference [of these]. What is the contradiction?

body.text: ahamarthasyā'tmatvaṃ nigamayati

children.translated_text: 'therefore' (<s>ata</s>)

children.text: iti / jānāmyahamiti jñānadharmitvena pratyakṣasiddhatvādahamarthasyaivā'tmatvam / ahantvena tasya muktāvapi bhāne 'numānamuktamāgamaśca / pratyaktvānyathānupapatitalakṣaṇastarko 'pyukta ātmano 'hamarthatvavyavasthāpakaḥ / sthūlo 'hamiti dehātmabhramarūpāvidyāsaṅgateśca jñātāhamartha evātmā, sa ca sarvadāhamiti bhāsate iti kārikārthaḥ / ātmā jñātaivetyatrāpi pratyakṣādikamastīti garbhitamatra / pratyakṣaṃ cāhaṃ jānāmītyādikaṃ prasiddhameva / jñānasya dehādidharmatvaniṣedhena pariśeṣānumānamapi siddham / sāstravacanāni cāgre mūla eva nirdekṣyante / jñānasamānāśrayatvādajñānasyājñātṛtve ātmano 'vidyānvayāyoga iti tarko 'pyaktaprāya iti / evaṃ jñāturahamarthasyātmatvaṃ vyavāsthāpi //14//
children.translated_text: and so forth. Because the 'I'-referent is established by perception as possessing knowledge as its property — [as in] 'I know' — the selfhood belongs to the 'I'-referent alone. Inference has been stated for its shining forth as 'I' even in liberation. And scripture [supports this]. Reasoning too — defined as the impossibility-of-being-otherwise of immediacy (<s>pratyaktva</s>) — has been stated as establishing the 'I'-hood of the self. And because of the connection with <s>avidyā</s> in the error of taking the body as the self [in usages] like 'I am gross' — the self is the knower, the 'I'-referent, and it always shines forth as 'I.' This is the meaning of the verse. That 'the self is the knower alone' — for this too, perception and the like exist — this is embedded here. And perception is well-known in [cognitions like] 'I know.' Inference by elimination (<s>pariśeṣa</s>) is also established — through the negation of knowledge being a property of the body and the like. Scriptural statements will be cited below in the root text itself. And the reasoning that — since ignorance (<s>ajñāna</s>) is co-located with knowledge, if there were no knower-hood of the self, <s>avidyā</s> could not be connected [with the self] — this too is mostly stated. Thus the selfhood of the 'I'-referent, the knower, is established. (Verse 14)

body.translated_text: He concludes the selfhood of the 'I'-referent with

body.text: atha jñānasyā'tmatve sādhakatvena parairupanyastamajaḍatvamapi vikalpya dūṣayati

children.translated_text: 'what was said' (<s>yadukta</s>)
and so forth. The explanation of 'the opposite of that' (<s>tadviparīta</s>) is
'invariably accompanied' (<s>avyabhicarita</s>)

children.text: tyādi / avyabhicaritaḥ-niyataḥ prakāśo yasyāḥ, evaṃbhūtā sattā yasya, tadajaḍamityarthaḥ / svasattāvyāpakaprakāśatvamajaḍatvamiti yāvat /
children.translated_text: and so forth. 'That whose manifestation is invariable' — that whose existence has such a character — that is non-inert. This is the meaning. Non-inertness means manifestation that pervades one's own existence. This is the purport.
'this being so' (<s>tathā satī</s>)

children.text: ti/ anātmasu sukhādiṣvapi niruktājaḍatvasya sattvāt vyabhicāra ityuktaṃ bhavati / ajaḍatvaprakārāntaraṃ dūṣayati
children.translated_text: and so forth. It has been stated that there is deviation [of the reason] because the stated non-inertness exists even in non-selves such as pleasure and the like. He refutes another variety of non-inertness with
'in one's own existence' (<s>svasattā</s>)

children.text: ti / yasya svasattayaiva prakāśaḥ, tatsvasattāprayuktaprakāśam, tattā jaḍatvamityapi pradīpādau vyabhicāri / dīpasya prakāśe hi na dīpāntarāpekṣā / nanu cakṣurāderapekṣāstyeva tatreti cet; astu nāma; tāvatā svasattāprayuktatāyā anapāyāt / svasattāmātraprayuktatvavivakṣā tu na saṃbhavati, saṃvidyasiddheḥ / vijātīyātmāpekṣatvāttatprakāśasya / etaccānantarameva sphuṭībhaviṣyati / dūṣaṇāntaramapyāha
children.translated_text: and so forth. 'That whose manifestation is produced by its own existence' — that is manifestation produced by one's own existence; that is non-inertness — but even this is deviant in lamps and the like. For the manifestation of a lamp does not depend on another lamp. [Objection:] But there is indeed dependence on the eye and the like. [Reply:] Granted; nevertheless, the character of being produced by one's own existence is not lost [for the lamp]. But the intention that [manifestation is produced] solely by one's own existence is not possible — because it is unestablished in cognition. Because the manifestation of that [cognition] depends on a self of a different class. And this will become clear immediately hereafter. He states another refutation with
'in knowledge' (<s>jñāna</s>)

children.text: ti / jñānato dharmo 'tiriktaḥ prakāśo nāma nābhimataḥ / jñānameva tu prakāśarūpam / tat svasattāprayuktaprakāśatvarūpo heturasiddhaḥ pakṣe jñāne / tatprakāśaṃ nityamabhyupagacchataḥ tasya svasattāprayuktatvakīrtanaṃ viruddhaṃ ca / yadvā prakāśavattvasya saṃvidyupagame 'bhimatanirviśeṣatvavirodha iti bhāvaḥ / svasmai svayaṃ bhāsamānatvarūpamajaḍatvamātmatve sādhakaṃ tu svarūpāsiddhamityāha
children.translated_text: and so forth. No manifestation (<s>prakāśa</s>) as a property distinct from knowledge is accepted [by the Advaitins]. Rather, knowledge itself has the form of manifestation. Therefore, the reason — having the form of 'manifestation produced by one's own existence' — is unestablished in the thesis, [namely] knowledge. And for one who accepts that manifestation [of knowledge] is eternal, the assertion that it is produced by its own existence is contradictory. Or, the acceptance that [cognition] possesses manifestation contradicts the accepted attributelessness (<s>nirviśeṣatva</s>) [of Brahman/consciousness]. This is the purport. He says that non-inertness — in the form of shining forth for oneself by oneself — is unestablished in its own nature [when applied to cognition as thesis], with
'if it is thought' (<s>yadi matam</s>)
and so forth. He states that the manifestation of knowledge depends on its substrate-connection with
'in the connection with that' (<s>tatsaṃbandha</s>)

children.text: ti / prakāśatā-jñānarūpatā, prakāśamānatā vā / svāśrayāya svaviṣayaprakāśakatvarūpaṃ jñānatvaṃ, prakāśamānatā cātmadharmatāhetuke eva / nahi svāśrayādanyasmai svaviṣayaṃ prakāśayati jñānaṃ, svayaṃ vā prakāśate iti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: and so forth. 'Manifestation' (<s>prakāśatā</s>) — the nature of being knowledge, or the state of being manifest. The nature of knowledge — which has the form of illuminating its own objects for its own substrate — and the state of being manifest depend solely on being a property of the self. For knowledge does not illuminate its own objects for someone other than its substrate, nor does it shine forth [for another] by itself. This is the purport.
'therefore' (<s>ata</s>)

children.text:
iti / svasmai svayaṃ bhāsa
mānatvamahamarthasyaiveti sa evātmetyarthaḥ / prakaṭatā-prakāśamānatā / ātmāntarasaṃbandham-āśrayāntarasaṃbandham / arthāntaraṃ-jñānādi /
children.translated_text: and so forth. The meaning is: the character of shining forth for oneself by oneself belongs to the 'I'-referent alone, and so that alone is the self. 'Manifestness' (<s>prakaṭatā</s>) — the state of being manifest. 'Connection with another self' — connection with another substrate. 'Something else' (<s>arthāntara</s>) — knowledge and the like.
'and this' (<s>etacca</s>)
and so forth.
'Self-established' (<s>ananyasādhana</s>)

children.text:
ityetadvivaraṇa iti bhāvaḥ /
saṃvida ātmatvamādhakamajaḍatvaṃ pradūṣya jñātrādeḥ saṃvidabhedasādhakaṃ prakaṭasaugatābhimataṃ sahopalambhaniyamaṃ dūṣayati
children.translated_text: — the purport is that this is an elaboration of that [term]. Having refuted non-inertness — which proves the selfhood of cognition — he refutes the invariable co-apprehension (<s>sahopalambhaniyama</s>) — which proves the non-difference of cognition from the knower — favored by the openly professing Buddhists, with
'nor with knowledge' (<s>na ca jñānena</s>)
and so forth.
'of knowledge too' (<s>jñānasyāpi</s>)

children.text: ti / mithyābhūtenāhamarthena sahopalambhanaiyatyataulyātsaṃvidastadabhedāt mithyātvaprasaktiriti bhāvaḥ / abhimataviruddhāpādakatvāddhetorbhavadīyasya viruddhatvamiti hetudoṣa udbhāvito bhavati / ahamarthena sahaivopalambhaṃ saṃvida upapādayati
children.translated_text: and so forth. The purport is: since the invariable co-apprehension of cognition with the 'I'-referent — which is [allegedly] false — is equal [in status], non-difference of cognition from that [I-referent] would entail the falsity [of cognition too]. Because the opponent's reason leads to a consequence contrary to what is desired, the fault of the reason being contradictory (<s>viruddha</s>) is brought out. He shows that the co-apprehension of cognition is established only in conjunction with the 'I'-referent, with
'that too' (<s>tadapi</s>)

children.text: ti / niyatena-svaprakāśavyāpakaprakāśavatā / tena-ahaṅkāreṇa / sahopalambho yasya tat sahopalambham / kiñca, tadupalambhavyāpyopalambhavattvarūpo hi sahopalambhaniyamaḥ paraiḥ tadabhedasādhako mataḥ / sa cāyamahamarthasya saṃvidabhedasādhane pakṣe 'siddha ityāha
children.translated_text: and so forth. 'Invariable' — possessing manifestation that pervades self-luminosity. 'With that' — with the <s>ahaṅkāra</s>. 'That which has co-apprehension' — that which is co-apprehended. Moreover, the invariable co-apprehension — which has the form of necessarily possessing apprehension that is pervaded by the apprehension of that [other item] — is regarded by the opponents as proving non-difference. And this [invariable co-apprehension] is unestablished in the thesis — [namely,] proving the non-difference of the 'I'-referent from cognition — he says with
'and unestablished' (<s>asiddhaśca</s>)

children.text: ti / atra vikalpaḥ-kiṃ jñānaviśeṣeṇa tena tena sahopalambhaniyamo 'hamarthasya vivakṣitaḥ, uta jñānaviśeṣamātreṇa, āhosvit jñānamātreṇeti / tatrādye 'siddhiḥ, cākṣuṣādijñānaprakāśamantarāpi ahamarthasya jñānāntaraprakāśe prakāśamānatvāditi
children.translated_text: and so forth. Here is the analysis: is the invariable co-apprehension of the 'I'-referent intended with each specific cognition, or with mere specific cognition [as a class], or with mere cognition [as such]? In the first [alternative], there is unestablished-ness — because the 'I'-referent is manifest even in the manifestation of another cognition without [the specific cognition such as] visual cognition and the like being manifest. Thus:
'because deviation is observed in each individual case'
— has been stated. He states the faults in the second and third alternatives with
'nor a [bare] particular' (<s>na ca viśeṣa</s>)
and so forth.
'There is no universal stripped of particulars'

children.text: iti nyāyāccākṣuṣādivyatiriktaṃ jñānaviśeṣamātraṃ jñānamātraṃ vā nāsti / tattadviśeṣaprakāśavyabhicāraścāhamarthaprakāśasyokta eva tattadviśeṣaprakāśābhāve 'pyahamarthaprakāśata iti bhāvaḥ / nanvevamapi jñānatvāvacchinnaprakāśenāvyabhicāra eva / ahamarthaprakāśe jñānatvāvacchinnaprakāśadhrauvyādityatrāha
children.translated_text: — by this principle, neither mere cognition-as-particular distinct from visual cognition and the like, nor mere cognition [as such], exists. And the deviation of the 'I'-referent's manifestation from the manifestation of each particular [type of cognition] has already been stated — [namely,] that the 'I'-referent is manifest even in the absence of the manifestation of each particular [cognition]. This is the purport. [Objection:] Even so, there is indeed non-deviation with manifestation delimited by cognition-hood (<s>jñānatvāvacchinna</s>). Because in the manifestation of the 'I'-referent, the manifestation delimited by cognition-hood is invariably [present]. To this he says:
'the universal' (<s>sāmānya</s>)

children.text:
iti /
anuvṛttasāmānyānupagamātsaugatairevaṃ hetusteṣāṃ durvaca iti bhāvaḥ / vināpi jñānaprakāśenāhamarthaprakāśo 'stītyāha siddhāntarītyā ca
children.translated_text: and so forth. Since the Buddhists do not accept a persisting universal, such a reason is difficult for them to state. This is the purport. He also states — according to the established doctrine — that the manifestation of the 'I'-referent exists even without the manifestation of knowledge, with
'when all [modifications] have ceased' (<s>samasta</s>)
and so forth.
'self-contradiction' (<s>svavāk</s>)

children.text: giti / sāhityasya bhedaniyatatvātsahaivopalambhamānatvahetuvyapadeśa eva bhedavyapadeśarūpa iti tena saṃvidahamarthayoraikyasādhane pratijñāhetuvākyayorvirodha ekaṃ dvitvāditivaditi bhāvaḥ / pratijñāhetughaṭakapadayorvirodhamuktvā pratijñāghaṭakapadayostamāha
children.translated_text: and so forth. Since togetherness (<s>sāhitya</s>) is necessarily determined by difference, the very characterization of the reason as 'being co-apprehended' amounts to a characterization of difference. Therefore, in proving the unity of cognition and the 'I'-referent, there is a contradiction between the proposition and the reason — like 'the one is two.' This is the purport. Having stated the contradiction between the proposition-constituting term and the reason-constituting term, he states [the contradiction] between the proposition-constituting terms, with
'moreover' (<s>api ca</s>)
and so forth.
'From the invariable co-apprehension, the non-difference of blue and its cognition'

children.text: rityevaṃ hi teṣāṃ pratijñā / dvitvaviśiṣṭe 'traikatvavidhirjananīvandhyātvavidhiriva vyāhata iti yāvat / jñānajñātrorabhedasādhanadūṣaṇaprasaṅge 'smin jñānajñeyayorabhedasādhakaprayogadūṣaṇādisādhamadūṣaṇaprakārasāmyādi ti dhyeyam / śabdadoṣamuktvār'thadoṣamanyamāha
children.translated_text: — for such is their [the Buddhists'] proposition. In a subject qualified by duality, the prescription of unity is contradicted — like a prescription that a mother is barren. This is the purport. It should be reflected upon that in this context — where the refutation of the proof of non-difference of cognition and the knower is at hand — the same refutation-method, the same proof-method, and the like apply [mutatis mutandis] to the refutation of the proof of non-difference of cognition and the knowable. Having stated the verbal fault, he states another substantive fault with
'and inconclusive' (<s>anekāntaśca</s>)

children.text:
ti / saṃvidaḥ svayaṃprakāśatvājjaḍatvādiprakāśakāle jñānaprakāśopi niyataḥ / tathā ca saṃvidā sahopalambhaniyamabhājāṃ jaḍatvamūrtatvādīnāṃ saṃvidabhede saṃvido jaḍatvamūrtatvādiprasaṅgaḥ / dharmadharmibhedānupagamāt, abhedepyādhārādheyabhāvapratītyupagamācca / evaṃ sarva
jñasya baddhajñānānāmupalambhe niyamena buddhajñānamapyupalamyate, teṣāṃ buddhajñānamahopalambhānāṃ buddhajñānābhede buddhasya baddhatvāpattiḥ / tatra tatrābhedānupagame cānaikāntyaṃ hetoriti bhāvaḥ / abhedasādhakaṃ hetvantaramapi tulyarītyā nirasyati
children.translated_text: and so forth. Since cognition is self-luminous, even at the time of the manifestation of inertness and the like, the manifestation of knowledge is also invariable. And so, if there were non-difference of inertness, corporeality, and the like — which share the invariable co-apprehension with cognition — from cognition, then cognition would have inertness, corporeality, and the like. And because the difference between property and property-bearer is not accepted [by them], and because even in [alleged] non-difference, the relation of substrate and superstratum is accepted in experience. Likewise, the cognitions of worldly beings are apprehended whenever the omniscient one apprehends [them] — the <s>Buddha</s>'s cognition too is invariably apprehended. And if there were non-difference of those [worldly cognitions] — which share the invariable co-apprehension — from the <s>Buddha</s>'s cognition, there would follow the consequence that the <s>Buddha</s> is in bondage. And if non-difference is not accepted in those cases, then the reason is inconclusive. This is the purport. He also refutes, by the same method, another reason adduced to prove non-difference, with
'invariably in a single [cognition]' (<s>niyamena eka</s>)

children.text: ti / ekajñānasiddhatvam -ekajñāne dvayoḥ prakāśamānatvam / nirāsaprakāraśca-ekajñānaviṣayatvenāhamarthe saṃvidabhedasya sādhane tulyanayenāhamarthābhedo 'pi saṃvidi prasajyeta / cākṣuṣādijñānaviśeṣeṇaiva siddhatvaṃ cāhamarthasyāsiddham / jñānāntarato 'pi siddheḥ, svāpe svataḥ siddheśceti / aprayojakatvamapyāha
children.translated_text: and so forth. 'Being established in a single cognition' — the manifestation of both in a single cognition. And the method of refutation [is]: if [one argues] that because the 'I'-referent is the object of a single cognition, cognition is non-different from [the 'I'-referent] — then by the same reasoning, the non-difference of the 'I'-referent from cognition would also follow. And the unestablished-ness [of the reason is also shown]: the 'I'-referent is not established solely through a specific cognition such as visual cognition — because it is established from other cognitions too, and because in deep sleep it is established through itself. He also states the non-probativeness [of the reason] with
In the counter-instance (<s>vipakṣa</s>),
thus. The absence in the counter-instance means refutation in the <s>vipakṣa</s>. He establishes precisely that impossibility.
existence

children.text: tviti / sādhyābhāvavati hetorvṛttāvāpādyamānāyāṃ bādhakastarko nāsti / ato 'prayojako heturiti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: thus. When the occurrence of the <s>hetu</s> (probans) in what possesses the absence of the <s>sādhya</s> (probandum) is being supposed, there is no countervailing reasoning (<s>tarka</s>) to serve as a defeater. Therefore the meaning is: the <s>hetu</s> is non-probative.
Does the blue and such conform to illumination because it is of non-luminous nature,
for the sake of practical activity, or is it rather because of its non-difference from that [illumination]? (verse 15)
Since this is a matter of doubt, non-difference cannot be determinately established.
And this invariable concomitance pertains to what is to be known (<s>bodhya</s>), not however to the relation between cognition and cognizer (<s>buddhi-boddhṛ</s>). (verse 16)

children.text: spaṣṭaśca pratyakṣabādhaḥ, sarvajñāneṣu vedyādiva vitterapi vediturbhedasyāparokṣatvāt / naca pratiyoginaḥ pratyakṣatvaṃ dṛśyatvaṃ vā bhedasyā'parokṣye tvapekṣitavyam, siddhimātreṇa tadupapattāvaprayojakatvena tadviśeṣasyānākṣepāt / anavabhāsamāne 'pi pratiyogini bhāvāḥ svarūpata eva vilakṣaṇāḥ pratyakṣyanta iti sarvalokasvasākṣikametat /
children.translated_text: And the perceptual refutation is evident: in all cognitions, just as the object of knowledge (<s>vedya</s>) is immediately apprehended, so too the difference between the cognition (<s>vitti</s>) and the cognizer (<s>veditṛ</s>) is immediately apprehended. Nor need one require that the counter-correlate (<s>pratiyogin</s>) be perceptible or visible for the immediacy of the difference, since when the difference is established by mere existence alone, the non-invocation of that particular condition renders it non-probative. That even when the counter-correlate does not appear, entities are perceived as intrinsically distinct — this is self-witnessed by all the world.

children.text: nanu jīvato bhedapratyakṣasya śirasi padanidhānena sahopalambhaniyamasyābhedena pratibandhagrahaṇamiti kathamiva tatastadvādhasaṃbhavaḥ / tathāsati hi jvālābhedānumānamapi tadekatvapratyabhijñayāpodyeta / aviśeṣajño devānāṃ priyaḥ / tatra hi kḷptakāraṇadoṣānuvṛttau satyāṃ jāyamāno 'parokṣāvabhāso na niravadyapratyakṣapūrvakamanumānaṃ bādhitumarhati / tathāhi-aciranirvāpitāropiteṣvekavartibhāgavartiṣu bahuṣudīpeṣu tadbhedādarśinaḥ susadṛśatayā sa evāyamiti smṛtirupajāyate iti dṛṣṭam / ato 'nyatrāpyapratibandhapuṣkalakāraṇakramopanipātādavayavaviśleṣācca susadṛśanirantarapravṛttapradīpapravāhālambanaiva tathā matiriti niścīyate / tathaikanānātvapratyayaḥ svataḥprāptendriyavṛttiviparyayaprayuktaḥ samasamayopajāyamānānekānavadyapratyakṣapratikṣiptaviṣayaścadvicandrādau dṛṣṭa iti nāsau tatraikatvānumānamabhibhavituṃ prabhavati / na caivamiha jñātṛjñānajñeyavivekasākṣātkārī pratyaya iti pratiruṇaddhyevāyamihābhedānumānodayaprasaktim / na copalabdhisāhityaniyamādeva tathātvamatrānumeyamiti yuktam, vipakṣe bādhakānupalabdheḥ / saṃvidadhīnasiddhitayāpi tathā niyamopapatteḥ / anaindriyikatvena ca tadvṛttiviparyayasyākiñcitkaratvāt / yogyānupalambhaparākṛtatvācca bādhakapratyayasya / api ca viṣayasiddhirhi saṃvit / sā ca svayaṃprakāśetyavivādaḥ / tenāvarjanīyastathā niyamaḥ / naca bhedo 'pi siddhimantareṇa sidhyedityanunmattena yuktamāpādayitumityalamanenānubhavaparāhatamatātivyākulīkaraṇena /
children.translated_text: Objection: since the invariable co-apprehension (<s>sahopalambhaniyama</s>) is established as the ground for apprehending the invariable connection with non-difference, how then is refutation from that possible, given that the perceptual apprehension of difference is being overridden? For if that were so, then even the inference of difference among flames would be overturned by the recognition of their unity. One ignorant of distinctions is dear to the gods. For when the defect of an established cause persists, the immediate appearance that arises does not deserve to override an inference preceded by flawless perception. Thus it is observed that when many lamps placed on a single stand are lit from one recently extinguished, one who does not see their difference generates the memory 'this is the same one' due to close resemblance. Therefore it is determined that elsewhere too, due to the sequential arising of unobstructed sufficient causes and the separation of parts, such cognition is based merely on a continuously flowing stream of closely similar lamps. Likewise the cognition of unity and plurality, being produced by a distortion of the naturally obtained sense-faculty operation, and having its object contradicted by multiple flawless perceptions arising simultaneously — as seen in the case of the double moon — therefore it cannot overpower the inference of unity there. But it is not so here: the cognition that directly witnesses the distinction of knower (<s>jñātṛ</s>), knowledge (<s>jñāna</s>), and known (<s>jñeya</s>) indeed blocks the very possibility of an inference of non-difference here. Nor is it proper to say that non-difference should be inferred merely from the invariable concomitance of co-apprehension, since no defeater is found in the counter-instance. For such invariable concomitance is also explained by the dependence of cognition on consciousness (<s>saṃvid</s>). And because the distortion of sense-faculty operation is ineffective since [the self] is not an object of the senses. And because the would-be defeating cognition is already eliminated by qualified non-apprehension (<s>yogyānupalambha</s>). Moreover, cognition of an object is indeed <s>saṃvit</s> (consciousness), and that is self-luminous — this is undisputed. Therefore such invariable concomitance is unavoidable. Nor would any sane person maintain that difference too cannot be established without establishment [of both terms] — enough of this bewildering of a position already defeated by experience!
(Thus concludes the refutation of the Buddhist-held conceptual distinction of apprehensible and apprehender, <s>grāhya-grāhaka-vikalpa</s>.)

children.text: aprakāśātmanaśca nīlādeḥ prakāśa ityanubhavasiddhatvānna samarthanāntaraṃ prārthayate / ātmā tu prakāśasvabhāva eva / na ca tāvatājñānatvam, svatantratvāt / paratantramāgantu yāvadarthendriyasannikarṣādikāraṇasannidhānamavatiṣṭhamānamarthāvacchinnarūpaṃ jñānamiti prāgevāvocāma / ātmā tu svatantro jñātā ahamiti pratyātmaṃ prathate / yadipunarīdṛśo 'pyayamananyādhīnasiddhitayā jñānamabhilapyate, abhilapyatāṃ kāmam / tathāpi jñānavadevedaṃ jñānam, na jñaptimātratayā /
children.translated_text: And since the illumination of blue and such, which are of non-luminous nature, is established by experience, no further justification is required. But the self (<s>ātman</s>) is of the very nature of luminosity. And it is certainly not ignorance (<s>ajñānatva</s>), because of its independence (<s>svatantratva</s>). We have already stated that dependent, adventitious knowledge (<s>jñāna</s>), which persists due to the proximity of causes such as the contact of object and sense-organ, and which is delimited by the object, is [mere knowledge]. But the self is an independent knower (<s>jñātṛ</s>) — it manifests to each person as 'I'. If even such a one, by virtue of its self-established nature, is called knowledge, let it be called so freely. Even so, this knowledge is like a possessor of knowledge (<s>jñānavat</s>), not as mere cognition (<s>jñaptimātratā</s>).
(Thus concludes the refutation of the Advaitin-held conceptual distinction of apprehensible and apprehender.)

children.text: ata eva hi cchandogāḥ-'atha yo vededaṃ jighrāṇīti sa ātmā' ityādyāmananti / tathā 'katama ātmā' iti praśnapūrvakamidameva lakṣaṇamāmananti vājasaneyinaḥ 'yo 'yaṃ vijñānamayaḥ prāṇeṣu hṛdyantarjyotiḥ puruṣaḥ' iti / atra hi yo 'yaṃ sarvalokānubhavasiddho vividhaviṣayavedanapracuraḥ prāṇeṣu prerakatayā sthito hṛdayāyatane antarjyotiḥ ahamiti pratyaktvena prakāśate, sa puruṣa iti yathoditamevātmasvarūpamupadiśyate / 'eṣa hi draṣṭā śrotā ghrātā rasayitā mantā boddhā kartā vijñānātmā puruṣaḥ' ityātharvaṇāḥ / tathā 'vijñātāramare kena vijānīyāditi' 'na paśyo mṛtyuṃ paśyati na rogaṃ nota duḥkhatām' 'sa uttamaḥ puruṣaḥ nopajanaṃ smarannidaṃ śarīram' 'evamevāsya paridraṣṭurimāḥ ṣoḍaśakalāḥ puruṣāyaṇāḥ puruṣaṃ prāpyāstaṃ gacchanti' 'tasmāddhā etasmānmanomayādanyo 'ntara ātmā vijñānamayaḥ' ityādyāḥ /
children.translated_text: For this very reason the followers of the <s>Chāndogya</s> teach: 'Now, he who knows "I am smelling this" — that is the self (<s>ātman</s>),' and so forth. Likewise, prefaced by the question 'Which is the self?', the <s>Vājasaneyins</s> (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s>) teach this very definition: 'This person (<s>puruṣa</s>) who consists of understanding (<s>vijñānamaya</s>), who is among the vital breaths (<s>prāṇas</s>), the inner light in the heart.' Here, this one who is established by the experience of all people, who is abundant in the cognition of diverse objects, who abides among the <s>prāṇas</s> as their impeller, the inner light in the abode of the heart, who shines as 'I' in direct self-awareness — that <s>puruṣa</s> is taught as the very nature of the self as described. The followers of the <s>Atharva Veda</s> (<s>Praśna Upaniṣad</s>) [declare]: 'For this is the seer, hearer, smeller, taster, thinker, knower, agent — the conscious self (<s>vijñānātman</s>), the <s>puruṣa</s>.' Likewise: 'The knower — by what, dear one, should one know him?'; 'The seer does not see death, does not see disease, does not see suffering'; 'That supreme <s>puruṣa</s>, not remembering this body, is not born again'; 'Thus for this onlooker, these sixteen parts (<s>kalās</s>) that tend toward <s>puruṣa</s>, having reached <s>puruṣa</s>, set'; 'Therefore, different from this self made of mind (<s>manomaya</s>), there is an inner self made of understanding (<s>vijñānamaya</s>)' — and so forth.

children.text: 'satyaṃ jñāna' mityatrāpi brahmalakṣaṇanirdeśe jñānaśabdo na jñānamātravacanaḥ ; api tu tadvadvacanaḥ / tadvacanatve 'liti' iti ādyudāttatvaprasakteḥ / antodāttaścāyaṃ jñānaśabdaḥ / matvarthīyācpratyayāntatve tathātvaṃ ghaṭate; nānyathetyetat paramātmanirūpaṇe atinipuṇamupapādayiṣyāmaḥ / aitareyopaniṣadapi 'prajñānaṃ brahye'tyuktvā 'sa etena prājñenātmanā' iti prakṛṣṭajñānavantameveśvaraṃ darśayati / tat siddhaṃ jñātaivāyamātmeti //
children.translated_text: Even in the statement '<s>satyaṃ jñānam</s>' ('truth, knowledge') in the definition of <s>Brahman</s>, the word <s>jñāna</s> does not merely denote knowledge; rather, it denotes 'one who possesses that' (<s>tadvat</s>). If it were to denote 'one who possesses that,' the initial-acute accent would be expected [by the suffix '<s>-li</s>']. But this word <s>jñāna</s> has a final-acute accent. When it is taken as ending in a <s>matvarthīya</s> (possessive-meaning) <s>ac</s>-suffix, such [final-acute accentuation] is accounted for; not otherwise — we shall demonstrate this most subtly in the section on the examination of the Supreme Self (<s>Paramātman</s>). The <s>Aitareya Upaniṣad</s> too, having said '<s>prajñānaṃ brahma</s>' ('consciousness is <s>Brahman</s>'), shows with 'with this conscious self (<s>prājñena ātmanā</s>)' that <s>Īśvara</s> is indeed one who possesses supreme knowledge. Thus it is established that this self (<s>ātman</s>) is indeed a knower (<s>jñātṛ</s>).
(Thus concludes the section on the examination of the nature of the inner self, which is distinct from the body and such.)

children.text: kiṃ punarasmin dehādivyatirekiṇi cetane pratyagātmani pramāṇam? / anu
children.translated_text: Now then, what is the means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) for this conscious inner self (<s>pratyagātman</s>) that is distinct from the body and so forth? Infer-

body.translated_text: Now he analyzes and refutes the non-inertness (<s>ajaḍatva</s>) that has been adduced by the opponents as proving the selfhood of knowledge, with

children.translated_text: ence — says <s>Akṣapāda</s>, the one skilled in logic (<s>nayavicakṣaṇa</s>). As he states:
Desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, and knowledge are the inferential mark (<s>liṅga</s>) of the self (<s>ātman</s>)
— thus.

body.text: kimamīṣāmātmanāvinābhāvo dhūmadhvajaviśeṣeṇeva dhūmaviśeṣasya dṛṣṭaḥ? hantaivaṃ tata eva tatpramiteḥ kimanumānena? / mābhūdviśeṣatodarśanam; sāmānyatastu bhaviṣyati / tathāhi-icchādayaḥ kāryatvānityatvaguṇatvādibhiḥ śabdādaya ivā'śritatayānumīyante / yaścaiṣāmāśrayaḥ sa ātmā / guṇatvaṃ ca pariśeṣāt / na sāmānyaviśeṣasamavāyābhāvāḥ anityatvāt / na dravyaṃ karma vā, vyāpakadravyasamavāyāditi / viśeṣaguṇatvaṃ cānityatve satyasmadādyekendriyagrāhyatvaniyamāt rūpādivat / evamāśrayamātramupasthāpayanto 'nvayavyatirekiṇo hetavaḥ dravyāntaraguṇatvaṃ ca pratyācakṣāṇaiḥ kevalavyatirekisādhanairātmagocaratayā niyamyante / tathā hi bhavati-icchādayo na mahābhūtaguṇāḥ, svātmana eva pratyakṣatvāt; abāhyendriyagrāhyatvāddhā / ye bhūtaguṇāste svātmaparātmapratyakṣāḥ bāhyakaraṇapratyakṣāśca, yathā rūpādayaḥ / na tathecchādaya iti na tadguṇāḥ / dikkālamanāṃsi punaḥ na viśeṣaguṇavanti; nāpi tadguṇānāṃ pratyakṣatvamiti na teṣāmapi guṇāḥ / akāraṇaguṇapūrvatvāt ayāvaccharīrabhāvitvādityādayaḥ śarīraviśeṣaguṇatvapratiṣedhahetavaḥ prācīnāścātrānukraṣṭavyāḥ / tenecchādayo na śarīraguṇāḥ tadguṇabhāvāpavādapramāṇavattve sati guṇatvāt / ye yathoktasādhyā na bhavanti, te yathoktasādhanā api na bhavanti; yathā rūpādayaḥ / yathoktasādhanāḥ punaricchādaya iti yathoktasādhyā eveti / vimatipadāspadebhyaḥ śarīrādibhyor'thāntaraguṇā icchādaya iti vā pratijñā / yathokta eva hetuḥ / udāharaṇaṃ ca prayoktavyam / sāmānyena vānvayaḥ pradarśanīyaḥ-yo yadguṇabhāvāpavādakapramāṇavattve sati guṇaḥ, sa tator'thāntarasya guṇaḥ; yathā pṛthivyādibhyaḥ śabda iti ākāśasiddhivadātmasiddhiriti /
body.translated_text: Is the invariable concomitance of these with the self observed specifically, like that of a particular smoke with a particular fire? Well then, if so, since the self would be known from that very [perception], what need is there for inference? Let there be no observation of the particular; but there will be [inference] from the general. Thus: desire and the rest, by virtue of being effects, non-eternal, and qualities, are inferred as requiring a substrate, just like sound and the rest. And that which is their substrate — that is the self. And their quality-hood is established by elimination (<s>pariśeṣa</s>): they are not universals, particularities, inherence, or absences, because of being non-eternal. They are not substances or actions, because of inhering in a pervading substance. And their being specific qualities [of a particular substance] is established — given their non-eternality — by the rule that they are graspable only by one's own sense-organ, like color and so forth. Thus, probans that establish [the self] through positive and negative concomitance (<s>anvaya-vyatireka</s>) present merely a substrate, while those that deny quality-hood in any other substance are restricted to the domain of the self by purely negative proofs (<s>kevala-vyatireki</s>). Thus it is stated: desire and the rest are not qualities of the gross elements (<s>mahābhūtas</s>), because they are perceptible only to oneself; or because they are not graspable by external sense-organs. Those that are qualities of elements are perceptible both to oneself and to others, and are perceptible by external instruments — like color and such. Desire and the rest are not like that, hence they are not qualities of those [elements]. Space, time, and the minds (<s>manas</s>) moreover do not possess specific qualities; nor is there perceptibility of their qualities — hence [desire etc.] are not qualities of those either. The absence of a prior [corresponding] quality in the cause, the fact of not lasting for the entire duration of the body — these and other arguments that negate quality-hood in the body are traditional and should be cited here. Therefore desire and the rest are not qualities of the body, since they possess quality-hood while there exist means of valid knowledge that refute their being qualities of that [body]. Whatever are not the probandum as stated are also not the probans as stated — like color and such. But desire and the rest are the probans as stated, hence they are indeed the probandum as stated. Or the thesis (<s>pratijñā</s>) may be: desire and the rest are qualities of something other than the body and such, which are the loci of dispute. The <s>hetu</s> is as stated. And the example should be adduced. Or the positive concomitance should be shown generally: whatever is a quality while there exists a means of valid knowledge refuting its quality-hood in a given thing, that is a quality of something other than that thing — just as sound [is a quality] of something other than earth etc. Thus, just as <s>ākāśa</s> (space) is established [from sound], so is the self established.

body.text: (iti vilakṣaṇātmana ānumānikatvapakṣanirūpaṇam)

children.text: idamapi na samīcīnamityeke / tathāhi-anvayavyatirekihetubhirdehādisādhāraṇamāśrayamātramavagamitam / na ca tāvatā'tmasiddhiḥ / kevalavyatirekī tu sādhanadaśāmeva nāsādayati, sapakṣānvayavirahāt, asādhāraṇavat / nacaivaṃ kevalānva
children.translated_text: Some say this too is not sound. Thus: by the probans of positive and negative concomitance, only a mere substrate common to the body and so forth has been established. But the self is not established by that alone. The purely negative proof (<s>kevala-vyatirekin</s>), however, does not even reach the stage of being a valid proof, due to the absence of positive concomitance in a similar instance (<s>sapakṣa</s>) — like an uncommon [probans] (<s>asādhāraṇa</s>). Nor [can one say] that in this way a purely positive proof (<s>kevalānva-

body.translated_text: (Thus concludes the examination of the position that the distinct self is known through inference.)

body.text: yino vipakṣavyatirekadarśanavikalatayā sādhāraṇavadasādhanatvam / deśakālādiśaṅgitopādhivigamepyanvayadarśanena sādhyānvitasvabhāvatayā pariniścitatvāt / naca sādhanābhāve sādhyābhāvadarśanamātreṇa sādhyānvitasvabhāvatvaṃ śakyaṃ niścetum / abhāvasyānantadeśavyāpitayānavayavena grahaṇasyaiva duṣkaratvāt, kalayāpyanyatravṛttau saṃbandhe niyamāsaṃbhavāt / sandehagrastatvācca-kiṃ sādhanābhāvaprayuktaḥ sādhyābhāvaḥ, kiṃ vā nimittāntaraprayukta iti / pṛthivyādibhyor'thāntaraguṇatvapratijñāpi dravyāntarāprasiddheraprasiddhaviśeṣaṇā /
body.translated_text: -yin</s>) would be invalid like a common [probans] (<s>sādhāraṇa</s>) due to lack of observed absence in the counter-instance (<s>vipakṣa</s>). For [in the purely positive case], since positive concomitance is observed even after removing suspected limiting conditions (<s>upādhi</s>) of place, time, and so forth, its nature as concomitant with the probandum is firmly ascertained. But one cannot ascertain the nature of being concomitant with the probandum merely from observing the absence of the probandum in the absence of the probans. Because absence, pervading infinite locations, is itself difficult to apprehend in its entirety; because even if [the probans] occurs elsewhere to the slightest degree, an invariable connection becomes impossible; and because there is doubt: is the absence of the probandum caused by the absence of the probans, or is it caused by some other factor? The thesis that [desire etc. are] qualities of something other than earth and so forth also [fails], because the other substance is not established — thus the distinguishing predicate is unestablished (<s>aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇā</s>).

body.text: (iti naiyāyikābhimatātmānumānanirāsaḥ)

children.text: etena sāṅkhyodīritasādhanabhedā apyapoditā veditavyāḥ saṅghātaparārthatvādayaḥ / tathā ca tāneva tāvadādito vyākurmahe-
children.translated_text: By this, the various proofs adduced by the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s> too — beginning with the composite-being-for-another's-sake (<s>saṅghāta-parārthatva</s>) — should be understood as refuted. And so we shall first expound those very [proofs] from the beginning:

body.translated_text: (Thus concludes the refutation of the <s>Naiyāyika</s>-held inference of the self.)

children.translated_text: Because of the composite being for the sake of another, because of the reversal of the three <s>guṇas</s> and such, because of [the need for] a presider (<s>adhiṣṭhāna</s>),
<s>Puruṣa</s> exists — because of the nature of being an experiencer (<s>bhoktṛbhāva</s>), and because of activity directed toward liberation (<s>kaivalya</s>).

children.text: ayamarthaḥ-dehendriyādayaḥ parārthāḥ saṅgātatvācchayanāsanaśaraṇādivat / pratyakṣaṃ ca śarīrasya saṅghātatvaṃ, bhūtānāṃ ca / avyaktamahadahaṅkārendriyāṇāṃ ca sukhaduḥkhamohātmatayā tathātvamanumeyaṃ tadvadeva / na cendriyāṇāmāhaṅkārikatvasyābhyupetasya, sādhyantvābhimatapārārthyadharmasya cāsaṃhataparārthatvasyānyathātvāpādanādubhayaviśeṣaviruddhatvaṃ hetoḥ; ahaṅkārānvayavyatirekānuvidhānena "
children.translated_text: The meaning is this: the body, sense-organs, and so forth serve another's purpose (<s>parārtha</s>) because they are composites (<s>saṅghāta</s>) — like beds, seats, shelters, and the like. And the composite nature of the body is directly perceived, as is that of the elements (<s>bhūtas</s>). The composite nature of the unmanifest (<s>avyakta</s>), the great principle (<s>mahat</s>), the ego-principle (<s>ahaṅkāra</s>), and the sense-organs is to be inferred from their being of the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion — in the same way [as beds etc.]. Nor is there the fault of the <s>hetu</s> being contradicted by both the particular properties (<s>ubhayaviśeṣaviruddhatva</s>), due to the accepted <s>āhaṅkārika</s> (ego-derived) nature of the sense-organs undermining the intended property of serving-another's-purpose that pertains to the non-composite — because the <s>āhaṅkārika</s> origin of the sense-organs is established by valid means through the conformity with the presence and absence of <s>ahaṅkāra</s>, by the authority of scripture (<s>āgama</s>) stating "
The gods are declared to be products of the <s>vaikārika</s> [<s>ahaṅkāra</s>],

children.text: ityādyāgamabalena prakāśalāghavaguṇānvayena ca vaikārikābhidhānasāttvikāhaṅkārabhedayonitvasyendriyāṇāṃ pramāṇasiddhasyāpavādānupapatteḥ / ātmanastu saṅghātatve tasyāpi saṅghātāntarārthatayānavasthāpattyā niṣpramāṇakānekakalpanāprasaṅgāt, aprayojakatvācca saṅghātatvasya śeṣitve, dṛṣṭāntadṛṣṭāśeṣadharmopasthāpane 'numānaprāmāṇya syaivāsambhavāpatteḥ tadasaṅghātatvasya cāpracālyatvāt / naca pramāṇāntarabalenānāhaṅkārikatvasaṅghātāntarārthatvayorbādhe 'bādhitena saṅghātaparārthatvenāpi na bhavitavyam / evaṃ ca saṃhatatvavyāpakāvaruddhatraiguṇyādirahito 'saṃhata ātmā siddhaḥ /
children.translated_text: and by the positive concomitance with the quality of luminosity and lightness — hence the refutation of the <s>pramāṇa</s>-established <s>vaikārika</s> (sāttvika-<s>ahaṅkāra</s>) origin of the sense-organs is untenable. But if the self too were a composite, then since it too would serve the purpose of yet another composite, there would be an infinite regress (<s>anavasthā</s>), entailing the groundless postulation of infinitely many [entities]; and because composite-nature is non-probative for being-subservient (<s>śeṣitva</s>); and because in presenting the properties of the example and the proved — whether seen or unseen — the very validity of the inference (<s>anumāna</s>) would become impossible — therefore the non-composite nature of the self is unassailable.
