children.text: nanu vedyasvabhāvo 'yam, yatsvaviṣayasaṃvidā sidhyatīti / vittistu vittireva, veditā ca veditaiveti kutastayorvedyasvabhāvānupraveśaḥ / uktaṃ hi tayormānasapratyakṣagocaratvam, anumeyatvāsambhavaśca / kutastarhi vittisiddhiḥ? svata eva / svayaṃprakāśā hi saṃvit /
children.translated_text: Now, [you may say:] their nature is to be known, and what is known is established by the cognition whose object it is. But cognition is merely cognition, and the knower is merely the knower — so how can knowability enter into them? For it has been stated that they are the objects of mental perception, and the impossibility of being objects of inference [has also been shown]. Whence then the establishment of cognition? From itself alone. For <s>saṃvid</s> (consciousness) is self-luminous.

children.text: maivam / sāpi hi viṣayavadevānyasyaiva prakāśamānatayā na svataḥsidhyati / svataḥsidhyantī ca sā kimiti kañcideva prati cakāsti, na sarvān prati / tatsamavāyāditi cet-yatsamavāyinī hi yā saṃvit tasyaiva sā cakāsti, netarasya, tadasamavāyāditi; yadyevam, āśritastarhi ātmasaṃbandhanibandhana eva saṃvidaḥ prakāśaḥ, tadbhāvābhāvānuvidhināt / yadyucyeta-prakāśasvabhāvāyā eva satyāḥ pratiyogiviśeṣāvacchedāyaiva tadapekṣā, na svarūpasiddhaya iti; kutaḥ khalvayaṃ niścayaḥ? yadi hi pratiyoginirapekṣaiva kadācidātmasvarūpamiva saṃvit prakāśeta, tata evamadhyavasyemāpi / na ca tathāsti / āśrayapratiyogisāpekṣaiva saṃyogaputratvāderiva tasyāḥ svarūpasatteti na pṛthaksiddhyutprekṣāvakāśaḥ / satyāḥ saṃvidaḥ prakāśavyabhicārābhāvāt svarūpaprayuktaḥ prakāśa iti cet, satyāḥ kiṃ tasyā ātmasaṃbandhavyabhicāro 'sti? / api caivaṃ sukhaduḥkhādayo 'pi tvanmate svataḥsiddhāḥsyuḥ / na hi te 'pi santo na prakāśante /
children.translated_text: Not so. For that [consciousness] too, like the object, is manifest only to another — hence it is not self-established. And if it were self-established, why does it shine forth only to a particular [subject] and not to all? If [you say] 'because of inherence (<s>samavāya</s>)' — since whatever consciousness inheres in, for that alone it shines, and not for another, due to the absence of inherence there — if so, then the illumination of consciousness is dependent precisely on its connection with the <s>ātman</s> (self), since it follows the presence and absence of that [connection]. If one were to say: 'the dependence [on the self] is only for the delimitation of a particular counter-correlate for consciousness whose nature is already illumination, not for the establishment of its own nature' — whence indeed this certainty? For if consciousness were sometimes to illuminate itself independently of any counter-correlate, just like the self's own nature, then we could accept this. But it is not so. Consciousness, being dependent on its locus as counter-correlate — like the reality of a conjunction or a son — [exists only] in that form; hence there is no scope for the fancy of independent establishment. If one says: 'because there is no deviation of illumination from existent consciousness, the illumination is due to its own nature' — is there then any deviation of the self-connection from existent [consciousness]? Moreover, on your view, pleasure, pain, etc. would also be self-established, for they too, when existing, are not unmanifested.

children.text: athārthāntarasādhakatayā sarvavādisaṃmatāyāḥ saṃvida eva paraṃ svayaṃprakāśatvamāśritam / tayaiva tathābhūtayā taditarabāhyābhyantarasakalapadārthasiddhyupapatteḥ kimanekasva
children.translated_text: Then, it is consciousness alone — accepted by all philosophical schools as capable of establishing other things — that alone is self-luminous par excellence. Since the establishment of all internal and external entities whatsoever is accounted for by that very [consciousness] in such a form, what is the need for admitting multiple self-luminous entities?
— this is the purport.
He justifies this very point:
'<s>Dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>'
— by means of this verse. 'Assisted by <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>' means: in a condition distinguished by having as auxiliary instruments the unseen [forces] of the nature of merit and demerit.
'Like the ear'

children.text: diti / karṇaśaṣkulyavacchinnākāśasyaiva śrotratvam / tasya cādṛṣṭasahakāre satyeva śabdagrahakaraṇatvam, na tadvirahe iti yathādṛṣṭanibandhanaḥ śrotrasyendriya bhāvaḥ tatheti yāvat / tathā cādṛṣṭavirahānmuktau manaso nendriyatvamiti bhāvaḥ //19//
children.translated_text: — thus. The space delimited by the auricle of the ear alone constitutes the organ of hearing. And that [organ] has the capacity to apprehend sound only when the cooperation of the unseen [karmic force] is present, not in its absence — just as the status of the ear as a sense-organ is dependent on the unseen, so too [is the mind's status] — that is the extent. And thus, in the absence of the unseen in liberation, the mind does not have sense-organ status — this is the purport. //19//

body.translated_text: He elaborates the meaning of the verse:

body.text: śaṅkate

children.translated_text: 'Nor [through] <s>yoga</s>-born'
— thus.

children.text: manassaṃyogasya yogajadharmānugṛhītatvam-yogajadharmasahakṛtatvam / yogajadharmaprabhāvānmuktāvapi manasa indriyabhāvo 'nuvartata iti mānasamātmajñānaṃ tadā sambhavatīti bhāvaḥ / muktau yogajadharmānuvṛttau śrutivirodhamāha
children.translated_text: 'The conjunction with the mind being assisted by <s>yoga</s>-born <s>dharma</s>' means: being assisted by <s>yoga</s>-born <s>dharma</s> as cooperating factor. The purport is: through the power of <s>yoga</s>-born <s>dharma</s>, even in liberation the mind's sense-organ status continues — hence mental cognition of the self is possible then. He states the scriptural contradiction to the continuation of <s>yoga</s>-born <s>dharma</s> in liberation:
'His <s>karmas</s> are destroyed'

— thus. 'Bright and otherwise' means: of the nature of merit and demerit. Now, if one says the scriptural passage intends the cessation of all <s>karma</s> except <s>yoga</s>-born <s>dharma</s>, to that he says:
'If [liberation] were the result of <s>dharma</s>'

children.text: ti / mokṣakāle jñānasyātmaviṣayakasya sarvaviṣayakasya vā dharmajanyatve janyabhāvasya vināśitvaniyamātpunarajñānādiprasaṅga ityarthaḥ / karmaphalasyānityatve śrutimudāharati
children.translated_text: — thus. The meaning is: if cognition — whether pertaining to the self or to all objects — were produced by <s>dharma</s> at the time of liberation, then since what is produced necessarily perishes, the unwanted consequence of ignorance etc. returning [would follow]. He cites a <s>śruti</s> for the impermanence of the fruit of <s>karma</s>:
'What is not done'

children.text: iti / nanu mokṣa ātmaiva jñānaheturastu / tatrāha
children.translated_text: — thus. Now, let the self itself be the cause of cognition in liberation. To that he says:
'Nor the self'
— 'ātmā sattayaiva' may be the original reading.
'kḷpte'

children.text: ti / jñānakāraṇatayābhimatasyendriyādeḥ tyāgaḥ, akḷptasyaiva kevalasyātmanaḥ jñānakāraṇatvena kalpanaṃ ca prasajyata ityarthaḥ / doṣāntaramapyāha
children.translated_text: — the meaning is: there would follow the consequence of abandoning the senses and the like that are accepted as causes of knowledge, and of postulating the self alone — which has not been postulated [for this role] — as the cause of knowledge. He states another fault too:
'tanmātre'

children.text: ti / ātmasvarūpamātranimittatve muktikālīnasya jñānasya sarvadaiva tat bhavediti saṃsārānavatāraprasaṅgaḥ, jñānasyājñānatanmūlasaṃsaraṇapratibandhakatvāditi bhāvaḥ / viśadatattvasākṣātkārarūpajñānabhāve 'pi saṃsāropagame ca doṣamāha
children.translated_text: — if the mere essential nature of the self were the sole cause, then the knowledge that [exists] at the time of liberation would exist at all times — and there would follow the consequence of never entering saṃsāra, because knowledge obstructs ignorance and the transmigration rooted in it. This is the sense. He states the fault even when there is an absence of knowledge in the form of vivid direct realization of truth and yet saṃsāra is accepted:
'bandhe'

children.text: ti / muktikālajñānasya saṃsārakāle 'pi sattve saṃsārāpekṣayā mokṣe vailakṣaṇyaṃ na syādityarthaḥ / nanu duḥkhadhvaṃsādireva mokṣeviśeṣa iti cet, tarhi tāvanmātrameva bhavenmokṣa iti kṛtaṃ jñānādināpārtheneti bhāvaḥ / ātmano muktikālīnajñāne hetubhūtasya nityatve 'pi na saṃsāre tatprasaṅgaḥ / dehādeḥ pratibandhakatvāditi śaṅkate
children.translated_text: — the meaning is: if the knowledge [present] at the time of liberation also exists during saṃsāra, there would be no distinctness in liberation as compared to saṃsāra. [Objection:] If it is said that the specific feature in liberation is precisely the destruction of suffering and the like — [Reply:] then let liberation be just that much, and knowledge and the like would be purposeless. This is the sense. [Objection:] Even though the cause that produces the knowledge of the self at the time of liberation is eternal, [that knowledge] does not [follow as a] consequence in saṃsāra — because the body and the like are obstructors — he raises the objection:
'na ca'
— he resolves it:
'tat khalu'
— having justified the impossibility of the obstructing function, he also states the contradiction there:
'kḷptajñāne'
— 'of that very' — of the body, senses, and the like.
'The statements that are thus are arthavādas (eulogistic passages)'
— he elaborates what was stated:
'tātkālike'

children.text: ti / duḥkhanivṛttiparā muktau sukhavādāḥ, jñānaprāgabhāvanāstitābhiprāyakāśca jñānavādāḥ / te cātmajñānapraśaṃsāmātraparāstadvidhiśeṣabhūtā evetyarthaḥ / prābhākaramatopasaṃhāraḥ
children.translated_text: — the statements about bliss in liberation pertain to the cessation of suffering, and the statements about knowledge are intended [to convey] the prior non-existence of knowledge. And those [statements] pertain merely to the praise of self-knowledge and are auxiliary to the injunction of that [knowledge] — this is the meaning. The conclusion of the <s>Prābhākara</s> position:
'ataḥ'

children.text:
iti / yathoktanītyā-viṣayaprakāśakasya jñānasyaiva svasvāśrayaprakāśakatvaṃ nyāyyamityuktanītyā /
prābhākaramataṃ pratikṣipati siddhāntī
children.translated_text:
— 'by the stated method' — by the method stated: that it is knowledge alone — which illuminates objects — that properly has the capacity to illuminate its own substrate as well.
The Siddhāntin refutes the <s>Prābhākara</s> position, with
'idam apy ātma'

children.text:
tyādinā / ātmatattvājñānakāryā
ātmaprakāreṣvayathāpratipattibhedā yeṣāṃ, teṣāmidaṃ nirarthakaṃ vacanamityarthaḥ / kathaṃ nirarthakatvaṃ gurukteḥ? tatrāha
children.translated_text: and so forth. The meaning is: this statement is meaningless for those who, due to ignorance of the truth of the self, have various misconceptions about the modes of the self. How is the statement of the teacher meaningless? To that he says:
'viṣaye'
('regarding the object').
'na hi'

children.text:
ti / ātmavittiḥ-ātmadharmabhūtaṃ jñānam / svarūpam-ātmasvarūpam / atra ātmā vittisvarūpaṃ vā iti pāṭhaḥ syādvā / seddhum-prakāśitum / atadviṣayatvāt-viṣayavittiviṣayatvābhāvāttayoḥ /
aviṣayayorapi jñānajñātrorjñānabalata eva siddhiriti śaṅkate guruḥ
children.translated_text:
— 'Self-awareness' (<s>ātmavitti</s>) — knowledge that is an essential attribute (<s>dharmabhūta</s>) of the self. 'Essential nature' — the self's essential nature. Here 'ātmā vittisvarūpaṃ vā' may be an alternative reading. 'To be established' — to be illuminated. 'Because of not being the object of that' — because of those two [awareness and the self] not being objects of object-cognition.
[Objection:] The teacher raises the objection that even though knowledge and the knower are not objects [of knowledge], their establishment is from the very power of knowledge:
'nanu vedye'

children.text: ti / vittireva, na tu vittiviṣayaḥ, viṣayavajjaḍā vā / veditaiva, na tu vedyaḥ, vedyavadajñātā vā / tathā ca vilakṣaṇasvabhāvatvādbhāvānāmaviṣayayorapi tayoḥ siddhirjñāvabalataḥ setsyatītyaviṣayatvenāsiddhirviṣayavattayordurbhaṇamiti bhāvaḥ / nanu jñānāntaraviṣayatvenaiva tayoḥ prakāśo 'stvityatrāha
children.translated_text: — [Awareness is] awareness itself, not an object of awareness, nor inert like an object. [The self is] the knower itself, not the known, nor unknown like the known. And thus, because these two — knowledge and the knower — have distinct essential natures from [ordinary] entities, their establishment even as non-objects will be accomplished from the very power of knowledge. Therefore, [the objection that] they are not established because they are not objects is difficult to maintain — this is the sense. [Objection:] But let their illumination be precisely through being objects of another knowledge — to this he says:
'uktaṃ hi'

children.text: ti / svabalata eva vitteḥ siddhiṃ śaṅkāsamādhānamukhenāha
children.translated_text: — he states, in the form of raising and resolving an objection, the establishment of awareness from its own power alone:
'kutaḥ'
('whence?').
'svata eva'

children.text:
ti / viṣayajñānakāle 'viṣayasyāpi tasya jñānasya prakāśo bhavatītyanāyatyā svīkaraṇīyam, tadāśrayatvenātmanaśceti hārdam /
tatra svaprakāśatvamākṣipati gurūktaṃ saṃvidaḥ siddhāntī
children.translated_text:
('from itself alone'). At the time of cognizing an object, the illumination of that knowledge too — which is a non-object — must be accepted without any further ado. And [the illumination of] the self as its substrate [must be accepted] — this is the core point.
The Siddhāntin challenges the self-luminosity of awareness asserted in the teacher's words:
'maivam'

children.text: mityādinā / svāśrayātmādhīnaprakāśatvādeva tasmā eva prakāśamānatvaṃ saṃvido ghaṭata iti svataḥsiddhatvāsiddhiriti bhāvaḥ/ atra paraḥ parihāraṃ śaṅkate
children.translated_text: ('not so') and so forth. The sense is: because awareness is luminous only through dependence on its own substrate, the self, it shines forth for that [self] alone — so the self-establishment [of awareness] is not established. The opponent raises a resolution here:
'tatsamavāyāt iti cet'
('if [you say] because of its inherence in that'). He elaborates his own statement:
'yatsamavāyinī'

children.text: ti / svayaṃprakāśāpi saṃvidātmāpṛthaksiddhatvādātmana eva prakāśata iti bhāvaḥ / pratikṣipatyākṣeptā
children.translated_text: — the sense is: although awareness is self-luminous, because it is inseparable (<s>apṛthaksiddha</s>) from the self, it shines forth for the self alone. The objector rejects this:
'yady evam'
('if so').
'tadbhāve'

— the meaning is: because the illumination of awareness conforms to the presence and absence of the connection with the self — i.e., has positive and negative concomitance [with it] — the causality of the connection with the self for the illumination of awareness is established. The opponent again raises an objection:
'yady ucyete'

children.text: ti / pratiyogī-viṣayaḥ, sa eva viśeṣaḥ-viśeṣaṇam, tadavacchedāyaiva-tatsaṃbandhāyaiva, viṣayaprakāśakatvāyaiveti yāvat / tadapekṣā-ātmasaṃbandhāpekṣā/ na tu svaprakāśāyetyarthaḥ / pariharati
children.translated_text: — 'the counter-correlate' — the object; that very thing is the qualifier (<s>viśeṣaṇa</s>); 'for the delimitation by that alone' — for the connection with that alone, i.e., for the capacity to illuminate objects alone. 'That dependence' — the dependence on the connection with the self — but not for its self-luminosity. This is the meaning. He resolves:
'kutaḥ'

children.text: evaṃ niścayo na saṃbhavatīti yāvat / niścayāsaṃbhavamevopapādayati
children.translated_text: — that is: such a determination is not possible. He justifies the very impossibility of the determination:
'yadi hi'

children.text: ti / pratiyoginirapekṣaiva viṣayanirapekṣaiva / evam-viṣayaprakāśanāyaivātmasaṃbandhāpekṣā saṃvido na svaprakāśaṃ pratītyevam /
children.translated_text: — 'independent of the counter-correlate' — independent of the object alone. 'Thus' — that the dependence of awareness on the connection with the self is only for the illumination of objects, not for [its] self-luminosity — [such a determination is impossible].
'na ca tathā'

children.text: ti / viṣayaprakāśakāla eva svāśrayāyaiva prakāśamānāyāḥ saṃvidaḥ svaprakāśe viṣayātmasaṃbandhasāpekṣatvameṣitavyamiti bhāvaḥ / atītādiviṣayajñāne 'pi viṣayeṇa saṃbandho jñānasya viṣayaviṣayibhāvalakṣaṇo vilakṣaṇaḥ svarūpasaṃbandhaviśeṣo 'styeveti hārdam / nanu nirviṣayā nirāśrayā ca saṃvit / antaḥkaraṇatadvṛttyupadhānaupādhikaṃ kevalaṃ tasyāḥ sāśrayatvādipratītimātramityatrāha
children.translated_text: — the sense is: since awareness shines forth for its own substrate alone even at the time of illuminating objects, it must be accepted that its self-luminosity is dependent on the connection with both the object and the self. Even in the case of cognition of past and other objects, the connection of knowledge with the object — characterized by the object-objectified relation — is of a distinct kind, [namely] a specific essential-nature relation. The core point [is this]. [Objection:] But awareness has neither an object nor a substrate. Its [apparent] having a substrate and the like is merely a perception conditioned by the limiting adjunct of the internal organ and its modifications — to this he says:
'āśraye'

children.text:
ti / bhūtale ghaṭasaṃyogasyāśrayo bhūtalam, pratiyogī
ghaṭaḥ / putratvasyā'śrayaḥ putraḥ, pratiyogī pitā / jñānasya pratiyogī viṣayaḥ, ātmā'śrayaḥ / siddhiḥ-sthitiḥ prakāśaśca / nirviṣayatvena nirāśrayatvena ca sthitiḥ prakāśo vā saṃvido nāstyeva / saṃvinmātrānubhavaścānupalambhabādhitaḥ / tathā ca saṃvitprakāśe ātmasaṃbandhāpekṣāpi durvāraiveti bhāvaḥ / svasattāvyāpakaprakāśatvena svaprakāśatvaṃ syātsaṃvida iti punaḥ śaṅkate
children.translated_text: ('regarding the substrate'). Of the conjunction of a pot on the ground, the substrate is the ground and the counter-correlate is the pot. Of son-hood, the substrate is the son and the counter-correlate is the father. Of knowledge, the counter-correlate is the object and the self is the substrate. 'Establishment' — subsistence and illumination. Awareness simply does not have subsistence or illumination through being without an object and without a substrate. And the experience of mere awareness [without object or substrate] is contradicted by non-apprehension. And thus, even the dependence on the connection with the self for the illumination of awareness is simply irresistible — this is the sense. He again raises the objection that awareness would have self-luminosity in the form of luminosity pervading its own existence:
'satyāḥ'
— he resolves:
'satyāḥ'

children.text: iti / tadā cātmasambandhasya niyatapūrvabhāvitvādapekṣitatvācca saṃvitprakāśe hetutvameṣṭavyameveti bhāvaḥ / niruktahetunā svayaṃprakāśatvasādhane doṣaṃ cāha
children.translated_text: — the sense is: in that case too, since the connection with the self is invariably antecedent and is required [for the illumination of awareness], its causality for the illumination of awareness must be accepted. And he states the fault in proving self-luminosity by the stated reason:
'api caivam'
— the sense is: the reason is inconclusive regarding pleasure and the like.
And in that case —

body.translated_text: He raises an objection:

body.text: sarvasyārthasya tadvitteḥ sākṣī sarvatra saṃmataḥ /
body.translated_text: The self — the witness of every object and every cognition of it, acknowledged as such everywhere —

body.text: ātmaivāstu svataḥsiddhaḥ kimanekaistathāvidhaiḥ //20//
body.translated_text: let it alone be self-established. What [need] for many [such entities] of that kind?

body.text: kiñca- yo yasya sākṣī tenaiva tasya siddhirna laukikī /
body.translated_text: Moreover — whoever is the witness of whatever, by that very [witness] the establishment of that [thing] is not mundane (i.e., not through experience).

body.text: arthasyevārthavitterapyātmā sākṣī hi lakṣyate //21//
body.translated_text: Just as of an object, so too of the cognition of the object — the self is observed to be the witness.

body.text: santu nāmārthavittayaḥ svataḥsiddhāḥ,tathāpi na tābhirayamātmā pratyakṣībhavati, tatsākṣitvāt / yatsākṣī khalvayaṃ puruṣaḥ, na tenāsau pratyakṣaḥ, ghaṭasākṣātkārīva ghaṭena / arthasaṃvidāṃ ca sākṣātkārī cetana iti so 'pi na tābhiraparokṣībhavati /
body.translated_text: Let the cognitions of objects be self-established — nevertheless, this self does not become directly perceived by them, because it is their witness. For whatever this person (<s>puruṣa</s>) is the witness of, he is not made directly perceivable by that — just as one who directly perceives a pot [is not made perceivable] by the pot. And the conscious self is the direct perceiver of the cognitions of objects — so it too does not become directly perceived by them.

body.text:
(iti siddhāntinā gurumatakhaṇḍanam)
nanu viṣayasaṃbandhasyevātmasaṃbandhasyāpi saṃvitprakāśe 'stu hetutvam / tāvatā na svayaṃprakāśatvasya hāniḥ / svasajātīyajñānāntarānapekṣaprakāśatvāttatsiddheḥ / ātmanastu na svayaṃprakāśatvameṣṭavyaṃ viṣayasyeva / kintu bāhyārthaprakāśakatveneṣṭasya jñānasyaivā'tmaprakāśakatvamapi kalpanīyaṃ lāghavāditi punaḥ śaṅkate guruḥ

children.translated_text: 'athārthāntare'
— he resolves:
'tathā sati'
('in that case').
'sarvasya'

children.text: ti / nānāsvayaṃprakāśakalpanāyāṃ gaurave sati sarvārthānāṃ sarvajñānānāṃ ca sākṣātkarturātmana eva svaprakāśatvaṃ kalpanīyam / natu jñānānāmityarthaḥ / viṣayāṇāmiva jñānānāmapyātmane prakāśamānatvādātmaikaḥ svaprakāśo bhavatu / anye sarve bhavantu tadadhīnaprakāśā eveti bhāvaḥ //20//
children.translated_text: ('of all'). When there is cumbersomeness in postulating self-luminosity for many [entities], the self-luminosity should be postulated for the self alone — who is the direct perceiver of all objects and all cognitions — not for cognitions. Just as objects, so too cognitions shine forth for the self — so let the self alone be self-luminous. Let all others have their luminosity dependent on it — this is the sense.

body.translated_text:
(Thus the Siddhāntin's refutation of the teacher's [Prābhākara] position.)
[Objection:] Let the connection with the self, just like the connection with the object, be a cause of the illumination of awareness. By that much, there is no detriment to self-luminosity [of awareness], since it is established from the luminosity that is independent of another knowledge of its own class. But the self need not be self-luminous — like an object. Rather, the capacity of knowledge itself — which is accepted as illuminating external objects — to illuminate the self too should be postulated, on grounds of parsimony — the teacher again raises the objection:

body.text: evaṃ saṃvidopyātmāyattaprakāśatvānna mukhyaṃ svaprakāśatvamityuktam / jñānāntarānapekṣaprakāśatvena bhavatu nāma jñānasya tatkathañcit / athāpi na jñānādhīnaprakāśa ātmetyāha-

children.translated_text: 'kiñ ca'
('moreover').
'yaḥ'
'yasya'

children.text: ti / sākṣīdraṣṭā, prakāśakaḥ / siddhiḥ prakāśaḥ / na laukikī-nānubhavasiddhā / lakṣyate-dṛśyate //21//
children.translated_text: — 'witness' — seer, illuminator. 'Establishment' — illumination. 'Not mundane' — not established through experience. 'Is observed' — is seen.

body.translated_text: Thus it has been said that because awareness has its luminosity dependent on the self, it does not have primary self-luminosity. Let knowledge have that [self-luminosity] in some sense, through luminosity independent of another knowledge — nevertheless, the self is not dependent on knowledge for its luminosity — he says:

body.text: ślokaṃ vyākhyāti svayameva

children.translated_text: 'santu nāma'
('let them be') and so forth. The sense is: since the illumination of the self by awareness is untenable in the manner stated, the self-luminosity of the self alone must be accepted.
All entities are such that their self-establishment is independent of homogeneous [entities] and of [entities] whose establishment depends on themselves.
Therefore, the self has self-establishment that is independent [of everything].

children.text: na hi kaścitpadārthaḥ svaprakāśāyāsādhāraṇasajātīyārthāntarāpekṣo dṛṣṭaḥ / na khalu ghaṭaḥ svasiddhaye ghaṭāntaramapekṣate; apekṣate tu vijātīyamālokādi / evamāloko 'pi prakāśamāno nālokāntaramapekṣate; nāpi svāpekṣaprakāśaṃ ghaṭādikamapekṣate; apekṣate tu vijātīyamindriyam / evamindriyamapi nendriyāntaraṃ svāpekṣaprakāśamālokādi ghaṭaṃ vāpekṣate; apekṣate tu vijātīyaṃ saṃvedanam / evaṃ saṃvedanamapi saṃvidantaraṃ svādhīnasiddhikamindriyādikaṃ vā nāpekṣate svasiddhau; apekṣate tu vijātīyaṃ svāśrayabhūtaṃ svatantramātmānam / evamātmāpyātmāntaraṃ svādhīnasiddhi saṃvidindriyādikamapi svāparokṣe nāpekṣata ityananyāpekṣā hyātmasvarūpasiddhiḥ /
children.translated_text: For no entity that shines forth is observed to depend on a homogeneous — extremely homogeneous — entity, or on an entity whose illumination depends on itself, [for its own illumination]. A pot, for instance, does not depend on another pot for its own establishment; but it does depend on a heterogeneous [entity such as] light and the like. Similarly, light too, when shining, does not depend on another light; nor does it depend on a pot and the like whose illumination depends on it; but it does depend on the heterogeneous sense-organ. Similarly, the sense-organ too does not depend on another sense-organ, or on light and the like or a pot whose illumination depends on it; but it does depend on heterogeneous awareness. Similarly, awareness too does not depend on another awareness, or on the sense-organ and the like whose establishment depends on it, for its own establishment; but it does depend on the heterogeneous, independent self that is its substrate. Similarly, the self too, for its own direct perception, does not depend on another self, or on awareness, the senses, and the like whose establishment depends on it — therefore the self-establishment of the self's essential nature is independent [of everything].

children.text:
(iti siddhāntinā'tmanaḥ svaprakāśatvasamarthanam)
saṃvidadhīnaprakāśatve bādhakamuktvā'tmanaḥ svaprakāśatve sādhakamapyāha
children.translated_text:
(Thus the Siddhāntin's justification of the self-luminosity of the self.)
Having stated the defeating consequence of awareness having its luminosity dependent [on the self], he also states the positive evidence for the self-luminosity of the self:
'sajātīya'

children.text: ti / sarve hi prakāśamānāḥ padārthāḥ sajātīyaṃsvātyantasajātīyam, svasādhyaṃ-svādhīnaprakāśaṃ cārthamanapekṣyaiva prakāśamānā iti ātmāpi prakāśamāna ātmāntaraṃ svāpekṣaprakāśaṃ jñānādicānapekṣyaiva prakāśata ityanumantavyam / tathāca svayaṃprakāśatvaṃ tasya phalatīti bhāvaḥ //22//
children.translated_text: ('homogeneous'). All entities that shine forth do so without depending on a homogeneous — extremely homogeneous — entity, or on an entity whose illumination depends on themselves. Therefore, it should be inferred that the self too, when shining forth, shines forth without depending on another self, or on knowledge and the like whose illumination depends on it. And thus its self-luminosity follows — this is the sense.

body.translated_text: He himself explains the verse:

body.text: ślokārthasya prapañcanaṃ

children.translated_text: 'na hi kaścit'

children.text: dityādi / atrāyaṃ niṣkarṣaḥ- svaviṣayakajñānāntarānapekṣaprakāśatvalakṣaṇaṃ svayaṃprakāśatvaṃ jñānātmanoḥ samānam / svetarasakalanirapekṣaprakāśatvalakṣaṇaṃ tu tadātmasvarūpasyaiveti /
children.translated_text: ('for no one') and so forth. Here is the conclusion: the self-luminosity defined as luminosity independent of another knowledge having oneself as its object is common to both knowledge and the self. But [self-luminosity] defined as luminosity independent of everything other than oneself belongs to the essential nature of the self alone.
Here those who know the truth of the self say: consciousness (<s>caitanya</s>) belongs to the self inherently,
because of being a property of its essential nature and limiting adjunct — like luminosity [belongs] to fire.
Apart from being the substrate of consciousness, there is no other essential nature of the self.
For whatever is devoid of consciousness is not the self — like a pot and the like.
And selfhood is not [established] through the power of consciousness (<s>citiśakti</s>), because of the consequence of destruction in liberation.
(If difference [from consciousness] were [established] through cognition (<s>bodha</s>) alone from another [source], the postulation of that power would be purposeless.)

children.text: buddhisukhaduḥkhādiniḥśeṣavaiśeṣikātmaguṇātyantikoparamalakṣaṇo hi mokṣaḥkaṇabhakṣākṣacaraṇamate / na cātyantaluptakāryaṃ vastu tatkāryajananaśaktamityatra kiñcitpramāṇaṃ kramate / dehādiviśiṣṭasaṃbandhitayā dṛśyamānasukhaduḥkhajñānādikāryaṃ viśiṣṭavartinīmevātmotpādaśaktiṃ kalpayati, dhūma ivārdrendhanasaṃbandhini dhūmadhvaje svotpādanasāmarthyam, vrīhyaṅkura iva ca satuṣataṇḍule / api ca bodhe satyevātmano 'nātmavyavacchede saṃbhavati kṛtaṃ tacchaktayāśrayaṇena /
children.translated_text: For liberation in the doctrine of <s>Kaṇabhakṣa</s> (i.e., <s>Kaṇāda</s>) and <s>Akṣacaraṇa</s> (i.e., <s>Gautama</s>) is characterized by the absolute and permanent cessation of all the specific qualities of the self according to <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> — such as cognition, pleasure, pain, and the like. And there is no valid means of knowledge to establish that an entity whose effects have been absolutely destroyed retains the capacity to produce those effects. The effects — pleasure, pain, knowledge, and the like — that are observed as connected with the body and the like as their substrate, postulate a capacity for production in the self that exists in that qualified [connection] — just as smoke [postulates] the capacity for its own production in fire connected with moist fuel, and just as a rice sprout [postulates the same] in a rice grain with its husk. Moreover, when cognition (<s>bodha</s>) exists, the discrimination of the self from the non-self is possible — so what is the use of resorting to that power [of consciousness separately]?

children.text: na caivaṃ sati bodha eva paramātmeti yuktam, tasyā'śrayapratiyogisāpekṣasvarūpatvādātmanaśca tadviparītasvabhāvatvāt; sākṣācca cetayiturahamarthasya sphuraṇāt; anubhavatarkāgamabalena citimata ātmabhāvasyānantarameva prapañcitatvācca / naca citimātrātmavāde 'pi tasyāgantukaviṣayasaṃbandhe bodhatvamadhyāropya boddhṛtvasamarthanaṃ sādhīyaḥ, saṃbandhasyobhayaniṣṭhatayār'thasyāpi boddhṛtvaprasaṅgāt / na ca kāryakāraṇabhāvavadvyavasthitvam, tatra janimato janayituśca parasparāpekṣāniyamalakṣaṇasaṃbandhaḥ / ihāpi sa eveti cenna, apekṣāhetvabhāvāt / kimarthamarthaḥ caitanyamapekṣate, caitanyaṃ vār'tham / siddhyarthamiti cet, kaḥ siddhyarthaḥ? na tāvadutpattiḥ, tasyā nirjñātanimittāntaratvāt / ghaṭādayo hi prasiddhamṛddaṇḍacakrabhramaṇādiparyāptanimittāntara śālino na citimapi nijajanane 'pekṣante / nirastaśca vijñānamātravādaḥ / nityasyātmana utpattyarthamarthāpekṣeti suvyāhṛtam / siddhiḥ prakāśa iti cet; kiṃ bhoḥ ātmā svayañjyotirapyarthādhīnaprakāśaḥ? yadasau tadarthamarthamapekṣate / mahanīyamidamātmaveditvam / prakāśaśca na saṃvidatirekī kaścidarthadharmaḥ saṃbhavatītyāveditam / saṃbhavannapyasau na citisvarūpamātranimittaḥ, sarvadā sarvārthaprakāśaprasaṅgāt / na hi sadā saṃnihitasamagrakāraṇaṃ kāryaṃ kadācidbhavati / āgantukātiśayāśrayaṇe vā nāmānta
children.translated_text: Nor is it proper, this being the case, [to maintain] that consciousness itself is the Supreme Self (<s>Paramātman</s>), because the essential nature of that [consciousness] depends on a substrate (<s>āśraya</s>) and a counter-correlate (<s>pratiyogin</s>), while the self has a nature opposite to that; and because directly, the self-luminous manifestation of the 'I'-meaning — that is, the cognizer — [is evident]; and because, by the force of experience, reasoning, and scripture, the selfhood of consciousness has been elaborated immediately [in what precedes]. Nor is [the following objection] stronger: that even on the doctrine that the self is mere consciousness, one can support the knower-hood [of the self] by superimposing upon it the character of cognition when it has an adventitious connection with objects — because since the relation inheres in both terms, the object too would absurdly become a knower. Nor can one appeal to a fixed arrangement as in the cause-effect relation, for there the relation is characterized by the invariable mutual dependence between what is produced and what produces. If one says the same applies here — no, because there is no basis for the dependence. For what purpose does the object depend on consciousness, or consciousness on the object? If [one says] for the purpose of accomplishment — what kind of accomplishment? Not origination, for that [origination] has its causal conditions already fully determined otherwise. For pots and the like, which possess fully sufficient causal conditions such as the well-known clay, stick, wheel-rotation, and so forth, do not depend upon consciousness even for their own origination. And the doctrine of consciousness-only (<s>vijñānamātravāda</s>) has been refuted. That the eternal self depends on an object for the purpose of origination — how well-spoken indeed! If [one says] accomplishment means illumination — then, sir, is the self, though self-luminous, dependent on objects for its illumination? That it depends on objects for that purpose — what a magnificent doctrine of self-knowledge this is! And it has been demonstrated that illumination (<s>prakāśa</s>) is not some property of the object distinct from consciousness (<s>saṃvid</s>). Even if [such illumination] were possible, it would not be caused solely by the essential nature of consciousness, for then all objects would absurdly be illuminated at all times. For an effect whose complete causal complex is always present does not occur only sometimes. And if one resorts to an adventitious excellence — then by that very [adventitious factor]

body.translated_text: The elaboration of the verse's meaning:

body.text: reṇa jñānamevāṅgīkṛtamiti tadvānevātmā'yātaḥ /
body.translated_text: one has simply accepted [another] cognition, and so the self has come to be precisely that [i.e., possessing cognition as an attribute].

body.text: (iti dharmabhūtajñānasya nityatvasādhanam)

children.text: nanvevamarthasiddhivyavasthāpakatayābhyupagataṃ jñānamāgantukaṃ kriyārūpamiti kathaṃ tadātmasvabhāvaḥ ? / tathāhi-arthāntaragatatve sati janakadravyāntara prati kāryatvādikena rūpeṇāsādhāraṇo gantavyadeśaprāptyādiryaṃ pratyasādhāraṇaḥ tatsamavetāgantukāsādhāraṇagamanādikriyājanyo dṛṣṭaḥ / tādṛśī cārthasiddhiryaṃ puruṣaṃ pratyasādhāraṇī tatsamavetatādṛśakriyājanyeti śakyamanumātum / maivam / akriyājanyenābhāvaprāptakṣetrādisvatvena kṣetriṇaṃ pratyasādhāraṇena kṣetrajavrīhyādisvatvena cānaikāntyāt / naca nirvyāpāratayā kṣetriṇastatrājanakatvam; vyāpārakālādinā vyabhicārāt, tadbhāvabhāvitvasya cāviśeṣāt / tajjīvanameva tatra janakavyāpāra iti cet, nanu tat sasyapālanādisādhāraṇamiti kathamasādhāraṇakriyājanyatvam? api caivaṃ sati tadevārthaprakāśe 'pi janakavyāpāro 'stu; kimakḷptakalpanayā? / satyapi tasminnartho na prakāśata iti cet, svatvaṃ vā kiṃ yathoditaṃ sati jīvane jāyata eva ? / vrīhyādisattāpyapekṣyata iti cet, ihāpīndriyādipratyāsaktiriti samānaścarcaḥ / ato yaṃ pratyasādhāraṇo yathoditadharmaḥ tadīyāsādhāraṇadharmanimitta ityetāvat / sa ceṣyata evātmanaścaitanyaṃ raveriva tejasvitvam /
children.translated_text: Objection: If knowledge, accepted as that which determines the accomplishment of objects, is adventitious and of the nature of an action (<s>kriyā</s>), how can it be the essential nature of the self? For thus — when something exists in another locus, there is an observed [relation wherein] the movement to the destination, which is unique to it, [occurs] through a form such as being an effect with respect to another producing substance, [and] this is produced by an adventitious action such as movement that is unique [to it and] inherent in it. And such accomplishment of an object, which is unique to a particular person, can be inferred to be produced by such an action inherent in him. This should not be so. Because there is deviation (<s>anaikāntya</s>) through [the counter-example of] ownership of a field obtained without any action, and through ownership of rice and the like produced from the field. Nor is there non-productiveness of the field-owner with respect to that [crop] due to his being without activity — because there is deviation through the time of activity and so forth, and because there is no distinction in the [crop's] being determined by the presence of that [owner]. If [one says] the owner's very livelihood is the productive activity there — well, that [livelihood] is common to the maintenance of crops and the like, so how can there be production by a unique action? Moreover, this being so, let that very [livelihood] be the productive activity in the illumination of objects too — why resort to unevidenced speculation? If [one says] even when that is present, the object is not illuminated — well, does ownership as described above necessarily arise when livelihood is present? If [one says] the existence of rice and the like is also required — here too the contact with the sense organs and the like [is required], so the objection is the same. Therefore, this much [is established]: a property that is unique to something is caused by a unique property belonging to it. And this is exactly what is accepted — the consciousness (<s>caitanya</s>) of the self, just as luminosity (<s>tejasitva</s>) belongs to the sun.

children.text: na ca hetubhedānuvidhāyitayā, jānābhyajñāsiṣamityādikālāvacchedapratītergamanāderiva jñānasyāgantukatvamanumeyam; ādityaprakāśenānaikāntyāt / asti hi tatrāpīmaṃ deśamādityaḥ prakāśayati prācīkaśat prakāśayiṣyatīti pratītiḥ / svārasikatve 'pyādityaprakāśasya prakāśyadeśasaṃbandhakādācitkatayā avacchedapratītirupapadyata iti cet; ihāpi tarhīndriyādipratyāsattisamāsāditayogyabhāvo 'nubhāvyabhedaḥ svābhāvikamātmanaścaitanyaguṇamavacchinattīti tadapekṣayaivendriyādyanuvidhānamatītānāgatapratyutpannatvapratyayaprayogau copapadyante /
children.translated_text: Nor should the adventitiousness of knowledge be inferred — as with movement — from the cognition of temporal limitation in [expressions like] 'I knew, I know, I shall know,' on the grounds that [knowledge] follows the diversity of causes; because there is deviation (<s>anaikāntya</s>) through the case of sunlight. For there too the cognition exists: 'The sun illuminates this region, it illuminated [it before], it will illuminate [it].' If [one says] even though the sunlight is intrinsic, the cognition of limitation is explained by the occasionality of its connection with the region to be illuminated — then here too, the differentiation of objects to be experienced, whose fitness is brought about by the contact with sense organs and the like, limits the natural quality of consciousness (<s>caitanya</s>) belonging to the self, and it is in dependence on that [contact] that the conformity with sense organs and the like, and the usage of past, future, and present cognitions, are both explained.

children.text: kathaṃ punaratra nirṇayaḥ, maṇidyumaṇiprakāśāderivaupādhiko 'yaṃ bhedaḥ, na tu gamanapacanāderiva svābhāvika iti ?
children.translated_text: But how is the determination made here that this differentiation is adventitious, like the light of a jewel or a lamp, and not intrinsic, like walking or cooking?

children.text: tādrūpyeṇaiva pratyakṣatvāt / na hi jātucidadrūpo 'yamātmā loṣṭādivaddaṣṭacaraḥ / yaśca yadguṇatayaiva sākṣādbhavati, sa tatsvabhāvaḥ,
children.translated_text: Because [the self] is perceived precisely in that form [i.e., as conscious]. For never is this self seen to operate as devoid of consciousness, like a clod of earth. And whatever is directly perceived as having a certain quality, that is of that nature,

body.translated_text: (Thus the establishment of the eternality of <s>dharmabhūtajñāna</s> [attributive knowledge].)

body.text: marudiva sparśaguṇatayaivādhyakṣyamāṇaḥ / yo yatsvabhāvo na bhavati, na tadviraheṇāpi svarūpata upalabhyate, gamanādirahitatayeva devadattādiḥ /
body.translated_text: just as wind (<s>marut</s>) is perceived as having the quality of touch. What is not of a certain nature is not apprehended in its own form even in the absence of that [quality], just as <s>Devadatta</s> and the like are [apprehended] precisely as devoid of movement and the like.

body.text: śarīravaditi cenna, asiddhatvāt / syādetat-yathaiva khlvasvabhāvabhūtenāpi śarīreṇa sadhrīcīna evāyaṃ cetanaścakāsti, tathā caitanyenāpīti / tannaivam, asiddhatvāt / na hi tanuviśiṣṭatayaivāyaṃ cetanaḥ parisphurati / yogināṃ praṇihitamanasāmuparatabahirindriyāṇāṃ ca dehānusandhānaviraheṇāpi ahamiti sphuṭamanubhavāt / jānāmīti pratyayaḥ śarīravarṇasanniveśanirbhāsaśūnyatayā tattvāntaragocara iti ca prāgevāvocam / karmānuguṇyena suramanujādijātīyatayā bhidyamānāsvāgamāpāyinīṣu tanuṣu manasa ivaikasya varṣmaṇaḥ svabhāvānubandhitvenāśrayitumaśakyatvāt / liṅgasya punaranuvṛttāvapi apratyakṣatvānna vyabhicāritvam /
body.translated_text: If [one says] 'like the body' — no, because that is not established. One might suggest: just as this conscious being always shines together with the body, which is not of its essential nature, so too with consciousness. That is not so, because it is not established. For this conscious being does not manifest as qualified by the body alone. For <s>yogins</s> with concentrated minds and those whose external senses have ceased [functioning], even without any apprehension of the body, there is the clear experience 'I.' And I have already stated that the cognition 'I know' is directed at a different reality, being devoid of any appearance of the body's color and configuration. Because the body, which changes according to the classes of gods, humans, and the like in accordance with <s>karma</s>, and which comes and goes — one's stature cannot be accepted as invariably connected to one's essential nature, like the mind [which also changes bodies]. And even though the subtle body (<s>liṅga</s>) persists [across lives], since it is not perceptible, there is no deviation [in the argument].

body.text: (iti jñānasyātmasvabhāvatvapratiṣṭhāpanam)

children.text: bodhasvābhāvye puṃsaḥ svāpamūrcchayoḥ prakāśaprasaṅga iti cenna, vikalpāsahatvāt / tathāhi-prakāśa iti padārthamātrasādhāraṇaṃ bodhajanyaṃ prakaṭatādipadaparyāyaṃ dharmamabhipretya vāyaṃ prasaṅgaḥ, atha bodhameva, tadaviprakarṣaṃ vā ? / ādye tadabhāvādeva na prasaṅgaḥ / abhāvaśca prakaṭita eva saṃvitsvatassiddhisamarthanasamaye / bhāve 'pi tamaḥpratibandhādapyanudayaḥ saṃbhavī / itarayorabhimatamevāpāditamityadoṣodbhāvanam / bodhasvābhāvye hi puruṣasya svāpādidaśāsu ca tathābhāvo 'bhimata eveti na hi tadāpādanaṃ doṣāya /
children.translated_text: If [one objects] that when a person's essential nature is consciousness, there would be the absurd consequence of illumination in sleep and unconsciousness (<s>mūrcchā</s>) — no, because [the objection] cannot withstand analysis. For thus — is this objection raised with reference to illumination as the property common to all objects, produced by cognition, synonymous with 'manifestation' and the like? Or with reference to cognition itself, or its non-remoteness? In the first case, there is no absurd consequence, precisely because of the absence of that [object-illumination]. And that absence has been made evident at the time of establishing the self-establishment of consciousness (<s>saṃvid</s>). Even if it were present, non-arising due to the obstruction of <s>tamas</s> (darkness) is possible. In the other two cases, what is charged as a fault is actually what is accepted — so there is no fault to be adduced. For when a person's essential nature is consciousness, the similar state [of consciousness] in the conditions of sleep and the like is indeed what is accepted — hence pointing that out is no fault.

children.text: atha matam-svāpādāvapi svānubhavasadbhāve jāgara iva vyavahāraprasaṅga iti; maivam, vyavahārāgocaratvāt / kaḥ khalvātmani vyavahāraḥ? na hyasāvādātuṃ hātumupekṣituṃ vā śakyaḥ / vyāhāraḥ prasajyata iti cet, kimaṅga! nirvikalpakabālamūkādivedanaviṣayo vyavahniyata eva? karaṇapāṭavavyavajihīrṣādisahakārivirahāttatra vyāhārānudaya iti cet, samāno 'yaṃ vidhiritaratrāpīti niranuyojyānuyogaḥ /
children.translated_text: Now if [one thinks] that even in sleep and the like, if self-experience exists, there would be the absurd consequence of worldly activity as in the waking state — this is not so, because [self-experience in sleep] does not fall within the scope of worldly activity. What worldly activity pertains to the self? For it cannot be seized, abandoned, or ignored. If [one says] verbal expression would follow — why, is the content of non-conceptual awareness of infants, mutes, and the like ever verbally expressed? If [one says] that verbal expression does not arise there due to the absence of cooperating factors such as proficiency of the instruments [of speech], desire to express, and the like — the same principle applies in the other case too [i.e., in sleep], so this is a groundless objection.

children.text: smṛtiprasaṅga iti cenna, avṛttitvāt /yadyucyeta-mūrcchādāvātmānubhavābhyupagamer'thāntarānubhava ivaivamahamanvabhūvamiti parastāt smṛtiḥ prasajyata iti; tanna, avṛtittvāt / na hi mūrcchā prasvāpo vā buddhivṛttiviśeṣo darśanasparśanādivat, yena
children.translated_text: If [one objects] there would be the absurd consequence of memory [of the sleep state] — no, because [sleep] is not a mental modification (<s>vṛtti</s>). If it were said that since one accepts self-experience in unconsciousness and the like, a subsequent memory 'I experienced thus' would follow, as in the case of experiencing other objects — that is not so, because [sleep] is not a [mental] modification. For neither unconsciousness nor deep sleep is a specific modification of the intellect, like seeing or touching, such that

body.translated_text: (Thus the establishment that knowledge is the essential nature of the self.)

body.text: smṛtibījaṃ saṃskāramādadhīyātām / kintūdbhūtena tamasoparatavyāpāreṣu karaṇeṣu nirvṛttikasāṃsiddhikabodhasvarūpeṇāvasthānamātramātmanaḥ / na ca bodhasvabhāvatvādevāsya saṃskārādhāyakatvam, anavaratopacīyamānasaṃskāratayānirmokṣaprasaṅgāt / anubhave ca svānurūpasaṃskārādhānaniruddhe sadṛśasaṃbandhidarśanādisamudbodhitanijabījānusāreṇa smaraṇamupajāyate / na cehātmasvarūpabodhasya jātucinnirodho janma vā; nityātmasattāprayuktatvāt / nimittāntarābhāvaścānantarameva vyākariṣyate? /tadevamanuvartamāna evānubhave kathaṃ smṛtirudayamāsādayet ? / ya evāhaṃ pūrvedyurāsaṃ sa evāhamadyāpīti smṛtisaṃbhinnapratyayo 'pi kālāvacchinnasvarūpagocaraḥ, na svarūpamātre / aviśadaśca svāpādau svānubhavo nirvikalpakaśca / paṭīyasā savikalpakenāvagamena smṛtibījamādhīyata iti ca kutastatprasaṅgaḥ / sāmyāccānanubhavābhimānaḥ śarīrataddhāraṇaprayatnānanusaṃdhānavat /
body.translated_text: they could deposit an impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) as a seed of memory. Rather, it is merely the self's abiding in its natural, innate, activity-free consciousness-nature, when <s>tamas</s> has arisen and the instruments [of cognition] have ceased their operations. Nor does [the self's consciousness] deposit impressions merely because of being of the nature of consciousness — for then, with impressions being accumulated without interruption, there would be the absurd consequence of never attaining liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>). And when, upon the cessation of experience depositing impressions in accordance with itself, remembrance arises following its own seed, awakened by the perception of something similar and related — in such a case, there is never any cessation or origination of the self's essential consciousness, because it is occasioned by the eternal existence of the self. And the absence of any other cause will be explained immediately hereafter. Thus, when experience continues uninterruptedly, how could memory arise [from it]? Even the cognition mixed with memory, 'The very same I who existed yesterday exist today too,' has as its object the self delimited by time, not the bare essential nature. And the self-experience in sleep and the like is indistinct and non-conceptual. Since the seed of memory is deposited by a more vivid conceptual cognition — how could there be such an absurd consequence? And due to similarity [between the states], there is the assumption of non-experience [during sleep], just as there is non-recollection of the effort to sustain the body and support it.

body.text: na cāvikṛtasvābhāvikabodhamātreṇāvasthāne svāpamokṣayoraviśeṣāpattiḥ; kleśavāsanānāṃ guṇābhibhavasya caikatra bhāvāt, itaratra tadatyantanivṛtteḥ / asaṃprajñātasamādhāvapi paramavairāgyaśālinā paṭutaranirodhasaṃskāreṇa caritādhikāriṇā apavargiṇā viśeṣaḥ /
body.translated_text: Nor is there the fallacy of no distinction between sleep and liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>) when [the self] abides merely in its unmodified, natural consciousness; for afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>) and their latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>), as well as the suppression by the <s>guṇas</s>, are present in one case, while in the other there is their complete and final cessation. Even in the <s>asaṃprajñāta</s> (objectless) <s>samādhi</s>, the distinction [from sleep] is maintained by one who possesses supreme dispassion (<s>vairāgya</s>), whose more potent impression of cessation (<s>nirodhasaṃskāra</s>) has fulfilled its function, and who is destined for final liberation (<s>apavarga</s>).

body.text: (iti jñānanityatve prasaktākṣepāṇāṃ pariharaṇam)

children.text: kathaṃ punarnidrāyā avṛttitve prabuddhasya pratyavamarśāḥ sukhamahamasvāpsamityādyāḥ? na hyananubhūtagocarāḥ smṛtayaḥ saṃbhavanti / sattvasacivasamullasitatamoguṇānubhavabhāvitabhāvanāyoniḥ khalu sukhamahamasvāpsaṃ, prasannaṃ me manaḥ, laghūni me gātrāṇīti pratyavamarśaḥ; rajastamassamudreke tu duḥkhamahamasvāpsaṃ, bhramatyanavasthitaṃ me cittamiti; sattvarajasī tvabhibhūya nitāntamudbhūte tamasi gāḍhamūḍhaṃ supto 'smi, gurūṇi me gātrāṇi, muṣitamiva manaḥ, mīlitamiva iti / satyamevam / dattottaraṃ hyetat / naivāmī vāsanāyonayaḥ pratyayāḥ / api tu tātkālikaśarīrendriyāmanovasthāviśeṣaparyālocananimittā
children.translated_text: But how, if sleep is not a [mental] modification, can the awakened person have reflective cognitions such as 'I slept happily' and the like? For memories without prior experience are impossible. The reflective cognition 'I slept happily, my mind is clear, my limbs are light' arises from a latent impression produced by the experience of the <s>tamas</s> <s>guṇa</s> that has manifested accompanied by <s>sattva</s>; while when <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s> predominate, [the reflection is] 'I slept unhappily, my mind wanders and is unstable'; and when <s>tamas</s> has arisen overwhelmingly, overpowering <s>sattva</s> and <s>rajas</s>, [the reflection is] 'I slept in deep stupor, my limbs are heavy, my mind is as if robbed, my [eyes are] as if closed.' True, this is so. But this objection has already been answered. These cognitions are not born from latent impressions. Rather, they are inferential,

children.text: ānumānikā iti / evaṃrūpā hīme-yataḥ prasannaṃ me manaḥ, samyagāhārapariṇāmavaśāllaghūni cāṅgāni, ataḥ sukhamahamasvāpsamiti / svāpāvasthāyāṃ vā
children.translated_text: arising from the examination of the particular condition of the body, sense organs, and mind at that time. For these are of such a form — 'Because my mind is clear and my limbs are light due to the proper assimilation of food, therefore I slept happily.' Or in the sleep state,

body.translated_text: (Thus the resolution of objections raised against the eternality of knowledge.)

children.text: indriyoparamatāratamyavaśādaviśadatātkālikatattadanukūlapratikūlaviṣayānusandhānanibandhanatayāpi smaraṇamupapadyata iti na vṛttyantaratvaṃ nidrāyāḥ / kathaṃ tarhi pāramarṣaṃ sūtram "abhāvapratyayālambanā vṛttirnidrā
children.translated_text: memory is also explained by its being grounded in the apprehension of favorable and unfavorable objects at that time, indistinct [though they are], in accordance with the varying degrees of cessation of the sense organs — so sleep is not another kind of [mental] modification. Then how [does one explain] the aphoristic <s>sūtra</s>, 'Sleep is the modification based on the cognitive content of absence' —

children.text: " iti / nirodhaparatvātprakaraṇasya na vṛttisvarūpe tātparyaṃ viparyayavat / nahyatadrūpapratiṣṭhaṃ mithyājñānaṃ kiñcidasti, sarvasaṃvidāmarthāvyabhicārāt / sa cādhikaraṇasiddhaḥ / sādhayiṣyate copariṣṭāt / kaivalyabhāgi yaccit tatpratyanīkatayā nidrādernirodhyatvenopadeśaḥ /
children.translated_text: ? Because the context pertains to cessation (<s>nirodha</s>), the purport is not about the essential nature of a [mental] modification, just as with erroneous cognition (<s>viparyaya</s>). For there is no erroneous cognition that is not grounded in a real [object], since all cognitions (<s>saṃvid</s>) are invariably [directed at] objects. And that [point] is established by the [present] topic. And it will be further established below. The instruction that sleep and the like are to be suppressed is given because they are opposed to that consciousness which tends toward <s>kaivalya</s> (isolation/liberation).

body.text: (iti nidrāyā vṛttirūpatvaniṣedhanam)

children.text: astu vā pūrvoktapramāṇādivṛttyabhāvakāraṇabhūtapracitatamatamoguṇāvalambanā vṛttireva nidrā; santu ca prabuddhapratyavamarśāśca smaraṇāni; tathā satya(pya) navaratānuvṛttabodhatayā sthitameva puṃso bodhasvabhāvatvam /
children.translated_text: Or let sleep indeed be a [mental] modification, based on the accumulated <s>tamas</s> <s>guṇa</s> that causes the absence of the previously mentioned valid cognition and other modifications; and let the reflective cognitions of the awakened person also be memories. Even so, the consciousness-nature of the person remains established, by virtue of consciousness continuing uninterruptedly [through sleep].

children.text: āha-bodhakāraṇānuvṛttyāpi bodhānuvṛttirupapadyata iti kathaṃ tathāsvābhāvyaniścayaḥ? ittham -
children.translated_text: He [the opponent] says: Even through the continuity of the cause of consciousness, the continuity of consciousness is explained — so how is the determination that it is [the self's] essential nature? Thus —

children.text: evaṃ viṣayaprakāśakādācitkatvenātmano dharmabhūtaṃ jñānamāgantukameva / ātmasvarūpaprakāśo 'pi na sarvadā, kintu viṣayajñānakāla eva jñānataḥ, na svataḥ iti pratyavasthānaprasaṅge jñānasya nityatvaṃ tāvadvyavasthāpayati

riti / ātmasvarūpaprayuktaṃ jñānam / taccātmano nityatvānnityameva / ātmasvarūpanirūpakadharmatvācca jñānasya na jñānarahitamātmanaḥ svarūpaṃ vyavatiṣṭeta prakāśarahitamiva tejaḥ / ato muktāvapi jñānavattvamupeyam, jñānaśūnyasyānātmatvāditi ślokadvayārthaḥ / nanu jñānābhāve 'pi jñānaśaktimadātmasvarūpaṃ muktikāla ityatrāha

ti / luptamuttarārdhamasya / tatsthāne 'smadīyaṃ pūraṇaṃ ( ) etaccihnāntarniveśitam / nityasya svarūpayogyatve phalāvaśyaṃbhāvaniyamājjñānaśaktimattve muktasya kadācijjñānamudiyāt / muktau kadāpi jñānasyānudayāttacchaktirapi tadā naṣṭaiveti ātmanāśa eva pratijñāto bhavet / svarūpanirūpakadharmanivṛttau svarūpanivṛtteravaśyambhāvādityarthaḥ / nanu jñānasya jñānaśaktervā nātmasvarūpanirūpakatvam / kintu āgantukamapi tadātmana eveṣyate dharmabhūtaṃ na ghaṭāderityātmanātmavyavasthopapadyata iti cet; maivam jñānasyātmasvarūpanirūpakadharmatāyāḥ sthāpayiṣyamāṇatvāt, jaḍātmavādasya trayyantaviruddhatvena sadbhiranādaraṇīyatvācceti hārdam //24//25//26//

body.translated_text: (Thus the denial that sleep is of the nature of a [mental] modification.)

body.text: citiśaktye tyādi vivṛṇoti

children.text:
ti / luptārdhavivaraṇaṃ syādidam /
nanu nityatve jñānasyā'tmatvamapīṣyatāṃ tasyaiveti śaṅkāmanūdya pariharati
ti / viṣayāśrayasāpekṣasya jñānasya tadanapekṣasvatantrātmasvarūpatvamayuktamityarthaḥ / kiñca, kalpanāyāmeva lāghavagauravacarcāvasaraḥ / natu sphuṭapratipanne boddhrātmanītyāha
ti / ahaṃ jānāmīti jñātrātmapratyakṣasya bhramatvamiti cettatrāha

ti / anantarameva-avyavahitapūrvameva / jñāturātmatvasamarthana iti yāvat / satpramāṇatarkānugrahāt jñātrātmapratyakṣasyābhrāntitvameva saṃmantavyamitibhāvaḥ / nanu caitanyamevā'tmā / viṣayasaṃbandha eva tasya bodho nāma / ato boddhṛtvapratipattirātmana upapadyata iti śaṅkate
ti / viṣayacaitanyasaṃbandhasya bodhatvābhimatasya saṃyogarūpatve tasya dviṣṭhatvādviṣayasyāpi boddhṛtvaprasaṅga ityāha

ti / yathā kāryakāraṇabhāvasya hetuhetumadubhayanirūpyatve 'pi hetuhetumatorvyavasthā idamasya kāraṇam, idaṃ tvasya kāryamiti, evaṃ cidviṣayasaṃbandhasya viṣayaviṣayinirūpyatve 'pi boddhṛbodhyavyavasthā ghaṭata iti śaṅkiturāśayaḥ / pariharati

ti / yadyapi kāryasya kāraṇasya ca saṃbandhaḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvaḥ kathyate / paraṃ tu kāryatvaṃ kāraṇanirūpitaṃ kāryaniṣṭhaṃ svapūrvavartikāraṇāpekṣatvalakṣaṇaṃ svaprākkālāvacchedena kāryavyāpakakāraṇakatvaparyasāyi, kāraṇatvaṃ ca kāryanirūpitaṃ kāraṇaniṣṭhaṃ svottarabhāvikāryāpekṣatvalakṣaṇaṃ kāryaniyataprākkālavartitvaparyavasāyi bhinnabhinnameva tatra praviṣṭam / atra tu eka evobhayasamavetaḥ saṃyoga iti vyavasthādurghaṭetyarthaḥ / yadyapi saṃyogasyobhayaniṣṭhatve 'pi anuyogitāsaṃbandhena tasya cinniṣṭhatvāccita eva boddhṛtvam, tatpratiyoginastu viṣayasya bodhyatvamiti vyavasthā ghaṭeta, athāpi na cinmātratvamātmanaḥ, kintu cityāśrayatvamapi śrautatvādupeyameveti dhyeyam / ciccetyayorapi parasparāpekṣāniyamalakṣaṇā eva saṃbandho 'stviti śaṅkate
ti / apekṣāyā hetuḥ prayojanarūpor'tho nāstītyarthaḥ / tasyaiva vivaraṇaṃ
mityādi / nanvarthānāṃ vāsanādoṣāccaitanya eva kalpitatvādadhiṣṭhānatayā cito 'pekṣā syādevetyatrā'ha

ti / evamarthasyotpattau cidapekṣāṃ pratikṣipya cita
utpattāvarthāpekṣāṃ pratikṣipati
ti / nityacaitanyasyārthāpekṣotpattivacanaṃ vyāhatataramiti bhāvaḥ / tatprakāśasyārthāpekṣāṃ nirasyati
iti / mahanīya mityādi sopālambham / anātmavettṛtvamevaivaṃ vaktuḥ phalati / arthānāṃ bhāsakasyātmajyotiṣaḥ svayaṃprākāśatvāditi bhāvaḥ / nanvastu prakāśer'thānāṃ cidapekṣā / tatrāha
ti / saṃvideva prakāśaḥ / tadarthaṃ saṃvidapekṣā cedātmāśraya iti bhāvaḥ / saṃvidatiruktaprakāśapakṣe 'pyāha
iti / caitanyamātrāpekṣatver'thaprakāśasya nityatvaprasaṅga ityarthaḥ / āgantukadharmavaccidapekṣatve ca tasya jñātrātmasiddhirapratyahetyāha

ti / āgantukātiśayaśca svadharmabhūtajñānavikāsarūpa eva / tadviśiṣṭaṃ jñānaṃ bodhaḥ / tadāśraya ātmeti na bodhamātramātmeti sāmpratamiti bhāvaḥ /
nanvevamātmano bodhasvarūpatvavadbodhasvabhāvatvamapi na saṃbhavati anityasya bodhasya nityātmasvabhāvatvāyogāt / arthiprakāśakādācitkatvāya bodhakādācitkatāyā eva mantavyatvāditi śaṅkate
iti / jñānasya kriyātvamāgantukatvaṃ ca sādhayituṃ sāmānyavyāptiṃ śikṣayati

ti / arthāntaraṃ-grāmādi / janakadravyāntaraṃ-gantā / gantavyadeśaprāptirgrāmapuruṣasaṃyogaḥ / ubhayaniṣṭho 'pyayaṃ puruṣapravṛttimūlatvena puruṣāsādhāraṇaḥ puruṣaniṣṭhāgantukagamanakriyājanyo dṛṣṭa ityarthaḥ / tādadhīnyādinā tadasādhāraṇārthāntaraniṣṭhadharmatvavyāpakaṃ tanniṣṭhāgantukakriyājanyatvamiti phalitam / udāharaṇamuktvopanayanigamane pradarśayati
ti / pratijñāhetū arthasiddhau / avayavatrayaprayogo vā yatheccham / jñeyaniṣṭhaśca prakāśastattatpuruṣāsādhāraṇaḥ tattatpuruṣīyāgantukajñānakriyājanyaḥ siṣādhayiṣito 'tra / vyāptimeva dūṣayati

ti / kulaparamparayā prāpte kṣetrādau janmata eva svatvaṃ yasya bhāgino 'nyasyābhāvāt, bhāve vā dāyataḥ; tatra tadasādhāraṇer'thāntarakṣetrādisvatve tanniṣṭhakriyājanyatvaṃ nāstīti vyabhicāra ityarthaḥ / abhāvaprāptetyatra bhāvaprāpteti svabhāvaprāpteti vānyathā vā pāṭhaḥ saṃbhāvyate / anyakriyayā daivena vā svakṣetre patitānāṃ bījānāṃ prarūḍhānāṃ svatve svāsādhāraṇe svīyāgantukakriyājanyatvaṃ nāstīti vyabhicāramapi pradarśayati

ti / yathā nirvyāpārasyāpi vyāpārāderanvayavyatirekābhyāṃ kāraṇatvam, tathā kṣetriṇaḥ sattva eva tannirūpitaṃ kṣetrādisvatvaṃ sidhyatīti tatra tata eva nirvyāpārasyāpi kṣetriṇo janakatvaṃ setsyatīti bhāvaḥ / nanu kṣetriṇo na nirvyāpāratvam, kintu jīvanameva vyāpāra iti śaṅkate

diti / kṣetriṇo jīvanaṃ hi sasyarakṣaṇādisādhāraṇakāraṇam / na tu kṣetrādisvatve 'sādhāraṇakāraṇam / tathā
cāsādhāraṇā- gantukakriyājanyatvānumāne 'naikāntyameveti bhāvaḥ / nanu tadvyāpārajanyatvameva sādhyate / na tvasādhāraṇakriyājanyatvam / nāto vyabhicāra iti cettarhyarthāntaramityāha

ti / indriyārthasannikarṣādisahakārisampattau boddhurjīvanamevārthaprakāśe janakamastviti bhāvaḥ / jīvanasyāpyuttarottarakālasattālakṣaṇasya na kriyārūpatvamiti na tadvyāpārajanyatvamapi sādhyam / kintu tadasādhāraṇadharmajanyatvamevetyupasaṃharati
iti / astvevam / tāvatā bhavato lābhaḥ kaḥ? / tatrāha

ti / asmadaniṣṭaṃ sādhayituṃ pravṛttasya bhavator'thāntareṇa nigrahaṇamevāsmākaṃ lābha iti bhāvaḥ/ svabhāvaprāptakṣetrādisvatve vyabhicārādevāgantukadharmajanyatvamapi na sādhayituṃ śakyata iti cānusandheyam /
evamarthaprakāśakādācitkatvena jñānāgantukatvasādhanaṃ dūṣitam / prakārāntareṇa ca tatsādhanaṃ dūṣayitumanuvadati

ti / jñānamāgantukaṃ kālāvacchinnatayā pratīteḥ, gamanādivat, jñānamindriyārthasannikarṣādijanyaṃ tadbhāvābhāvānuvidhāyibhāvābhāvatvāt indhanādijanyapākādivaditi prayogadvayamatra garbhitam / vyabhicāreṇaiva dūṣayati
ti / svābhāvikasyāpyādityaprakāśasya tattatprakāśyadeśasaṃbandhasya kālatrayaparicchinnatayā tadviśiṣṭaviṣayiṇī kālaparicchinnatvapratītiḥ na prakāśasvarūpasya kādācitkatvasādhiketi śaṅkate
viśiṣṭe vidhiniṣedhau viśeṣaṇamupasaṅkāmataḥ sati viśeṣye bādhe

iti nyāyena viśiṣṭe kālāvacchedapratītirviśeṣaṇe paryavasyati / anityatvānumānaṃ ca viśiṣṭaviṣayam, natu svarūpamātraviṣayam / tathā ca yadrūpāvacchinnasya kālāvacchedapratītiḥ tasyānityatvameva svarūpamātrasya ca na kālāvacchedapratītiriti na vyabhicāra iti bhāvaḥ / svarūpamātrasya kālāvacchedapratītiḥ pakṣe 'pyasiddheti pariharati
ti / yogyabhāvaḥ-prakāśayogyatā / avacchinattikālāvacchinnatvaṃ yathā bhavettathā svasaṃbandhena viśinaṣṭi caitanyamityarthaḥ / hetuviśeṣānuvidhānasyāpyanyathāsiddhimāha

ti / arthasaṃbandhāpekṣayaivetyarthaḥ / tathā ca prathamānumānasyāprayojakatvamiti hārdam /
kālāvacchedāderaupādhikatvaṃ svābhāvikatvaṃ tatra tatra dṛṣṭam / jñāne tasyaupādhikatvaniścaya ekāntataḥ kuta iti punaḥ śaṅkate
children.translated_text:
— with reference to the connection of meaning alone — this is the sense. And thus the first inference is ineffective — this is the essential point.
The adventitious nature (<s>aupādhikatva</s>) of time-delimitation and the like has been observed to be natural in various cases. He raises a further objection as to how there can be certainty that it is adventitious in the case of knowledge:
'How then'

and so forth. 'This distinction is adventitious' — the distinction of past, future, and so on in knowledge is adventitious, being dependent on the limiting adjunct (<s>upādhi</s>) of connection with objects.
'By that very nature'

children.text: ti / jñānasya nityātmasvabhāvatvānnityatvamiti tatkālāvacchedapratīteraupādhikatvaṃ suniśceyamiti bhāvaḥ / jñānavattvenaiva sākṣātkriyamāṇatvādātmā jñānasvābhāva ityarthaḥ / sākṣātkāro vṛttiviśeṣaḥ / sa cātmano jñānavattvenaiveti yāvat / tenātmanaḥ svarūpata eva prakāśamānasya svāpe jñānavattvenāprakāśe 'pi na kṣatiḥ /na caivamapi ahaṃ sukhī, ahaṃ duḥkhī, ahamicchāmi, ahaṃ dviṣyāmītyātmanaḥ sākṣātkāre jñānavattvenāprakāśādasiddhatvaṃ hetoriti vācyam; tatrāpyahamiti anukūlapratikūlaviṣayakajñānavattvasyollekhāt; sukhāderapi jñānāvasthāviśeṣatvācca / icchādipratyakṣakāle jñānasya svayaṃprakāśatvādicchādyanubhavavattvenāpyātmano bhānācca jñānavattvenaivātmana upalambhaḥ setsyatīti cānusandheyam / yadyapi jñānasyātmasvabhāvatvādau śrutireva jāgarti / athāpi yuktipradhānatvātprakaraṇasyāsya yuktirevātra nidarśitā / śāstraṃ cāgre pradarśayiṣyate /
children.translated_text:
and so forth. Since knowledge is eternal by being the essential nature of the eternal self, its eternality is certain; hence the adventitious nature of the apprehension of time-delimitation is well-established — this is the purport. The meaning is: the self is of the essential nature of knowledge, because it is directly apprehended precisely as possessing knowledge. Direct apprehension (<s>sākṣātkāra</s>) is a specific modification of cognition (<s>vṛtti</s>). And that [apprehension] of the self occurs precisely through its possessing knowledge — this much [is meant]. Therefore, for the self that inherently shines forth through its own nature, even the non-manifestation as possessing knowledge in deep sleep causes no harm.
Nor should it be said that in the direct apprehension of the self as 'I am happy,' 'I am suffering,' 'I desire,' 'I hate,' the reason is unestablished due to non-manifestation as possessing knowledge; for even there, the 'I' involves a reference to the possession of knowledge pertaining to favorable and unfavorable objects; and because pleasure and the like are also specific states of knowledge. Since at the time of perceiving desire and the like, knowledge is self-luminous, and since the self also shines as possessing the experience of desire and the like, the apprehension of the self is precisely through its possessing knowledge — this too should be considered. Although scripture itself is vigilant regarding the essential nature of knowledge belonging to the self, nevertheless, since this section is predominantly concerned with reasoning, only reasoning has been presented here. Scripture will be shown later.
'For not'

children.text:
ti / acidrūpaḥ-caitanyānāśrayaḥ / śiṣṭaṃ spaṣṭam /
atra śaṅkate
children.translated_text:
and so forth. '<s>Acidrūpa</s>' (of non-conscious nature) — not being a locus of consciousness. The rest is clear.
He raises an objection here:
'Like the body'

children.text: ti / tadvattayaivopalabhyamānatvaṃ na tatsvabhāvakatvavyāpyam / śarīravattayaivopalabhyamānasyāpyātmanaḥ śarīrasvabhāvakatvābhāvādityarthaḥ / pariharati
children.translated_text: and so forth. The meaning is: being apprehended only as possessing that [body] does not entail being of the nature of that [body], for the self, though apprehended only as possessing a body, is not of the nature of the body. He resolves [the objection]:
'Because of being unestablished'

children.text: diti / śaṅkāgranthasya vivaraṇam syādeta dityādi / sadhrīcīna eva-sahita eva / parihāragranthasya vivaraṇam
children.translated_text: and so forth. The explanation of the objection-passage is 'Would it be the case' and so forth. '<s>Sadhrīcīna</s>' means 'combined, together with.' The explanation of the resolution-passage is
'That is not so'

children.text: mityādi / śarīravattayaivopalambha ātmano 'siddhaḥ / yogadaśāyāmavadhānadaśāyāṃ mānasānubhavadaśāyāmapi śarīraṃvinaivātmano bhānāt / tathāca na vyabhicāra iti bhāvaḥ / yogipratyakṣe ātmacintane ca dehaṃ vinā'tmabhānamuktvā laukikapratyakṣe 'pi tadāha
children.translated_text: and so forth. The apprehension of the self only as possessing a body is unestablished. Because the self shines without the body in the state of <s>yoga</s>, in the state of focused attention, and even in the state of mental experience — this is the purport. And thus there is no deviation [of the reason] — this is the intent. Having mentioned the manifestation of the self without the body in yogic perception and self-contemplation, he states [this] also regarding ordinary perception:
'I know'
and so forth. He strengthens the thesis that the body is not of the essential nature of the self:
'The instrument'

children.text: ti / tattanmanuṣyādiśarīraviśeṣavattayaivopalambhaścātmano 'siddha iti ca hārdam / manasa iveti vaidharmyadṛṣṭāntaḥ / mano yathānuvartate na tathā śarīramekamiti yāvat / muktāvasthāyāmapi mano 'nuvṛttyāśayenedam / nanu sthūlaśarīrasya nivṛttāvapi sūkṣmaśarīrasya sarvadānuvṛttirvartate / tasya ca nātmasvabhāvatvamiti tatra vyabhicāra iti mandāśaṅkāmapanudati
children.translated_text: and so forth. The essential point is that the apprehension of the self as possessing specifically such-and-such a human or other body is also unestablished. 'Like the mind' is the dissimilarity-example (<s>vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta</s>). The meaning is: the body does not follow [the self] in the way the mind does. This is said with the intention that the mind continues even in the state of liberation. Now, even upon the cessation of the gross body, the subtle body (<s>sūkṣmaśarīra</s>) always continues. And since that is not of the nature of the self, there is deviation [of the reason] in that case — he dispels even this mild objection:
'Of the <s>liṅga</s> [body]'

children.text:
ti / apinānuvṛttireva nāsti pralaye mokṣe ceti vyajyate / liṅgaśarīrasyātīndriyatvāddhetvabhāvānna vyabhicāra iti ca bhāvaḥ /
atredaṃ bodhyam-ātmadharmabhūtajñānasvarūpaṃ tāvannityameva / kintu saṅkhocavikāsaśālinastasya indriyādidvārakaprasaraṇādarthaprakāśakatvamiti
punararthaprakāśakatvaviśiṣṭasyānityatvamiṣyate / ato viśiṣṭaviśeṣeṇānityatvaṃ svarūpato nityatvaṃ ca vyavasthāpitaṃ tasyātreti /
atha nityatve jñānasya caturdhā'kṣepamupakṣipya pratikṣipati
children.translated_text:
and so forth. The word 'also' (<s>api</s>) suggests that [the subtle body] does not continue at all in dissolution (<s>pralaya</s>) and liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>). And since the subtle body (<s>liṅgaśarīra</s>) is beyond the senses, there is no deviation due to the absence of the reason — this too is the purport.
Here the following should be understood: the essential nature of the <s>dharmabhūtajñāna</s> (attributive knowledge) of the self is indeed eternal. However, since it undergoes contraction and expansion, its capacity to illuminate objects arises through the channels of the senses and the like;
furthermore, the non-eternality of [knowledge] as qualified by the capacity to illuminate objects is accepted. Thus, non-eternality with respect to the qualified particular and eternality with respect to the essential nature have been established — such is [the position] here.
Now, he presents and refutes a fourfold objection against the eternality of knowledge:
'The essential nature of cognition'

children.text: ityādinā / jñānasvabhāvatve puṃsaḥ svāpamūrcchayoḥ svarūpaprakāśaḥ syāditi prathamākṣepaḥ / prakāśapadārthavikalpenainaṃ pariharati
children.translated_text: and so forth. The first objection is: if knowledge is the essential nature of the person (<s>puṃs</s>), then there should be self-luminosity in deep sleep and unconsciousness. He resolves this through a distinction in the meaning of the word 'luminosity' (<s>prakāśa</s>):
'In the distinction'

children.text: tyādinā / jñānātiriktasya jñānajanyasya prakāśasya sattve 'pi ātmani bodhena tasyājananaṃ svāpe tamoguṇapratibandhādgāḍhāndhakārapratibandhādiva cākṣuṣasyājananamiti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: and so forth. Even though luminosity — distinct from knowledge and produced by knowledge — exists, its non-generation in the self through cognition during sleep is due to the obstruction by the quality of <s>tamas</s> — just as visual [perception] is not generated due to obstruction by dense darkness — this is the purport.
'Such a state'

children.text:
iti / bodhavattvamityarthaḥ /
bodhasya sattve svāpa ātmano vyavahāraprasaṅga iti dvitīyākṣepaḥ / tamanubhāṣate
children.translated_text:
— the meaning is: the state of possessing cognition.
The second objection is: if cognition exists [in sleep], there would be the undesirable consequence of activity (<s>vyavahāra</s>) of the self in sleep. He restates [the objection]:
'If it is held'
and so forth. He resolves:
'Not so'

children.text: iti / vyavahāraḥ kāyiko viciko vā'pādyate / ādyo na sambhavatītyāha
children.translated_text: and so forth. Activity (<s>vyavahāra</s>) is either bodily or verbal. He states that the first is not possible:
'Who indeed'
and so forth. The word <s>kim</s> is used in the sense of censure.
'For not'
and so forth. The purport is: because the essential nature of the self is eternally attained [and thus requires no activity]. He restates the second [type of activity]:
'Speech'
and so forth. He resolves:
'What then'

children.text:
ti / nirvikalpakaṃ vācakaśabdādiviśeṣaṇānullekhi yajjñānaṃ bālamūkādeḥ, tatsattve 'pi na tadviṣayasya vyāharaṇaṃ dṛśyata ityarthaḥ / tathāca svaviṣayavyāhāravyāptirjñānasya nāstītyasthāne prasaṅga iti bhāvaḥ /
anubhave sati svāpa ātmano jāgaraṇe smṛtiprasaṅga iti tṛtīyākṣepaḥ / tamanuvadati
children.translated_text:
and so forth. The meaning is: even when non-conceptual (<s>nirvikalpaka</s>) knowledge exists — knowledge that does not involve specific qualifiers such as signifying words — as in the case of an infant or a mute person, verbal expression regarding its object is not seen. Thus knowledge is not pervaded by verbal expression regarding its own object — and so the objection is misplaced — this is the purport.
The third objection is: if there is experience during sleep, there would be the undesirable consequence of memory upon waking. He restates [the objection]:
'Memory'
and so forth. He resolves:
'Because of non-occurrence'
and so forth. The elaboration of the objection is
'If it be said'
and so forth. The elaboration of the resolution is
'That is not'
and so forth.
'For not'

children.text: ti / buddhivṛttiviśeṣaḥ- dharmabhūtajñānāvasthāviśeṣaḥ / svāpādikālikātmānubhavaḥ svabhāvalakṣaṇa eva, natu dharmabhūtajñānāvasthāviśeṣalakṣaṇa iti yāvat / yene ti / jñānavṛttereva smṛtibījasaṃskārajanakatvamiti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: and so forth. 'A specific modification of the intellect' — a specific state of <s>dharmabhūtajñāna</s> (attributive knowledge). The experience of the self during sleep and the like is only of the nature of the essential nature [of the self], not of the nature of a specific state of <s>dharmabhūtajñāna</s> — this much [is meant]. 'Because' — the purport is that only a cognitive modification (<s>jñānavṛtti</s>) is the producer of the impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) that is the seed of memory.
'But'

children.text: iti / svāpādau svābhāvikadharmabhūtajñānavattvenāvasthānamevātmanaḥ, na tu jñānasya vṛttaya iti bhāvaḥ/
children.translated_text: and so forth. In sleep and the like, the self merely abides as possessing natural <s>dharmabhūtajñāna</s> (attributive knowledge), but there are no modifications of knowledge — this is the purport.
'And if in cognition'

children.text:
ti / nityasvaviṣayakabodhasvabhāvakatvādityarthaḥ / dharmabhūtajñānaṃ tāvat nityamātmaviṣayakam, indriyārthasannikarṣādisahakārisaṃpattyā
punarviṣayagrāhīti ekadeśimatenedam / yadvā bodha eva svo bhāvaḥ svarūpam, tattvāccidrūpatvādevāsya-ātmanaḥ svaviṣayakasaṃskārajanakatvaṃ kiṃ na syāditi śaṅkā / paraṃ prakaraṇavaśātpūrvoktarītyaivārtho 'tra susaṅgataḥ / asya-nityabodhasya / nityabodhasya saṃskārajanakatvaśaṅkāṃ pariharati
children.translated_text:
and so forth. The meaning is: because [the self] is of the essential nature of cognition that eternally has itself as its object. <s>Dharmabhūtajñāna</s> (attributive knowledge) is indeed eternally directed toward the self; additionally, through the cooperation of auxiliaries such as the contact of senses with objects,
it grasps [other] objects — this is according to the <s>ekadeśin</s> (partial-agreement) view. Alternatively, cognition itself is its own nature (<s>svabhāva</s>), its essential being; because of that — because of being of the nature of consciousness — would it not be the case that this self would produce impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>) regarding its own object? — this is the objection. However, by the force of the context, the meaning as stated earlier is well-fitting here. 'Of this' — of the eternal cognition. He resolves the doubt about the eternal cognition producing impressions:
'Unceasing'

children.text:
ti / tathā-sati sāmagrībalātpratikṣaṇaṃ saskārodayasaṃbhavena saṃskāradhārāviśramābhāvaprasaṅga / tathā
ca kleśakarmavipākāśayānāmātyantikanivṛttilakṣaṇamokṣasyāsiddhiprasaṅgaḥ ityarthaḥ / nityabodhasvarūpasya saṃskārajanakatvedoṣamuktvā niṣprayojanatvamapyāha
children.translated_text:
and so forth. 'In that case' — there being so, since impressions would arise at every moment by the force of the causal complex, there would be the undesirable consequence of the absence of cessation of the stream of impressions. And
thus there would be the undesirable consequence of the impossibility of liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>), which is defined as the absolute cessation of afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>), actions (<s>karma</s>), fruitions (<s>vipāka</s>), and latent deposits (<s>āśaya</s>) — this is the meaning. Having stated the defect in the eternal cognition's being a producer of impressions, he also states its purposelessness:
'And if experience'

children.text: ti / saṃskārakalpanaṃ hi anubhūtacarasyānanubhūyamānasya pratipattyartham / nityānubhava eva jāgrati kaḥ saṃskārakalpanāyā artha iti bhāvaḥ / svānurūpatvam- anubhavasamānaviṣayakatvam / nijabījam-smṛtibījaṃ, saṃskāraḥ / nanvātmaviṣayiṇyapi smṛtirdṛṣṭetyatrāha
children.translated_text: and so forth. For the postulation of impressions is for the purpose of apprehending what has been experienced but is not currently being experienced. If experience is eternally present, what purpose does the postulation of impressions serve? — this is the purport. 'Conformity to itself' — having the same object as the experience. 'Its own seed' — the seed of memory, i.e., the impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>). Now, since memory directed toward the self is also observed, he states regarding this:
'I who am the very same'

and so forth. 'A cognition mixed with memory' — a cognition regarding the essential nature of the self that is of the nature of memory with respect to the portion delimited by the prior time, and of the nature of experience with respect to the portion delimited by the present time.
'In the time-delimited'

children.text: ti / ātmasvarūpamātrasya sadā prakāśe 'pi tattatkālādyavacchinnasya vṛttigrāhyatayā vṛtteśca saṃskārajanakatayā nirukta pratyaya upapadyata ityarthaḥ / na svarūpamātre-na svarūpamātraviṣayakaḥ / nityātmabodhasya saṃskārajanakatve bādhakaṃ prayojanābhāvaṃ cābhidhāya tasya svāpādikālikasya saṃskārajanakatvāsaṃbhavamapyabhidhatte
children.translated_text: and so forth. The meaning is: even though the bare essential nature of the self is always luminous, that which is delimited by such-and-such time and the like is grasped by a cognitive modification (<s>vṛtti</s>), and since the modification is a producer of impressions, the aforementioned cognition is well-accounted for. 'Not regarding the essential nature alone' — not having only the bare essential nature as its object. Having stated the counter-evidence and purposelessness in the eternal self-cognition's production of impressions, he also states the impossibility of the sleep-time [cognition] producing impressions:
'And if unclear'

children.text: ti / tamoguṇābhibhavādaviśadaḥ, bāhyāntaraviśeṣaṇānavagāhanānnirvikalpaścetyarthaḥ / paṭīyasā-anabhibhūtena / smṛtibījaṃ saṃskāraḥ / ādhīyate-utpādyate /
children.translated_text: and so forth. 'Unclear' due to the dominance of <s>tamoguṇa</s> (quality of darkness); 'non-conceptual' (<s>nirvikalpaka</s>) because of not apprehending specific external and internal qualifiers — this is the meaning. 'By a stronger one' — by one that is not overpowered. 'The seed of memory' — the impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>). 'Is deposited' (<s>ādhīyate</s>) — is produced.
Here the following should be understood:
