children.text: yadyapi suptotthitasya sukhamahamasvāpsa mityādipratisandhānabalātsvāpakālikātmasvarūpānubhavasyāpi saṃskārajanakatvameṣṭavyam / athāpi ekadeśimatāśritavādo 'yam / ata evāgre astu vā ityādinā pakṣāntaraṃ vakṣyati / anubhave vartamāne tāvanmātraviṣayakasmṛterudayāyoge 'pi pratyavamarśasyādhikaviṣayasya saṃskārabalādudaye na kṣatiriti / adhikamagre / nanu sarvadā'tmasvarūpānubhava ityanupapannam / viṣayānubhavakāla eva sukhādināhamarthaprakāśasyānubhavasiddhatvādityatrāha
children.translated_text: Although, on the strength of the recognition upon waking from sleep — 'I slept happily' and so on — the production of impressions even by the experience of the self's essential nature during sleep must be accepted, nevertheless this argument is stated from the standpoint of the <s>ekadeśin</s> (partial-agreement) position. For this very reason, later he will present an alternative view with 'let it be so' and so forth. Even when experience is present, though memory having only that [bare self] as its object does not arise, there is no harm in the arising — through the force of impressions — of reflective cognition (<s>pratyavamarśa</s>), which has additional content. More on this later. Now, the claim that there is always experience of the self's essential nature is unjustified [from the opponent's perspective]. Since the illumination of the self by the meaning 'I' is established through experience only at the time of object-experience such as pleasure and the like — regarding this he says:
'Because of sameness'

children.text:
ti / ekākāreṇānubhūtamāne viśeṣākārāsphūrterananubhavabhramaḥ / atra nidarśanaṃ śarīrādi / yathā jāgare sadānubhūyamānasyāpi karacaraṇādilakṣaṇasya śarīrasyāgantukaviśeṣasphuraṇavelāyāmeva viśeṣataḥ pratipattyānyadānanubhūyamānateva, yathā vā'ntarasya jāgaraṇe śarīradhāraṇaprayatnasya sadānuvartamānasyāpi buddhipūrvahastādyutkṣepaṇakāla eva sphuṭāvabhāsenānyadānanubhūyamānateva, tathā prakṛte 'pīti bhāvaḥ / yadyapi śarīradhāraṇaprayatnasya
jīvanayoniśabditasyātīndriyatvamiṣyate tārkikaiḥ / athāpi adṛṣṭata eva jīvanasyopapatteratīndriyayatnakalpanaṃ gurubhūtam / jāgare tu prayatnato 'pi śarīratadavayavadhānaṇamiṣyate / sa ca prayatnaḥ pratyakṣayogya eva / nidrāyāṃ tvadṛṣṭata eva śarīradhāraṇamiti hārdamācāryataraṇānām / tat dṛṣṭāntasyāsya nānupapattiriti dhyeyam /
svāpe 'pi bodhānuvṛttau samādhimuktayoḥ svāpāviśeṣaprasaṅga ityākṣepāntaramanūdya pariharati
children.translated_text:
and so forth. When something is experienced in a uniform manner, due to the non-manifestation of a distinct form, there is the illusion of non-experience. The illustration here is the body and the like. Just as the body — characterized by hands, feet, and the like — though always experienced during waking, is specifically apprehended only at the time when an adventitious particular manifests, and at other times seems as if not experienced; or just as the internal effort of maintaining the body during waking, though always continuing, is clearly manifest only at the time of deliberate raising of the hand and the like, and at other times seems as if not experienced — so too in the present case — this is the purport. Although the <s>Tārkikas</s> (logicians) accept the effort of maintaining the body — called the source of life (<s>jīvanayoni</s>) — as supersensible, nevertheless, since life can be accounted for through <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen merit) alone, the postulation of a supersensible effort is an unwarranted burden. In waking, however, the maintenance of the body and its parts through effort is accepted. And that effort is indeed capable of being perceived. But in sleep, the maintenance of the body is through <s>adṛṣṭa</s> alone — this is the essential view of the master-teachers (<s>ācāryatara</s>). Therefore, there is no inapplicability of this illustration — this should be noted.
Having restated and resolved a further objection — that if cognition continues even in sleep, there would be the undesirable consequence of no distinction between sleep and <s>samādhi</s> (meditative absorption) and liberation —
'And if in the unmodified'

children.text: ti / avidyādikleśaḥ, tamoguṇābhibhavādatyantasaṅkucitajñānatvaṃ ca svāpe / na hi tadā jñānena svātmaprakāśo 'pi / mokṣe tu kleśātyantanivṛttiḥ, āvaraṇanivṛttyā nityāsaṅkucitasarvaviṣayajñānatā ceti viśeṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: and so forth. In sleep, there is <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) and other afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>), and extremely contracted knowledge due to the dominance of <s>tamoguṇa</s> (quality of darkness). For at that time, there is no self-manifestation even through knowledge. But in liberation, there is absolute cessation of afflictions, and — due to the removal of the covering — eternally uncontracted knowledge directed toward all objects — this is the distinction.
'In the <s>asaṃprajñāta</s> [samādhi]'

children.text: ti / saṃprajñāteti kvacit pāṭhaḥ / samādhau ca puṃsaḥ paramavairāgyanirodhasaṃskārapāṭavātmaikapravaṇamanaskatvaprayuktamokṣopāyasiddhikṛtaḥ svāpato mahān viśeṣo 'stīti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: and so forth. In some readings, '<s>saṃprajñāta</s>' [is found]. The purport is: in <s>samādhi</s>, the person's great distinction from sleep consists in the accomplishment of the means to liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>), brought about by supreme dispassion (<s>vairāgya</s>), mastery over cessation-impressions (<s>nirodhasaṃskāra</s>), and the state of mind exclusively directed toward the self.
'By one who has completed the course'

children.text:
ti tu samīcīnaḥ pāṭhaḥ / kṛtādhikāreṇetyarthaḥ / apavargiṇā-apavargopadhāyakena / kaivalyāvasthātmasākṣātkaraṇayogyeneti yāvat / manasā iti viśeṣyamadhyāhāryam / caritādhikāriṇeti pāṭhe tu kṛtātmanetyarthaḥ, kṛtakṛtyeneti vā / evaṃ citsvarūpatvaṃ citsvabhāvatvaṃ copapāditaṃ prasaktākṣepapariharaṇena /
atha svāpe 'pi anutyayā vṛttyaivātmanaḥ prakāśaḥ setsyati, kṛtaṃ svaprakāśatvenetyantarnidhāya svāpe 'pi buddhivṛttireṣṭavyeti śaṅkate
children.translated_text:
— this is the correct reading. The meaning is: by one who has completed the qualification (<s>adhikāra</s>). '<s>Apavargin</s>' — one who bestows liberation (<s>apavarga</s>); that is, one who is fit for the direct realization of the self in the state of <s>kaivalya</s> (absolute isolation). 'Mind' (<s>manas</s>) is to be supplied as the qualified noun. In the reading '<s>caritādhikāriṇa</s>,' the meaning is: 'one who has accomplished the self,' or 'one who has fulfilled his purpose.' Thus, both the nature of being consciousness (<s>citsvarūpatva</s>) and the nature of having consciousness as one's essential attribute (<s>citsvabhāvatva</s>) have been established through the resolution of incidental objections.
Now, harboring the thought that if even in sleep the self is luminous through a continuous cognitive modification (<s>vṛtti</s>), then what need is there for self-luminosity — he raises the objection that a cognitive modification must be posited even in sleep:
'How then'

children.text: riti / atrāyaṃ samuditāśayaḥ-svāpo nāma tamoguṇānubhavaḥ / riṣadudbuddhasattvasahakṛtatama ālambanatve tasya sukhatvaṃ, sattvakāryaṃ ca laghutvādir / iṣadudbuddharajaḥsahitatama ālambanatve duḥkhatvaṃ calatvādi ca / sattvarajasoratyantābhibhāvakaprodbuddhatama ālambanatve ca gāḍhamūḍhatvādi / svāpe tama anubhave satyeva tajjasaṃskārataḥ prabodhe sukhamasvāpsamityādipratisandhānasyopapattiḥ nānyatheti / ardhāṅgīkāreṇa pariharati
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Thus. Here the cumulative intent is this: sleep is indeed the experience of the <s>tamoguṇa</s> (quality of darkness). When <s>tamas</s>, accompanied by slightly awakened <s>sattva</s>, serves as the object of [mental] modification, it has the nature of pleasure, and the effects of <s>sattva</s> are lightness and the like. When <s>tamas</s> accompanied by slightly awakened <s>rajas</s> serves as the object, there is the nature of pain, restlessness, and the like. And when <s>tamas</s> fully awakened overpowers <s>sattva</s> and <s>rajas</s> and serves as the object, there is deep stupefaction and the like. In sleep, when the experience of <s>tamas</s> is present, the justified account of the post-waking recognition 'I slept happily' is from the impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>) produced by that [experience] — not otherwise. He refutes [this] with partial acceptance:
"True indeed [is that]" —

children.text: iti / niruktapratītāvabhyupagamaḥ / svāpasya tamoguṇālambanavṛttirūpatve, smṛtirūpatve ca svāpādau niruktapratīteranabhyupagamaḥ / tadāha
children.translated_text: thus. There is acceptance of the cognition described [above]. [But] there is non-acceptance of the described cognition when sleep is held to be a mental modification (<s>vṛtti</s>) with <s>tamoguṇa</s> as its object, or when it is of the nature of memory. Therefore he says:
"The answer has been given" —
thus.
"Inferential" —

children.text:
iti / vṛttisāmānyaviraha eva svāpaḥ / yogyāsmaraṇaliṅgācca prakāśasvabhāvāyā vṛtterabhāvasya tatkālīnasyānumānam / dehendriyalāghavādiliṅgācca sukhatvādestatrānumānam / pūrvadinakṛtasyāparasmin dine
pratyabhijñābalātsvāpakālikātmasattāṃśe 'pyanumānarūpaiveyaṃ pratītiriti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: thus. Sleep is simply the absence of mental modifications in general. And from the inferential mark of the absence of recollection of suitable [objects], the inference of the absence of modification (<s>vṛtti</s>) — which is by nature luminous — at that time [of sleep] is [established]. And from the inferential mark of lightness of the body and senses, the inference of pleasure and the like in that [state] is [established]. Even regarding the portion of self-existence during sleep, this cognition 'I slept' is of the nature of inference alone, based on the force of recognition of what was done the previous day on the following day — this is the purport.
"Not another kind of mental modification" —

children.text: iti / na tamoguṇaviṣayakabuddhivṛttirūpatvaṃ nidrāyā upagantavyam / svāpānumānādeva niruktapratīternirvāhādityarthaḥ / nidrāyā vṛttirūpatvābhāve pātañjalasūtrasya kā gatiriti śaṅkate
children.translated_text: thus. Sleep should not be accepted as having the nature of a mental modification (<s>buddhivṛtti</s>) pertaining to <s>tamoguṇa</s> — because the described cognition is accounted for by inference from sleep alone. This is the meaning. He raises an objection regarding what becomes of <s>Patañjali</s>'s <s>sūtra</s> if sleep is not of the nature of a <s>vṛtti</s>:
"How then" —
thus. He answers:
"In cessation" —

children.text:
ti / bhāvālambanavṛttisāmānyābhāvo nidreti tātparyam / asyāśca vṛttivanniroddhatvasāmānyādvṛttitvopacāra iti bhāvaḥ / atra
nidarśanaṃ
children.translated_text: thus. The purport is: sleep is the absence of mental modifications in general that have an existent object as their support. And because it shares in common with [other] modifications the property of being suppressible (<s>niroddhatva</s>), the figurative designation as a 'modification' [is applied] — this is the meaning. Here the illustration:
"Like <s>viparyaya</s> (error)" —

children.text: diti / anyathākhyāterabhāvena bhedāgrahasyaiva bhramasthalābhiṣiktasya viparyayaśabditasya niroddhavyatvatātparyeṇa vṛttitvavannidrāyā api vṛttitvaṃ kīrtyata iti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: thus. Since <s>viparyaya</s> — which, in the absence of cognition of the actual [thing], is simply the non-apprehension of difference, and which has been coronated on the throne of delusion and is denoted by the word <s>viparyaya</s> — because of the intent that it too is to be suppressed, its designation as a modification is proclaimed, and similarly for sleep — this is the purport.
"If it be so" —

children.text:
ti / sarvasaṃvidāmarthāvyabhicāraḥ-yathārthakhyātitvalakṣaṇonyāyatattvasāstrīyādhikaraṇasiddha ityarthaḥ / niroddhavyatvaṃ caiṣāṃ kaivalyasādhanaparipanthitayetyāha kaivalye ti / kaivalyabhāgi yaccit-mokṣādhikṛtamātmasvarūpam, tatpratyanīkatayā-tadabhimatasādhanasiddhivighātakatayaiteṣāṃ niroddhavyatvamityarthaḥ /
sukhamahamasvāpsamiti pratīteḥ pratisandhānarūpatvamupagamyāpyāha
children.translated_text: thus. The non-deviation from objects of all cognitions — characterized as <s>yathārthatva</s> (correspondence with reality) — has been established in the treatise on the <s>Nyāyatattva</s> in the relevant section. This is the meaning. And the suppressibility of these [modifications] is because they are obstacles to the means of attaining <s>kaivalya</s> (isolation), thus he says 'in <s>kaivalya</s>.' That which is the <s>kaivalyabhāgin</s> — the essential nature of the self that is qualified for <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation) — their suppressibility consists in obstructing the accomplishment of the means desired for that [liberation]. This is the meaning. Having accepted the nature of post-waking recognition as <s>pratisandhāna</s> (reconnection), he says:
"Let it be so" —

children.text: ti / jñānavattayaivopalabhyamānatvādātmano bodhasvabhāvatvamuktam / niruktarītyā svāpe 'pi bodhānuvṛttipratipādanācca tadeva pratiṣṭhāpitaṃ bhaviṣyatīti nāsmākaṃ kācit kṣatiḥ / yatti hṛdayaṃ vṛttyaivātmanaḥ prakāśo na svarūpata iti, tattvāśāmodakāyitamiti ca pūrvottarābhyāṃ sunirūpitaṃ bhaviṣyatīti bhāvaḥ / smaraṇāni-pratisandhānarūpāṇi /
children.translated_text: thus. Since the self is apprehended only as possessing knowledge, the nature of the self as essentially cognitive (<s>bodhasvabhāva</s>) has been stated. And since even in sleep, the continuation of awareness (<s>bodhānuvṛtti</s>) has been demonstrated through the method described — that very [thesis] will have been established, so there is no harm to our [position]. As for the heart [of the opponent's position] — that illumination of the self is only through mental modification, not through its own essential nature — that will be well refuted by the preceding and subsequent [arguments], like a sweetmeat of truth — this is the purport. 'Recollections' — those of the nature of reconnection (<s>pratisandhāna</s>).
[Verse:] Since, without the inherent awareness (<s>bodha</s>) of the self, existing by itself,
The darkness (<s>tamas</s>) during sleep and similar states, as described, would not be established — due to the unestablishedness of the reason. // 27 //

children.text: uparatāni hi prasvāpakāle sarvāṇyevendriyāṇi saha manasā / saṃskārasya ca na smṛteranyatra sāmarthyam / na ca svaprakāśaṃ tamaḥ; arthāntaravartino 'pyaniśaṃ prakāśaprasaṅgāt / kḷptaśca sarvārthasādhanatayā bodha iti tenaiva karaṇavirahiṇā satā svabhāvabhūteno(dbhūteno)dbhūtavṛttestamaso 'nyasya vā'tmavartino guṇasya sphuraṇamiti balādabhyupagamanīyam /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] For in sleep, all the senses together with the mind have indeed ceased. And the impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) has no capacity [to produce anything] other than memory. Nor is <s>tamas</s> (darkness) self-luminous — because even of something residing in another [entity], there would be the unwanted consequence of perpetual illumination. And awareness (<s>bodha</s>) has been established as the accomplisher of all purposes. Therefore, it must be forcefully accepted that it is by that very [awareness] — existing by its own nature, without instruments — that the manifestation of <s>tamas</s> or some other quality residing in the self occurs.

children.text: nityaprakāśaścātmā pramātṛtvāt / apramātṛtvavyāpakabaddhaṃ hyanityaprakāśatvaṃ vyāpakaviruddhapramātṛtvabhāginyātmani nātmānaṃ labhate /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] And the self is eternally luminous, because it is a knower (<s>pramātṛ</s>). For non-eternal luminosity, being pervaded by non-knower-hood, does not obtain in the self which partakes of knower-hood — [which is] contradictory to the pervader.

children.text: svāpasya vṛttitvopagame 'pi na jñānanityatvasiddhiḥ / vṛtteḥ karaṇajanyatvāditi parasya śaṅkāmanuvadati
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Even if sleep is accepted as a [mental] modification, the eternality of knowledge is not established — because modification is produced by an instrument. He restates the opponent's objection:
"He says" —
thus. He refutes:
"In this manner" —
thus. The meaning is: the ascertainment of the nature of knowledge [will be established] through the method to be stated next.
"Since" —

children.text: iti / svāpe kāraṇāyogātsvataḥsiddha eva tamaḥprakāśako bodha ityeṣṭavyamityarthaḥ //27//
children.translated_text: thus. The meaning is: in sleep, due to the absence of a cause [for it], the awareness that illuminates <s>tamas</s> must be accepted as self-established. // 27 //

body.text: ślokaṃ svayameva vivṛṇoti

children.translated_text: "Have ceased" —

children.text:
ti / anyasya vā-sukhādervā / uparatavyāpāratvātkaraṇānāṃ svāpe na jñānavṛtteravasaraḥ / ataḥ svābhāvikena bodhenaiva tamoguṇaprakāśa
iti balādeṣṭavyaṃ yadi tamo 'nubhavaḥ svāpa iṣyate / tatsiddhaṃ bodhasvabhāvatvamiti bhāvaḥ / vastuto jñānasya na svāpe tamaḥprakāśakatvamatisaṅkucitavṛttitvāt / svarūpānubhavabalātsukhatvena tadā bhāsamānasyātmanaḥ parāmarśaḥ paraṃ prabodha iti tu siddhāntaḥ /
children.translated_text: thus. 'Or of another' — or of pleasure and the like. Since the instruments have ceased functioning in sleep, there is no occasion for a cognitive modification. Therefore, it is by the natural (<s>svābhāvika</s>) awareness alone that <s>tamoguṇa</s> is illuminated — this must be forcefully accepted if the experience of <s>tamas</s> is admitted in sleep. Thus, the nature of the self as awareness is established — this is the purport. In reality, knowledge does not illuminate <s>tamas</s> in sleep, because of its extremely contracted functioning. Rather, due to the force of self-experience, the reflective awareness of the self appearing as pleasurable at that time is the awakening — this, however, is the established doctrine.
"I slept" —

children.text:
iti svāpakālāṃśayostvanumitirūpaiva niruktapratītiḥ / nityānubhavasya saṃskārājanakatve tu sākṣādeva svāpakālīnātmasvarūpānubhavasya niruktapratisandhānahetutvaṃ sukhatvenātmāgāhanāṃśa iti ca bodhyam /
bodhasvabhāvasyāpyātmano vṛttikāla evāstu prakāśo na sarvadetyatra tāvannityaprakāśatvaṃ sādhayati
children.translated_text: thus. The described cognition regarding the sleep-time portion is indeed of the nature of inference alone. But it should also be understood that if the eternal experience does not generate impressions, then the direct experience of the self's own nature during sleep itself is the cause of the described reconnection, [specifically] the portion that is the immersion into the self as pleasure. He now establishes the eternality of luminosity, [even] for the self whose nature is awareness, which exists only during the time of [mental] modification:
"And eternally luminous" —
thus.
"Non-knower-hood" —
thus. That which has the form of non-knower-hood is the pervader; [non-eternal luminosity] is the pervaded — this is the meaning.
[Verse:] The self-established luminosity (<s>prakāśatva</s>) of this [self] arises from its nature as a knower (<s>jñātṛbhāva</s>);
For dependence-on-another for illumination is pervaded by non-knower-hood. // 28 //
(Thus [is] the establishment of the eternally self-luminous nature of the self, whose essential nature is knowledge.)

children.text: kaḥ punarayaṃ prakāśaḥ, yo 'sya nityo 'bhyupeyeta svābhāvikaśca? kaścāsyātmanā saṃbandhaḥ? / yadi jñānameva; saṃbandhaścāśrayāśrayitvam; tato hetvabhāvena sādhyābhāvasya vyāptimupadarśayituṃ nidarśanatayā ghaṭādyupādātavyam-yadanityaprakāśamanyādhīnaprakāśaṃ vā tadapramātṛ, yathā ghaṭādīti / tatra ca viśeṣaniṣedhasya sāmānyābhyanujñākṣepakatvādāgantukaṃ jñānaṃ ghaṭādāvanumatamāpadyeta / atha tanmābhūditi viṣayaviṣayibhāva eva saṃbandhaḥ saṃgīyeta, tato nityavajjñānaviṣayatvamātmanaḥ prasatyeta / jñānaviṣayīkāraśca sādhanaviśeṣāyattatvena niyata iti na
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] What, then, is this luminosity (<s>prakāśa</s>) that is to be accepted as eternal and natural to it? And what is its relation to the self? If it is knowledge (<s>jñāna</s>) itself, and the relation is that of substratum and attribute (<s>āśrayāśrayitva</s>), then to show the pervasion of the absence of the probandum through the absence of the reason, an illustration such as a pot should be adduced: 'Whatever is of non-eternal luminosity or dependent on another for illumination is a non-knower — like a pot.' And therein, since the negation of a particular [i.e., non-eternal luminosity] implies the permission of the general [i.e., some luminosity], adventitious knowledge in a pot would be inadvertently admitted. If, to avoid that, the relation is asserted to be that of object and objectifier (<s>viṣayaviṣayibhāva</s>), then the self's being an object of knowledge would be perpetual, as for things known eternally. And the objectification by knowledge, being dependent on particular means, is determinate — thus it would not be

body.translated_text: [Commentary:] He himself glosses the verse:

body.text: svābhāvikatvasambhavaḥ / acetanagocara eva tathā niyama iti cenna, cetanāntaraviṣayīkāre 'pi tathābhāvadarśanāt / na cānātmagocara eva sādhanasāpekṣatvaniyama iti vācyam / ātmano 'pyānumānikāgamikayogajñānaviṣayīkāre tatsāpekṣatvadarśanāt / viruddhe caikasyaikakriyāyāṃ karmakartṛtve, sūcyagrasyevātmanivedhyavedhakatve / nityatvaniratiśayasūkṣmatvavyāpitvacitsvābhāvyādirūpeṇa pratyagarthasyaupadeśikatvamānumānikatvaṃ vā, na svarūpataḥ / svarūpāpekṣayaiva svataḥsiddhirabhyupeyata ityasamādheyo virodhaḥ / rūpabhedena gamyagamakatvāṅgīkārapakṣe 'pakṣasyeva śabdāderna svataḥsiddhatvam /
body.translated_text: possible for it to be natural. [The objection] 'the restriction [of means-dependence] applies only to non-conscious objects' is not valid, since the same is observed even in the objectification of other conscious beings. Nor can it be said that the restriction of means-dependence applies only to non-self objects — because even for the self, means-dependence is observed in inferential, scriptural, and yogic cognition of the self. And it is contradictory for one and the same thing to be both the object and agent in a single action — like the impossibility of a needle-point piercing itself. The fact that the self has the character of being teachable and inferable with respect to [its qualities of] eternality, surpassing subtlety, all-pervasiveness, consciousness-nature, and the like, is [only] secondary, not primary. Self-establishment is to be accepted precisely with reference to the essential nature — thus the contradiction is irresolvable. In the view that accepts the self as both knowable and knower through difference of aspects — like a word, it would not be self-established.

body.text: (iti jñānāśrayatvaviṣayatvayoḥ prakāśamānatvarūpatve doṣānukīrtanam /)

children.text: athocyeta-na prakāśo jñānam / api tu tannimittaścetanetarasarvapadārthasādhāraṇo dharmaḥ, yadvaśāt prakāśata iti prakhyopākhyepratāyete sarvapadārtheṣvaviśeṣeṇa; āśrayāśrayitvalakṣaṇaśca saṃbandhastena saha sarvabhāvānām / sa ca yathoditasādhanabalādeva sāṃsiddhiko nityaścātmana iti / parākṛto 'yaṃ pakṣaḥ / na jñānātirekī prakāśo nāma / yadvyavahāropajananānuguṇaṃ jñānaṃ, tatprakāśata ityucyate / jñeyasya jñātuḥ svātmanaśca vyavahārānuguṇaṃ jñānamudayata iti yuktaḥ triṣvapi ekarūpaḥ prakāśatevyavahāraḥ / tattvāntaraprakāśābhyupagametātsvābhāvye
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Now if it is said: luminosity (<s>prakāśa</s>) is not knowledge (<s>jñāna</s>), but rather a property common to all entities — both conscious and non-conscious — caused by knowledge, by virtue of which [an entity] 'shines forth' — thus the expressions <s>prakhyā</s> (clarity) and <s>upākhyā</s> (designation) apply indiscriminately to all entities; and the relation of all entities with it is that of substratum and attribute; and it is natural and eternal for the self, [arising] from the power of the means described — this position has been rejected. For there is no luminosity (<s>prakāśa</s>) that is different from knowledge. That knowledge which is conducive to generating practical activity — that is said to 'shine forth.' The practical activity appropriate to the knowable, the knower, and one's own self — the knowledge that arises for all three is appropriately called uniform 'shining forth.' If another principle called <s>prakāśa</s> is accepted, then regarding its naturalness —
[garbled text]
no
[garbled text]

children.text: ca punaḥ kiṃ caitanyāśrayaṇena? / na ca prakāśa eva taditi vācyam, ghaṭāderapi prakāśavattayā cetanatvaprasaṅgāt / yadyucyet-sati cetanāvattve puṃsaḥ prakāśamānatvamiti: saṃvidīdānīṃ kā vārtā? cetanaiva hi sā, na cetayate / atha saṃvidastatsaṃbandhādhīnaḥ sa dharma iti cet; kastayā saṃbandhaḥ, yastannibandhanam? / nāśrayāśrayitvam; ghaṭādestadabhāvaprasaṅgāt / na viṣayaviṣayibhāvaḥ, tasyaivānirūpaṇāt / anirūpaṇaṃ ca bhrāntyadhikaraṇasiddhāntārambhe saṃvitsiddhau cānusandhātavyam / ātmanastasya cāprakāśa prasaṅgaśca / jñānādhīnaprakāśāśrayataiva siddhiḥ, tayā cānumeyaṃ jñānamiti pakṣaḥ prāgeva pratikṣiptaḥ /
children.translated_text: And then, what [is gained] by resorting to consciousness? Nor can it be said that <s>prakāśa</s> itself is that [consciousness] — for then a pot and the like, being luminous, would absurdly be conscious. If it is said that a person's being illuminated depends on possessing consciousness — then what of consciousness (<s>saṃvid</s>)? It is indeed consciousness, [but] it does not cognize [by itself]. If it is said that its property [of making things illuminated] depends on its relation with consciousness — then what relation with it would be the basis of that? It is not the relation of substratum and attribute, because of the unwanted consequence of its absence in pots and the like. It is not the relation of object and objectifier, because that very [relation] is unascertainable. And its unascertainability should be considered in the beginning of the established doctrine of the section on error and in the section establishing <s>saṃvid</s> (consciousness). And there would be the unwanted consequence of the non-illumination of that [consciousness itself] and of the self. The position that establishment [of the self] depends on knowledge-dependent illumination, and that knowledge is to be inferred from that [illumination] — that position has already been rejected.

children.text: svaprakāśasaṃvidvādino 'pi vyavahārānukūlye vairūpyamaśakyaparihāram / ātmani samavetaṃ jñānamasaṃbandhinyarthe prakāśaṃ vyavahāraṃ vā kathaṃ prasuvītetyapi cintyam / indriyaliṅgādisvakāraṇapratyāsattivasāditi mā vocaḥ / na khalu labdhātmakaṃ kāryaṃ svanimittakāraṇamanurudhya kāryamārabhate / mā bhūdudakāharaṇādi ghaṭādeḥ kulālādisamānādhiṣṭānam / na ca nimittakāraṇanāśe kāryanāśaḥ / naśyati cendriyasaṃprayogādināśe rūpādijñānam / ata indriyeṇa saha caitanyamapi nissṛtya tena tenārthena sannikṛṣyate, hastādineva tvagindriyam / tathā sati hi tadupādhikatvāttajjñānasya yuktaṃ tadbhāvānuvidhāyitvam / anyathotpannaṃ jñānamindriyārthasannikarṣanivṛttau kimiti nivartate? / jñānajanyārthadharmaprakāśavādino 'pi samāno 'yaṃ doṣaḥ / nimittakāraṇaṃ hi jñānam / kutastannivṛttau arthaprakāśo nivartate? kuto vā yāvattadbhāvamavatiṣṭhate ? /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Even for the proponent of self-luminous consciousness (<s>svaprakāśasaṃvid</s>), the incongruity with practical activity is unavoidable. It is also questionable how knowledge inhering in the self could give rise to illumination or practical activity with respect to an object that is unconnected [with the self]. And do not say: 'Through the proximity of its own causes — the senses, inferential marks, and the like.' For a product that has already attained its being does not conform to its efficient cause in order to initiate a [further] effect. Let there be no water-fetching and the like from a pot [guided] by its potter; nor is there destruction of the effect upon the destruction of the efficient cause. Yet the knowledge of form and the like does perish upon the destruction of sense-contact and the like. Therefore, consciousness too, going forth together with the sense, comes into contact with such-and-such an object — just as the tactile sense [extends via] the hand and the like. For in that case, since [knowledge] would be conditioned by that [sense-contact], it would be reasonable for the knowledge of that [object] to conform to the existence [of that contact]. Otherwise, why would the knowledge that has arisen cease upon the cessation of the sense-object contact? Even for the proponent that knowledge produces the property of illumination in the object — the same defect [applies]. For knowledge is the efficient cause; why would illumination of the object cease upon the cessation of that [knowledge]? Or why would it persist as long as it [knowledge] exists?

children.text: nanu nityaprakāśatvaṃ svābhāvikabodhakṛtameva kiṃ na syādityatrāha
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Objection: Why would not eternally luminous nature arise from natural awareness itself? To this he says:
"Self-established" —

children.text: ti / vyāptā-vyāpyā / vyāpakābhāvādvyāpyābhāva iti yāvat / jñātṛtvasvābhāvyādevānanyādhīnaprakāśatvasiddhiriti bhāvaḥ / jñānasya prakāśo jñānāntarānapekṣo 'pyātmasambandhāpekṣa iti jñāne 'nanyādhīnaprakāśatvalakṣaṇaṃ sādhyaṃ nāsti, tena sapakṣe jñāne sati pakṣamātravṛtti jñātṛtvaṃ bhavatyasādhāraṇamiti śaṅkānavakāśaḥ /yadyapi kevalavyatirekiṇo na pramāṇatvaṃ siddhānte / athāpi paraprakriyayā parān pratyetatsamarthanaṃ sambhavatyeva / siddhānte tu pūrvoktānvayinaiva svaprakāśatvasiddhirātmanaḥ / nityatvagrāhakapramāṇabalāccātmanaḥ tatprakāśasyāpi nityatvamarthasiddham / śrutibhiśca sakalārthapratiṣṭeti paramācāryāṇāmāśayaḥ //28//
children.translated_text: thus. 'Pervaded' means: is the pervaded [term]. From the absence of the pervader, [there follows] the absence of the pervaded — this is the meaning. From the very naturalness of knower-hood, the establishment of non-dependent-on-another luminosity [follows] — this is the purport. Even though the luminosity of knowledge is not dependent on another knowledge, it is dependent on the self-relation; so there is no probandum of non-dependent-on-another luminosity in [the case of] knowledge. Therefore, with knower-hood — which occurs in the thesis-locus (<s>pakṣa</s>), namely knowledge alone — being an uncommon [reason], there is no room for the objection [that it is asādhāraṇa]. Although in the established doctrine, purely negative [inference] is not accepted as valid — even so, by way of the opponent's framework, this establishment for the opponent's sake is indeed possible. In the established doctrine, however, the self's [self-luminosity] is established by the very anvaya-type [concomitance] previously stated. And by the force of the valid means that grasp the self's eternality, the eternality of its luminosity too is established as a matter of course. And through the <s>śruti</s> (scripture), which is the foundation of all things — this is the intent of the supreme teachers. // 28 //

body.translated_text: (Thus the enumeration of defects in [treating] illumination-nature as consisting in either being the substratum of knowledge or being the object of knowledge.)

body.text: atha prasaṅgāt

children.translated_text: "luminosity" —
He introduces an examination to determine the meaning of the term:
'What then'
and so forth. Since this examination serves to justify the assignment-to-each-object (<s>pratikarmavyavasthā</s>) even of eternal knowledge, it has relevance to the topic at hand.
'If'

children.text: ti / prakāśata ityatra dhātvarthaḥ prakāśo jñānam / ākhyātārthaścāśrayatvamiti yadi kathyate ityarthaḥ / etaddūṣayati
children.translated_text: and so forth. In 'prakāśate' ('it shines'), the verbal root meaning is <s>prakāśa</s> (luminosity), which is knowledge (<s>jñāna</s>). And the verbal ending means 'being the substrate of' — if this is what is being stated, that is the meaning. He refutes this:
'Then'
and so forth.
'If in that case'

children.text: ti / vyatirekyudāharaṇavākye nityaprakāśarūpaviśeṣaniṣedhasya prakāśasāmānyābhyupagamaparyavasāyitvācca ghaṭādāvāgantukajñānavattvamabhyupagataṃ bhavedityarthaḥ / na caivaṃ sati tatra hetvabhāvo 'jñātṛtvaṃ na syāditi vācyam / anātmatvasyātrājñātṛtvapadena vivakṣitatvāt / prakāśāśrayatvamātrasya tu sādhanāyogaḥ siddhatvāditi ca bodhyam / uktadoṣaparihārāya prakārāntaraṃ śaṅkate
children.translated_text: and so forth. Since the negation of the specific [attribute of] being of the nature of eternal luminosity (<s>nityaprakāśarūpa</s>) in the dissimilar example (<s>vyatireka</s>) sentence would culminate in the acceptance of luminosity in general (<s>prakāśasāmānya</s>), it would follow that even a pot and the like possess adventitious knowledge — this is the meaning. Nor should it be said that in that case, the absence of the reason — non-knower-hood — would not obtain there, because what is intended by the word 'non-knower' here is non-selfhood (<s>anātmatva</s>). And it should be understood that mere substrate-hood of luminosity cannot serve as the probandum, since it is already established. To avoid the stated fault, he raises an alternative objection:
'Let that not be so'

children.text: diti / yadi jñānaviṣayatvaṃ prakāśamānatvamucyata iti yāvat / etadapi dūṣayati
children.translated_text: and so forth. The meaning is: if being an object of knowledge is what is meant by 'being luminous.' He refutes this too:
'Then'

children.text: iti / nityaprakāśavattvasādhanenātmanaḥ sārvadikaṃ jñānaviṣayatvaṃ prasajyata ityarthaḥ / iṣṭamevedamiti cettatrāha
children.translated_text: and so forth. The meaning is: by proving that the self possesses eternal luminosity, it would follow that the self is an object of knowledge at all times. If [one says] 'this is exactly what is desired,' to that he says:
'In knowledge'

children.text:
ti / jñānasya viṣayaprakāśanavyāpāro hi indriyādidvārakaḥ / ata itarānapekṣo
nityaśca jñānaviṣayabhāva ātmano duḥsādha ityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: and so forth. The operation of knowledge in illuminating its object is indeed dependent on the senses and other [instruments]. Therefore, the state of being an object of knowledge that is independent of other [instruments] and eternal is difficult to establish for the self — this is the meaning.
'And the rule'
and so forth. The meaning is: the rule is that objectification (<s>viṣayīkaraṇa</s>) occurs only in dependence upon an instrument (<s>karaṇa</s>).
'And when [such] is the case'
and so forth. The meaning is: because dependence on the operation of an instrument is observed.
'And not'

children.text: ti / svātmabhinnaviṣaya eva viṣayīkārasya karaṇāpekṣatvamucyata iti na ca vācyamityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: and so forth. The meaning is: nor should it be said that the dependence on an instrument for objectification applies only to objects other than one's own self.
'Of the self too'

children.text: / svātmaprakāśane 'pi śabdaliṅgādikaraṇasāpekṣatvadarśanāt niyamasaṅkoco na karaṇīya ityarthaḥ / nanu svarūpamātraviṣayakaṃ nityajñānaṃ siṣādhayiṣitam / asya cātmaviṣayīkaraṇe na karaṇāpekṣetyatrāha
children.translated_text: and so forth. The meaning is: since dependence on instruments such as scripture (<s>śabda</s>), inference (<s>liṅga</s>), and the like is observed even in the self-illumination of one's own self, the restriction should not be narrowed. Now, what is sought to be established is eternal knowledge having only one's own essential nature (<s>svarūpamātra</s>) as its object. And that this self-objectification does not depend on instruments — to this he says:
'Contradictory'

children.text: iti / svarūpamātrasyaiva kartṛtvakarmatvayorupagamo viruddhaḥ / svarūpamātrajñāne ākārabhedādavirodhasamarthanamapi na sambhavatītyāha
children.translated_text: and so forth. The acceptance of both agent-hood (<s>kartṛtva</s>) and object-hood (<s>karmatva</s>) for the same essential nature alone is contradictory. He says that a reconciliation through a distinction of aspects is also not possible in the case of knowledge of mere essential nature:
'In the case of eternality'

children.text: tyādivākyadvayena / nanu svarūpasyaiva gamyatvepi tasyaiva gamakatvaṃ sāmānyaviśeṣadharmabhedāddhaṭetetyatrāha
children.translated_text: and so forth, with two sentences. Now, even if the essential nature itself is both what is known and what makes known, these two are compatible due to the distinction between generic and specific properties (<s>sāmānyaviśeṣadharmabheda</s>) — to this he says:
'By a distinction of form'

children.text:
ti / yathā śabdaśabdasya śabdaśabdavācyatve 'pi vācyatā śrotragrāhyaguṇatvākāreṇa, vācakatā cānupūrvīviśeṣeṇeti na svayaṃprakāśatvamapakṣasya śabdasya, evaṃ grāhyagrāhakatāvacchedakadharmabhede pakṣīkṛtasyāpi ātmano na svaprakāśatvaṃ sidhyedityarthaḥ/ evaṃ vimarśakena pakṣadvayaṃ dūṣitam /
atha bhāṭṭaprakriyāmanuvadati
children.translated_text:
and so forth. Just as the word 'śabda' (sound), even though it is denoted by the word 'śabda,' has its denotability in the aspect of being a quality apprehended by the ear, and its denotative capacity in the specific sequence [of phonemes] — yet sound is not self-luminous in your view, similarly, even if the distinguishing properties that delimit what-is-to-be-grasped and the grasper are different, self-luminosity cannot be established for the self that has been made the subject — this is the meaning. Thus the examiner has refuted both alternatives.
Now he restates the <s>Bhāṭṭa</s> position:
'Now it is said'

children.text: ti / prākaṭyaṃ prakāśaḥ, āśrayatvaṃ ca saṃbandhaḥ / prakāśata iti pratītivyavahārau ca prākaṭyāśrayatvārthakāveva prācuryeṇa pravartete / jñānajanyaḥ prakāśaśca cetanācetanasarvapadārthasādhāraṇaḥ / sa eva nityaḥ svābhāvikaścātmanaḥ sādhyatāṃ jñātṛtvabalāditi śaṅkāgranthārthaḥ / prābhākaramukhena nirākarotīmaṃ pakṣaṃ
children.translated_text: and so forth. <s>Prākaṭya</s> (manifestness) is <s>prakāśa</s> (luminosity), and being-the-substrate is the relation (<s>saṃbandha</s>). The cognition and usage 'it shines' (<s>prakāśate</s>) predominantly operate with the meanings of manifestness and substrate-hood. And the <s>prakāśa</s> generated by knowledge is common to all entities, both sentient and insentient. That very [manifestness], when eternal and natural to the self, is what is to be proved, by the force of knower-hood — this is the purport of the objection passage. He refutes this position through the <s>Prābhākara</s> standpoint:
'Rejected'

children.text: iti / jñātatāvyavahārasya svaprakāśajñānata evopapatterna jñānajanye jñātatākhye dharmāntare pramāṇaṃ kimapīti parākaraṇaprakāraḥ /
children.translated_text: and so forth. Since the usage of 'being known' (<s>jñātatā</s>) is explained precisely from self-luminous knowledge (<s>svaprakāśajñāna</s>), there is no evidence whatsoever for a separate property called 'being-known' (<s>jñātatā</s>) produced by knowledge — this is the manner of refutation.
'Some [say] in all three'

children.text: ti / prakāśo jñānam, tadadhīnavyavahārānuguṇyaṃ sambandhaḥ prakāśata ityatrākhyātārtha iti pakṣa eva jñeyajñānajñātṛṣu ekārthakatā prakāśatevyavahārasya ghaṭata ityarthaḥ / tritayavyavahārānuguṇyāpādanaṃ ghaṭādijñānasya svabhāva iti hārdam / jñānātiriktasya prakāśasya nityasyātmanyupagame tatra jñānaṃ vyarthamiti cāha
children.translated_text: and so forth. The meaning is: the position that <s>prakāśa</s> is knowledge, that the relation is conformity to the usage dependent on it, and that in 'prakāśate' the verbal ending [carries this meaning] — in precisely this position, the unitary meaning of the usage 'prakāśate' can be shown to apply to the knowable (<s>jñeya</s>), to knowledge (<s>jñāna</s>), and to the knower (<s>jñātṛ</s>). The essential point is that producing conformity to all three usages is the very nature of knowledge of pots and the like. And he also says that if an eternal <s>prakāśa</s> distinct from knowledge is accepted in the self, knowledge would be rendered purposeless there:
'In another category'

children.text: ti / svaviṣayakajñāne satyevātmanaḥ prakāśamānateti kṣemasādhāraṇaprayojakatopagamānnātmani caitanyasya vaiyarthyamiti śaṅkate
children.translated_text: and so forth. Since when there is knowledge of one's own object, the self's being-luminous is accepted as having a purpose common to both [knowledge and prakāśa] — there is no purposelessness of consciousness (<s>caitanya</s>) in the self. He raises this objection:
'If it is said'
and so forth. He challenges:
'Consciousness' (<s>saṃvid</s>)

children.text: ti / saṃvit jñānameva, na jñānāśrayaḥ / tathā ca caitanyasamavāyitvasya prakāśamānatāprayojakatve caitanye tadabhāvātprakāśamānatā na ghaṭeteti bhāvaḥ / nanu caitanyasambandha eva prakāśaheturupeyata iti cettatrāha
children.translated_text: and so forth. <s>Saṃvid</s> (consciousness) is knowledge itself, not the substrate of knowledge. And thus, if the substrate-in-which-consciousness-inheres is accepted as the cause of being-luminous, then since consciousness itself lacks that [inherence-relation], being-luminous would not be possible — this is the purport. Now, if one holds that connection with consciousness itself is the cause of luminosity, to that he says:
'Who, by that'

children.text: ti / tayā-cetanayā / saṃbandhavikalpena dūṣaṇamatra kriyate / caitanyavadātmasamavetatvasya caitanyasaṃbandhatve ghaṭāderaprakāśāpattiḥ / tadāha
children.translated_text: and so forth. 'By that' — by consciousness. The refutation here is carried out through the alternatives of relation. If being-possessed-of-consciousness through inherence in a substrate that possesses consciousness constitutes the connection with consciousness, then even pots and the like would absurdly become luminous. He states this:
'Of a pot and the like'

children.text: riti / caitanyaviṣayatvasya tattve ca caitanyasyātmanaścāprakāśāpattiḥ / tadāha
children.translated_text: and so forth. And if being-an-object-of-consciousness is [the relation], then consciousness and the self would absurdly become non-luminous. He states this:
'Of the self'

children.text: iti / ātmanaḥ-saṃvidaḥ / tasya-puṃsaḥ / prakāśaprayojakasya caitanyaviṣayatvasyāṅgulyagreṇeva svātmasparśasyāśakyatvāccaitanye, karmakartṛtvavirodhādātmani cāsambhava iti hārdam / nanu karmakartṛvirodhopagame 'stu jñānāśrayatayaivātmani prakāśatevyavahāraḥ / jñānasya tvatīndriyasya jñātatāliṅgakānumānātprākaṭyaṃ sambhavati prakāśatevyavahāranidānamityatrāha
children.translated_text: and so forth. 'Of the self' — of consciousness (<s>saṃvid</s>). 'Of that' — of the person. The essential point is: since being-an-object-of-consciousness, which is the cause of luminosity, is impossible for consciousness — like the impossibility of touching one's own fingertip with that same fingertip — and is also impossible for the self due to the contradiction of being both agent and object (<s>karmakartṛtvavirodha</s>). Now, if one accepts the contradiction of being both agent and object, let the usage 'it shines' apply to the self merely by virtue of being the substrate of knowledge. As for knowledge — since it is supersensory, its manifestness is possible through an inference marked by the sign of being-known (<s>jñātatā</s>), and this serves as the ground for the usage 'it shines.' To this he says:
'Dependent on knowledge'

children.text:
ti / jñānānumānapratikṣepācca jñānasya jñānarūpatayaiva prakāśatevyavahāro vācyaḥ / tathā ca prākaṭyena jñānajadharmeṇārtheṣu, jñānarūpatayā jñāne, jñānāśrayatayaiva
cātmani prakāśatevyavahāra iti triṣvapi tasyaikarūpyāsambhava etanmata iti sthitam /
evaṃ bhāṭṭamate jñeyajñānajñātṛṣu prakāśatevyavahārasyaikarūpyāsambhavaṃ gurumukhena procya gurumate 'pi triṣu vyavahārānuguṇye aikarūpyāsambhavaṃ vimarśaka udbhāvayati

children.translated_text: 'In self-luminosity'

children.text: ti / jñānaviṣayatayār'the, jñānarūpatayā jñāne, jñānāśrayatayā cātmani vyavahārānuguṇyaṃ vaktavyamiti gurumate 'pi vairūpyamaśakyaparihāramityarthaḥ / dūṣaṇāntaramapyāha matadvaye
children.translated_text: and so forth. The meaning is: the conformity to usage must be stated as being through 'being an object of knowledge' for the object, through 'being of the nature of knowledge' for knowledge, and through 'being the substrate of knowledge' for the self — thus, even in the teacher's view, the disparity is impossible to avoid. He also states another objection, common to both views:
'In the self'
and so forth. Here is the objection:
'The sense organ'

children.text: ti / yadarthasaṃbaddhendriyaliṅgādinā yajjñānaṃ janitam, tat tasminnarthe prakaṭatāṃ vyavahārānuguṇyaṃ vā niṣpādayatīti śaṅkārthaḥ / pratikṣipati
children.translated_text: and so forth. The meaning of the objection is: whatever knowledge is generated by a sense organ and the like that are connected with an object, that [knowledge] produces manifestness or conformity to usage with respect to that object. He rejects this:
'Not when obtained'

children.text: ti / kāryasya svotpattāveva nimittakāraṇāpekṣā / na tu samutpannasya svakāryajanane 'pi / anyathā kulālasannidhāna eva ghaṭena jalasyāharaṇam, nānyatrepi syādityarthaḥ / jñānasyaiva svakāryaniṣpādane svanimittāpekṣetyāśrayaṇe cedamapi vaiṣamyaṃ prasajyata iti bhāvaḥ / kulālādisamānādhiṣṭhānam-kulālādisamānādhikaraṇam / vaiṣamyāntaramapyāha
children.translated_text: and so forth. An effect depends on its material cause only for its own origination, not for the production of its own effect once it has already arisen. Otherwise, only in the presence of the potter would the pot fetch water, and not elsewhere — this is the meaning. The purport is that if one insists that knowledge too depends on its own material cause for producing its own effect, even this asymmetry would follow. 'Having the same locus as the potter and the like' — having the same substrate as the potter and the like. He also states another asymmetry:
'And not'

children.text: ti / anyatra nimittanāśe kāryanāśasyādarśanāt jñānasyaiva nimittanāśena nāśābhyupagamenāpi vaiṣamyaṃ prasaktaṃ pakṣadvaye 'pītyarthaḥ / kaṃ tarhi prakāśasya vyavahārasya vopapattiḥ? tatrāti / iti indriyādidvārā prasṛtasya tena sahārthasannikṛṣṭasya jñānasyārthaprakāśakasyārthapkāvyavahāra- janakatvaṃ svīkāryamanāyatyeti hārdam / siddhāntināṃ pakṣo 'yam /
children.translated_text: and so forth. Since the destruction of the effect is not observed upon the destruction of the material cause elsewhere, even with the acceptance that knowledge is destroyed upon the destruction of its material cause, this asymmetry would arise in both positions — this is the meaning. What then is the explanation of manifestness or usage? To that [he says]: the meaning is — thus, knowledge that has proceeded through the senses and the like, that is thereby connected with the object, and that illuminates the object, must be accepted as producing the usage of object-manifestness. There is no other way. This is the <s>Siddhāntin</s>'s position.
'And when such is not the case'

children.text: ti / indriyeṇa saha pravṛttyādimattve hi jñānasya tadarthasannikṛṣṭasya tatprakāśakasyendriyārthasannikarṣānvayavyatirekānuvidhāyyanvayavyat irekopapattirityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: and so forth. The meaning is: when knowledge operates together with the sense organ, being connected with that object and illuminating it, its co-presence and co-absence with the contact between sense organ and object is established — this is the meaning.
'Otherwise'

and so forth. The meaning is: if one does not accept the contact between knowledge and the object through the medium of the senses and the like, then since the destruction of the material cause would not be a reason for the destruction of the effect, the cessation of knowledge would not follow upon the cessation of the contact between sense organ and object.
And it is not proper to counter this with the example of number (<s>saṅkhyā</s>) and the like;

body.translated_text: [Commentary:] Now, incidentally,

body.text: asiddhatvena nāśasya saṅkhyāyā buddhināśataḥ /
body.translated_text: Because the destruction of number is through the destruction of the cognition, [and] the destruction [of number] is [itself] unestablished;

body.text: ekasaṅkhyava saṅkhyātvādanyāpyādravyabhāvinī //29//
body.translated_text: Like the number one, [other] numbers too, by virtue of being numbers, are not inherent in substance alone. //29//

body.text: sarvā hyekāśrayā saṅkhyā nityānityārthavartinī /
body.translated_text: For every number, residing in a single substrate, whether in eternal or non-eternal entities,

body.text: yāvadāśrayasatyeva saṃmatā sarvavādinām //30//
body.translated_text: Is accepted by all theorists as existing as long as its substrate exists. //30//

body.text: dvitvādikā parārdhāntā saṅkhyā yānekavartinī /
body.translated_text: The numbers beginning with two up to <s>parārdha</s> (the highest number), which reside in single [entities],

body.text: sāpi saṅkhyātvasāmānye sati kasmānna tādṛśī //31//
body.translated_text: They too, given the commonality of being numbers — why would they not be similar [to the number one]? //31//

body.text: nanu naikatvaṃ saṅkyā; svarūpānatirekāt / ataḥ sādhanavikalamudāharaṇam /
body.translated_text: Now, [one may object:] oneness (<s>ekatva</s>) is not a number, because it is not different from the essential nature [of the thing]. Therefore, the example lacks the probandum.

body.text: maivam / saṅkhyaiva sā; dravyāntare 'pyanuvṛtteḥ / yadi ghaṭādeḥ svarūpamevaikatvam, tato ghaṭa ekaḥ, paṭa eka iti sarvadravyasādhāraṇyamekatvasya na syāt / nahi ghaṭasvarūpasya paṭasvarūpeṇa saṃbhavati sāmānādhikaraṇyaṃ ghaṭaḥ paṭa iti / asti tu tadekatvasya /
body.translated_text: This is not so. It is indeed a number, because it persists across different substances. If oneness were merely the essential nature of a pot and the like, then the common applicability of oneness to all substances — as in 'the pot is one,' 'the cloth is one' — would not obtain. For the essential nature of a pot cannot have co-referentiality (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) with the essential nature of a cloth, as in 'pot is cloth.' But oneness does have that.

body.text: nanu nimittanāśasyāpi kāryanāśe hetutvaṃ kvacideṣṭavyam / anyathāpekṣābuddhināśādditvādernāśasyānupapatteḥ / tathā prakṛte 'pi bhaviṣyatīti śaṅkate

children.translated_text: 'And not'
and so forth. He resolves it:
'Because [it is] unestablished'

children.text: ti / apekṣābuddhināśena dvitvādināśasyāsiddhatvena na nimittanāśena kāryanāśe dvitvādernāśasya nidarśanatvaṃ saṃbhavatītyarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: and so forth. The meaning is: since the destruction of duality and the like through the destruction of the cognition of mutual dependence is itself unestablished, [duality and the like] cannot serve as an example for the destruction of an effect through the destruction of its material cause.
'One'

children.text: ti / yāvadāśrayabhāvitvādekatvasyeva dvitvādeḥ saṅkhyātvānnāpekṣābuddhināśānnāśa ityarthaḥ / asiddhatvametenopapāditaṃ bhavati / phalito 'tra prayogaḥ-dvitvādiryāvadāśrayasatī saṅkhyātvādekatvavaditi //29//30//31//
children.translated_text: and so forth. The meaning is: just as oneness persists as long as its substrate exists, so too duality and the like, being numbers, are not destroyed through the destruction of the cognition of mutual dependence. By this, the unestablished-ness [of the counter-example] is demonstrated. The resulting inference here is: duality and the like persist as long as their substrate exists, because of being numbers — like oneness. //29//30//31//

body.translated_text: Now, the destruction of the material cause must sometimes be accepted as a cause for the destruction of the effect too. Otherwise, the destruction of duality (<s>dvitva</s>) and the like upon the destruction of the cognition of mutual dependence (<s>apekṣābuddhi</s>) would be inexplicable. So likewise in the present case — he raises this objection:

body.text: dṛṣṭānte hetvāsiddhiṃ śaṅkate

children.translated_text: 'Now, oneness is not [a number]'
and so forth. He resolves it:
'This is not so'
and so forth.
'If'

children.text: ti / tattadvyaktisvarūpasyaivaikapratītivyavahāraniyāmakatve ghaṭa ekaḥ, paṭa eka ityādyanugatapratītivyavahārānupapattiḥ / tattadvyaktitvasyānanugatatvāt / ekatvasaṅkhyāyāstathātve tu ekatvenānugamādanugatapratītyādyupapattiriti bhāvaḥ / tārkikaprakriyayedam /
children.translated_text: and so forth. If the essential nature of each particular instance were itself the determinant of the cognition and usage 'one,' then the persisting cognition and usage such as 'the pot is one,' 'the cloth is one' would be inexplicable, because the particular-instance-hood of each is not something that persists [across instances]. But if oneness is a number [that is a real property], then since it does persist [across instances] by virtue of [being] oneness, the persisting cognition and the like are explicable — this is the purport. This follows the <s>Tārkika</s> (logician's) procedure.
Moreover — number and oneness are contradictory, therefore only duality is a number, just as other numbers are;
'One, two' — for there is no co-referential cognition [of these]. //32//

children.text: yattu anekadravyavṛttitve sati guṇatvāt saṃyogavadayāvaddravyabhāvinīdvitvādisaṅkhyeti, tannanātve 'naikāntikama / na hi satorapi ghaṭapaṭayostannānātvaṃ naśyati / na ca tat dvitvasaṅkhyaiva / trayāṇāṃ tadabhāvaprasaṅgāt / na ca tadekatvābhāvamātram / tucchasyāpi nānātvāpatteḥ /
children.translated_text: As for [the argument] that duality and other numbers are non-enduring like conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>), because they are qualities that reside in multiple substances — that is inconclusive with respect to their mutual distinctness. For even when the pot and the cloth both exist, their mutual distinctness does not perish. Nor is that [distinctness] the number duality itself, because the absurd consequence would arise for three [things too having] its absence. Nor is it mere absence of oneness, because even a non-entity (<s>tuccha</s>) would absurdly become plural.
He raises the objection of unestablished reason in the example —
'Now, oneness is not [a number]'
— and so forth. He resolves it —
'This is not so'
— and so forth.
'If'

children.text:
' ti / tattadvyaktisvarūpasyaivaikapratītivyavahāraniyāmakatve ghaṭa ekaḥ, paṭa eka ityādyanugatapratītivyavahārānupapattiḥ / tattadvyaktitvasyānanugatatvāt / ekatvasaṅkhyāyāstathātve tu ekatvenānugamādanugatapratītyādyupapattiriti bhāvaḥ / tārkikaprakriyayedam /
svarūpatve bādhakamuktvaikatvasya saṅkhyātve sādhakamapyāha '
children.translated_text:
— and so forth. If the essential nature of each particular instance were itself the determinant of the cognition and usage 'one,' then the persisting cognition and usage such as 'the pot is one,' 'the cloth is one' would be inexplicable, because the particular-instance-hood of each is not something that persists [across instances]. But if oneness is a number [that is a real property], then since it does persist [across instances] by virtue of [being] oneness, the persisting cognition and the like are explicable — this is the purport. This follows the <s>Tārkika</s> (logician's) procedure.
Having stated the defeater against [oneness being] mere essential nature, he also states the positive proof for oneness being a number —
'The number'

children.text: ' ti / atra prayogaḥ-ekatvaṃ saṅkhyā saṅkhyāntaraviruddhatvāt dvitvādivaditi / hetuṃ pakṣe ghaṭayati '
children.translated_text: — thus. Here the argument [is]: oneness is a number, because it is contradicted by other numbers, like twoness and so forth. He applies the reason to the thesis:
'one' —

children.text: 'm iti / atredaṃ bodhyam-uddeśyatāvacchedakāvacchinnaparyāpterdvitvādisaṃbandhatayā bhānāt ekatvāvacchinnaparyāpteśca dvitvādisaṃbandhatvābhāvena na ekaṃ dvāviti prayogaḥ / ekaṃ dvitvavaditi tu syānnāma, atra dvitvasamavāyasyaiva svarūpasaṃbandhena bhānāt, tasya caikasminnapyabādhāt / saṅkhyāntaraviruddhatvaṃ ca saṅkhyāntaraparyāptyavacchedakāvacchinnaparyāptikavṛttikatvābhāvalakṣaṇamiti / dvitvāderyāvadāśrayabhāvitvānumāne dṛṣṭānte sādhanavaikalyaṃ parahṛtametāvatā // 32 //
children.translated_text: thus. Here this should be understood: since the comprehension delimited by the delimitor of the designatum appears as related to twoness etc., and since the comprehension delimited by oneness does not have the property of being related to twoness etc., the formulation 'one is two' is not [valid]. However, 'one is like twoness' might work, since in this case the inherence of twoness itself appears through the relation of its own nature, and since that [relation] is not negated even in a single [entity]. And 'being contradicted by other numbers' is defined as the absence of the property of being present in what is delimited by the delimitor of the comprehension of another number. [The objection of] deficiency of the proof in the inference and example, due to twoness etc. being present wherever there is a substratum, is thus refuted. // 32 //

body.translated_text: He raises an objection regarding the unestablished-ness of the reason in the example:

body.text: āpekṣikatvāt dvitvādeḥ pratiyegyavavagrahāt /
body.translated_text: Because twoness etc. are relative, because of the non-apprehension of the correlate,

body.text: bubhutsoparamāccāpi satyā evānavagrahaḥ // 33 //
body.translated_text: and because of the cessation of the desire to know, there is indeed non-apprehension of what is real. // 33 //

body.text: ataścaitanyasyaivendriyadvārār'thasannikarṣa eva tadbhāvānuvidhānopapattiḥ /
body.translated_text: Therefore, it is justified that it is consciousness alone, through the door of the senses, through contact with objects, that conforms to their existence.

body.text: anyacca, arthasya prakāśakaṃ hi jñānaṃ bhavatām / sarvaṃ ca prakāśakaṃ prakāśyavastusannikṛṣṭameva prakāśakaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ dīpaprabhādi / atastadapi tatheti yuktamāśrayitum / vyomavadamūrtasya na kriyāvattvamiti cet, keyaṃ mūrtirnāma ? yadvirahiṇaḥ kriyāyogaḥ / yadi paribhāṣikī dravyatve sati kvācitkateti /
body.translated_text: Moreover, knowledge is what illuminates the object, according to you. And everything that illuminates is seen to illuminate only when in proximity to the object to be illuminated — like lamp-light and the like. Therefore it is reasonable to maintain that [knowledge] also is like that. If [you object that] being incorporeal like space, it cannot have activity — what then is this 'corporeality' called? That whose absence entails the absence of activity? If it is a technical term — being a substance yet being occasional —

body.text: iṣyata eva sā caitanye / na hi tatsarvagataṃ dravyam, tathāsati yugapat sarvārthasiddhiprasaṅgāt / kvācitkatve tu tadvi yadaikadaikendriyeṇa saṃprayuktaṃ tadarthābhimukham, na tadendriyāntaramadhitiṣṭhati / ata eva hi yugapajjñānānutpattiḥ / niratiśayavegaṃ ca tat, yugapadivātiśīghramanekendriyādhiṣṭhānadarśanāt / ato yathoditamamūrtatvamasiddham / sparśavattā mūrtiḥ, tadvitarahānniṣkriyatvamiti cet ; śabdenānaikāntaḥ / sa khalu śaṅkhamukhāderdavīyaso 'pi deśāt nodanaviśeṣeṇa loṣṭādiriva yāvadvegaṃ pratiṣṭhate sparśavihīno 'pi / sparśarahitasyāpi manaindriyasya kriyāvattvaṃ padārthavākyārthavidāmubhayeṣāmapi saṃmatameva /
body.translated_text: that is accepted in the case of consciousness. For that [consciousness] is not an omnipresent substance; if it were, there would be the unwanted consequence of accomplishing all objects simultaneously. But being occasional — when it is connected with one sense-organ at one time and directed toward that object, it does not preside over another sense-organ. This is precisely why simultaneous cognitions do not arise. And its velocity is unsurpassed, since it is seen to preside over multiple sense-organs almost simultaneously, as if instantaneously. Therefore, the incorporeality stated above is unestablished. If [you say] corporeality is possession of touch, and from its absence there is inactivity — this is inconclusive, because of [the counter-example of] sound. For sound, even from a less [dense] region such as the mouth of a conch, by a particular impulse, like a clod of earth, travels as far as its velocity [carries it], even though devoid of touch. And the activity of the mind-faculty, which is also devoid of touch, is accepted by both — by those who know word-meanings [Vaiśeṣikas] and by those who know sentence-meanings [Mīmāṃsakas].

children.text: kathamatītānāgatayorasatoścaitanyena saṃprayoga iti cet, kathaṃ vā viṣayabhāvaḥ, prakāśamānatvam, saṅkhyādiyogo vā tayoḥ ? yastatra nirvāhaḥ, sa evātrāstu / api cātītatayānāgatatayā ca tāvapyadyāpi vidyete iti tena rūpeṇa bodhasannikarṣe kānupapattiḥ ? kiñca, yathā davīyasi deśe satā dhruvaśiṃśumārādinā dṛk tu sannikṛṣyate, tathā davīyasi kāle satā kalpādyantavartinā svayaṃbhuvādineti nālokaṃ kiñcit / kiñca-
children.translated_text: If [you ask]: how can consciousness be connected with the past and future, which are non-existent? And how can they be objects? [The answer is:] because they are being illuminated;
He raises the prima facie objection:
'but many' —
thus. He refutes it:
'that' —

children.text:
' ti / nānātvaṃbahutvam / tasya ca vyāsajyavṛttitvāddvitvādivadguṇatvameva / na tu bhedarūpatvam / bhedasyāvyāsajyavṛttitvāditi bhāvaḥ /
nanu yāvadāśrayaṃ sattve āśrayopalambhakāle niyamata ekatvasyeva dvitvāderupalambhaḥ prasajyate iti cettatrāha '
children.translated_text: thus. Plurality means multiplicity. And since it has an extended occurrence, it is itself a quality, like twoness etc. But it is not of the nature of difference. Difference
'because of being relative' —

children.text: ' diti / saṃbandhyantaragrahasāpekṣagrahasya dvitvādeḥ pratiyoginaḥ saṃbandhyantarasyāgrahaṇāt, grahaṇe vā dvitvādibubhutsāyā apekṣābuddheśca tadvodhe sahakāriṇyā viraheṇa na sadā graha iti bhāvaḥ / evaṃ ca nimittanāśanāśyatvasya na nidarśanībhavitumalaṃ dvitvādatyuktaṃ bhavati / vastuto 'pekṣābuddhiviśeṣātiriktaṃ dvitvādikamevāprāmāṇikamiti tannāśādhīnatannāśasya na tarāṃ prasaktiriti bodhyam // 33 //
children.translated_text: thus. Since the apprehension of twoness etc. depends on the apprehension of the other relatum, [and] since there is non-apprehension of the other relatum, the correlate — and since the apprehension

body.text: nātītānāgate buddherdūre bhavitumarhataḥ /
body.translated_text: The past and future cannot be far from cognition;

body.text: buddhyā prakāśamānatvādbuddhiboddhṛsvarūpavat // 34 //
body.translated_text: because they are illuminated by cognition, like the nature of cognition, the cognizer, and the cognized. // 34 //

children.translated_text: And thus, of consciousness,

children.text: niratiśayavegitayāntarāladeśakālāgrahaṇābhimāno 'lātacakragatakramavaddeśabhedasaṃyogavibhāgāgrahaṇābhimānavat / api cendriyaliṅgasaṃskārāderyadarthapratiniyataṃ rūpam, tainaivopaśliṣya nissaraccaitanyamapi tadgocareṇaiva sannikṛṣṭate ; yathā gavādipadaśaktirekabuddhisiddhe 'pi sāmānyaviśeṣātmake vastuni sāmānyāṃśenaiva saṃbadhyate, yathā vā vidhiḥ prāptāṃśaparihāreṇāprāptāṃśameva bhāvanāyāḥ spṛśati / ata indriyādidvāreṇa caitanyaṃ tadarthābhimukhaṃ nirgacchatīti nyāyyam / yathā'ha bhagavān "
children.translated_text: due to its unsurpassed velocity, the non-apprehension of intervening space and time [gives rise to] the misconception — like the non-apprehension of spatial differentiation, conjunction, and disjunction in the case of a whirling firebrand —
'That carries away his wisdom, as wind carries a boat on water' —
thus. And <s>Manu</s> [says]:

children.text: indriyāṇāṃ hi sarveṣāṃ yadyekaṃ kṣaratīndriyam / tenāsya kṣarati prajñā dṛteḥ pādādivodakam //
children.translated_text: 'If even one of all the senses leaks, through that his wisdom leaks away, like water from a leather bag through its foot.'
Thus.

body.text: yattu guṇaścaitanyaṃ guṇinamapahāya kathamanyato yātīti ; tadayuktam, prahāṇānabhyupagamāt / aprahāyaivātmānamitastataścetanā indriyādidvārānniścarati / vicchinnāyāśca tasyāḥ sandhānāsaṃbhavaḥ śāsra evoktaḥ / dṛśyante ca guṇā api śabdagandhasūryālokaratnaprabhādayo gatimanto dharmyativartinaśca / atisūkṣmo dūragamanadharmā bhautiko hi śabdaḥ /
body.translated_text: But [the objection:] if consciousness is a quality, how can it go elsewhere without leaving its possessor? — that is unjustified, because we do not accept [its] leaving. Without leaving

body.text: nanu nabha iva vibhuḥ śabdo vyañjakadhvanivaśena prādeśika iva gatvara iva copalabhyate / tathāhi-śabdaḥ sarvavyāpī ekadravyavartitve satyākāśaguṇatvāt tatparimāṇavat / maivam, atadguṇatvāt / vāyavīyaḥ śabdaḥ, tena niyatasahotpattikatvāt, tadīyasparśavat / yaśca yena dravyeṇa niyatasahotpattirguṇaḥ sa tadguṇa eva, yathā tathāvidhā rūpādayaḥ / niyatasahotpattiśca vāyunā śabdaḥ / ubhayorapi bherīdaṇḍavaṃśadalanādisaṃyogavibhāgajatvaniyamāt / utpadyate ca śabdaḥ indriyagrāhyatve sati guṇatvāt gandhādivat / kṛtakaśca, kriyottaramevopalabhyatvāt saṃyogādivat / na cābhivyañjakatvaṃ prayatnādeḥ kalpyam, gauravāt / tatpratītikāraṇatvakalpanādapi tatkāraṇatvakalpanaiva hi laghvī / abhivyañjakāśca ekadeśāvasthitānekendriyagrāhyān yugapadabhivyañjanti, yathā pradīpo rūpasaṅkhyāparimāṇāni karakādīṃścaikapradeśavartinaḥ / na caivaṃ tālvādisaṃyogavibhāgajanitapavana iti nāsau vyañjakaḥ /
body.translated_text: Now, just as sound, though omnipresent like space, is perceived as if localized and as if moving due to the manifesting sound [vibration] — for indeed, sound

body.text: jñānasyārthasannikarṣānupagame bādhakamuktvār'thasannikarṣe sādhakaṃ cāha '

children.translated_text: 'moreover' —
thus. He raises the objection of the contradiction with incorporeality regarding knowledge's external projection:
'like space' —
thus. He rejects this objection through the alternative regarding corporeality:
'what is this' —
and so forth.
'for that [consciousness] is not' —
thus. The purport is that in the state of bondage, knowledge is indeed non-omnipresent.
'it does not [preside over] that [other sense]' —

children.text: ' ti / ekendriyādhiṣṭhānakāle indriyāntarasaṃpṛktaṃ sattanna pravartayati tadarthasannikarṣāyetyarthaḥ / evaṃ cāvibhudravyatvalakṣaṇamūrtatvasya jñāne satvādamūrtatvamasiddhamiti bhāvaḥ / sparśavattvaṃ mūrtatvamiti pakṣe doṣamāha '
children.translated_text: thus. The meaning is that at the time of presiding over one sense-organ, that existing [consciousness] connected with another sense-organ does not operate toward proximity with that [other] object.
'by sound' —

children.text: ' ti / yasyāsparśatvaṃ tasyākriyatvamiti niyamo 'siddhaḥ / śabdasyāmūrtasyāpi kriyāvattvāt / tathā cāsparśasyāpi jñānasya prasaraṇādau nānupapattiriti bhāvaḥ / anaikāntyapradarśanaṃ śabde tasya dravyatvamatena / tasya dravyatve vimatyāmapi saṃpratipannasthalāntare taddarśayat '
children.translated_text: thus. The rule that whatever lacks touch is inactive — that is unestablished, because even sound, which is incorporeal, has activity. And thus
'touch' —

children.text: ' ti / yadvā nanu śabdasyāśrayadvāraiva gatirvācyā / śabdāśrayaśca vāyuḥ sparśavāniti na niruktaniyame kṣatiriti cettatrāha '
children.translated_text: thus. Alternatively: but the movement of sound should be stated as being only through its substratum. And the substratum of sound is air, which possesses touch — so the stated rule is not violated.
'touch' —

children.text:
' ti / padārthavidaḥ kāṇādāḥ, vākyārthavido jaiminīyāḥ / ubhayeṣāmapi sammataṃ manaso niḥsparśasyāpi kriyāvattvamityarthaḥ /
arthasannakarṣeṇa jñānasyārthaprakāśakatve 'tītenānāgatena vār'thena sannikarṣāyogājjñānana tattadarthaprakāśavyavahārau na ghaṭete iti śaṅkate '
children.translated_text: thus. Those who know word-meanings are the <s>Kaṇādas</s> (Vaiśeṣikas); those who know sentence-meanings are the <s>Jaiminīyas</s> (Mīmāṃsakas). It is accepted by both that even the mind, which is devoid of touch, has activity.
'how, regarding the past' —
thus. He states the objection:
'how indeed' —

children.text: ' ti / atītānāgatayorvartamānajñānaviṣayatvaṃ vaiśeṣikamate, vartamānajñānādhīnaprakāśākhyadharmasamavāyitvaṃ bhāṭṭamate, matadvaye 'pi dvitvādisaṅkhyā ca vartamānāpekṣābuddhijanyātayoḥ kathaṃ ghaṭata ityarthaḥ / uttarataulyaṃ sphorayati '
children.translated_text: thus. According to the Vaiśeṣika view, the past and future being objects of present knowledge, being possessed of the property called 'illumination' dependent on present knowledge —
'that, there' —

children.text: ' ti / jñānaviṣayatve jñānādhīnadharmabhāktve vā jñānādhīne vartamānatvamarthasya nāpekṣitamityakāmenāpi svīkāryam / asmābhirapi jñānasannikarṣastathaivopapādyata iti bhāvaḥ / vastutaḥ siddhānte dhvaṃsaprāgabhāgabhāvalakṣaṇāvasthāntareṇa tayorapi jñānakāle sattvājjñānasannikarṣa upapadyata evetyāha '
children.translated_text: thus. Whether it be object-hood of knowledge, or possession of a property dependent on knowledge, present-ness of the object is not required by either, so it follows without need.
'even if' —

children.text: ' ti / kānupapattirityatra kvacit kā nāmānupapattiriti pāṭhaḥ / nanvevamapi tattatkālasya jñānena grahaṇaṃ na syādadyatanena, tasyedānīmabhāvādityatrāha '
children.translated_text: thus. What impossibility? — here, in some readings: 'what impossibility indeed?' But even so, [the objection that] a particular time cannot be grasped by knowledge —
'furthermore' —

children.text:
' ti / jñānāsyātivegitayā tattatkālasannikarṣeṇa tattadgrahaṇamupapannamityarthaḥ / vyavahitakālasannikarṣe jñānasya nidarśanaṃ vyavahitadeśasannikarṣo 'tivegino nāyanatejasaḥ /
dūratve 'pi buddhyā sannikarṣo ghaṭata ityuktam / idānīṃ buddhyapekṣayādūratvameva netyāha '
children.translated_text: thus. The meaning is that due to the extreme velocity of knowledge, the apprehension of each [past and future object] through contact with each respective time is justified. Contact with an intervening time —
'the past' —

children.text: ' ti / buddhyadūratvameva buddhisannikarṣo bodhyabodhaboddhṛsādhāraṇa iti tu siddhāntaḥ // 34 //
children.translated_text: thus. Not being far from cognition is itself proximity to cognition — that is common to the cognizable, cognition, and the cognizer — this is the established conclusion. // 34 //

body.translated_text: Having stated the refutation of [the objection to] knowledge's proximity to the object, and the proof in favor of object-proximity, he says:

body.text: nityatvavādinaḥ śabdā nirbhāgavyomavartinaḥ /
body.translated_text: For those who maintain that words are eternal, partless, and abide in space,

body.text: śrāvaṇāścetyabhivyaktiniyame nāsti kāraṇam // 35 //
body.translated_text: and are auditory — there is no reason to restrict manifestation. // 35 //

body.text: deśaikye grāhakaikye ca vyañjakaikyaṃ hi darśitam /
body.translated_text: For identity of place, identity of perceiver, and identity of manifesting agent have been shown;

body.text: tadabhāvātprayatnotthamārutaḥ kāraṇaṃ dhvaneḥ // 36 //
body.translated_text: in their absence, the air produced by effort is the cause of sound. // 36 //

body.text: ata eva ca nānātvaṃ pratyuccāraṇamiṣyatām /
body.translated_text: For this very reason, let difference be accepted with each utterance,

body.text: kṛtasya kāraṇāyogāddhetupauṣkalyabhedataḥ // 37 //
body.translated_text: since what is [already] produced cannot be a cause, and because of the difference in the completeness of causes. // 37 //

body.text: kiñcodāttānudattatvadīrghatvahrasvatādayaḥ /
body.translated_text: Moreover, <s>udātta</s> (high pitch), <s>anudātta</s> (low pitch), long, short, and other [properties],

body.text: gādisthā yugapadbhānto na bhindyuḥ svāśrayān katham // 38 //
body.translated_text: residing in [sounds like] 'ga' etc., appearing simultaneously — how could they not differentiate their substrata? // 38 //

body.text: sthānaikyāpātasādṛśyāt pratyabhijñāpi naikyataḥ /
body.translated_text: Owing to the similarity of the initial impression from identity of locus, recognition too [is explained] — not from identity;

body.text: pradīpapratyabhijñeva jñāpitā bhedahetavaḥ // 39 //
body.translated_text: just as the recognition of a lamp — [these are] indicators of difference. // 39 //

body.text: nanvevaṃ caitanyasaṃyogaḥ, saṃyogajo vā kaścitprakāśaḥ prāptaḥ / ubhayamapi tanna caitanye saṃbhavati, bhedāpekṣatvāt saṃbandhasya / ātmano 'pi na caitanyena saṃyogaḥ, taddharmitvāt / na hi dharmadharmiṇoḥ saṃbandhaḥ saṃyogaḥ / samavāyo hi saḥ ; ayutasiddhasaṃbandhatvāt / saṃyogastu pṛthaksiddhayordravyayoḥ kriyānimittā prāptiḥ, akārya kāraṇayorvā tayornirantarasthitiḥ / caitanyasaṃyogasamavāyayoranyatarasya, saṃbandhamātrasya vā prakāśatve jñātṛjñānajñeyaśarīrendriyeṣvavyāptyativyāptī yathāyogamādarśayitavye / tattvāntaraprakāśābhyupagamastvanupalabdhibādhito na dūṣaṇāntaraṃ prayojayati / ato yadvyavahārodayānuguṇaṃ jñānam, tat prakāśata ityevābhyupagamo yuktaḥ / tritayavyavahārānuguṇyaṃ saṃvidastu svabhāva ityaparyanuyojyaṃ nimittavairūpyam / na hi svabhāvāḥ paryanuyogamarhanti / evaṃ cetsaṃyogasamavāyavirahiṇo 'pi padārthasya nimittabhedānusāreṇa vyavahārahetuḥ saṃviditi yuktamāśrayitum /
body.translated_text: Objection: In this case, either conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>) with consciousness (<s>caitanya</s>), or some illumination (<s>prakāśa</s>) born of conjunction, would follow. Neither of these is possible in the case of consciousness, since relation (<s>saṃbandha</s>) requires distinction [between the relata]. Nor can the self (<s>ātman</s>) have conjunction with consciousness, since it is the substrate (<s>dharmin</s>) of that [consciousness]. For the relation between a property (<s>dharma</s>) and its substrate (<s>dharmin</s>) is not conjunction — it is inherence (<s>samavāya</s>), since it is a relation between inseparable entities (<s>ayutasiddha</s>). Conjunction, on the other hand, is the contact (<s>prāpti</s>) between two independently existing substances caused by activity, or their uninterrupted co-location when they are not in a cause-effect relation. If illumination (<s>prakāśatva</s>) consisted in either conjunction or inherence with consciousness, or in mere relation, then under-extension (<s>avyāpti</s>) and over-extension (<s>ativyāpti</s>) with respect to the knower (<s>jñātṛ</s>), knowledge (<s>jñāna</s>), the known (<s>jñeya</s>), the body (<s>śarīra</s>), and the sense organs (<s>indriya</s>) would have to be shown as appropriate. The acceptance of illumination as a separate category (<s>tattvāntara</s>), however, is refuted by non-apprehension (<s>anupalabdhi</s>) and does not require a separate objection. Therefore, the proper position is simply this: that knowledge (<s>jñāna</s>) which is conducive to the arising of cognition (<s>vyavahārodaya</s>) is what illuminates. That awareness (<s>saṃvid</s>) is by its very nature (<s>svabhāva</s>) conducive to the threefold cognition — this is an unquestionable ground of distinction. For intrinsic natures (<s>svabhāva</s>) do not admit of further inquiry. If so, it is proper to hold that awareness (<s>saṃvid</s>), even without conjunction or inherence, is the cause of cognition in accordance with differences in its occasioning conditions (<s>nimittabheda</s>).

body.text: ucyate / uktamatra, na nimittakāraṇamanurudhya kāryaṃ svakāryamārabhata iti / vyavahārānuguṇasaṃvedanatve 'pi prakāśapadārthe pravṛttinimittabhedo duṣparihara eva / bahuvrīhisamāsāśrayaṇe saṃvidantarābhāvena tasyāṃ tadabhāvaprasaṅgāt / karmadhārayāśrayaṇe jñātṛjñeyayorasaṃvedanatvenāprakāśaprasaṅgaḥ / vyavahārodayānuguṇyaṃ ca vyavahārato 'vagantavyam / tataḥ prāgeva ca bhavati viditatvapratītirvyāhāraśca/
body.translated_text: Reply: It has been stated here that an effect does not produce its own effect in conformity with its occasioning cause (<s>nimittakāraṇa</s>). Even granting that the object of illumination (<s>prakāśa</s>) is awareness that is conducive to cognition (<s>vyavahāra</s>), the distinction of the ground of application [of the term] is indeed difficult to avoid. If one resorts to a <s>bahuvrīhi</s> compound [for 'prakāśa'], then since there is no other awareness (<s>saṃvid</s>) [besides the one in question], the absence of that [illumination] in it would follow. If one resorts to a <s>karmadhāraya</s> compound, then the knower (<s>jñātṛ</s>) and the known (<s>jñeya</s>), not being awareness, would be unilluminated (<s>aprakāśa</s>). Moreover, the conduciveness to the arising of cognition must be ascertained from cognition itself; but even prior to that, there already exists the apprehension of something being known (<s>viditatva</s>) and verbal expression.

body.text: yadyevam, kastarhi prakāsatepadārthaḥ ? / na hi niravadyamekarūpaṃ jñātṛjñeyajñānānugataṃ tamupalabhāmahe / ucyate / nūnaṃ bhavānaśrutapūrvī prathamādhikaraṇasya nyāyatattve / abhihitaṃ hi tatredamanubhave smṛtimupapādayadbhiḥ, 'anubhavādūratvaṃ smṛtinimitta'm iti / etaduktaṃ bhavati-saṃvidadūratvaṃ prakāśa iti /
body.translated_text: If so, then what is the referent of the word 'illuminates' (<s>prakāśate</s>)? For we do not find any single, flawless nature that pervades the knower (<s>jñātṛ</s>), the known (<s>jñeya</s>), and knowledge (<s>jñāna</s>). Reply: Surely you have not previously heard of the first chapter of <s>Nyāyatattva</s>. For there, while establishing memory (<s>smṛti</s>) on the basis of experience (<s>anubhava</s>), it was stated: 'Non-remoteness from experience (<s>anubhava</s>) is the cause of memory (<s>smṛti</s>).' What this means is: non-remoteness (<s>adūratva</s>) of awareness (<s>saṃvid</s>) is illumination (<s>prakāśa</s>).

body.text: āha-kimidamadūra iti ? dūrādanyastadviruddhastadabhāvo vā ? tathā viśeṣaṇamupalakṣaṇaṃ vā adūra iti ? viśeṣaṇatve pakṣatraye 'pi saṃvedanadūratvānusandhānapūrvikayā prakāśata iti pratītyā bhavitavyam / na ca tathāsti / upālakṣaṇatve svarūpāntaraṃ vācyam / na ca davagamyata ityuktam / ucyate ; alamasthāne saṃbhrameṇa /
body.translated_text: He asks: What is this 'non-remote' (<s>adūra</s>)? Is it something other than 'remote' (<s>dūra</s>), or opposed to it, or the absence of it? Also, is '<s>adūra</s>' a qualifier (<s>viśeṣaṇa</s>) or an indicator (<s>upalakṣaṇa</s>)? If it is a qualifier, in all three alternatives, there would have to be an apprehension of 'illuminates' preceded by the investigation of the remoteness of awareness — but that is not the case. If it is an indicator, then some other nature must be specified — but it has been said that it cannot be ascertained. Reply: Enough of this confusion over a non-issue.

body.text: nanvevamapi vyavahitadeśakālasannikarṣasya madhyavartideśakālasannikarṣanāntarīyakatayā madhyavartināmapi grahaṇaṃ syāditi prasaṅgamiṣṭatvena pariharati '

children.translated_text: 'If so' (<s>evaṃ cet</s>).

children.text: ' ti / nanvevamapi cakṣuṣā prasṛtasya jñānasya rasādibhirapi sati sannikarṣe tena rūpasyaiva prakāśanaṃ na tu rasāderiti vyavasthā kathamityatrāha '
children.translated_text: But even so, when knowledge that has extended through the eye has contact with taste (<s>rasa</s>) and other [qualities] as well, how is the determination that it illuminates only form (<s>rūpa</s>) and not taste etc.? To this he says
'Moreover' (<s>api cet</s>).

children.text: ' ti / yadarthapratiniyataṃ rūpam-yadartha eva vyavasthitaṃ bodhajananasāmarthyam / tena-tadarthapratiniyatarūpeṇendriyādinā / tadgocareṇaiva-tattādindriyādiyogyārthenaiva / evaṃ ca cākṣuṣajñānasya na rasādinā sannikarṣa iti bhāvaḥ / yogyāṃśenaiva saṃbandhe laukikaṃ vaidikaṃ ca nidarśanaṃ '
