children.translated_text: That which has a form (<s>rūpa</s>) determined for a particular object — whose capacity to generate cognition (<s>bodha</s>) is established only for that particular object — through that, i.e., through the sense organ etc. whose form is determined for that particular object, and only in the domain of that — i.e., only with respect to the object suitable for that particular sense organ. Thus the sense is that visual knowledge (<s>cākṣuṣajñāna</s>) has no contact with taste (<s>rasa</s>) and the like. For the principle that relation obtains only through the suitable aspect, he gives both a worldly and a Vedic illustration with the words
'Just as' (<s>yathā</s>)
and
'Just as, indeed' (<s>yathā vai</s>).

children.text:
' ti ca / gavādipadaśaktestadvyaktilakṣaṇaviśeṣeṇa sambandhe tattatpadādvyaktyantarabodho na syāt / sāmānyāṃśena saṃbandhe tu syāditi gavādipadasaṃbandhayogyatvaṃ sāmānyasyaiva matam / vidheśca prāptārthe 'nvayasya nirarthakatvādaprāptenaivānvayayogyatā matā / tena tena ca tattadanvaya iṣyate yathā, evaṃ tattadaindriyikādijñānasya tattadindriyādyarthenaiva saṃbandho mantavyaḥ ; anyathāndhabadhirādivilopaprasaṅgāt, avyavasthāprasaṅgācceti bhāvaḥ / bhāvanāyāḥ sādhyasādhanetikartavyatānvayitve 'pi bhāvanānyayinyaprāpte sādhanāṃśa eva vidhitātparyamiti mīmāṃsakāḥ / tadarthābhimukhameva-indriyayogyārthaprakāśanaikatatparam / saṃbandhamātraṃ na sannikarṣaḥ / kintu saṃbandhaviseṣaḥ / sa ca tattadindriyayogyārthenaiva tattadaindriyikajñanasyeti na cākṣuṣādinā
rasādeḥ prakāśa iti hārdam / cākṣuṣādijñānasya rasādina saṃbandha eva nāstīti tu kaścana pakṣaḥ / prāguktapakṣa eva tu yuktaḥ / indriyārthabhimukhatayā jñānasya prasaraṇe śrīmadgītāvākyaṃ pramāṇayati '
children.translated_text: If the denotative power (<s>śakti</s>) of words like 'cow' (<s>go</s>) etc. were related to the particular distinguishing characteristics of individual instances (<s>vyakti</s>), then from those respective words, cognition of other individuals would not arise. But if related through the universal (<s>sāmānya</s>) aspect, it would — thus it is held that eligibility for relation with words like 'cow' belongs to the universal alone. And since the connection of an injunction (<s>vidhi</s>) with what is already obtained (<s>prāptārtha</s>) would be purposeless, eligibility for connection is held to be only with what is not yet obtained (<s>aprāpta</s>). Just as connection with each respective [element] is accepted through each respective [aspect], similarly the relation of each respective type of sensory knowledge with each respective sense-object must be understood — otherwise, the absurd consequence of the abolition of blindness, deafness, etc. would follow, as would the consequence of indeterminacy. This is the purport. The <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s>s hold that even though <s>bhāvanā</s> (productive force) involves the connection of the goal (<s>sādhya</s>), the means (<s>sādhana</s>), and the procedure (<s>itikartavyatā</s>), the purport of the injunction lies only in the means-aspect, which is what is not yet obtained. [Knowledge] is directed solely toward that — i.e., exclusively devoted to illuminating the object suitable for the [respective] sense organ. Mere relation is not proximity (<s>sannikarṣa</s>); rather, it is a specific type of relation. And that [specific relation] of each respective type of sensory knowledge is only with the object suitable for that respective sense organ — hence there is no illumination (<s>prakāśa</s>) of taste etc. by visual cognition etc. This is the essential point. That visual cognition etc. has absolutely no relation with taste etc. is yet another view. But the previously stated view is the correct one. To cite authoritative evidence for the extension (<s>prasaraṇa</s>) of knowledge toward the objects of the senses, he adduces a statement from the blessed <s>Gītā</s>:
'Of that' (<s>tad asya</s>).
The verse is:
'Of the senses that rove about,
the mind that follows them' —

children.text: " iti pūrvārdham / ātmagrahaṇapravṛttaṃ jñānamindriyārthapravaṇaṃ mana indriyadvārā viṣayābhimukhaṃ nayatītyarthaḥ indriyadvārājñānasya prasaraṇe manorvākyam '
children.translated_text: this is the first half. The meaning is: knowledge, which initially grasps the self (<s>ātman</s>), being inclined toward the objects of the senses, is led by the mind (<s>manas</s>) through the sense organs toward the objects. The statement regarding the extension (<s>prasaraṇa</s>) of knowledge through the sense organs via the mind is
'Of the senses' (<s>indriyāṇām</s>).

children.text: 'm iti / kṣarati-bāhyaviṣayamabhisarati / tenendriyadvāreṇa caitanyamipi nissarati carmabhastrikācchidradvāreva jalamityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'Flows out' — it moves toward external objects (<s>bāhyaviṣaya</s>). By this, consciousness (<s>caitanya</s>) too exits through the gateway of the senses, just as water [exits] through the opening of a leather bellows — this is the meaning.
'Without abandoning' (<s>aprahāya</s>) —

children.text: ti / saṅkocavikāśaśālino jñānasyātmadharmasyāparityajyaivātmasaṃbandhaṃ vikāsāvasthayā bāhyārthasaṃbandho ghaṭata iti yāvat / guṇasyāpyāśrayādanyatra gamane nidarśanamāha '
children.translated_text: Knowledge (<s>jñāna</s>), which is an attribute of the self (<s>ātman</s>) and which possesses the capacity for contraction and expansion (<s>saṅkocavikāśa</s>), connects with external objects (<s>bāhyārtha</s>) in its expanded state without relinquishing its connection with the self — this is the meaning. To provide an illustration for the case of a quality (<s>guṇa</s>) also going beyond its substrate (<s>āśraya</s>), he says
'Are seen' (<s>dṛśyante</s>).

children.text: ' iti / dharmyativartitvandharmideśādhikadeśasaṃbandhitvam / guṇatvaṃ cāyutasiddhaprakāratvalakṣaṇaṃ dravyādravyasādhāraṇamatra vācyam, śabdagandhayoradravyayorālokaprabhayośca dravyayorguṇatvenopādānāt / guṇasya gatimattvādi tu āśrayāṃśadvārā / na caivaṃ dharmyativartitvamasiddhamiti vācyam / prasiddhāśrayaśaṅkhapuṣpādyativartitve tātparyāt / '
children.translated_text: Exceeding the substrate (<s>dharmin</s>) means being connected with locations beyond the location of the substrate. And the sense of 'quality' (<s>guṇatva</s>) here should be understood as having the character of being an inseparable mode (<s>ayutasiddhaprakāratva</s>), which is common to both substances (<s>dravya</s>) and non-substances — since sound (<s>śabda</s>) and smell (<s>gandha</s>), which are non-substances, and light (<s>āloka</s>) and radiance (<s>prabhā</s>), which are substances, are all cited as qualities. The movement etc. of a quality, however, is through its substrate. Nor should one say that the exceeding of the substrate is unestablished, since the intent is to refer to well-known cases like the exceeding of [the substrate of] conch-shell, flower, and so forth.
'Smell wafts from afar' —

children.text: ' tiśrutirgandhasya gatimāha / śabdasya gatimattvaṃ 'śaṅkhanādo 'ya' mityādyupalabdherdūre 'pi / nanvākāśaguṇatvācchabdasyāśrayadvārāpi gatirnopapadyata ityatrāha '
children.translated_text: this <s>śruti</s> passage describes the movement of smell (<s>gandha</s>). The movement of sound (<s>śabda</s>) is [established] from the perception such as 'this is the sound of a conch,' even at a distance. To the objection that since sound is a quality of space (<s>ākāśa</s>), its movement cannot be explained even through its substrate, he replies
'Extremely subtle' (<s>atisūkṣma</s>).

children.text:
' iti / bhautikaḥ-bhūtajanitaḥ / bherīdaṇḍābhighātādinodbhūte vāyau śabdo jāyate / āśrayavāyyaṃśaviśaraṇavaśācca nānādikṣu tasyāpi sambandho ghaṭata iti bhāvaḥ / atisūkṣmatvāddūragantṛtvaṃ vāyoḥ / āśrayadharmaścāśrayayiṇyupacarita iti bodhyam /
nanvākāśaguṇasya śabdasya vibhutvādeva na gamanāpekṣā / yatkṛte vāyavīyatvaṃ kalpyeta / vyañjakayogideśa evopalambhaniyamācca na vibhutve 'pi sarvatropalambhaprasaṅga iti śaṅkate '
children.translated_text: Physical (<s>bhautika</s>) — produced by the elements (<s>bhūta</s>). Sound arises in the wind (<s>vāyu</s>) that is generated by the striking of a drum-stick and the like. And through the dispersal of the wind-aspect of its substrate, its connection in various directions is also established — this is the purport. Because of its extreme subtlety, wind can travel far. And the property of the substrate is figuratively attributed to what resides in it — this should be understood. Now, since sound is a quality of space (<s>ākāśa</s>), which is all-pervading (<s>vibhu</s>), there is no need for movement — for which one would have to posit its being of the nature of wind. And since apprehension is restricted to the location where there is contact with a manifester (<s>vyañjaka</s>), there would be no consequence of apprehension everywhere even if [sound] were all-pervading. This is the objection raised with the words
'But surely, space' (<s>nanu nabhas</s>).
He establishes the all-pervasiveness (<s>vibhutva</s>) of sound with the words
'Sound' (<s>śabda</s>).

children.text: ' iti / ghaṭākāśasaṃyogādau vyabhicāravāraṇāya hetau viśeṣaṇadalam / ghaṭādyekatvādau tadvāraṇāya viśeṣyam / etaddūṣayati '
children.translated_text: The qualifying term in the inferential reason (<s>hetu</s>) is to exclude deviation (<s>vyabhicāra</s>) in cases like the conjunction of pot-space (<s>ghaṭākāśa</s>) etc. The qualified subject is to exclude cases like the oneness of a pot etc. He refutes this with the words
'Not so' (<s>maivam</s>).
He states the non-establishment of the essential nature [of the reason] with the words
'Because it is not a quality of that' (<s>atadguṇatvāt</s>).

children.text: ' diti / ākāśaguṇatvābhāvādityarthaḥ / nanvākāśaguṇatvaṃ śabdasya śāstrasiddhaṃ kathaṃ pratikṣipyata iti cet ; ucyate / āgamānusāre ākāśasyaiva na vibhutvamiti na tarāṃ tadguṇasya vibhutvam / yuktyā tu kevalayā vāyavīyatvameva setsyati śabdasyeti hārdam / yuktimevāha '
children.translated_text: The meaning is: because of the absence of being a quality of space (<s>ākāśa</s>). Objection: How can the scriptural teaching that sound is a quality of space be rejected? Reply: According to scripture (<s>āgama</s>), space itself is not all-pervading, so still less is its quality all-pervading. By reasoning (<s>yukti</s>) alone, the nature of sound as belonging to wind (<s>vāyavīyatva</s>) will be established — this is the essential point. He states the reasoning with the words
'Belonging to wind' (<s>vāyavīya</s>).

children.text: ' iti / vibhutvaṃ pratikṣipya nityatvamapi śabdasya pratikṣipati mīmāṃsakābhimatam '
children.translated_text: Having rejected all-pervasiveness, he also rejects the eternality (<s>nityatva</s>) of sound as maintained by the <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s>s with the words
'It is produced' (<s>utpadyate ca</s>).

children.text:
' ti / anena vāyavīyatvānumāne śabdasya hetuviśeṣyāṃśāsiddhirapi parihṛtā / nanu taduttarakālopalabhyatvaṃ tadvyaṅgyatvādapi ghaṭetetyaprayojakatvaṃ hetoriti śaṅkāṃ
pratikṣipati '
children.translated_text: By this, the objection of the non-establishment of the subject-aspect of the inferential reason (<s>hetu</s>) in the inference of sound's belonging to wind is also resolved. Now, to the objection that the property of being apprehended after [the striking] could also be explained by the hypothesis that it is manifested (<s>vyaṅgya</s>) [rather than produced], making the inferential reason inconclusive — he rejects this with the words
'Not so' (<s>na ca</s>).

children.text: ' ti / gauravāt-taddhetutvakalpanātastadabhivyaktihetutvakalpanāyāṃ gauravāt / vipakṣe gauravaprasaṅgaḥ svapakṣasyānugrāhakastarka iti hṛdayam / abhivyaktipakṣe 'nupapattimapyāha '
children.translated_text: Because of the greater ontological burden (<s>gaurava</s>) — because in positing that [striking] as the cause of manifestation (<s>abhivyakti</s>) rather than as the cause of production, there is greater burden. The possibility of this greater burden in the opponent's position is a corroborative reasoning (<s>tarka</s>) that supports one's own position — this is the essential point. He also states the impossibility in the manifestation view:
'And the manifesters' (<s>abhivyañjakāś ca</s>).

children.text:
' ti / uccāraṇasya varṇābhivyañjakatve yugapadeva nānāvarṇābhivyaktiprasaṅgaḥ / abhivyañjakasyaikadeśasthaikendriya grāhyasarvābhivyañjanasvābhāvyāditi bhāvaḥ / varṇābhivyañjakapavane vaijātyaparikalpane tvatigauravam-vyaktihetutvakalpanam, vyaktivyavasthityai vyañjakai vaijātyakalpanaṃ cetyapi bodhyam /
vyañjakatve doṣamevopapādayati sārdhaślokena '
children.translated_text: If utterance (<s>uccāraṇa</s>) were the manifester of phonemes (<s>varṇa</s>), there would be the absurd consequence that all phonemes would be manifested simultaneously. This is because a manifester, being located in a single place and apprehensible by a single sense organ, would by its very nature manifest everything — this is the purport. But if one were to posit heterogeneity (<s>vaijātya</s>) among the winds that manifest phonemes, there would be excessive ontological burden (<s>atigaurava</s>) — both positing the cause of manifestation and positing heterogeneity among manifesters for the sake of ordered manifestation — this should also be understood. He further establishes the defect in the manifestation theory in a verse and a half:
'If [sounds are] eternal' (<s>nityatve</s>).

children.text: ' ti / nityatvavādina iti ṣaṣṭhyantam / mate iti śeṣaḥ / ekāśrayakatvamekandriyagrāhyatvaṃ ca viśeṣaṇadvayeva sūcitam / tathā caikoccāreṇe sarvavyañjanaprasaṅgo vyañjakatvapakṣe iti nigamayati '
children.translated_text: Here, 'of the proponent of eternality' (<s>nityatvavādinaḥ</s>) is in the genitive case, with 'in the view' (<s>mate</s>) to be supplied. The two qualifications — having a single substrate and being apprehensible by a single sense organ — have already been indicated. And thus he concludes that in the manifestation theory, a single utterance would manifest everything:
'When there is identity of location' (<s>deśaikye</s>).
The words
'Because of the absence of that' (<s>tadabhāvāt</s>)

children.text: ' diti / ekavyañjakavyaṅgyatvābhāvāt dhvaneḥ-varṇasyoccāraṇaprayatnotthitaḥ koṣṭhyamārutastālvādisthāne 'bhighātaṃ prāpta utpādaka eva tasya tasya varṇasyetyarthaḥ / vyaṅgyatvāsaṃbhavādutpādyatvapakṣe prasaktaṃ pratyuccāraṇaṃ gakārāderbhinnatvamapi sammantavyamevetyāha '
children.translated_text: [mean]: because of the impossibility of being manifested by a single manifester — the air from the chest (<s>koṣṭhyamāruta</s>) arising from the effort of utterance, upon striking the place of articulation such as the palate (<s>tālu</s>) etc., is simply the producer (<s>utpādaka</s>) of each respective phoneme — this is the meaning. Since manifestation (<s>vyaṅgyatva</s>) is impossible, in the production theory, the distinctness of <s>ga</s>-kāra etc. at each utterance, which follows as a consequence, must also be accepted. He says:
'For this very reason' (<s>ata eva</s>).
He also establishes the distinctness of <s>ga</s> etc. through the apprehension of contradictory properties (<s>viruddhadharmopalambha</s>):
'Moreover, in the acute accent' (<s>kiñca udātte</s>).

children.text: ' ti / ādipadena tāratvamandatvādi grāhyam / ekasyaiva kālabhedena viruddhānvayasambhavādyugapadbhānta ityuktam / bhāntaḥ-bhāsamānāḥ / vyañjakatvāsambhavādeva vyañjakadharmā vyaṅgyesamāropyanta ityapi durvacamityāśayaḥ / nanu so 'yaṃ gakāra ityādipratyabhijñā kathaṃ pratyuccāraṇaṃ bhede ? tatrāha '
children.translated_text: The word 'etc.' (<s>ādi</s>) includes loudness (<s>tāratva</s>), softness (<s>mandatva</s>), and so forth. Since the same entity could have contradictory connections at different times, it is said that they [the contradictory properties] appear simultaneously. 'Appearing' (<s>bhāntaḥ</s>) means being manifest. The suggestion is that it is also untenable to say that the properties of the manifester are superimposed onto the manifested, since manifestation itself is impossible. Objection: How can there be distinctness at each utterance, given the recognition 'This is the same <s>ga</s>-kāra'? To this he says:
'When there is identity of the place of articulation' (<s>sthānaikye</s>).
The sense is that this [recognition] is an erroneous cognition (<s>bhrānti</s>) based on similarity (<s>sādṛśya</s>). // 35 // 36 // 37 // 38 // 39 //

body.translated_text: But even so, since the contact with an intervening place and time is necessarily entailed by contact with a remote place and time, the apprehension of intervening objects would also follow — he dismisses this objection as desired [i.e., accepted] with the words

body.text: bhavatvanubhavādūraṃ dūrādanyadvirodhi vā /
body.translated_text: Let non-remoteness from experience, or something other than remoteness, or its opposite,

body.text: tadbhāvaśca prakāśatvaṃ (stu) kimatra bahu jalpyate // 40 //
body.translated_text: and that state itself be illumination (<s>prakāśatva</s>) — why belabor the point further? // 40 //

body.text: prakāśata iti pratibhāso 'pi buddhiviprakarṣapratyanīkabodhatatsaṃsṛṣṭa padārthasvarūpavimarśa eva, bāhyaprakāśavat /
body.translated_text: Even the appearance 'it illuminates' is itself a discernment (<s>vimarśa</s>) of the intrinsic nature of the object conjoined with a cognition that is the counterpart of the remoteness of the intellect (<s>buddhi</s>) — just like external light (<s>prakāśa</s>).

body.text: tatrāpi hyāloke tadvyāptabhūbhāgādau ca prakaṭādiprakhyopākhye ālokādūratvanimitte / yathā ca tatra tannimittā santamasanivṛttiḥ, evamihāpi jñānadūratvanimittā ajñānanivṛttiḥ / ata eva cānubhūte anubhave cottarakālatulyatsmaraṇam /
body.translated_text: For even there, in the case of light and the ground-surface pervaded by it, the appearances of being manifest (<s>prakaṭa</s>) etc. are caused by non-remoteness from light. And just as there, the cessation of darkness is caused by that [non-remoteness from light], so too here, the cessation of ignorance (<s>ajñāna</s>) is caused by non-remoteness from knowledge (<s>jñāna</s>). And for this very reason, there is equal recollection (<s>smaraṇa</s>) at a later time of what has been experienced and of the experience itself.

body.text: evaṃ ca caitanyasaṃbandhaviśeṣaviṣayavikalpo 'pyalabdhāvakāśa iti niranuyojyānuyoga eva / nairantaryapadaprayāyamatyantasāmīpyamātraṃ ca saṃyogaḥ / sa eva paratantrāśritaḥ samavāyapadaparibhāṣābhūmirvaiśeṣikāṇāmiti nārthāntaratvamūrīkṛtya vikalpaḥ saṃbhavati / yathā ca saṃyogāntarbhāvaḥ samavāyasya, tathā saṃbandhavimarśe darśayiṣyāmaḥ / jñānādūratva prayukto vyavahārakṣamatālakṣaṇo vā paraḥ prakāśaḥ / sa ca satyapi svanimittapauṣkalye pratibandhāt yogyatāvirahādvā vyāpitvasaṅgitvādyātmadharmāntareṣu dehendriyādau ca na sañjāyate, cakṣussannikṛṣṭa iva kālindīpayasi rūparasādayaḥ /
body.translated_text: And thus, even an alternative regarding a specific relation with consciousness finds no scope — so this is merely questioning what need not be questioned. Uninterrupted proximity alone is conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>). That very [conjunction], when dependent on another and abiding in a substrate, becomes what the <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s> designate by the term <s>samavāya</s> (inherence) — so the alternative does not arise by admitting a real difference [between them]. And as inherence is subsumed under conjunction, we shall demonstrate in the discussion of relations. Or, the other illumination (<s>prakāśa</s>) is the capacity for practical activity (<s>vyavahāra</s>) produced by remoteness from knowledge. And that does not arise — even when its own causal conditions are complete — in other properties of the self such as pervasiveness (<s>vyāpitva</s>), attachment (<s>saṅgitva</s>), etc., or in the body, senses, and so forth, due to obstruction or absence of fitness (<s>yogyatā</s>) — just as color, taste, and the like [do not manifest] in the water of the <s>Kālindī</s> (Yamunā) even when in contact with the eye.

body.text:
evaṃ nityatvavibhutvapratikṣepeṇa vāyavīyaguṇatvaṃ vyavasthāpitaṃ yuktyā śabdasya visṛtvaratvaṃ ca / ātmaguṇasya caitanyasyānyatra saṃbandhamātre dṛṣṭāntaḥ śabdo gandaśca / āśrayamantarānyatra gamane dṛṣṭāntaḥ sūryāloko maṇiprabhā ca / dravyarūpvādanyatra gamanaṃ saṃbhavati / āśrayasaṃbandhāvicchedāttaddharmatvaṃ ca susthitamiti praghaṭṭakārthaḥ /
evamarthasaṃbandhaścaitanyasyoktaḥ / prakāśatevyavahāraśca caitanyasaṃbandhaprayukta ityabhipretam / atra prābhākaraḥ śaṅkate '

children.translated_text: 'But if it is so'

children.text: 'm iti / caitanyasaṃyogasya prakāśamānatāvyavahāraniyāmakatve caitanye tadāśraye tadāśraye ca tadvyavahārānupapattiḥ / caitanyasamavāyasya tathātve ca caitanyatadviṣayayostadvyavahārānupapattiḥ / caitanyasaṃbandhamātrasya tathātve cendriyāderapi prakāśaprasaṅgaḥ / ato nimittaviseṣādeva tattajjñānasya tattadarthavyavahārahetutvaṃ svabhāvataśca svasvāśrayavyavahārahetutvameṣṭavyamityanarthakamartacaitanyasaṃbandhakalpanamiti samuditāśayaḥ / vibhudvayasya saṃyogo 'stīti pakṣe kriyāyā abhāvāttatra saṃyogaṃ prakārāntareṇa nirvakti '
children.translated_text: — thus. If the conjunction with consciousness is what determines the practical activity of 'being illuminated,' then such practical activity would be impossible in consciousness itself, in its substrate, and again in its substrate. And if inherence (<s>samavāya</s>) of consciousness [is posited as the determinant], then such practical activity would be impossible in consciousness and its object. And if mere relation with consciousness [is posited], then there would be the undesirable consequence that even the senses and the like would be illuminated. Therefore, it is only due to a specific causal condition that a particular cognition serves as the ground for the practical activity regarding a particular object, and naturally [each cognition] serves as the ground for the practical activity regarding its own substrate — so the postulation of a relation between an object and consciousness is pointless. This is the combined purport. In the position that there is conjunction between two omnipresent [entities], since there is no action [to produce it], he explains conjunction in another way:
'In what is not an effect'

children.text: ' ti / avayavāvayavibhinnayordravyayorantarālāvyavahitasthitiḥ saṃyoga ityarthaḥ / sa cāvibhau kriyayā / vibhvostu svata eveti bhāvaḥ / arthasaṃbandhasya nirāsādeva tajjanyadharmāntaraprakāśapakṣo nirastaḥ / dharmāntaraprakāśe 'nupalabdhibādhamapyāha '
children.translated_text: — thus. The meaning is: conjunction is the state of two substances — which are partless and without parts — standing in uninterrupted proximity. And in non-omnipresent [substances], that [conjunction arises] through action. But for omnipresent [entities], it exists by their very nature — this is the purport. Since the relation with objects has already been refuted, the position of illumination of other properties produced by that [relation] is also refuted. Regarding the charge of non-apprehension against the illumination of other properties, he also states:
'In another category'
— thus.
'Not open to further questioning'

children.text:
'm iti / svayameva svasya vyavahārahetuḥ, svāśrayasya svasamavāyāt, viṣayasya tu svanimittānusāratā iti prayojakavaiṣamyaṃ na dūṣaṇāvahamityarthaḥ /
gurumate 'pyukte doṣamāha vimarśakaḥ '
children.translated_text:
— thus. The meaning is: [consciousness] is itself the cause of its own practical activity, [it illuminates] its own substrate by virtue of its inherence therein, and regarding its object, it follows its own causal conditions — so this asymmetry in the causal factors does not constitute a defect.
The critic (<s>vimarśaka</s>) states the fault even in the teacher's position:
'It is replied'

children.text:
' iti / svanimittakāraṇavatyeva deśe svakāryajanakatvamadṛṣṭamanyatreti indriyasannikarṣavatyevārthejñānena vyavahāro niṣpādyata iti na
samyagiti bhāvaḥ / dūṣaṇāntara mapyāha '
children.translated_text: — thus. The purport is: it is unprecedented that [consciousness] produces its own effect only in a location where its own causal conditions are present, and not elsewhere — therefore, practical activity is accomplished by cognition only in an object that is in contact with the senses, so [the teacher's position] is not entirely correct. He states another objection as well:
'In practical activity'

children.text: ' ti / jñātṛjñeyayoḥsvavyavahārānuguṇajñānakatvalakṣaṇaḥ prakāśaḥ / jñānasya tu svavyavahārānuguṇajñānatvalakṣaṇaḥ sa iti triṣvanugataḥ prakāśapadārtho nāstyanugatavyavahāraniyāmaka ityarthaḥ / nanu jñānādhīnaṃ vyavahārānuguṇyamevāstu prakāśaḥ / sa cānugata ityatrāha '
children.translated_text: — thus. For the knower and the knowable, illumination (<s>prakāśa</s>) has the character of being cognition that accords with their respective practical activities. And for cognition, that [illumination] has the character of being cognition that accords with its own practical activity — thus there is no single common referent of the word <s>prakāśa</s> that uniformly determines practical activity across all three [knower, knowable, and cognition]. Now, let illumination simply be the accordance with practical activity that depends on cognition, and let that be common [to all three] — to this he says:
'When practical activity arises'

children.text:
' ti / vyavahārayogyatārūpaprakāśasya vyavahārata evānumeyatayā vyavahārātpūrvameva jāyamānau viditatvapratītivyavahārāvanupapannāvityarthaḥ /
evaṃ vimarśakena prakāśapadārtha ākṣipte taṭasthaḥ śaṅkate '
children.translated_text:
— thus. The meaning is: since illumination in the form of fitness for practical activity is inferable only from practical activity itself, the cognitions of 'being known' and the corresponding practical dealings that arise prior to [actual] practical activity would be unjustified.
Thus, when the referent of the word <s>prakāśa</s> is challenged by the critic, a neutral observer raises an objection:
'If indeed so'
— thus.
'For indeed not'

children.text: ' ti / jñānasaṃbandhamātrasyāprakāśamānārthasādhāraṇyāt samavāyādeścānanugatatvādanyūnānatiriktaḥ prakāśatepadārtho durnirūpa ityarthaḥ / prakāśatepadārthaḥ-prakāśatepadaghaṭakaprakṛtipratyayārthaḥ / siddhāntī samādhatte '
children.translated_text: — thus. The meaning is: since mere relation with cognition is common even to objects that are not illuminated, and since inherence (<s>samavāya</s>) and the like are not common [to all cases], the referent of the word <s>prakāśate</s> ('is illuminated') — being neither less nor more [than what is required] — is difficult to determine. 'The referent of the word <s>prakāśate</s>' means the meaning of the root and suffix that constitute the word <s>prakāśate</s>. The <s>siddhāntin</s> (proponent) resolves [the difficulty]:
'It is replied'

children.text: ' ityādinā / prathamādhikaraṇasyeti śaiṣikaṣaṣṭhī / anubhave smṛtim -anubhavavisayiṇīṃ smṛtim / '
children.translated_text: — and so forth. 'Of the first chapter' — the sixth case ending is in the sense of belonging. 'A memory regarding experience' — a memory that has experience as its object.
'Remoteness from experience'

children.text: 'm iti / viṣayasyevānubhavasyāpyanubhavādūratvamastyeveti smṛtarupapadyata iti yāvat / nanvastu nāmaitat / prakṛta kimāyātam ? tatrāha '
children.translated_text: — thus. The point is: just as the object has remoteness from experience, so too does experience itself have remoteness from [another] experience — and thus memory is accounted for. Now, granted this may be so; what does it yield for the matter at hand? To this he says:
'This has been stated'

children.text:
'm iti / saṃvidadūratvaṃ saṃvido 'pyastītyuktaprāyam / tadrūpa eva prakāśapadārthastriṣvanugata ityuktaṃ bhavatītyarthaḥ/
śaṅkate '
children.translated_text:
— thus. The meaning is: it has been virtually stated that even cognition (<s>saṃvid</s>) possesses non-remoteness. That very form [of non-remoteness] is the referent of the word <s>prakāśa</s>, common to all three [knower, knowable, and cognition] — this is what has been said.
He raises an objection:
'What is this'

children.text: 'm iti / naño nānārthatvātprakṛteta kor'tha iti jijñāsayā śaṅkā / naño yaṃ kañcanāpyarthamabhyupagamya śaṅkāntaraṃ '
children.translated_text: — thus. Since the particle <s>nu</s> has multiple meanings, the objection arises from the desire to know what meaning is intended in this context. Accepting some meaning of <s>nu</s>, [the opponent raises] a further objection:
'If so'

children.text: ' ti / dūrabhedādeḥ prakāśapadārthatve dūrajñānāpūrvikayaiva tatpratītyā bhavitavyam / na ca tathopalabhyate / tasyopalakṣaṇateve tūpalakṣyākārāntaraṃ vācyam / nacatadasti / evaṃ pakṣadvaye 'pyanupapattipratītiḥ śaṅkabījam / vikalpāsahatvātsaṃvidadūratvaṃ na prakāśaḥ syādityākṣepo vā '
children.translated_text: — thus. If the difference of remoteness and the like is the referent of the word <s>prakāśa</s>, then the cognition of that [prakāśa] must be preceded by the cognition of remoteness. But it is not experienced thus. And if [remoteness] is merely an indicator (<s>upalakṣaṇa</s>), then the other form of what is indicated must be specified. But there is no such [form]. Thus in both alternatives the basis of the objection is the impossibility of [accounting for] the cognition. Or the challenge is: since the alternative [explanations] are untenable, the non-remoteness of cognition cannot be <s>prakāśa</s>.
'What'
— and so forth. He resolves [the objection]:
'It is replied'

— thus.
He responds to the first alternative:
'Let it be in experience'
— thus. He responds to the second alternative:
'And its nature'

children.text: ' ti / anubhavadūrabhinnatvamanubhavadūravirodhitvaṃ vā prakāśatvam-prakāśamānatvam, prakāśapadārtha iti yāvat / atrānubhavapadaṃ jñānasāmānyārthakam / atredaṃ hārdam-śākhā candra ityādivadupalakṣyopalakṣaṇayoḥ sāmānādhikaraṇyanirdeśaḥ '
children.translated_text: — thus. Being non-different from the remoteness of experience, or being opposed to the remoteness of experience — that is <s>prakāśatva</s> (being illuminated), i.e., the referent of the word <s>prakāśa</s>. Here the word 'experience' has the general meaning of cognition. Here the essential point is: just as in [the expression] 'the branch-moon' and the like, there is co-referential designation (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) of indicator and indicated.
'And its nature'
'being illumination'

children.text: 'm iti / tathā ca saṃvidadūratvopalakṣito dharmaḥ prakāśa iti // 40 //
children.translated_text: — thus. And accordingly, the property indicated by the non-remoteness of cognition is <s>prakāśa</s> (illumination). // 40 //

body.translated_text:
Thus, by refuting eternality and omnipresence, the status of sound (<s>śabda</s>) as a quality of air (<s>vāyu</s>) has been established through reasoning, as well as its capacity for spreading. Sound and odor serve as examples for consciousness — a quality of the self — having a relation elsewhere [than its substrate]. The light of the sun and the luster of a gem serve as examples for traveling elsewhere without [leaving] the substrate. Since [consciousness] has the nature of a substance, traveling elsewhere is possible. And its being a property of that [self] is well-established due to the non-severance of the relation with the substrate — this is the purport of the <s>praghaṭṭaka</s> (introductory passage).
Thus the relation of consciousness with objects has been stated. And the practical activity of 'being illuminated' is occasioned by the relation with consciousness — this is the intended meaning. Here, the <s>Prābhākara</s> raises an objection:

body.text: ato yathoktanītyā'tmā svataścaitanyavigrahaḥ/
body.translated_text: Therefore, by the method stated, the self is by its own nature an embodiment of consciousness (<s>caitanya</s>);

body.text: jñā(bhā)nasvabhāva evānyatkaraṇaiḥ pratipadyate //41//
body.translated_text: Being of the essential nature of knowledge (<s>jñāna</s>/<s>bhāna</s>), it apprehends other things through instruments [such as the senses]. // 41 //

body.text:
yattu sukhādinidarśanenātmaviśeṣaguṇatayā citerāgantukatvamupapāditam, tadapi guṇavṛttāparijñānena; yataḥ
prakāśapadārthavicāro vṛttaḥ prāsaṅgikaḥ / viṣayavittivelāyāmevātmano vittyadhīnaḥ prakāśa iti vādasya nirāsārthaṃ prāg yatsamarthitaṃ jñānasvabhāvatvamātmano 'nyāpekṣaprakāśatvaṃ ca, tannigamayati ata iti kārikayā / yato jñeyajñānajñātṛsādhāraṇaḥ prakāśo nirvaktuṃ śakyate, ataḥ pakṣasapakṣānugataprakāśasiddhyā sajātīyetikārikoktayuktayā svādhīnasvaprakāśa ātmā siddhaḥ / sa ca jñānasvabhāvaka eva / natvāgantukamasya jñānam / cakṣurādinā prasṛtācca dharmabhūtajñānādarthāntarasyāpi prakāśako bhavatyātmeti kārikārthaḥ / hānasvabhāva iti prācīnamudritapāṭhastu na samīcīnaḥ //41//
body.translated_text:
As for what was argued — that consciousness is adventitious (<s>āgantuka</s>) to the self, being a specific quality of the self as demonstrated by the examples of pleasure and the like — that too [fails] due to incomplete understanding of the function of qualities; because:
The examination of the referent of the word <s>prakāśa</s> was conducted incidentally. To refute the doctrine that the self's illumination depends on the occasion of contact with objects, what was earlier established — namely the self's essential nature as knowledge and its self-dependent illumination — he concludes with the verse beginning 'therefore' (<s>ataḥ</s>). Since illumination common to the knowable, knowledge, and the knower can be articulated, therefore — by the reasoning stated in the verse that establishes <s>prakāśa</s> as pervading one's own class — the self is established as self-dependently self-luminous. And it is of the very nature of knowledge (<s>jñāna</s>). Its knowledge is not adventitious. And through the attributive knowledge (<s>dharmabhūtajñāna</s>) that extends outward via the eye and other [senses], the self illuminates other objects as well — this is the meaning of the verse. The earlier printed reading '<s>hānasvabhāva</s>' is not correct. // 41 //

body.text: svarūpopādhayo dharmā yāvadāśrayabhāvinaḥ /
body.translated_text: Properties that are qualifiers of the essential nature (<s>svarūpa</s>) exist as long as the substrate exists;

body.text: naivaṃ sukhādi bodhastu svarūpopādhirātmanaḥ //42//
body.translated_text: Pleasure and the like are not thus, but knowledge (<s>bodha</s>) is a qualifier of the essential nature of the self. // 42 //

body.text:
yathā ca bodhopādhirātmabhāvaḥ, tathopapāditam / sukhaduḥkhe ca nātmadharmo, indriyasauṣṭhavanāśayoreva tadbhāvopapādanāt / vyākariṣyate caitadantimapadārthasamarthanāvasara iti sādhanavikalatā ca nidarśanasya / rāgadveṣādayo 'pi manovasthāviśeṣāḥ na sākṣādātmaguṇāḥ / vijñāyate hi "kāmaḥ saṅkalpo vicikitsā śraddhāśraddhā dhṛtiradhṛtirhnīrdhīrbhīrityetatsarvaṃ mana eve"ti / gīyate ca 'icchā dveṣaḥ sukhaṃ duḥkha'miti / 'cetanādhṛti'riti kṣetralakṣaṇamaikapadyena / cetanayā dhriyamāṇaḥ saṅghāto hi dehaḥ / svavṛttyanuguṇacaitanyamātrādeva pravartamānaṃ kṣetramiti yāvat / ata eva hyantaryāmibrāhnāṇe 'yasya pṛthivī śarīram' 'yasyāpaḥ śarīram' 'yasyātmā śarīra'mityādinirdeśaḥ / 'tāni sarvāṇi tadūpu'riti ca purāṇe /
kimidaṃ dhīriti ? utprekṣābhiprāyaṃ tat, na jñaptiviṣayam / tasyāḥ svābhāvikatvasya tasyāmeva śrutau śrūyamāṇatvāt / śrūyate hi "na vijñāturvijñātorviparilopo vidyate" iti, "na hi draṣṭurddaṣṭerviparilopo vidyate avināśitvā"diti ca / jñāturavināśitvādeva jñānasyāvināśamupapādayantīyaṃ śrutirjñātuḥ svarūpaprayuktaṃ jñānamiti darśayati / na ca dṛṣṭiviśeṣaṇatayā draṣṭurupādānamiti sāmpratam, puṃlliṅganirdeśavirodhāt; hetośca sādhyasamatvāpatteḥ / draṣṭuḥ svarūpanirdeśaparatve 'pi

children.translated_text: 'Just as luster is not created in a gem by washing away impurities,
so too knowledge is not created in the self by the removal of faults;

body.translated_text:
And how knowledge is a qualifier of the self's essential nature has been demonstrated. Pleasure and pain, however, are not properties of the self, since their existence is accounted for by the proper functioning and impairment of the senses alone. And this will be elaborated in the context of establishing the final category — so the example [of pleasure etc.] suffers from deficiency of the proof. Desire, aversion, and the like too are specific states of the mind, not directly qualities of the self. For it is known: 'Desire, intention, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, shame, intelligence, fear — all this is indeed the mind.' And it is declared [in the <s>Bhagavadgītā</s>]: 'Desire, hatred, pleasure, pain' — and 'consciousness, firmness' is [stated] as a characteristic of the field (<s>kṣetra</s>) in a single compound. For the body is an aggregate sustained by consciousness. The field operates solely through consciousness that accords with its own functioning — this is the sense. Therefore indeed, in the <s>Antaryāmī Brāhmaṇa</s>, [there are] such statements as 'whose body is the earth,' 'whose body is the waters,' 'whose body is the self.' And in the <s>Purāṇa</s>: 'all those are his forms.'
As for the question 'What is this <s>dhī</s> (cognition)?' — that is [asked] with the intent of speculative supposition, not as a matter for determination. For its naturalness [to the self] is heard in that very <s>Śruti</s> itself. For it is heard: 'There is no cessation of the knower's knowing,' and 'There is no cessation of the seer's seeing, because of [its] indestructibility.' This <s>Śruti</s>, establishing the indestructibility of knowledge from the very indestructibility of the knower, shows that knowledge is intrinsic to the essential nature of the knower. And it is not proper [to say] that the knower is mentioned merely as a qualifier of seeing, because of the contradiction with the masculine gender designation; and because the reason would be equal to the thing to be proved. Even if the word <s>dṛṣṭi</s> (seeing) is taken as referring to the essential nature [of the seer], its being a groundless [designation] cannot be resolved, and [there would be] the defect of abandoning one's own position. But the eternality of the self — established through many lines of reasoning and scriptural authority (<s>āgama</s>) as unshakable — is properly adduced as a reason. For when an entity exists, its essential qualifiers cannot but exist — just as yellowness [cannot but exist] when gold exists, and radiance [cannot but exist] in a lamp. Therefore the meaning is this: of consciousness (<s>citi</s>), which is the essential nature of the self, which — through the modes of connection with specific external and internal objects — acquires the designations of seeing, smelling, tasting, speaking, hearing, thinking, touching, and knowing, and which is self-illuminating — there is never any cessation in either the state of <s>saṃsāra</s> (bondage) or <s>apavarga</s> (liberation). Thus [the <s>Śruti</s> states]: 'Just as a mass of salt is without interior, without exterior, entirely a mass of flavor — even so, indeed, this self is without interior, without exterior, entirely a mass of consciousness (<s>prajñāna</s>)'; likewise, 'by its own light, by its own radiance'; and 'The self is [his] light, O Emperor — thus he said.' And regarding the state of liberation, the <s>Chāndogyas</s> [state]: 'The seer does not see death, does not see disease, does not see any suffering; the seer who is all-seeing sees all'; 'not recollecting birth'; and 'He, with that divine eye, with his mind, sees those desires and rejoices.' And other <s>Śrutis</s> too — such as 'This person indeed knows, but there is nothing to be known' — which declare the self's awareness even upon the cessation of all instruments [of cognition], confirm its essential nature as knowledge. And in the <s>Purāṇa</s>: 'This self is of the nature of pure bliss (<s>nirvāṇa</s>), of the nature of knowledge, and untainted.' And in the <s>Itihāsa</s>: 'The light even of lights.' And the venerable <s>Śaunaka</s> [says]:

children.translated_text: Just as the water and the sky are not created by the digging of a well,
what already exists is merely brought to manifestation — how can what does not exist come into being?'

body.translated_text: "Likewise, through the destruction of deficiencies that are to be abandoned, qualities such as awareness and the like are manifested, not produced — for they are indeed eternal [qualities] of the self." Thus. For this very reason, the <s>sūtrakāra</s> (author of the <s>sūtras</s>) also [states]: 'A knower, for that very reason.' (Thus ends the establishment through <s>śruti</s> and other [authorities] of the eternality of <s>dharmabhūtajñāna</s> (attributive knowledge).) That being so, the consciousness (<s>caitanya</s>) that constitutes the essential nature of the self — in its specific connections with objects — manifests the differentiation of practical dealings such as certainty, doubt, and the like; or [that differentiation occurs] in consciousness partaking of those specific [connections]. For the firm connection of consciousness with an object is certainty (<s>niścaya</s>); the simultaneous infirm connection of that very [consciousness] with many [objects] is doubt (<s>saṃśaya</s>); the connection that follows the traces (<s>vāsanās</s>) of [previous] knowledge is memory (<s>smaraṇa</s>) — and so forth. And it has been said: 'The connection of consciousness, which is a property of the self, with an object is called knowledge (<s>jñāna</s>).' Nor does this entail the absurd consequence that the object too becomes a knower, on the grounds that contact resides in both [relata] — because there is no contact [initiated] by the object. For the contact is of consciousness with it, like external light. For just as, even though there is a relation of light [with objects], the capacity to illuminate belongs to the sun and the like alone, not to the pot and the like. Now, if it is said that since light is dependent on the sun and the like, that [sun] alone, being the possessor of that property, is said to be the illuminator of other things through its connection — then here too, since consciousness is a property of the self, the self alone, touching other things through it, is properly said to be the knower. Thus it is established: this self, being of the very nature of consciousness, abides ever knowing itself; but as for other things, it knows or does not know in accordance with the difference of occasions. (Thus ends the establishment of the sub-varieties such as doubt etc. of <s>dharmabhūtajñāna</s> (attributive knowledge).) That being so, this self, though being of the nature of consciousness and fully shining forth, does not shine forth distinctly and discriminately — like a fish moving in a deep lake, and like milk mixed with water. Therefore, the varieties of earlier inferences that follow the method of demonstrating this, as well as [scriptural] statements, are respected. And those not satisfied even by these strive for direct realization (<s>aparokṣajñāna</s>) — [a knowledge] that is unlike all other object-cognition — [attained by] having the impurity of the obscuring veil of ignorance cleansed through the practice of the limbs of <s>yoga</s> such as <s>yama</s> (restraint), <s>niyama</s> (observance), and the rest; and having the blemish of <s>rajas</s> (passion) and <s>tamas</s> (darkness) shaken off through the maturation of the practice of <s>nirodha</s> (cessation), [resulting in] the predominance of <s>sattva</s> (purity). And that direct knowledge arises at the culmination of contemplative intensity (<s>bhāvanāprakarṣa</s>) — this is undisputed among all philosophers — therefore no effort is made here today to establish it. Now, he restates and refutes what was said earlier — namely, the adventitious nature [of knowledge], as the contrary of its being natural to cognition — with 'but as for pleasure etc.' 'That too' — [refers to] the function of qualities, i.e., the nature of qualities. And what is that? To this he says 'qualifiers of the essential nature' (<s>svarūpopādhayaḥ</s>). Being a qualifier of the essential nature means being a determining attribute of the essential nature. The natural state of properties that are of such a character is their existence as long as the substrate exists. Others, however, are adventitious — this is the function of qualities. Granted that this is so; then what follows? To this he says 'not so.' The adventitious nature of objective pleasure and the like would indeed [be admitted]. But since cognition (<s>bodha</s>) is a determining attribute of the essential nature of the self, and since the eternality of the self is about to be established, the adventitious nature [of cognition] cannot be proven — this is the purport. //42//

dṛṣṭiścākṣuṣamadhyakṣam / ghrātirghrāṇajam / rasayatiḥ-rāsanam / vaktiḥ-śābdaṃ jñānam / śrutiḥ-śrāvaṇamadhyakṣam / matiranumānam / spṛṣṭiḥ-spārśanamadhyakṣam
/ vijñātirupāsanam, yogajaḥ sākṣātkāro vā / svātmāvabhāsinyāḥ-svaprakāśāyāḥ / jñānasyātmasvabhāvatve nityatve cānyā api śrutīrudāharati sa yatheti / anantara iti bāhyaḥ, abāhya iti āntaraśca pradeśaḥ sāmastyena
vivakṣitaḥ / kātsnaryaṃ cātmanaḥ svarūpato dharmataśca / tathāca jñānasvarūpatvaṃ jñānasvabhāvatvaṃ cātmanaḥ sadā labhyate / ukter'the śrutyantaraṃ svena bhāsā svena jyotiṣeti / svarūpato dharmataśca prakāśarūpatvamatrocyate / ātmajyotirityapi niruktārthameva /sūryādijyotirhijyotiṣmajjyotīrūpaṃ ca, tathā'tmāpi / sūryādijyotiṣaḥ prakāśa iva, ātmano jyotīrūpaṃ jñānaṃ svābhāvikamiti cātra vivakṣitam / muktau jñānānuvṛttau śrutimupakṣipati tathāpavargeti / svābhāvikākārāvirbhāvalakṣaṇāyāṃ muktau jñānānuvṛttyā jñānasyātmasvabhāvānubandhitvaṃ prasidhyatīti bhāvaḥ / svāpe 'pi jñānānuvṛttiparāṃ śrutimāha anyāśceti / sato 'pi jñānasyārthasannikarṣābhāvātsvāpe nārthaprakāśa iti jānātyevetyāderarthaḥ / nityatva ātmasvabhāvatve ca jñānasya smṛtīścodāharati nirvāṇeti / purāṇe-śrīmati vaiṣṇave / jñānamaya iti / mayaṭ prācurye / evakāro 'trāpi saṃbadhyate / jñānapracura evetyavadhāraṇena niruktārthalābhaḥ / jyotiṣāmapīti mahābhārate śrībhagavadgītāyām / jñānanityatvādau sphuṭaṃśrīviṣṇudharmavacanamupakṣipati bhagavānityādinā / āhetyadhyāhāryam /
uktārthe sūtramapi pramāṇamityāha ata eva hīti / ataḥ-śrutita eva ātmā jñaḥ-jñātaiveti sūtrārthaḥ / jña evetyanena nityatvamātmasvabhāvatvaṃ ca jñānasya sūtrakṛdabhimatam / ata eva jñānanityatve svāpe 'pi prakāśaḥ syādityāśaṅkya parihṛtaṃ puṃstvādivadityanena /
nanvevaṃ jñānasyātmadharmabhūtasya svābhāvikatve tasya saṃśayaniścayādibhedaḥ smṛtyanubhavabhedaśca katham? tatrāha tadevamiti / yugapatjhaṭiti, nairantaryeṇeti yāvat / jñānavāsanā-anubhavādhīnasaṃskāro jñānasūkṣmāṃśaḥ / caitanyārthasaṃśleṣaviśeṣaḥ, arthasaṃśleṣaviśeṣaviśiṣṭaṃ caitanyameva vā saṃśayaniścayādivyapadeśabhāgityuktam / tatra prathamapakṣe śaṅkate na caivamiti / saṃyogasya dviṣṭhatvena cityarthasaṃyogasya jñānatve viṣayasyāpi jñātṛtvaprasaṅga ityarthaḥ / caitanyasya jñātṛtvaprasaṅge kathañcidiṣṭāpattisambhavādviṣayasya jñātṛtvaṃ prasañjitam / yadvā viṣayasya-viṣayāśrayasya / yathāśrute ātmano 'pi
tattajjñānāśrayatvaṃ na syāt pakṣe 'smin / ataḥ svāśrayāśrayatvasaṃbandhena jñānavattvameva jñātṛtvamatra pakṣe vācyamiti viṣaye na jñātṛtvaprasaṅga iti / pariharati viṣayeṇeti / viṣayeṇeti hetau tṛtīyā / viṣayaśabdo viṣayavyāpāraparaḥ / evamagre cātanyenetyatrāpi / ayaṃ bhāvaḥ-arthagrahaṇārthaṃ vyāpriyamāṇaṃ hi caitanyameva / tathāca
viṣayacaitanyasaṃyogasya tattadarthajñānatve 'pi tasya svānukūlavyāpṛtimaccaitanyāśrayatvasaṃbandhenātmanyeva sattvāttasyaiva jñātṛtvaṃ nārthāderityupalambhabalādvyavasthāpyam, yathā ālokārthasaṃyogasyaiva prakāśatve 'pi prakāśakatvaṃ svadharmabhūtālokaprasaraṇavaśātsūryādereva nārthasya tadvaditi / yadvā viṣayānuyogikasaṃyogābhāvāditi viṣayeṇetyāderarthaḥ / tasya saṃyogaḥ-viṣayapratiyogikasaṃyogaḥ / evaṃ prathamaṃ pakṣamupapādya tattadarthasaṃbaddhaṃ caitanyameva tattadarthajñānamiti dvitīyaṃ pakṣaṃ śaṅkāsamādhānamukhena vyavasthāpayati atheti / prakāśaḥ-prakāśakaḥ / sūryāditantratvam-sūryādyadhīnasvarūpasthitipravṛttikatvaṃ tadapṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇatvaṃ ca / tattadarthasaṃbaddhālokāśrayasyaiva sūryādeḥ prakāśakatvamiva tattadarthasaṃbaddhacaitanyavata ātmana eva jñātṛtvamityarthaḥ / ayameva mukhyaḥ pakṣaḥ / jñātṛtvasya sākṣādātmani saṅgateriti bhāvaḥ / ananyasādhana ityuktamananyādhīnasiddhitvaṃ caitanyasvabhāvatvaṃ cātmano nigamayati tatsiddhamiti / caitanyasvabhāva eva-jñātṛtvasvabhāva eva / anena jñānasyāgantukatvaṃ nirastam / ātmanaṃ vidannevāste-nityānanyādhīnasvaprakāśavānevāste / anenātmanaḥ prakāśasyāgantukatvaṃ
jñānaprayuktatvaṃ ca vyāvartitam / nimittabhedānusāreṇa- indriyaliṅgādijñānārthasannikarṣopādhyanvayavyatirekānuvidhānataḥ / śiṣṭaṃ spaṣṭam /
svayaṃprakāśasyātmanaḥ śābdādipramāṇadhīgocaratvamapi sādhayati tadevamityādinā / asphuṭaprakāśe mīno nidarśanam; avivekagrahaṇe ca kṣīram / tadupapādananyāyānugatāḥ-ātmānātmavivekopapādakāvayavapañcakātmakanyāyaprayojyāḥ, anumānabhedāḥ-anumānaviśeṣāḥ / vacanāni-pramāṇavākyāni śāstrānugatāni / tairapi iti / anumānāgamānāṃ parokṣaikahetutvena prasphuṭaprakāśāsampādakatvāttāvanmātre 'paritoṣaḥ prasphuṭātmaprakāśākāṅkṣiṇāṃ yukta eva hi / mana ādigatajñānāvāraṇadoṣakṣapaṇaṃ yogāṅgānuṣṭhānena sampadyata iti yamaniyameti dyotitam / nirodhābhyāsaḥ-yogābhyāsaḥ / yogāścittavṛttinirodha iti hi yogasūtram / yogābhyāsaparipākato rajastamaḥkāluṣyanivṛttyodriktaviśuddhasattve manasi ātmavivekasākṣātkārayogyateti nirodhābhyāsetyāderarthaḥ / vailakṣaṇyasyātmagatasyāparokṣajñānāya, prayatante-āsiddhiniṣpatternintaramātmatattvacintanapravṛttimācaranti / bhāvaneti / ātmano
nirantarānucintanalakṣaṇe yoge bhāvanāprakarṣaparyante niṣpanne sati, cāparokṣajñānam-yogajadharmānugṛhītaviśuddhamanojanyātmatattvasākṣātkāraḥ,udayate-jāyata ityarthaḥ /

children.translated_text: Thus the <s>ātman</s> (self), being self-established, not through scripture nor through inference,
is clearly manifested through direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) born of the practice of <s>yoga</s> (<s>yogābhyāsa</s>). //43//

children.text:
(ityātmapramāṇanirūpaṇaprakaraṇam)
athāsya kālāvacchedaparīkṣā / tatra sugatamatānusāriṇaḥ sanmātrānubandhinīṃ kṣaṇikatāmācakṣāṇā nityātmadarśanameva sarvānarthamūlaṃ manyamānāḥ kṣaṇabhaṅginamenaṃ saṅgirante; yat sat tat kṣaṇikam, saṃścāyamātmeti / kathaṃ punaḥ sanmātrānubandhinī kṣaṇikatā? / akṣaṇikasya sattānupapatteḥ / yanna kasmaicitkāryāya, antataḥ sārvajñyavijñānagotaratvāyāpi na prabhavati, na tasya sadbhāvaḥ saṃbhāvyata ityarthakriyākāritaiva sattā bhāvānām / na ca sā svavyāpakabhūtakramayaugapadyavirahiṇyakṣaṇike saṃbhavinītyanyatra niravakāśatayā kṣaṇikatayaivānubadhyate / kathaṃ punaḥ kramayaugapadyayorarthakriyāvyāpakatvam? kathaṃ vā tayorakṣaṇikānnivṛttiḥ? / śrūyatām /
uktamarthaṃ saṅgṛhṇāti evamātmeti / svaprakāśasyātmano dharmabhūtaṃ jñānaṃ viṣayādigrahaṇe dehādivailakṣaṇyagrahaṇe cātmana upayujyata ityetāvatā siddham / evamātmani pramāṇaparīkṣā vṛttā //43//
children.translated_text:
(Thus ends the section on the examination of the means of knowledge regarding the self.)
Now begins the examination of its temporal limitation (<s>kālāvaccheda</s>). There, those who follow the doctrine of the <s>Sugata</s> (Buddha), declaring momentariness (<s>kṣaṇikatā</s>) as invariably concomitant with mere existence (<s>sanmātra</s>), considering the view of an eternal self to be the root of all misfortune, assert that this [self] is momentary and perishing; [the argument being:] whatever exists is momentary, and this self exists. But how is momentariness invariably concomitant with mere existence? Because existence is impossible for what is non-momentary. That which is not capable of producing any effect whatsoever, not even for the sake of attaining the state of omniscient consciousness (<s>sārvajñyavijñāna</s>), its real existence cannot be conceived — thus the existence of entities consists solely in causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyākāritā</s>). And that [causal efficacy] is not possible in a non-momentary [entity] which lacks sequence (<s>krama</s>) and simultaneity (<s>yaugapadya</s>), which are its pervaders; therefore, having no scope elsewhere, it is invariably concomitant with momentariness alone. But how are sequence and simultaneity pervaders of causal efficacy? And how are they excluded from the non-momentary? Listen!
He summarizes the meaning stated [in the foregoing] with 'Thus the self' (<s>evamātmā</s>). It is established to this extent: for the self-luminous <s>ātman</s>, the <s>dharmabhūtajñāna</s> (attributive knowledge) is useful for the self in apprehending objects and in grasping [the self's] distinction from the body and the like. Thus the examination of the means of knowledge regarding the self is concluded. //43//

body.translated_text:
The phrase 'yathā ca' ('and as'): '<s>bodhopādhi</s>' (having cognition as its limiting adjunct) is a <s>bahuvrīhi</s> compound. The meaning is: the entity denoted by the word '<s>ātman</s>' (self) has as its defining attribute a property that is non-different from <s>jñāna</s> (knowledge). The <s>bodhopādhitva</s> (nature of having cognition as limiting adjunct) of the self has been established through the reasoning that it is apprehended only as possessing knowledge. Even though the occasional nature of object-contact makes cognition tinged by objects appear occasional, the essential nature of <s>jñāna</s> (knowledge) is eternal — this is the purport. Although scripture will be cited later as authority for knowledge being the essential nature of the self and for its eternality, still, since this section is predominantly reason-based, reasoning alone is given precedence — this should be understood. By this it is stated that in the inference for the adventitious nature of knowledge, the <s>upādhi</s> (limiting condition) is 'being different from the defining attribute of the essential nature.' Now he also states the unestablished-ness of the reason in the illustration, with 'sukha' ('pleasure'): In the established doctrine, favorable and unfavorable cognitions themselves are of the nature of pleasure and pain. And since these fall within the <s>pakṣa</s> (thesis-locus), they cannot serve as illustrations. And pleasure and pain, as distinct from particular cognitions, are characterized by excellence and non-excellence of the instruments. Since these two are not qualities of the self, the reason is unestablished in the illustration — this is the purport. 'Antima' ('final') — the meaning is: this is the occasion for establishing the portion 'inherently blissful.' Objection: Even so, <s>rāga</s> (desire/attachment) and the like could serve as illustrations, since they are particular qualities of the self and are adventitious. To this he says 'rāga' ('desire'): <s>Rāga</s> and the like, being modifications of the mind, are not properties of the self. Rather, just as the heat that is a property of fire appears in a pot in contact with it, so too the properties of the mind merely appear in the self. And thus it has been stated: 'This self is verily of the nature of cessation (<s>nirvāṇamaya</s>), consisting of knowledge, pure; suffering, ignorance, and impurity are properties of <s>prakṛti</s>, not of the self' — this is the purport. That <s>rāga</s> and the like are properties of the internal organ is understood from <s>śruti</s> (scripture) as well — he says 'vijñāyate' ('it is known'). He also corroborates this meaning with the words of the Lord — 'gīyate ca' ('and it is sung'). Because the internal organ is situated in the <s>kṣetra</s> (field/body), its properties such as <s>rāga</s> are stated as properties of the <s>kṣetra</s>. Objection: But 'cetanādhṛti' ('consciousness-support') is also read there; therefore knowledge too is not a property of the self. To this he says 'cetanādhṛti': 'cetanā' and 'dhṛti' are not two separate words; rather, 'cetanādhṛti' is a single compound meaning 'that whose support is through consciousness' — thus what is necessarily the body is indicated, and this is a characteristic of the body — this is the purport. Therefore he says 'svavṛtti' ('own existence/activity'): <s>vṛtti</s> means existence or activity. 'Pravartamāna' means 'continuing excellently' or 'endowed with activity, having attained stability.' The purport is: the body has its own existence and activity dependent on the connection of the self with consciousness. This alone is a proper characteristic of the body, since definitions through having hands, feet, etc. suffer from the defect of under-extension and the like — keeping this in mind, he adduces <s>śrauta</s> (Vedic) statements that declare earth and the like to be the body of the Supreme Self, with 'ata eva' ('therefore'). Since everything has its essential nature, stability, and activity obtained solely through the knowledge that is the will of the Lord, the scriptural teaching of its being His body is entirely primary — this is the purport.
'Kim' ('what'): Objection: Among the properties of the internal organ, <s>dhī</s> (intellect/understanding) is also listed; therefore knowledge cannot be the essential nature of the self — this is the implicit objection here. He resolves it: 'utprekṣā' ('conjecture') — the meaning is: among the particular modifications of the mind, conjecture is called '<s>dhī</s>.' Although desire and the like are admitted to be properties of the self [by some], they are not natural to the self but are caused by limiting conditions such as <s>karma</s> and the like. And because desire and the like possess the capacity to cause the respective mental modifications, the statement of their non-difference from the mind in <s>śruti</s> is figurative — this is the established conclusion. Moreover, if knowledge in a particular state-modification is itself of the form of <s>rāga</s> and the like, then in the inference for the occasional nature of knowledge, <s>rāga</s> and the like cannot serve as illustrations. Nor can it be said that the adventitious nature of knowledge-in-general is to be proved through a qualified illustration, because only the state-qualified [knowledge] is apprehended, and there is no means of proving the adventitious nature of unqualified knowledge-in-general. And if its eternality is established by <s>śruti</s>, then the eternality too is established by <s>śruti</s> itself, resulting in contradiction of the means of cognition that apprehends the <s>dharmin</s> (subject).
Since the non-existence of states is impossible, the eternality of knowledge alone is supported by reasoning — this is the inner meaning. The literal reading, however, is by way of provisional acceptance. He cites <s>śruti</s> for the eternality of knowledge: 'śrūyate hi' ('for it is heard'). The eternality of the essential nature of knowledge, which partakes of states such as being <s>vijñāti</s> (discernment), <s>dṛṣṭi</s> (vision), and so forth, is what is intended here. <s>Viparilopa</s> means destruction. Objection: Only indestructibility is stated here, not the beginningless-ness and endlessness of knowledge. To this he says 'jñātu' ('of the knower'): Since knowledge is a defining attribute of the essential nature, the eternality of the eternal self implies that knowledge too is ancient — this is the purport. 'Na ca' ('but not'): The word '<s>draṣṭṛ</s>' (seer) as a qualifier of <s>dṛṣṭi</s> (vision) in non-difference is not appropriate, because in that case, the feminine form '<s>draṣṭhyā</s>' would have to be used — this is the purport. Having stated the verbal contradiction, he states the meaning-contradiction: 'hetoś ca' ('and of the reason'): <s>sādhyasamatva</s> means unestablished-ness. The meaning is: the reason in the form of indestructibility is also unestablished, just like the <s>sādhya</s> (probandum) in the form of eternality characterized by existence at all times. Or: since indestructibility itself is the <s>sādhya</s>, it is improper as the <s>hetu</s> (reason). Anticipating an alternative interpretation, he resolves it: '<s>draṣṭu</s>' ('of the seer'). In the construction here, the word '<s>dṛṣṭi</s>' is used in the sense of an entity (bhāva-pradhāna). What is to be proved is the exclusion of the impossibility of being knowledge, of the seer. And here, the non-productivity of the reason as a non-reason — i.e., its non-probative character — is difficult to resolve — this is the purport. 'Svapakṣa' ('own position'): The meaning is that for the proponent of adventitious knowledge, the acceptance of knowledge being the nature of the self constitutes self-contradiction (<s>apasiddhānta</s>). And against the meaning of this <s>śruti</s> as interpreted by the <s>Advaitin</s>, the refutation intended here is as follows: When the <s>sādhya</s> (probandum) is the non-difference of the seer from the essential nature of knowledge, the eternality of the self is a non-reason due to being unestablished in a different locus (<s>vyadhikaraṇāsiddha</s>). And accepting that the <s>jñātṛ</s> (knower) — the I-object — is the self and is indestructible, constitutes self-contradiction. To state the intended meaning of this <s>śruti</s>, he clarifies the subject-matter with two sentences: '<s>ātmanas tu</s>' ('but of the self') and '<s>nahi satī</s>' ('for indeed the existent'). That knowledge being a defining attribute of the eternal self's essential nature is the reason for its eternality — this has been indicated by the two sentences. Now he states the meaning of the <s>śruti</s> passage: 'tena' ('therefore'). '<s>Draṣṭu</s>' (of the seer) is a qualifier in a different substrate (<s>vyadhikaraṇa</s>) of <s>dṛṣṭi</s> (vision), i.e., of <s>dharma-bhūta-jñāna</s> (attributive knowledge). The eternality of the self is stated through 'being indestructible, of the self.' And from the <s>dharmin</s>-indicator '<s>draṣṭu</s>' (of the seer), the nature of knowledge as a defining attribute of the self's essence is established. And thus, stating the resultant reason: '<s>ātmasvabhāvabhūtāyā</s>' ('of that which has become the essential nature of the self'). Being the essential nature of the eternal self is the reason. By this, the objection of unestablished-ness in a different locus is set aside. The particular mode of connection with particular objects — characterized by the specific relation between consciousness and objects that is dependent on the different extensions through instruments such as the senses, inferential marks, and so forth — by which the designations of <s>dṛṣṭi</s> (vision) and the like are obtained — this is the compound. <s>Dṛṣṭi</s> is visual perception. <s>Ghrāti</s> is olfactory [perception]. <s>Rasayati</s> is gustatory [perception]. <s>Vakti</s> is verbal knowledge. <s>Śruti</s> is auditory perception. <s>Mati</s> is inference. <s>Spṛṣṭi</s> is tactile perception.
<s>Vijñāti</s> is meditation (<s>upāsana</s>), or yogically produced direct realization. '<s>Svātmāvabhāsinyā</s>' means 'of that which is self-luminous.' He cites other <s>śrutis</s> also for the essential nature and eternality of knowledge of the self: 'sa yathā' ('just as'). 'Anantara' means external, 'abāhya' means internal — these locations are collectively intended. 'Entirety' refers to the self both in its essence and in its attributes. And thus both being-of-the-nature-of-knowledge and having-knowledge-as-essential-attribute are always obtained for the self. For the meaning stated, another <s>śruti</s> [is cited]: 'svena bhāsā svena jyotiṣā' ('by its own light, by its own radiance'). Being of the nature of illumination both essentially and attributively is stated here. '<s>Ātmajyoti</s>' (self-luminous) also has the same explained meaning. Just as the light of the sun and the like is a radiance that possesses luminosity, so too is the self. Just as the radiance of sunlight and the like, so too the luminosity (<s>jyotī-rūpa</s>) of the self — namely <s>jñāna</s> (knowledge) — is natural. This is what is intended here. He introduces a <s>śruti</s> for the continuation of knowledge in liberation: 'tathāpavarga' ('likewise in liberation'). When liberation, characterized by the manifestation of the natural form, is attained, the continuation of knowledge establishes that knowledge follows the essential nature of the self — this is the purport. He cites a <s>śruti</s> teaching the continuation of knowledge even in sleep: 'anyāś ca' ('and others'). Though knowledge exists [in sleep], due to the absence of object-contact in sleep, there is no illumination of objects — this is the meaning of 'jānāti eva' ('he indeed knows') and similar [expressions]. He also cites <s>smṛtis</s> (remembered texts) for the eternality and essential-nature-hood of knowledge: '<s>nirvāṇa</s>' — in the <s>Purāṇa</s>, the auspicious <s>Vaiṣṇava</s> one. '<s>Jñānamaya</s>': the suffix <s>mayaṭ</s> [is used] in the sense of abundance. The particle 'eva' is connected here too. Through the restrictive emphasis 'consisting predominantly of knowledge alone,' the explained meaning is obtained. '<s>Jyotiṣām api</s>' — in the <s>Mahābhārata</s>, in the <s>Śrī Bhagavad Gītā</s>. He introduces a clear statement from the <s>Śrī Viṣṇudharma</s> regarding the eternality of knowledge and related matters, with '<s>bhagavān</s>' ('the Lord') and so forth. The word 'āha' ('says') is to be supplied.
He states that a <s>sūtra</s> also is authority for the stated meaning: 'ata eva hi' ('for this very reason'). The meaning of the <s>sūtra</s> is: 'therefore' — from <s>śruti</s> itself — the self is a knower, indeed a knower. Through 'a knower indeed,' the eternality and essential-nature-hood of knowledge are intended by the <s>sūtrakāra</s> (author of the sūtras). Therefore, anticipating the objection that if knowledge is eternal, there should be illumination even in sleep, the resolution is offered: 'puṃstvādivat' ('like masculinity and the like').
Objection: If knowledge, which is an attribute of the self, is thus natural, how can its differentiations into doubt, certainty, and the like, and its differentiations into memory and experience, [be explained]? To this he says 'tad evam' ('that being so'): 'Simultaneously' means 'all at once,' i.e., continuously. '<s>Jñānavāsanā</s>' (knowledge-impressions) — the subtle aspect of knowledge consisting of <s>saṃskāras</s> (dispositions) dependent on experience. The specific connection of consciousness with objects — or consciousness itself as qualified by the specific connection with particular objects — is what receives the designations of doubt, certainty, and the like. Regarding the first view, he raises an objection: 'na ca evam' ('but not so'): Since contact (<s>saṃyoga</s>) resides in both relata, if the contact of consciousness with objects were knowledge, then the object too would absurdly become a knower — this is the meaning. Since, in the case of the absurd consequence that consciousness becomes a knower, some form of <s>iṣṭāpatti</s> (desired consequence) is possible, the absurdity of the object becoming a knower is presented. Alternatively, '<s>viṣaya</s>' means the locus of the object. In this view, even the self — as read literally — would not be the locus of various cognitions. Therefore, in this view, knower-hood should be stated as knowledge-possession through the relation of being the locus of one's own locus — and thus there would be no absurd consequence of knower-hood in the object. He resolves: 'viṣayeṇa' ('by the object'): The instrumental 'viṣayeṇa' is used in the sense of reason. The word '<s>viṣaya</s>' refers to object-directed activity. Similarly in what follows, 'caitanyena' ('by consciousness') [also refers to the activity of consciousness]. The purport is: It is consciousness alone that is engaged in grasping objects. And thus, even though the contact of object and consciousness constitutes knowledge of particular objects, since that [contact] exists in the self alone through the relation of being the locus of consciousness that is engaged in activity favorable to itself, knower-hood belongs to the self alone, not to objects and the like — this must be determined by the force of apprehension, just as even though the contact of light with objects constitutes illumination, the capacity to illuminate belongs to the sun and the like alone, by virtue of the extension of light that is their own attribute, and not to the objects — similarly here. Alternatively, the meaning of 'viṣayeṇa' and so forth is: because there is no contact that has the object as its correlate [in the self]. 'Tasya saṃyogaḥ' — contact having the object as its counter-correlate. Having thus established the first view, he establishes the second view — that consciousness itself as connected with particular objects is the knowledge of those objects — through the device of objection and resolution: 'atha' ('now'). '<s>Prakāśa</s>' means illuminator. 'Being dependent on the sun and the like' means having one's essential nature, stability, and activity dependent on the sun and the like, and being a non-separately-established qualifier of them. Just as the capacity to illuminate belongs to the sun and the like alone, which are the locus of light connected with particular objects, so too knower-hood belongs to the self alone, which possesses consciousness connected with particular objects — this is the meaning. This is indeed the primary view, because knower-hood directly pertains to the self — this is the purport. Having stated 'ananyasādhana' ('not dependent on anything else'), he concludes the self's nature as not dependent on anything else for its establishment and as having consciousness as its essential nature: 'tat siddham' ('that is established'). 'Of the essential nature of consciousness alone' means 'of the essential nature of knower-hood alone.' By this, the adventitious nature of knowledge is refuted. '<s>Ātmānaṃ vidan eva āste</s>' ('abides knowing the self alone') — means abides as eternally self-luminous, not dependent on anything else. By this, the adventitious nature of the self's luminosity and its being caused by knowledge are excluded. 'In accordance with the difference of occasions' — means: in conformity with the presence and absence of the specific conditions of contact between the object of consciousness and the senses, inferential marks, and other means of knowledge. The rest is clear.
He also establishes that the self, though self-luminous, is also an object of cognition through <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony) and other <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge), with 'tad evam' ('that being so') and so forth. A fish is the illustration for indistinct illumination; and milk for apprehension without discrimination. 'Following the method of that demonstration' — meaning: inferences that are to be employed, consisting of the five-membered syllogism demonstrating the discrimination of self from non-self. 'Varieties of inference' means particular inferences. 'Statements' means authoritative scriptural sentences. 'By these also' — since inference and scripture, being exclusively causes of indirect knowledge, do not produce fully distinct illumination, the dissatisfaction with merely that much is indeed appropriate for those who desire fully manifest self-illumination. That the removal of the defect of obstruction of knowledge acquired through the mind and the like is accomplished through the practice of the limbs of <s>yoga</s> is indicated by '<s>yama-niyama</s>' and so forth. '<s>Nirodhābhyāsa</s>' (practice of cessation) means practice of <s>yoga</s>. For the <s>Yoga Sūtra</s> states: 'Yoga is the cessation of the modifications of the mind.' Through the maturation of yoga practice, when <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s> impurities subside and the mind becomes predominantly pure <s>sattva</s>, it becomes fit for the direct realization of self-discrimination — this is the meaning of '<s>nirodhābhyāsa</s>' and so forth. For the direct knowledge of the distinctness belonging to the self, they 'strive' — they engage in the activity of continuous contemplation of the self's true nature until the attainment of <s>siddhi</s> (perfection). '<s>Bhāvanā</s>' (contemplation): When <s>yoga</s>, characterized by uninterrupted contemplation of the self, reaches the culmination of contemplative intensity, direct knowledge (<s>aparokṣajñāna</s>) — i.e., the direct realization of the self's true nature produced by a purified mind graced by yogically cultivated qualities — arises — this is the meaning.

atha nityatvaṃ vyavasthāvayituṃ vicāramupakramate athāsyeti / asya-ātmanaḥ, kālāvacchedaparīkṣā-kālasaṃbandhaviṣayavicāraḥ / pravartate iti śeṣaḥ / tatreti / ātmanaḥ kālasaṃbandhe vicāraviṣaye kṣaṇamātrakālasaṃbandhinaṃ vināśinamātmānamāmananti kecana vādinaḥ (saugatāḥ) iti yāvat / kālasaṃbandhaḥ kṣaṇikatvalakṣaṇa evetyamīṣāmāśayaḥ / sattvāt kṣaṇikatvamātmana ityuktam / sattvasya kṣaṇikatvavyāpyatve siddhe śobhanamidam / tadeva kuta
ityataḥ sattvaṃ kṣaṇikatvavyāptyarhaṃ pariṣkaroti yanneti / arthakriyākartṛtvameva sattvam, tacca kṣaṇikatvavyāpyamityāśayaḥ / sārvajñyavijñānam-buddhajñānam / kṣaṇikatvavyāptimevopapādayati na ca seti / arthakriyākartṛtvavyāpakaṃ kramākramānyatarat / taccākṣaṇike sthire 'ghaṭamānaṃ kartṛtvaṃ kṣaṇike vyavaśtāpayatīti sattva kṣaṇikatvavyāpyamevetyāpatatīti bhāvaḥ / kramayaugapadyānyatarasya kartṛtvavyāpakatvam, tasya
sthire 'sambhavaṃ copapādayituṃ praśnaḥ kathaṃ punariti / uttaraṃ śrūyatāmityādinā /

children.translated_text: In [producing] causal effects (<s>arthakriyā</s>), the efficacy of entities has a twofold course:
either sequentially (<s>krameṇa</s>) or simultaneously (<s>yugapat</s>) — no third mode is possible. //44//

children.text:
bhāvābhāvavadanayoranyataranivṛttāvanyataravyavasthānādarthakriyājanane bhāvānāṃ na tṛtīyaprakārasaṃbhava iti kramākramapratibaddhaivārthakriyā / na cākṣa
ṇike kramayaugapadye saṃbhavataḥ /
(etāvānevātmasiddhigranthābhāga upalabhyate)
children.translated_text:
Just as with existence and non-existence, when one of the two [modes] is excluded, the other is established; therefore in the production of causal effects, there is no possibility of a third mode for entities — thus causal efficacy is bound to either sequence or non-sequence [simultaneity]. And in a non-momentary [entity], neither sequence nor simultaneity is possible.
(Only this much of the <s>Ātmasiddhi</s> text is available.)
Thus, in the <s>Siddhitraya</s>, graciously bestowed by the supreme teacher (<s>paramācārya</s>),

body.translated_text:
Now, to establish the eternality [of the self], he begins the inquiry with 'Now, of this' (<s>athāsya</s>). 'Of this' — of the <s>ātman</s>; 'examination of temporal limitation' (<s>kālāvacchedaparīkṣā</s>) — inquiry concerning the relation to time. The remainder is 'proceeds.' 'There' (<s>tatra</s>) — in the subject of inquiry concerning the self's relation to time, certain disputants (the Buddhists, <s>saugatāḥ</s>) declare the self to be perishable, having a relation to time of only a moment's duration — this is the meaning. The view of these [Buddhists] is that the relation to time is characterized by momentariness alone. It has been stated that the self is momentary because of [its] existence. This would be fine if the pervasion of existence by momentariness were established. Then whence [is that pervasion established]?
Therefore he refines [the argument that] existence is fit for pervasion by momentariness with 'that which' (<s>yat</s>). The purport is: existence is nothing but causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyākartṛtva</s>), and that is pervaded by momentariness. '<s>Sārvajñyavijñāna</s>' means the knowledge of the <s>Buddha</s>. He establishes the pervasion by momentariness with 'and not' (<s>na ca</s>). Either sequence or non-sequence [i.e., simultaneity] is the pervader of causal efficacy. And that [sequence or simultaneity], being impossible in a non-momentary, stable [entity], establishes the efficacy in the momentary — thus it follows that existence is pervaded by momentariness alone; this is the purport. To establish that either sequence or simultaneity is the pervader of efficacy, and that it is impossible in a stable [entity], the question 'But how?' (<s>kathaṃ punar</s>) [is raised]. The answer [begins] with 'Listen' (<s>śrūyatām</s>) and so on.

body.translated_text: the foremost champion of establishing the <s>Viśiṣṭādvaita</s> doctrine, the blessed sage <s>Yāmuna</s> (<s>Śrī Bhagavad Yāmunamuni</s>), [this is] the <s>Ātmasiddhi</s>. //

artheti / kiñcidarthakriyākaraṇaṃ krameṇa, kiñciccākrameṇa-yugapat / yaugapadyāsaṃbhave kramaḥ, tadabhāve ca yaugapadyaṃ niyatamiti kramayaugapadyānyataravyāpyaivārthakriyā bhavatītyarthaḥ //44/
bhavatvevam / athāpi sthire kathaṃ na sā? tatrāha na ceti /

children.translated_text: The subsequent portion of the text is not found anywhere from here onward.
The commentary has been composed on what has been obtained, [presenting] its essence.

body.translated_text:
'Causal effect' (<s>artha</s>) — some causal action is [done] sequentially, and some non-sequentially, i.e., simultaneously. When simultaneity is impossible, there is sequence; and in the absence of that [sequence], simultaneity is necessarily [the case] — thus causal efficacy is pervaded by either sequence or simultaneity; this is the meaning. //44//
Let it be so. But then, how is that [causal efficacy] not [possible] in a stable [entity]? To that he says, 'And not' (<s>na ca</s>).

body.translated_text: Thus, the commentary on the <s>Ātmasiddhi</s> named <s>Siddhāñjana</s>, composed by <s>Śrī Vaiṣṇavadāsa</s> Pra.Bha. <s>Aṇṇaṅgarācārya</s>, an ornament of the lineage of <s>Prativādibhayaṅkarācārya</s>, born in the sacred place of <s>Nāgapurī</s> (<s>Tirunāṅgūr</s>), the son of the eminent teacher <s>Śrī Kṛṣṇamācārya</s>, who has traversed the ocean of the four <s>Tantrīs</s>, whose fame extends to all quarters, an embodiment of compassion, descended in the divine lineage of <s>Śrīmad Bhāṣyakāra</s> [<s>Rāmānuja</s>], a resident of <s>Śrī Bhūtapurī</s>, a connoisseur, the sovereign among scholars, of the <s>Hārīta</s> [lineage], who has mastered the heart of the <s>padavākya</s> and <s>pramāṇa</s> systems through devoted service at the lotus feet of the preceptor-king <s>Śrīmad Āsūri Rāmānujācārya Deśikendra</s>, a master of <s>Nyāya</s> and <s>Vyākaraṇa</s>, learned in both <s>Vedāntas</s> — may it be victorious for a long time!
